text_en:
Nearly six years had passed since the sky first began to close. The sun still existed somewhere beyond the ceiling of ash-grey cloud, but most days it left only a pale smear of light behind, just enough for people to tell day from night. Those who had once fled south in search of warmth no longer spoke of the desert's scorching heat. Snow had buried the Atlas Mountains, frozen the irrigation channels solid, and turned the fields around Marrakesh into ground as hard as stone.

In a small stone house on the edge of the city, Juliet Spencer woke before the wooden clock on the wall struck five. Four years there had taught her body the rhythm of a household that counted every log, every bucket of water, every hour of warmth that might still be coaxed from the stove. She slipped from beneath the goatskin blanket, fastened her collar, then rested a hand on Edward's shoulder to make sure her husband was still asleep.

He lay turned towards Remi, one arm stretched across the seven-year-old boy by instinct. Even in sleep, his hand had found the posture of a man guarding something.

Juliet watched them for a moment before leaving the bed. A thin skin of ice had formed over the water bucket beside the stove. She broke it with the handle of a spoon, measured out only enough for a small pot, then stirred the embers buried beneath the ash.

Three oak logs went on the fire in a neat little pyramid. No more. One extra log today could mean one cold evening next week.

When steam began to rise, Juliet dipped a rough cloth into the water and washed her face and neck quickly before wrapping herself again. She no longer cursed the cold as she had during their first winters. It had become another household duty, like mending clothes, checking the stores, or remembering which pair of Remi's socks still needed drying by the stove.

A creak of timber behind her made her turn. Edward was sitting up. His chestnut hair was still disordered from sleep, but the first things he checked were the stove, the window, and the latch on the door, the reflex of a man who had once lived by the watch.

"You're up before me again."

Juliet hung the cloth over the side of the pot and nodded towards the stable door. "The fire was already going before you managed to say that. If you're truly desperate to make amends, you can go clean the cattle shed before Remi wakes."

Edward glanced at their son, still curled beneath the blankets, and suppressed a laugh. "Very well. I shall atone with an heroic quantity of cow dung."

She shook her head, although the reproach had already left her voice. "If you say it, do it."

He pulled on his goatskin coat. Before leaving, he bent and kissed her temple. Juliet was laying slices of hard bread into a pan, but her hand paused long enough to catch his wrist.

"Don't stay out there too long."

"I'll see if the cattle are willing to negotiate."

The look she gave him was answer enough.

Edward drew up his hood and opened the door. Cold air rushed through the house, forcing him to raise his collar before he had even stepped outside. There were scarcely twenty paces between the house and the cattle shed, yet the night's snow reached nearly to his ankles. He followed yesterday's packed path, cleared the drainage groove with a shovel, and only then pushed open the stable door.

The breath of more than forty cattle turned the air inside white. Condensation clung to the frozen beams, while old goatskins laid across the animals' backs had become damp with cold. Several beasts were pressed together so tightly that one could scarcely tell where one set of legs ended and another began.

Edward ignored the feed troughs and went straight to the far corner. He crouched beside a chipped earthenware jar and carefully lifted away the sackcloth covering it.

Inside lay a dull grey mass nearly the size of a man's fist. Fine cracks webbed its surface, glowing a sullen red like an ember that refused to die. The heat was barely strong enough to melt ice within a few paces, and it carried a sulphurous smell that caught at the back of the throat.

Market traders called it red lime. Castilian officials had a longer name for it. To Edward, it was simply a cheap Vestigium that could keep forty cattle alive for a few more nights without burning through the family's winter wood.

He brought two fingers near the surface without touching it. The red glow was visibly weaker than the night before.

"Three nights at most."

Using an iron rod, he turned the jar until the largest fracture faced the wall. If the shell split completely, the thing would vent poisonous gas before cooling. Edward had learned that lesson during their first winter at the price of one calf and two days spent coughing blood.

Small footsteps hurried through the snow outside. Remi appeared in the doorway with his woollen cap sitting crooked over one ear and a bucket clutched in both hands. It was nearly half his size. He lowered it beside his father with great care, then blew into fingers already red with cold.

"Mama said to bring you warm water."

Edward tested the weight of the bucket and looked at him. "Did your mother give you that job, or did you volunteer before she could stop you?"

Remi pulled his cap lower. "Both, Father."

Edward snorted. He lifted the bucket to the trough while Remi took up a broom and dragged the wet straw aside. The boy's work was clumsy, but he knew to stand downwind and to keep more than an arm's length from the Vestigium jar.

No seven-year-old should have needed to know either thing. Edward had never allowed himself the comfort of pretending the world was still normal.

"Father, was winter in England this cold?"

The iron hook stopped halfway through the hay.

"Cold enough," Edward said. "But the sky was bright."

Remi leaned on the broom. "Bright like the Vestigium lamps at the market?"

"No." Edward looked through the gap in the door at the colourless sky beyond the yard. "Brighter than that. Much brighter."

"Could I imagine it?"

That made Edward turn.

Remi had been born in 1708 and was scarcely more than a year old when London fell. Whatever England existed in his mind had been assembled from his parents' memories, a few yellowing pages, and an old leather map worn soft at the folds.

Marrakesh was what the boy actually knew. Snow lying over Moorish domes. The smell of hot roasted potatoes that Uncle Omar slipped him whenever they crossed the market. The red walls and frozen lanes of a city that had somehow learned to live beneath a deadened sun.

His father's homeland, by comparison, was almost a myth.

Edward rested a hand on his knee and crouched until they were eye to eye. "It doesn't matter if you can't remember it. I'll tell you what I remember, and you can keep as much or as little as you like. When you're older, you can decide for yourself whether England deserves to be called home."

Remi blinked. "Then why should I remember it at all?"

Edward looked at him for a moment. "You don't have to. I lost my homeland, Remi. I won't turn it into a debt you have to repay."

He ruffled the boy's hair and stood before the thought could become a lecture. Remi did not ask again. He returned to the straw instead and occasionally poked the handle of his broom against his father's boots until Edward was forced to pretend to kick back.

By the time they went inside, Juliet had set three bowls of barley porridge on the table. The smell of beef fat and fried onion rose with the steam. Remi lunged for his chair so eagerly that it rocked beneath him. Juliet caught the back of his collar before he could overturn it.

"Hands first, Remi."

"But they're freezing, Mama."

"Dirty hands still get washed. Go."

He trudged towards the basin like a condemned man who had exhausted his right of appeal. Edward sat down and noticed half a slice of salted meat beside his bowl. He looked at his wife. Juliet did not bother raising her head.

"Don't ask. You ate less than he did last night."

Edward opened his mouth to protest, but Remi returned from the basin in time to betray him with enthusiasm.

"That's true. I saw it."

Edward put an elbow on the table. "Apparently no one in this house is on my side any longer."

Remi pointed towards the stable. "You still have the cows."

Juliet turned towards the stove, but not quickly enough to hide her laugh. Breakfast passed through the kind of small things that no one thought to call happiness. Juliet reminded Remi to chew properly. The boy tried to hide a piece of bread in his coat and received a tap across the back of his hand when Edward caught him. There were no campaign maps on the table, only three bowls of porridge and the salted meat Juliet refused to take back from her husband.

After breakfast, she prepared for the market. She checked the purse twice, wrapped a scarf across the lower half of her face, and tucked a bundle of tanned hides into her basket to trade for salt. Edward stood beside the door repairing the clasp of her cloak.

"I'll come with you."

"You said you needed to look at the roof over the storehouse this morning."

"It can wait until the afternoon."

Juliet hesitated, then nodded towards Remi, who was bent over a stained scrap of paper practising his letters.

"Stay and teach him instead. I'll go to the market, stop by Uncle Omar's, and come straight home."

Edward had not yet answered when she tugged his collar down, kissed him, and let go.

"I've walked that road for four years." She opened the door and the wind immediately caught her cloak. "Besides, I bargain better than you."

The door closed behind her.

Edward looked at his son. "You see that, Remi? Your mother has just insulted my commercial talents."

Remi did not look up from his letters. "She isn't wrong."

Edward decided that the morning lesson might benefit from a little additional discipline. By noon, Marrakesh was fully awake. For centuries the city had lived in the red of its earthen walls, the green of its palms, and the heat rising from the desert. Now snow lay thick across Moorish domes, paths had been dug like trenches between banks of ice, and every conversation sent clouds of white breath into the air.

Juliet crossed the central market without fighting the cold as she once had. When the wind came hard across the square, she simply lowered her centre of gravity, turned one shoulder into it, and kept walking without letting her basket strike anyone passing in the opposite direction.

Beneath the market roof, the air was warmer.

Small Vestigium lamps hung from the wooden beams, each no larger than a fist. They gave off a steady amber light and a cleaner heat than the red lime in the Spencer stable. One lamp cost enough to feed a poor household for weeks, so the city paid for their upkeep.

People said that as long as the market still burned warm, Marrakesh still had a heartbeat. Juliet liked the phrase, though she had never admitted it aloud.

She traded the hides for salt, argued a handful of pepper down by nearly a third, then bought two onions for supper. On her way out, she noticed a crowd around the government notice post and slowed.

A clerk had just pasted three fresh bulletins to the board. They still smelled of ink. The flow of people through the market immediately bent towards them.

This was different from the usual postings about coal prices and ration allotments. Those who finished reading did not move away. They stood before the board, exchanged short words, and looked north.

Juliet stayed outside the crowd. She watched the faces as people turned away. An old sailor tightened his grip on the brim of his cap. A Castilian man gathered his wife and children and left the market earlier than planned. Two traders argued quickly in a local dialect Juliet could not follow, but both kept glancing towards the same quarter of the sky.

"News from the fronts," someone said behind her.

The basket in Juliet's hand seemed heavier.

For years, war had existed somewhere beyond Marrakesh, distant enough that the city could continue through habit. She did not know what those three sheets of paper had changed, and she had no desire to invent an answer from rumours whispered beneath a market roof.

She adjusted her scarf and went home.

When she stepped through the door, Edward was seated beside Remi at the table. Their worn leather map lay open between them. He was showing the boy the names of the seas.

"This is the Atlantic." Edward placed a finger on the broad stretch of water west of Europe.

Remi traced the coast down towards Morocco. "And this is where we live?"

"Here." Edward touched Morocco.

When Remi asked about England, his finger rested a little longer on the island to the north.

"And England is here."

The basket touched the tabletop with a soft thump. Edward looked up at once.

"They've posted new bulletins at the market," Juliet said. "Three at once."

He waited when she stopped. "Anything certain?"

"Nothing I could hear. But people stayed after reading them. A few families left the market early."

Edward folded the map in half, hiding Europe beneath old leather. "Then let's not bring rumours to the dinner table. When there is something real to know, the people responsible for it will deal with it."

Juliet looked at the folded map but did not press him.

Remi broke the silence by pointing at the word he had written. "Father, how many T's are there in Atlantic?"

Edward glanced down. "More than you've written."

"I did it on purpose."

"Then you can do it on purpose correctly five more times."

Remi groaned. Juliet laughed and carried the basket to the stove. The house settled back into its small obligations, while three government notices remained outside among the crowd.

That afternoon Edward repaired the storehouse roof. He nailed two boards over a cracked section, packed the gaps with straw and pine resin, then moved sacks of barley further from the damp wall. Remi stood below passing him nails. Juliet counted the salted meat, set aside provisions for the last three days of the week, and wrote the totals into a small ledger.

Life continued. Edward had often thought that this was the strangest thing about the end of the world. People still mended socks, patched leaking roofs, and argued over whether the last onion belonged in tonight's soup or tomorrow's. A city could fall a thousand miles away, yet if a cow developed a fever, a farmer would still spend the night beside it.

Near what passed for dusk, the grey outside the window deepened towards black. Juliet set the soup pot over the fire. On the floor, Remi fitted scraps of wood into the shape of a three-masted ship. A few paces away, Edward sat on a low stool trying to mend a rein.

After threading the needle through the same hole in the leather three times, he finally lowered his hands in defeat. He pulled the bad stitch free, checked the hole, and began again. Juliet stirred the soup in the warmth of the kitchen while Remi remained absorbed in the unfinished bow of his little ship.

"Tired?" she asked.

Edward looked up. "Perhaps."

Juliet tapped the ladle against the rim of the pot. "Then wash your hands and eat. There will still be work tomorrow."

He obeyed.

The three of them had barely settled around the table when someone knocked at the door. Three blows, evenly spaced and hard enough to shake a fine crust of ice from the frame.

Edward and Juliet both stopped.

Neighbours seldom called at this hour unless something was wrong, and no one they knew knocked like a man demanding entry. Remi shifted as if to stand. Juliet caught his shoulder and kept him seated. Edward rose without a word, crossed the room, and placed one hand on the latch.

The knock came again.

This time a low male voice, deliberately flattened until it carried almost no emotion at all, reached them through the timber.

"Edward Spencer?"

Edward's hand stopped on the latch.

"That depends on who's standing outside."

Silence held for several seconds. Then a second voice answered, lower than the first and somehow even more unpleasant.

"Open the door. We have orders to verify your identity."

Juliet set down the ladle. Her hand moved towards the bread knife at the corner of the table, not drawing it, only bringing it within reach where Edward could see. Remi looked from one parent to the other, curiosity draining quickly from his face.

Edward braced one hand against the door before turning the lock. "Whose orders?"

The reply came at once, smooth with authority. "You are not in a position to ask."

Too smooth.

Edward opened the door only far enough for one man to pass while keeping his rear foot behind the threshold. Snow-laden wind entered with two tall figures wrapped from shoulder to boot in heavy cloaks. Dark scarves hid most of their faces, and their hoods had been pulled low enough to leave only the eyes visible.

The man in front stepped inside but did not advance. His gaze moved over Edward, Juliet, then settled on Remi.

"Edward Spencer. Former Admiral of the Royal Navy of England. Confirm your identity."

Edward shifted just enough to place himself between the strangers and the table.

"You have the right address. Whether I confirm anything depends on what you intend to do next."

The second man closed the door behind him. He removed his gloves slowly and folded both hands behind his back like an official preparing to pronounce sentence.

"You may be required to come with us."

Juliet moved half a step forward. "My husband is going nowhere until you tell us who you are."

Both strangers looked at her.

The man in front held his silence long enough for the bubbling soup and crackling fire to become painfully clear.

Then his shoulders began to shake.

Edward had barely registered it when the man behind him made a strangled sound. He tried to swallow it, failed, turned towards the door, and burst out laughing.

The first man lasted two seconds longer.

"Damn it, I told you not to look at Juliet!"

He tore the scarf from his face. Wet platinum-blond hair spilled from beneath the hood, clinging in places to his forehead. A long scar crossed his chin, and the grin beneath it destroyed the last trace of menace.

"God above, Ed. That face alone was worth the entire journey."

His companion pulled down his own scarf and drew a long breath in a doomed attempt to recover his dignity.

"I had intended to sustain the performance for at least another half minute. This is a grave injustice."

Edward remained beside the door.

Juliet recovered first. She lowered the bread knife onto the table and leaned one hand against the back of a chair.

"Romeo? Marco?"

Romeo spread both arms as though standing on a stage awaiting applause. "At last. Someone in this house recognises old friends."

Edward still did not move.

Romeo's arms lowered. His smile faded as the possibility dawned on him that the joke might have gone too far.

"Ed?"

Edward crossed the room and drove a fist into Romeo's shoulder.

Romeo staggered sideways. "That hurt! You heartless bastard. I crossed half of Morocco to visit you."

Edward did not let him finish. He hooked an arm around Romeo and dragged him into a crushing embrace, then reached out and pulled Marco in as well.

Marco laughed aloud, thumping Edward repeatedly between the shoulders. "Easy. Easy. I'd prefer to keep my ribs."

Edward held them for another moment before letting go. Then he studied both men from head to foot as though he needed to confirm that flesh and bone had truly followed memory into his kitchen.

"Bastards." He gripped each of their shoulders once more. "You're really alive."

Romeo planted his hands on his hips. "We're the ones who should be saying that. Word was that Admiral Spencer vanished somewhere in the south. Nobody mentioned he had retired to become lord of a cattle shed."

Marco brushed snow from his shoulder. "I suggested we introduce ourselves like civilised men. He insisted on staging an arrest."

"Slander." Romeo pointed at him. "The line about him not being in a position to ask questions was yours."

Juliet finally laughed. "You two nearly had me defending the house with a bread knife."

Marco bowed with absurd solemnity. "Then we are profoundly grateful for your restraint."

Romeo glanced at the knife and looked back at Edward. "You see? I told him the most dangerous person in this house wasn't you."

Remi had stayed close to his mother, but now he looked up at the strangers, searching through stories he had heard before. "You know my father?"

Romeo immediately crouched until they were eye to eye. "Oh, we know him. We knew him when he thought three hours of sleep was proof of genius."

Edward frowned. "Do not fill his head with nonsense."

Marco removed his hood and smiled at the boy. "Don't worry. There is an entire list of things more ridiculous than that."

Remi's eyes brightened.

Edward pointed at both men. "Every story passes through me first."

Romeo stood again. "Hear that, Marco? Four years of cattle and he's turned into a proper stern father."

Edward laughed, and Romeo wisely used the opportunity to step out of striking distance. When Romeo stepped in for another embrace, the collar of his cloak shifted. A metal chain slipped free and struck the clasp of his coat with a small chime. Almost at the same moment, Marco's pendant slid from beneath his shirt when he bent to retrieve a fallen glove.

Edward stopped smiling.

Both pendants bore the same finely carved Castilian lion. Tiny orange-red Vestigium crystals sat in the eyes, no larger than peas, yet warm enough to melt the condensation from the metal into droplets. A serial mark had been engraved beneath each lion's jaw.

Edward did not need to read it.

His gaze moved from Romeo's token to Marco's. "Royal Guard?"

Romeo looked down at his chest like a thief who had just discovered the stolen silver hanging in full view. He shoved the chain back beneath his coat. "Ah. That."

Marco made no effort to hide his own. He rested the lion in his gloved palm. "It's a long story."

Edward folded his arms. "You have hot soup and the whole evening."

Romeo pulled out a chair without waiting for an invitation. "Then I shall begin with the most important point. Service to the Castilian Crown is considerably less glamorous than the public has been led to believe."

Marco dragged the next chair closer but remained standing. "Do not listen to him distort everything."

Romeo turned on him at once. "Did you or did you not spend half the day riding through snow because our superior changed the schedule three times?"

Marco considered this. Then he sat.

"On that point, listen to him."

Edward laughed. "Work going well?"

Romeo leaned his head back as if he had just been asked whether he fancied execution at dawn. "Splendidly. Provided your definition of splendid includes sleeping in barracks for three nights, being dragged awake on the fourth because someone remembered an order that should have gone out yesterday, then riding at speed to discover the plan has already changed."

Marco accepted the cup Juliet placed before him and added, "Our superior possesses the remarkable talent of assigning a third duty before you've begun the second."

"Exactly." Romeo nodded violently. "And the first duty has not, of course, been cancelled."

Juliet placed two extra bowls on the table. "You both sound very fond of this superior."

Marco wrapped his hands around the bowl for warmth. "I respect the ability to carry that much work."

Romeo sampled the soup. "I respect the fact that our superior is not in this kitchen while I'm complaining."

Edward sat opposite them. "Weren't you two always allergic to babysitting powerful people?"

"Still am," Marco said at once.

Romeo finished the piece of bread Juliet had passed him before answering. "The title is grander now. The cloak is better. Most importantly, the person tormenting us possesses the fully legitimate authority to have our heads removed."

Marco looked at him. "Do not say things like that in front of a child."

Remi slid his chair nearer to Edward. "Do they really cut people's heads off, Father?"

Edward placed a hand against his son's cheek and gently turned him back towards the soup. "Eat."

Romeo bowed over his bowl to hide a smile.

Only after both men had eaten several mouthfuls did Edward ask, "How did you find me?"

Marco wiped his hands. "You were not especially difficult to locate. We asked for an English former naval officer living with his family outside Marrakesh, keeping more than forty cattle and occasionally buying enough red-lime Vestigium to heat an entire stable. Three conversations."

"Four," Romeo corrected. "The first red-lime merchant tried to sell me a whole crate before he told me where you lived."

Edward shrugged and glanced around the kitchen as though the room itself proved his point. "It smells of cattle dung, the storehouse roof leaks whenever the storms come in, and every winter we count firewood one log at a time. In exchange, I sleep without a flintlock beneath my pillow and no longer wake because ship guns are tearing the night apart. I call that an excellent bargain."

Marco watched him in silence. "I thought this place would wear you down."

"You were wrong." Edward looked towards Juliet and Remi. "There is nothing idle about it. I have a seven-year-old boy to raise, a herd of cattle that chooses the worst weather imaginable to fall ill, and a wife so skilled at finding my mistakes that she notices them before I do."

Juliet set down a bowl with deliberate gentleness. "How fortunate that today you chose to admit that in front of witnesses."

Romeo pointed his spoon at her. "Juliet, I support this statement without reservation."

Marco leaned back. "As do I. But first I'd like an explanation for why he's become thinner."

Edward pointed across the table at Romeo. "Because men like him keep arriving to steal my food."

Romeo looked at his nearly empty bowl, considered the accusation, and nodded. "Compelling evidence."

For a time, the conversation turned to things that required no map. Who was alive. Who had vanished. Which old habits had somehow survived everything else.

Romeo described spending a night in a horse shed after snow blocked a convoy. Marco complained that he still had to rewrite Romeo's reports because his handwriting looked increasingly like knife wounds. Edward told them how Remi had once tried to feed bread to a cow and lost an entire glove to it.

The stories could not replace the missing years, but they made the distance between them feel less like an abyss. Juliet spoke rarely. She refilled cups, corrected Edward when he remembered a detail incorrectly, and watched Remi discover with fascination that his father had once possessed a life in which these two loud men appeared regularly.

Then Edward noticed that Romeo had never removed the sword from his hip. Marco's combat gloves also remained beside his dominant hand. The lion pendants had disappeared beneath their collars, but once Edward had seen them, he could no longer pretend this was merely a reunion.

He placed his bowl on the table. "All right. The performance, supper, and complaints about your superior have gone on long enough. Tell me what the two of you are trying not to say."

Romeo looked at Marco. The smile vanished from his face.

Marco straightened in his chair. "We are not the only ones who came to see you."

"I assumed as much."

Before Marco could continue, the sound of wheels grinding through snow reached them from the road. It was too heavy and too measured for a merchant's cart. Hooves kept disciplined pace on either side.

Romeo tapped two fingers against the haft at his hip. "That is why we avoided saying too much."

Juliet looked through the window. A black carriage had stopped before the gate. Four mounted guards flanked it in pairs. No flag advertised their arrival, yet the fittings on their saddles and uniforms carried the same lion Edward had just seen carved into the pendants.

Edward glanced at Romeo. "Your superior?"

Romeo bent over his bowl and finished the last of the broth with great concentration. "I have made no such statement."

Marco rose. "The person travelling with us wanted to speak with you in person."

"Who?"

Marco tucked the lion beneath his coat and turned towards the door. "Come out and see."

As Edward passed, Juliet touched his arm. "I'll receive the guest. You change out of the coat with straw on the shoulder."

Edward looked down at himself. "I thought it made me look honest and rustic."

"It probably works on the cows."

Romeo made a sound halfway to a laugh and suppressed it the instant Marco opened the door. A woman stepped down from the carriage. Edward caught only a glimpse of a deep red cloak trimmed in white fox fur before Juliet went out to meet her and brought her into the front room.

Marco and Romeo separated automatically to either side of the doorway. Romeo stopped smiling. Marco closed the door and took position to the left of the curtain without needing an order.

Isabella had not yet spoken. The two men who would once have argued with an Academy instructor in Edward's presence now needed only to see her enter a room to know exactly where they belonged. Edward brushed several strands of straw from his shoulder, straightened his coat, and walked towards the small sitting room separated from the kitchen by a heavy curtain. Just before lifting it, he looked back once.

Romeo was no longer laughing. Marco gave him a single nod. Edward drew the curtain aside.

The woman beside the stove did not rise. A deep crimson velvet cloak fell over the side of her chair, its white fox trim carrying almost no snow. Dark brown hair had been gathered neatly behind her head. Her amber eyes were the only warmth on a face held almost perfectly still.

A ceremonial sword bearing the Castilian arms rested beside the chair. On the table, the tea Juliet had poured still steamed.

At twenty-seven, Isabella Testarossa could still change the rhythm of a room by sitting quietly inside it. The velvet cloak, the ceremonial blade, and the straight-backed posture belonged to a Queen. The scarred wooden table, the scent of soup, and the cramped kitchen belonged to the Spencers. The two worlds had never intended to share the same space.

Juliet checked the nearly empty teapot and stood. "I'll fetch more hot water. You two can speak."

The moment she disappeared behind the curtain, Isabella's courteous smile vanished. Her eyes travelled from Edward's snow-stained boots to the goatskin coat and the dirt still caught at one cuff. Then they settled sharply on his face.

"You truly chose to bury yourself here with that woman? She looks at you with the ordinary devotion of a servant. You should have been beside someone who understood what you were worth."

Edward breathed out. Six years had changed many things. Apparently that particular piece of Isabella had survived untouched. "That's what you've never understood," he said quietly. "In a world like this, ordinary warmth is the rarest luxury left."

Water poured into the kettle beyond the curtain. Isabella watched him for another moment, plainly unconvinced. When Juliet's footsteps returned, the irritation disappeared from her face as completely as if it had never existed. She accepted the refilled cup with perfect courtesy.

"Thank you, Juliet."

Then she looked at Edward. "Well. You are still alive."

He rested one hand against the doorframe. "You crossed half of Morocco in winter to confirm that?"

Isabella placed her cup on the tray and allowed him to wait. "Of course not." Her voice softened. "I came to tell you that tomorrow will no longer be as quiet as today."

Wind struck the window. Edward looked at Isabella, then at the ceremonial sword beside her chair. Behind the curtain came Remi's voice and the lingering smell of supper, but the room before him had already filled again with maps, orders, and the people who had known him before Marrakesh.

Whatever Isabella had brought south with her, she had already carried it across the threshold.

Isabella said nothing more after her warning. She waited for Edward to answer, giving him no room to dismiss the words as the opening move of some negotiation.

Juliet stepped from behind her husband. "I'll leave you to speak privately."

"No." Isabella turned to her. The Queen's manner still carried its formal distance, but she did not push Juliet away from a decision that concerned her family directly. "Stay. What I am about to say will decide where Edward goes, and if he goes, where you and Remi will live. I would rather you hear it now than have your husband repeat it later as though it were someone else's affair."

Juliet looked at Edward. He drew out the chair beside him and kept a hand on its back until she sat.

Marco and Romeo remained near the doorway. Neither had smiled since Isabella crossed the curtain.

"Map," Isabella said.

Marco removed the leather tube from his shoulder at once. The map he unrolled was far larger than the worn sheet Edward used to teach Remi geography. Its edge covered a wooden plate and pushed the boy's spoon aside. With that one movement, the Spencer family's dining table became the sort of place Edward had spent years trying to escape.

Isabella placed one finger on the North African coast. "The truth is much worse than the rumours reaching Marrakesh. The Western Roman advance did not begin at Tunis. Before turning towards North Africa, Ravenna's armies drove the Ottomans from most of their European territories and swallowed regions no one would have believed they could reach only a few years ago. Winter came, and they did not stop. They simply continued south."

Marco pointed across the land stretching from the Balkans to the Mediterranean.

"The Ottomans asked Castile for help. We sent troops, artillery, supplies, everything we could spare to hold the line with them. The combined strength of both empires failed to save Libya. Egypt fell soon after."

Isabella moved her finger west and stopped at Tunis.

"And now this. Tunis is gone."

Juliet looked at the little name printed on the map. She could not have said how many days of marching lay between Tunis and Marrakesh, but she understood the meaning of Isabella's hand moving nearer to their home.

"Fes and Taza still stand," Isabella continued, "but do not let two names remaining on a map mislead you. My forces are stretched thin enough that if one link breaks, the entire southern line falls back another city. Tunis gives Ravenna a port, warehouses, and supply routes. From now on, every city we lose is another step towards Marrakesh."

Edward did not interrupt. One hand rested on the back of Juliet's chair, his thumb touching the place where her wrist lay beneath her sleeve.

Isabella moved north to the Pyrenees.

"Here, almost the whole weight of the Castilian field army is pinned in place. The Emperor of Holy France murdered the Pope in Vienna and tore up the Non-Aggression Treaty as if it had never existed. France has not yet broken the entire Pyrenean line, but if I strip troops from it to save North Africa, I open Iberia myself."

Juliet did not understand every consequence of a Pope dying in Vienna. She understood the silence that fell over Marco and Romeo when Isabella spoke of it. If a treaty strong enough to keep a frontier quiet could disappear with one murder, then things Juliet had once imagined permanent were no more permanent than the ice outside the window.

Marco leaned over the map and indicated two overlapping supply routes. "The southern burden has already forced the north to surrender one legion. The reverse is also true. If artillery goes north, Fes works with whatever remains."

Isabella did not answer him. Her finger crossed the map again, this time towards the west.

"In the New World, we have lost more than a fleet. In practical terms, the entire theatre has slipped beyond our control."

Edward raised his eyes when she mentioned seven Mythic-grade Vestigia. Isabella noticed and continued without pause.

"The Portuguese Navy sailed with seven Mythic-grade Vestigia. They have learned to integrate them into fleet formations, one compensating for the weakness of another. The strategic fleet Castile sent to intercept them was destroyed before it could alter the situation."

She gave no casualty figure. "Once the force meant to command the sea was broken, our remaining positions in the New World could no longer support one another as a single defence. Those not already taken by Portugal are isolated, cut from reinforcement, and surviving on whatever they still possess."

A log split in the stove. No one spoke over it.

"The Portuguese remain on the far side of the Atlantic," Isabella said. "But we no longer have sufficient strength there to contain them. If they turn their bows towards Iberia and attempt to reclaim their homeland, I cannot promise that any Castilian fleet left in European waters can stop them."

Marco looked at Edward. "Three jaws closing at once. France from the north. Western Rome from the south-east. Portugal waiting beyond the ocean. Castile has lost the initiative in every theatre."

Edward did not ask how many shells remained at Fes, how many men held the Pyrenees, or how many ships could still fight. He looked instead at Marrakesh and measured the distance from Tunis with his eyes.

The city was no longer far enough away to pretend the war belonged elsewhere. Juliet shifted her hand in her lap. Edward found it immediately and laced his fingers through hers.

"You did not cross half of Morocco simply to tell me the world is ending," he said. "Say what you actually came for."

Isabella did not answer with words. She untied the red cord around the documents she had brought and laid three orders side by side before him.

"I came to give you three choices."

She pushed the first to the left.

"The first road is the Atlantic. You take command of every combat-capable formation remaining in the Castilian fleet. Your immediate task is to hold Gibraltar, Lisbon, and the sea route linking Iberia to North Africa, then find a way to prevent the Portuguese Navy from bringing the war back to Europe."

Edward read the order without touching it.

Isabella moved it aside and placed the second before him.

"The second road is Ravenna."

Marco straightened the instant he heard the name.

Isabella pressed two fingers to the document. "I have sufficient evidence to believe the Crown of Ravenna is more than a symbol of Western Roman authority. It is itself a Mythic-grade Vestigium kept at the very centre of their power. We still do not understand the full extent of what it can do, but too many anomalies in Western Roman campaigns cannot be explained by manpower, artillery, or logistics alone."

She let the implication settle before continuing.

"If you choose this road, you infiltrate Ravenna, locate the Crown, and seize it. If seizure proves impossible, you destroy it."

Romeo came away from the wall.

Edward still did not touch either order.

Isabella laid her hand over the third sheet. An English lion had been pressed faintly into one corner.

Juliet's eyes lowered to the emblem.

"And the last road," Isabella said, placing a finger on the British Isles, "goes north."

Edward waited.

"You return to England."

The words outweighed every place-name around them.

"Not to resurrect a dead empire," Isabella continued. "You go with a Reliquiario detachment small enough to move through regions where armies and governments no longer exist. You find surviving communities, recover valuable ownerless Vestigia, and open contact with the Kingdom of the Danes."

Her fingertip drew a line north from the islands.

"If the Danes have not yet been crushed between France and Novgorod, a northern front could force France to look in another direction. Even a partial shift of pressure away from the Pyrenees buys Castile time."

Edward remained still.

Isabella leaned back and rubbed her thumb over the mark her glove had left on her wrist.

"Do not mistake these orders for three chances at victory. The Atlantic may drown you with another fleet. Ravenna may bury you before you ever see the Crown. England may contain nothing but ice, corpses, and things mankind should never have disturbed."

Her fingertips touched each order in turn. "Every road leads into death, Edward. I did not come because I possess a safe one. Death no longer asks anyone's permission in this age. The least I can still give you is the right to choose how you walk towards it."

Juliet tightened her grip on Edward's hand.

He read the three orders again and stopped at a word he had never seen.

"Reliquiario?"

"The Latin records call them Venator Reliquia, Vestigium Hunters. In Castilian we call them Los Reliquiarios."

Isabella removed an appendix from the file but kept it in her own hand. "They are not Church agents, monks, magicians, or executioners. They are specialists trained to enter forbidden regions where ordinary soldiers cannot operate. They deal with ownerless Vestigia and anomalous zones that have already killed enough people that no sane commander sends another regiment merely to see what happens."

Marco drew the appendix closer so Edward could read the notes in its margins. "Their resistance to exposure is much better than a normal soldier's. They are trained to approach, contain, and if necessary suppress Vestigia. But they remain flesh and blood. They bleed, they die, and sometimes they die very quickly."

Edward looked at Isabella. "I understand."

The three orders remained between them, each promising a different kind of ruin. For the first time since Isabella entered the house, Edward looked away from the map and towards the room around it. Before he could choose a road, there was something more important he needed answered.

Edward did not ask about troop strength, the limits of his authority, or how long any of the missions were expected to last. He turned to Juliet, took her hand, and asked the question that mattered first.

"If I go, what happens to Juliet and Remi?"

Isabella did not need to consult her papers. "Barcelona, for now. It is still the place where I can protect them best."

Edward looked up.

"A properly heated apartment in the central district, food under the royal allotment, clean water, physicians, and a school for Remi. My Guard will be directly responsible for their security. If events force the court to move its administrative centre to Madrid before your family reaches Iberia, the protection order moves with them. It is not tied to a single city."

Juliet lowered the document to the table but kept one finger against its edge. "How long does the protection last?"

"Until Edward returns," Isabella said. "Or until you choose to leave and circumstances permit it."

Edward still had not touched the mission orders. He placed a finger over the city named on the protection paper.

"Is Barcelona truly the safest place, or do you also want them close enough to make certain I do not betray Castile?"

Isabella removed her remaining glove and placed it beside her cup. When she sat straighter, the Queen returned fully to the room. "If you want the answer from the Crown, then both. Barcelona is among the safest places left to us. A man sent somewhere he may die fights better when he knows his wife and child are alive and have somewhere to receive him if he returns. But I will not pretend that keeping Juliet and Remi under direct Castilian protection places no obligation upon you."

Her amber eyes did not leave his. "Politics does not disappear because we give it a kinder name."

Edward rested one finger on the document. "At least you are willing to say it plainly."

"You ask. I answer. I did not come to Marrakesh to make you think well of me."

Juliet kept her hand on the protection order. The conversation had moved too far beyond shelter and rations to remain a matter of paperwork.

Isabella turned to her first. "But Juliet, I want one thing understood." Then she looked back at Edward. "Do not call them hostages. If you betray me, I will strip you of command, issue a warrant, and bring you back for trial. If you resist, my people may kill you. If one day you must abandon Castile because your wife and son are trapped somewhere about to burn, I will judge you after they are safe."

She laid her palm flat against the table. "Juliet and Remi will not pay for your choices. I will say that once."

Only then did Edward draw the paper closer. His gaze settled on the royal seal. "Does this survive me? And what happens if you die first?"

"Yes. They remain protected if you die. If I die, the document still bears the royal seal and the Council's signatures. Their rights do not depend on my continued existence."

"Barcelona can fall."

"Yes. If it ceases to be safe, the court moves them before it moves the silver reserves."

Juliet spoke next. "And if my son and I do not want to go where the court chooses?"

Isabella turned fully towards her. "If it is not an emergency evacuation, the decision is yours. I am protecting you and Remi, not owning you."

Juliet read the page again and nodded. "Then I understand."

Edward kept asking questions. He wanted to know where the food came from, who commanded the security detail, who possessed authority to alter a route if a railway failed, and where Remi would be treated if he became ill. Not once did he ask the size of the fleet he might inherit, how many Reliquiarios would accompany him, or what authority he would hold in the field.

Isabella answered everything until he was satisfied that his family would not simply disappear into a promise stamped with wax.

Only then did she say, "You may now ask about the mission."

Edward settled back in his chair. "I still have one more question."

She waited.

"What if I say no?"

Marco turned sharply. Romeo came away from the wall.

Edward ignored both. "What if I take Juliet and Remi out of Marrakesh tonight, reject every order and every offer of protection, and disappear from your life completely?"

Isabella lifted her hand from the table and sat upright. "I will not have you dragged back in chains."

Marco looked up. Romeo straightened, but Isabella's eyes remained on Edward. "If you reject the orders and the protection, I let you leave. From that moment, the consequences are yours. I will not take food from my army, divert Royal Guards, or open emergency stores to rescue a man who deliberately walked away from that protection."

"And if we die out there?"

"Then that is the consequence you chose."

Isabella's voice remained level. "But do not dress it in the word protection. You are not merely asking whether you have the right to refuse. You are testing whether I will stand here and call removing Juliet and Remi from every organised supply line a sensible plan."

Edward did not answer.

"You know Marrakesh is no longer safe. You also know that beyond Castilian control you possess no escort, no reserve stores, and no secure route. Yet the first alternative you test is disappearance."

She leaned forward slightly. "Do not ask me to pretend that is a plan."

Edward frowned. "Lower your voice. Remi is resting in the next room."

Isabella's chair scraped hard against the stone floor as she rose. "Remi being in the next room is exactly why I am saying it."

Edward stood as well.

"You may hate war. You may hate my throne. You may hate the fact that I came here to pull you back towards a life you abandoned. But do not stand in front of me and call taking your wife and child somewhere no one can protect them an act of protecting your family."

"Bella."

"Where exactly do you intend to run this time?"

The words stopped her as soon as they left her mouth. Her hand fell from the edge of the table. "You were an admiral of an empire. You pulled thousands of people out of London while the city burned. You taught me that when people are cornered, they will call anything in front of them an escape route simply because it leads away."

Her voice failed for a moment. Isabella turned her face aside, but the first tear had already crossed her cheek. "And all these years, I have still thought of you as my brother." She wiped her face with the back of her hand and braced herself against the table again. Marco and Romeo did not move. "I crossed half of Morocco through a snowstorm because I will not stand aside and watch you, Juliet, and Remi freeze to death in some forgotten place simply because you want to believe resigning from the military was enough to make war forget your family."

Edward had known what to do beneath naval gunfire, in hurricane winds, and during a retreat collapsing around him. Isabella crying in his kitchen left him without words for several seconds. "Bella." He stepped nearer. "I did not say I was leaving. But I had to ask."

She pressed her lips together and said nothing. When she looked at him again, her eyes were still red, but the next question had returned to the cadence of state business. "Have you made a decision?"

Edward glanced at Juliet. She neither nodded nor shook her head, but both of her hands closed around his. He looked again at the three orders. "Give me two days. Two days to arrange what can be arranged and speak properly with Juliet before I answer. I understand your strategic position. There is no need to send anyone else to explain it."

Isabella sat down. "Two days."

Edward nodded once.

"Forty-eight hours," she said. "Marco will return here. If the answer is no, I want to hear you refuse me yourself."

"Agreed."

She folded the documents together. "If the answer is yes, you choose freely among the three missions."

Edward left that unanswered. Isabella did not press.

A small wooden knock came from behind the curtain.

Juliet turned her head. "Remi again."

A head appeared first, followed by half a body. Remi held a wooden cup in both hands and tried to wear the solemn expression of a child engaged in important household business.

"I only wanted to ask whether anyone needs more water."

Edward looked at the cup. "The empty cup?"

Remi inspected it. He turned it slowly as if water might somehow be hiding on the other side, then moved the evidence behind his back.

"I was going to ask first and fetch it afterwards."

Romeo laughed aloud. Marco turned towards the window to hide his face. Juliet pressed two fingers to her brow.

Isabella lasted several seconds longer before she laughed as well. It was not the courteous laugh she used before courtiers. It came freely enough to dissolve what remained of the coldness in her face. Remi stood beside the curtain with the empty cup hidden behind him and stared from one adult to another, entirely uncertain what he had done.

"Come here." Isabella beckoned. Remi looked immediately to his father. Edward nodded, and only then did the boy approach. She bent to his level. "I heard everyone call you Remi. Is that your proper name, or only what they use at home?"

"Everyone calls me Remi."

"Reminisce," Edward said behind them.

Isabella looked over.

"Reminisce?"

"Yes. Remembrance." Edward glanced at Juliet before continuing. "So we remember what we lost, and what we still have to keep."

Isabella's smile faded as she looked back at the boy, who was still waiting to be told why he carried such a name. "That is a heavy name for a child."

Edward folded his arms. "He'll grow into it."

Remi finally surrendered to the question he had been holding since Isabella first arrived. "Are you really a Queen?"

Romeo coughed and looked away.

Isabella answered with exactly the seriousness the boy had given the question. "I am."

Remi straightened. "Do you own a castle?"

"I own several."

"Several?"

Isabella had to tighten her lips to preserve a calm expression. "Several. Although I should warn you, most of them are terribly cold."

Remi considered this. A Queen with several castles apparently became less impressive if the castles could not stay warm. "Do the castles have schools?"

Her hand paused against the rim of her cup. "Not inside the castles. But in Barcelona you would find schools, more books than you could finish, teachers, and many children your own age."

His eyes widened. "I could go to school?"

"If your family moves to Iberia, then yes."

Remi turned at once towards his parents. Juliet's fingers tightened around the fabric of her skirt.

Isabella noticed and placed a hand on the boy's shoulder before he could speak. "But whether your family goes or stays is for your parents to decide. You are not allowed to use school to lure your father into saying yes. Understood?"

Remi looked up, considering the wording carefully. "What if I remind him only once each day? That would not count as luring him, would it?"

Romeo dropped his face towards the table. Marco turned fully towards the window.

Isabella looked at Edward and laughed. "Seven years old and already searching for loopholes. If he ever enters my court, I will have every document he signs read twice."

Edward pointed at his son. "Do not learn Uncle Romeo's tricks."

"I haven't even done anything," Romeo protested.

Remi giggled despite not quite understanding why the accusation was funny.

Isabella adjusted the boy's crooked woollen cap. "Does your father teach you to read here?"

"Yes. But if I make a mistake, he makes me write it five times."

Edward defended himself immediately. "This morning he left a letter out of Atlantic."

"I did it on purpose."

"Which is why you deserved five repetitions even more."

Isabella shook her head at Edward. "What sort of admiral loses an argument to a seven-year-old?"

"I am clearly winning."

Remi interrupted. "You are not, Father."

Isabella laughed into her hand. Edward, recognising that the entire room had defected to the opposition, ended the argument before the situation became worse.

A little later, Remi found himself studying Isabella again. Her crimson cloak, silver embroidery, and immaculate white gloves had captured his attention far more completely than any discussion of empires.

She caught him looking. "What is it?"

"Nothing."

"I am a Queen," Isabella said with a smile. "I am very good at noticing when someone is hiding something."

He hesitated, then surrendered. "I was only looking because you're very beautiful."

Juliet turned away to hide a smile. Edward looked at Isabella with the expression of a man who already knew where this was going.

She seized the opportunity immediately. "Then answer something for me, Remi. When you grow up, what sort of wife would you like?"

"Isabella," Edward warned.

She ignored him.

Remi scratched his head and thought with such seriousness that even Romeo and Marco waited for the result. His gaze moved to his mother, then back to Isabella.

"I would like someone beautiful and clever, and kind to me the way Mama is."

Juliet went still.

Remi quickly smiled at Isabella. "And if she knew how to dress as splendidly as you, that would be perfect."

The room froze for one beat.

Then Isabella broke into laughter so bright she had to cover her mouth. Romeo slapped the table. Marco surrendered every attempt at dignity. Juliet bent and kissed her son's hair.

Edward sighed theatrically. "I spend seven years feeding and raising you, and this is how you repay me? Defeated by a cloak?"

"But her clothes really are beautiful, Father."

"I know."

Still laughing, Isabella ruffled Remi's hair. "The boy has excellent taste."

"I shall remember this as the day you began corrupting my son's mind."

"Too late. He plainly has opinions of his own."

Remi did not know what victory he had apparently achieved, but he enjoyed it. The smile left him only when he remembered the words he had overheard beyond the curtain. "Father."

Edward saw the change immediately and crouched before him. Remi gripped the edge of his goatskin sleeve.

"Do you have to go somewhere?"

"Maybe." Edward covered the small hand with his own. "Your mother and I still need to talk."

"Far away?"

"Perhaps very far."

Remi inspected the old goatskin coat as if this were now the most urgent strategic problem in the room. "Then take your thickest coat."

Edward laughed, but the sound caught before it fully left him. "I will."

"And the gloves Mama repaired."

"Yes."

"Not the pair with the hole."

"I understand."

Remi still looked unconvinced. Juliet came over and rested a hand on his shoulder. "All right. Go fetch the water properly this time, and remember to bring water back with the cup."

He looked at the empty cup still hidden behind him, caught for the second time in one afternoon. "Yes, Mama."

He ran from the room.

Romeo waited until the footsteps faded before laughing again. Isabella rose. The smile remained on her face for another moment before duty reclaimed it.

She straightened her collar and looked at Juliet. "I am leaving the protection order here. Read every line. If there is a term you will not accept, write directly on the paper and I will have it reviewed."

Juliet took the document in both hands. "I will."

Isabella turned to Edward. "Forty-eight hours. That is all I can give you."

"I remember."

Marco opened the door. Snow-laden air entered at once and bent the flame in the stove.

Isabella crossed the threshold, then stopped. "Edward."

He looked at her.

She did not turn around. "Do not choose because I cried."

Edward said nothing.

"If you return to war out of pity for me, I will be the first person to despise you for it."

This time he understood exactly what she needed to hear. "I know."

Isabella nodded, raised her collar, and stepped into the snow. The door closed behind her. Marco followed her to the carriage. Romeo pulled up his hood and went towards the mounted escort. Neither man asked Edward what he would choose.

Inside the carriage, the wind became a low, constant rumble behind thick wooden walls. Isabella sat opposite Marco, removed her gloves, and placed both hands on her knees. The emotions of the Spencer house were behind her. The skin around her eyes still felt tight from tears wiped away too quickly.

Marco did not speak at first. Through the fogged window, the stone house receded until only one yellow square of light remained in the snow.

Isabella looked at her hand. When she stood to leave, Remi had taken hold of one finger the way children did when they forgot who the person before them was supposed to be. The touch was gone, but the meaning Edward had given the boy's name remained.

Reminisce.

A child named so that his parents would remember what they had lost, and what they still had to protect.

Marco finally broke the silence. "He resembles Edward. Especially the questions. The boy refuses the first answer merely because an adult gave it. Edward was exactly the same when he was young. Insufferable."

Isabella laughed once and looked towards the window. "The smile is Juliet's."

Marco did not comment on the second name. He had spent enough years around other families to recognise that some observations did not improve by becoming arguments.

Isabella rested her head lightly against the carriage wall. She had prepared herself to find Edward broken, a man surviving by habit and waiting for one strong reason to return to the life he had abandoned. Instead she had found a house that smelled of soup, a child leaving toys on the floor, a wife who knew exactly how much her husband had eaten, and Edward Spencer laughing sincerely about cow dung. That was what made the mission she had brought south harder.

"He looks better than I expected," Marco said. "Her Majesty seems to have noticed."

"I noticed."

Isabella was silent for a while.

"And that is not the problem. It is why I hated coming here."

Marco did not ask.

"If Marrakesh were still safe, I would have left his life alone. But Tunis is gone. If Western Rome advances again, Edward will no longer be choosing between war and family." She drew the woollen blanket over her knees. "War will choose for him."

Marco looked back towards where the house had vanished. "So Your Majesty wants him to choose first."

"I want him to retain the right to choose."

After a moment, Marco asked, "And if he truly refuses?"

"I let him refuse."

He turned to her.

"I told him the choice was his. I do not withdraw my word simply because I dislike the answer." Isabella adjusted the blanket. "But neither am I obliged to rescue him from the consequences of that answer."

Marco accepted that. "Do you think he will choose the north?"

Isabella did not answer immediately. Of the three orders, only the last had contained a name heavy enough to make Edward remain silent longer than usual. She also knew him well enough to understand that silence was not consent. "I don't know."

Marco raised an eyebrow. Perhaps it was the first time that day he had heard Isabella admit ignorance without attaching a contingency plan.

She closed her eyes. "And this time, I do not want to decide for him."

The carriage moved through Marrakesh, carrying the Queen back towards maps, reports, and a chain of cities falling one after another. In the stone house behind her, Edward Spencer had forty-eight hours to decide whether he would step again into the storm.

* * *

Night had settled completely by the time Remi fell asleep. He curled beneath the blankets with the little three-masted ship clutched against his chest as though letting go might cause it to disappear.

Juliet sat beside the stove for a long time without speaking. Edward did not hurry her. He gathered the three orders from the dining table, moved them to one side, and placed the protection document in the centre.

At last Juliet crossed the room. She ignored the chair opposite him, knelt beside his knees, and rested her forehead against one of them. "Edward, I'm afraid."

His hand settled at the back of her neck.

She tried to continue, swallowed, then tried again. "I look at Marco and Romeo, at their armour, at the map on the table, and I see London."

Edward closed his eyes.

"I know this isn't London." Her fingers tightened in his coat. "But I can still hear the guns. I remember people trampling each other at the harbour. I remember Remi screaming himself hoarse in my arms while you kept running away and coming back, away and back, as though one moment of delay would kill all three of us."

Edward pulled her to her feet and held her. "I'm here."

"I know." The words caught in her throat. "That's what frightens me."

There was no better answer, so he only kept his arms around her.

A long time passed before Juliet raised her head. "You are going to choose one of them, aren't you?"

Edward looked at the three orders. "I have not answered Isabella."

"I didn't ask Queen Isabella." Juliet wiped her cheek with her wrist. "I'm asking my husband."

Edward turned fully towards her. This time he did not reach for the map. "If I stay, I don't know whether I'm protecting you and Remi or simply waiting for the war to find our door."

Juliet did not contradict him.

"If I go, Isabella can at least move you somewhere safer." He looked at the protection order. "I hate that your future sits on a piece of paper carrying someone else's seal. But right now that paper means a roof, food, and a school for Remi."

Juliet looked at the three mission orders and touched the first. "If you must go, isn't the navy the road closest to the man you used to be?"

Edward shook his head. "It is closest to what I used to be good at, which is probably why Isabella placed it first. But taking the fleet means reacting to whatever day Portugal chooses to come home. I would spend the campaign holding sea lanes and waiting for someone else to move first." He tapped the page lightly. "I can do that. But all it does is stop one door from closing."

Juliet moved to the second document. "And Ravenna? You don't believe the Crown is worth gambling your life."

"Too much depends on a Vestigium even Isabella does not understand. Striking directly at the enemy capital and betting everything on one Crown is a campaign built around a wager. I cannot build our future on that."

Juliet did not ask about the third. Her hand stopped over the English lion.

Edward placed his fingertip beside hers. "I want to return to England."

Juliet closed her eyes. The hand holding the paper folded one corner without her noticing.

Edward took that hand into his. "The north is no safer than the other roads. But it is the only one that can create another strategic direction instead of holding a line already breaking or staking everything on a single raid."

Juliet looked at the last order. "Are you choosing the north because it is truly the best road, or because England is at the end of it?"

"Both, perhaps." He spoke more slowly now. "I do not know what remains there. If the Danes still stand, if there are surviving communities on the islands, and if we can connect the two, France will have to look north as well. Castile buys time." His eyes settled on the lion embossed in the paper. "And I learn whether my homeland is actually dead."

Juliet tightened her grip on his hand. "What about Remi? Are you looking for a front, or a homeland for our son?"

Edward looked towards the room where the boy slept. "I can't promise him a homeland. But if there is still somewhere people can live, I want to know it exists before I accept that his whole life will be a series of shelters other people permit him to use."

Juliet did not let go. "And if you do not come back? Do not comfort me. I want the true answer."

Edward needed several seconds. "I don't know."

She kept looking at him.

He drew her closer.

"If there are only graves, I come home. If there are still people alive, I want to help them open a road out."

Juliet rested her forehead against his chest. "I hate that answer."

Edward kissed her hair. "So do I."

She held him a little longer. "But I understand."

They remained beside the dying fire until the flames had collapsed into red coals.

Before standing, Juliet looked around their house. "Where do we begin tomorrow? Remi, the cattle, our things, then Isabella?"

Edward looked at the wooden chest, the old leather map, and the child sleeping in the next room. "Tomorrow morning I answer Isabella first. Then we tell Remi properly and start packing. We slaughter part of the herd for a farewell meal. The rest go to the Governor and to households that can still keep them alive."

He moved the other two orders aside. Only one remained in the middle of the table.

England.

For six years, England had existed in the Spencer house only through maps, old books, and stories told to Remi. Tonight the name lay beneath Edward's hand in the form of an order that might carry him back.

The next morning, Edward opened the door and briefly wondered whether he had properly awakened. Marco was leaning against the fence with both arms folded. A few paces away, Romeo sat on an overturned crate struggling with a piece of bread hard enough to make him look as though he were interrogating an unusually stubborn prisoner.

Both still wore Castilian cloaks, though the heavy armour was gone. Their horses stood tied near the fence, breathing white into the early air. A skin of ice still clung to the saddles, proof that neither man had enjoyed a short journey.

Edward remained in the doorway. "What the hell are you two doing here?"

Romeo finally broke the bread. Half of it slipped from his fingers and planted itself upright in the snow. He stared at it as though weighing whether the rescue effort would be worthwhile. "Good morning to you too, old friend."

Edward refused to be diverted and looked at Marco. "Last night Isabella said someone would return in two days. I have not grown senile since supper."

Marco drew his collar closer and brushed snow from one shoulder. "Correct. Last night we also expected to wake this morning in Tangier."

Edward frowned. "Then why are you standing outside my house?"

"Because we'd travelled more than halfway there when Her Majesty stopped the carriage."

Romeo swallowed the last of the bread still in his hand. "More accurately, she threw us out."

Edward looked at him. "On the road?"

"On the road." Romeo nodded. "Snow to the knees. Wind attempting to remove the skin from our faces. An excellent environment for meditating on the honour of serving in the Royal Guard."

Marco almost smiled. "Her Majesty said you had forty-eight hours. Whether you accept or refuse, you may need a carriage, travel papers, a courier, or anything else involving the Crown during those two days. She did not want you wasting half a day searching for an official willing to sign something."

Edward leaned against the frame. "So she exchanged two Royal Guards for a pair of errand boys."

"She used the word assistance," Marco said. "And she was very specific. We are not to ask what you have decided, pressure you in any direction, or stand in your house watching you pack like two crows waiting for a corpse."

Romeo raised one finger. "The crow portion is my interpretation."

"The rest is accurate."

Edward laughed. Whatever sleep remained in him disappeared. "You rode halfway to Tangier and came back for that?"

Romeo pointed at Marco. "He suggested continuing and pretending we had not heard."

"I asked whether both of us were strictly necessary."

"And then she looked at him." Romeo paused and imitated a dead expression so exaggerated that it ceased to resemble any human face. "Thus, we turned the horses around."

The door opened behind Edward.

Juliet stepped out carrying a large basket, her scarf already tied firmly around her head and a folded list tucked into her belt. She looked at the two men who had arrived before sunrise, then at her husband. "I told them to wait inside. They said it was easier to breathe out here."

Marco coughed politely. "We did not want to wake the household."

Romeo lowered his voice. "And Juliet assigns tasks very quickly. Going inside might have produced more."

She heard him. "Correct."

Romeo fell silent.

Edward looked at the basket.

"You're going to the market this early?"

"If I go now, I can buy flour before the northern convoys take the better stock. I also need the distribution office to tell me how we transfer the cattle, and we need more rope." Juliet tightened her gloves. "You stay with Remi. These two arrived at the right moment. Make use of them."

Marco put his hands behind his back like a man receiving orders. "What do you need?"

Juliet pointed at the woodpile. "My husband said yesterday that he would split another stack before we left. It remains remarkably unsplit."

Edward frowned. "I haven't even had breakfast."

"I didn't tell you to do it now. I told them."

Romeo turned towards Edward with the expression of a betrayed ally. "Are you not going to defend our honour?"

Edward stepped down from the threshold and picked up the shovel resting against the wall. "I have just learned that the Queen kicked you out of her carriage and sent you back to assist with chores. Your honour is your own problem."

Juliet laughed and settled the basket against her hip. "I'll be back before noon. Remi is eating in the kitchen. Do not let him follow these two around learning anything strange."

"That wounds me," Romeo said, placing a hand over his heart.

"You'll survive."

She passed through the gate, then turned once more. "And don't forget you need to see Victoria."

Edward nodded. "I remember."

Juliet disappeared down the snow-covered road towards central Marrakesh. The three men watched until she vanished behind a line of stone houses.

Romeo turned first. "Your wife remains as terrifying as I remember."

Edward tossed him an axe. "You've known her again for less than a day."

"Enough time to form an informed opinion."

Marco took the second axe and pulled his gloves tight. "At least she did not leave us in the middle of a snowfield."

"No. She has sentenced us to firewood. I have not decided which is worse."

Edward planted the shovel in the snow. "Work. If you want lunch, we need something to cook it with."

Romeo muttered that he had once been a naval officer and was now performing labour in exchange for porridge. He still dragged the first log into place.

Soon the yard settled into the rhythm of axes.

Romeo complained throughout, yet always pulled the next log into position before anyone had to tell him. Marco had changed less. He checked the handle, read the grain, and only then swung.

Romeo did everything faster than necessary. By the fourth strike, his blade landed off-centre.

Edward watched him once. "Your hands are still too high."

Romeo stopped. "You remember that?"

"I remember you breaking an axe handle at Caen and blaming the weather."

Marco laughed. "I wrote the report."

Romeo looked at him. "And you believed me."

"No. I wrote 'cause undetermined' because I did not want to explain to a colonel that an officer had been defeated by a piece of wood."

Romeo pointed the axe at both of them. "You two hold grudges for an unreasonable length of time."

Edward did not answer. He bent to clear snow from the path leading towards the stable. While Marco dragged another log out, Edward spoke as though he were merely continuing the conversation. "I accepted Isabella's offer."

Romeo's axe stopped in mid-air. Marco released the log. Neither asked whether they had heard correctly.

Edward stood the shovel beside the wall. "After she left last night, Juliet and I talked. I am taking the mission."

Romeo spoke first. "The fleet?"

Edward shook his head.

Marco watched him longer. "Ravenna, then?"

"No."

Edward looked at both men. "The north."

For several seconds, no one said anything. Wind swept across the fence and lifted a thin veil of snow from the stable roof.

Romeo lowered the axe. "England?"

"Yes. I chose England."

No one joked.

All three men were English, though Marco and Romeo now wore Castilian lions and answered to another Queen. England still meant harbours, fog, barracks that no longer existed, streets that had disappeared, and people who had failed to reach the last ships.

Marco rested his axe against the log. "Are you certain?"

"I'm certain I want to go. Whether the choice is right, I'll discover when I get there."

Romeo bent to pick up the split wood. "I thought you would choose the sea."

"So did I until last night."

Romeo opened his mouth, but Edward shook his head. "The reasons can wait. I wanted the two of you to know before the news travelled beyond this house."

Marco glanced towards the window. Behind the fogged glass, Remi's shadow crossed and vanished. "Juliet cannot be pleased. You're still leaving Marrakesh?"

"She isn't pleased, and I don't expect her to be." Edward rested both hands on the shovel. "But this was never about Juliet granting or denying permission. We decided as a family that we leave Marrakesh. I take the mission. Juliet and Remi travel under protection to Iberia."

Marco did not correct a word. He only nodded.

Romeo leaned on the axe. "What do you need from us?"

"For the moment, nothing concerning the north. I do not want half a story outrunning me. If Isabella asks, tell her I have decided and will send my answer myself."

Marco waited. "That's all?"

"For this morning."

Edward pointed at Romeo's axe. "Now split the wood."

The kitchen door opened.

Remi stood there holding a wooden cup and watched the three adults as though they were engaged in some incomprehensible game.

"Father."

Edward turned. "What is it?"

"I brought water."

Romeo bent immediately to inspect the cup. "Is there actually water in it this time?"

Remi hugged it to his chest and regarded him with suspicion. "Yes."

Edward laughed. "Leave him alone."

Remi brought the cup to his father, then looked at the two Royal Guards chopping wood. "Are you going with Father?"

Marco set his axe down. "No. We have other work."

Romeo leaned against his own handle. "Extremely important work that no one has the decency to call heroic."

Remi considered that. "Will you come back for supper?"

Romeo looked at Edward. "That is already more practical than most questions from General Staff."

Edward gave the cup back to his son. "Go inside. It's cold."

Remi took several steps, then turned. "Father, you really chose England?"

Edward looked at him. They had not explained everything the night before, but the boy had heard enough broken pieces to guess. "Yes. I'll explain it properly later."

Remi nodded and pointed at the goatskin coat. "Remember the thick one."

Romeo immediately turned away to laugh.

Edward closed his eyes for a moment. "I remember."

The boy ran back inside.

Marco picked up his axe. "You already have a junior quartermaster in the house."

"Do not teach him anything."

"I don't think he needs us. It appears to be developing naturally."

They returned to work.

Snow disappeared from the path. The stack beneath the eaves grew. Their conversation drifted away from old campaigns and towards small things: a crooked storehouse hinge, which sacks of fodder had to be moved first, which tools Edward meant to leave behind. No one mentioned the mission again. For a little while, they split wood, repaired hinges, shovelled snow, and argued over trivialities in much the same way they had when they were young. In that frozen yard, no one needed to be an admiral or a Royal Guard.

When the last of the wood had been stacked, Romeo planted both hands on his hips. "For the record, if Juliet orders me to clean the cattle shed before lunch, I intend to claim Royal Guard immunity."

Marco looked at him. "You have no such immunity."

"Then I shall invent it."

Edward picked up the shovel. "Please do. I would like to watch Juliet resolve a constitutional dispute."

The soft grind of cart wheels in the lane announced Juliet's return before the debate could continue. She entered carrying a basket heavier than the one she had left with. Flour, salt, new rope, several packets of herbs, and two loaves still warm from the oven filled it. Remi ran out to meet her, immediately accepted the lightest bundle, and declared himself useful.

Juliet surveyed the split firewood, the cleared path, and the repaired storehouse door. "Not bad."

Romeo straightened. "I request that this achievement be entered into my service record."

"You still haven't finished the eastern stall."

His shoulders sank.

Edward took the basket from his wife. "What did the distribution office say?"

"The cattle require the Governor's signature, or that of an official she authorises. The original breeding stock came through the municipal fund." Juliet brushed snow from her sleeves. "I took the forms. But you should speak to Victoria before we start moving animals anywhere."

Edward nodded. "I was going this afternoon."

"Don't wait. I passed the administrative square on the way home. The Governor's residence is quieter than usual, probably because half the officials are running towards Tangier and Ceuta. Normally you'd wait behind merchants and farm owners for half the day. Today there were only a few carriages outside."

Romeo brushed his hands together at once. "Excellent. We need to report as well."

Marco was already turning towards the horses when Juliet called them back. "Edward goes first. You two promised to assist, so do not celebrate yet."

Both Royal Guards stopped.

Marco glanced at Edward with the unmistakable question of whether rescue was forthcoming.

Edward carried the basket inside. "I hear nothing."

Juliet pointed towards the stable. "Marco, one of the boards in the eastern feeding trough is rotten. Replace it. Romeo, move the fodder sacks from the outer store beneath the inner roof. The snow may be heavier tonight."

Romeo stared at the sky. "I am beginning to understand why the Queen sent us back."
