Juliet showed no remorse. "Finish those two jobs and you may go to the Governor, the battlefield, or the moon for all I care."

Edward had just stepped inside when she called after him. "And you."

He turned.

Juliet looked from his muddy boots to the goatskin coat covered in wood dust. "Do not go to the Governor looking as though you have just crawled out of a cattle stall."

Edward looked at himself. "Victoria has seen me worse."

"I believe you. The gate guards may not have."

Romeo laughed so hard that he had to lean on the fence. Fifteen minutes later Edward emerged again in a clean woollen shirt, his goatskin coat brushed free of sawdust, and his hair forced into rough order with water.

Juliet adjusted his collar before allowing him past. "Acceptable."

Edward bent and kissed her forehead. "I'll be home before dark."

"If you drink with Victoria, remember the way home."

He paused. Juliet had already turned back to the basket and offered no explanation.

Romeo gave a quiet whistle. Marco immediately kicked him in the shin.

Edward decided he had heard nothing. He left alone.

At noon, Marrakesh still carried the strange appearance of a city born beneath sun and now surviving under a white-grey sky. Cart wheels and boots had ground the snow into dirty tracks through the streets. Timber braces supported earthen roofs against the weight of ice.

Edward crossed the market Juliet had just left. Traders now covered vegetables beneath two layers of cloth. Meat hung inside recesses protected from the wind. Merchants whose grandparents might once have used fans against the desert heat burned charcoal beneath their feet.

The war had arrived here long before Isabella.

People spoke of Tunis, the eastern road, rising flour prices, and military convoys passing through Tangier. Yet as Edward walked among them in a plain goatskin coat, none knew that the man beside them carried a decision that might return him to the place he had sworn six years ago never to see again.

At the end of the market street, Edward turned into the administrative square and kept walking.

The Governor's residence stood above the administrative square, a broad stone building altered and expanded by Castilian hands across several generations. Two flags snapped from its low tower, one royal and one belonging to the government of Marrakesh.

Juliet had been right. The courtyard beyond the gate was quieter than usual.

A guard recognised Edward before he could introduce himself. The man checked the visitor ledger, looked once at the goatskin coat, and opened the door.

"Governor Valdes is in her office. You may go straight in, Sir."

Edward grimaced. "I am not a 'Sir' anything yet."

The guard plainly had no idea how to respond and chose the safest option: silence.

Edward followed the familiar stone corridor. Four years in Marrakesh had brought him to this building often enough for distribution papers, breeding stock, land taxes, and a dozen other matters the Admiral he had once been would never have imagined caring about. The first time he entered, however, he had carried no farm ledger.

He had carried Juliet half-dead with exhaustion, Remi barely older than one, and what remained of their life stuffed into two bags soaked through with seawater. Victoria Valdes had stood at the end of this same corridor. She had not asked how many ships Edward lost, how many men were dead, or why England had fallen. She looked at the child in Juliet's arms and ordered a room with a working stove prepared. Edward remembered that more clearly than any words of consolation.

He knocked.

"Come in."

The Governor's office had barely changed since his last visit. A map of Morocco covered one wall. Distribution tables and convoy lists hung beside it. A large fire burned in the corner, and three stacks of files on the desk had been tied with different colours of cord.

Victoria Valdes stood near the window with a report in one hand and the other resting against the stone sill. Her blond hair was tied neatly behind her head. A red pencil remained between her fingers, poised above the page she had been marking.

She looked Edward from head to foot and laughed. "Edward, you still dress exactly like the cadet who used to skip tactics lectures."

"I changed before coming."

"Then send Juliet my thanks. I refuse to believe that was your idea."

Edward closed the door. "You are still as vicious as ever."

"And you still begin by defending yourself from attacks no one has made."

Victoria lowered the report. "Sit."

She did not summon a servant. Instead she opened the cabinet near the hearth, took out two glasses and a bottle of red wine.

Edward raised an eyebrow. "It's not even noon."

Victoria glanced at the ice on the window. "You used to drink rum before breakfast at sea and explain that it was cold. Look outside. I fail to see why the argument should become weaker in Marrakesh."

Edward surrendered.

She poured two glasses and handed one to him.

The heat of the room and the scent of wine drew an old memory out of the Academy common rooms, back when four people not yet twenty had believed the map of the world was a permanent thing.

Victoria sat opposite him. "Four years, and this is the first time you've come here of your own accord without paperwork forcing you. Do not try to count the annual breeding-register closure. That is paperwork."

Edward drank a small mouthful.

Victoria watched the way he set the glass on the table. "You are preparing to say something difficult. I know because you have been sitting there for several minutes and have yet to say what you actually came to say."

She rested one elbow on the arm of her chair. "Fifteen years, Edward, and you still have the same habit. The more you dread the real subject, the more you begin with things that can be counted. Cattle. Powder barrels. Days of provisions." Her mouth curved. "At the Academy, before admitting you'd lost the map-room key, you spoke to me for nearly ten minutes about how badly the lock had been designed."

Edward rubbed two fingers against his forehead. "I did not lose it. Romeo took it. I only held it for him and forgot where I put it."

Victoria raised her glass. "I remember. I remember a great many things about you that you assume everyone else has forgotten."

Edward turned his own glass between his fingers. "Such as?"

"Such as a second-year cadet who stood in the rain for nearly two hours waiting for my training session to end because he wanted to ask whether I would have supper with him."

Edward covered half his face with one hand. "Must you bring that up? It was not raining when I began waiting."

"Correct. The rain started half an hour later. A sensible man would have gone home. You had apparently promised yourself that you would remain there and therefore stood beneath it until you were soaked like an idiot."

Victoria laughed first. Edward resisted for several seconds and then failed. They laughed together until the old memory lost some of its power to embarrass him.

Victoria set her glass down. "Do you remember the street behind the Academy? The bakery that stayed open until midnight. Winter festival."

He did. Victoria had lost one glove down a drain. Her hand became so cold that when she took his, Edward assumed she only wanted warmth. They had walked nearly the length of the street without either one letting go first. "I remember."

"At the time, I thought that if you were slightly less foolish, perhaps we would have become a different story."

Edward did not laugh immediately.

Victoria did not look at him for an answer. She only drank.

"Perhaps." He took another sip. "I am trying not to excavate holes for myself. Juliet is very good at discovering things I believed safely buried."

Victoria laughed louder. "Does she know about me?"

"She knows you were an old Academy friend, Governor of Marrakesh, and the person who helped my family survive our first winter."

"All very safe facts." Victoria propped her chin in one hand. "You neglected the part where you haunted the corridor outside the women's wing just to wait for my evening walk?"

"I was not haunting anything. I stood where I thought we were supposed to meet, though in retrospect I cannot remember anyone formally arranging the meeting."

"Or the graduation ball, when you complained that my dress was absurdly elaborate and ten minutes later asked me to dance?"

Edward drank again. "I was young."

"You were over twenty."

"Still young."

Victoria laughed hard enough to set down the glass. When it passed, she pushed the wine aside and drew the papers on her desk closer. "Very well. You have entertained me sufficiently. Speak."

Edward set down his own glass. "The cattle."

Victoria closed her eyes. "You are incurable."

"I genuinely came about the cattle."

"I know. And something else."

Edward took the form Juliet had given him from inside his coat. "The breeding stock the city assigned us four years ago has grown to more than forty head. According to the register, part remains municipal stock. The rest belongs to the household under the original agreement."

Victoria understood before she looked at the paper. "You are leaving Marrakesh and want the transfer settled before you go."

"Yes. I do not want someone else cleaning up an unfinished matter after I've gone."

She pulled a large ledger from the corner of the desk and opened the section for farms south of the city. "You do not need to return the entire herd to one place. The city only needs the public share counted, marked, and reassigned to households short of breeding animals. Your family's share can be kept, sold, given away, or transferred as you wish."

Edward touched the form. "I don't want to sell ours. Most can go to Omar, the Thompsons, and several English families short of stock. The city portion goes back according to the ledger. I'd prefer not to reach departure day and have an official arrive demanding to know where half the cattle disappeared."

Victoria made several notes. "I'll send someone tomorrow. No need to drive the entire herd to the residence like last time."

"That was the tax officer's idea."

"I know." She grinned. "I still remember more than thirty cattle blocking the gate. And yes, I laughed. Governors must take their pleasures where they find them."

She wrote again. "The inspection happens at the farm. We mark the public animals and move them later. Keep everything in your stable until the family convoy leaves. No one is asking you to march cattle through a blizzard merely to prove that you are honest."

Edward looked at her. "Thank you."

Victoria's pencil stopped. "Do not thank me as though I have granted a favour. You and Juliet honoured every term for four years. The herd has grown better than most around Marrakesh. The city receives more than it issued. This has been a useful transaction for both sides."

Edward smiled. "You still hate being thanked."

"I hate the way you turn everything into a debt."

That removed his smile.

Victoria closed the ledger. "Four years ago I gave your family an empty house, a few cattle, and residence papers. You turned those things into a life. Stop telling the story as though Victoria Valdes saved Edward Spencer."

She leaned back. "I opened a gate. The three of you walked through it."

Edward rested his hands on his knees.

"Then I still owe you a gate."

"You are genuinely beyond repair."

Victoria shook her head and tapped her pencil twice on the ledger. "Now the other matter."

Edward knew he had reached the end of his evasions.

"Isabella visited your house yesterday. A royal carriage and an escort riding through the city are difficult to hide."

Edward leaned back. "Then I can stop pretending you do not know."

"I know only that she wanted to meet you privately and specifically told me I did not need to attend. I asked no further questions." Victoria nodded towards the cattle form. "But you came here this morning to transfer the herd. The rest does not require genius."

Edward put the wine down. "You know I accepted."

"I know you accepted. I do not need every detail. The first thing you did after making your decision was arrange Marrakesh properly. You are not preparing for a journey you expect to end quickly."

She studied him. "You are closing one door before opening another."

Edward did not argue. "I chose England."

Victoria only nodded. "I suspected that as well."

"Because people say it is dead?"

"Not only because of that."

She leaned forward. "You chose it because you cannot tolerate an unanswered question. Most people can live with 'perhaps no one survived'. You cannot. If there is even a chance that someone remains in Scotland, Ireland, or elsewhere on those islands, you will need to see it before accepting that they are gone."

Edward lowered his glass rather than drinking.

Victoria continued. "You will tell Isabella it creates a northern front. You will tell Juliet the war will eventually find Marrakesh, so another road must be opened before the old ones close. Both arguments are true."

She pointed at him. "But I know the other sentence too. The one you hate most is: what if I had tried once more?"

Edward stopped smiling. Footsteps passed in the corridor outside. Neither of them looked towards the door.

"You think you understand me that well?"

Victoria settled back. "I possess one advantage Isabella and Juliet do not."

Edward waited.

"I knew you before anyone called you Admiral."

She set down the glass. "Isabella met again an Edward already old enough for people to lean on. Juliet met you after you had learned that everything could be lost. I remember the idiot standing in the rain because he had made himself a promise no one else had asked him to make."

Edward covered half his face. "Could you stop using that story as evidence?"

"No."

She smiled, then became serious again. "I am not claiming to know everything about you. I am saying that certain habits survived from before all four of us became the people we are now."

Edward was quiet. "Which habit worries you most?"

Victoria answered without hesitation. "You always believe the last person to remain behind should be you."

This time Edward had no ready reply.

"It has saved many people. It has also nearly killed you often enough for me to lose patience."

Edward looked at the hands roughened by four years of farm work. "Juliet said something similar last night."

"Then for once in your life two people have told you the same thing. Consider listening."

He turned the wine glass half a circle on the table. "I thought you would tell me to stay."

"If I wanted you to stay, I would have said so the moment you entered."

Victoria rose and crossed to the map on the wall. "I do not like your choice. I understand it."

Her hand settled over the British Isles. "Strategically, it is not as mad as it sounds. If the Danes retain sufficient strength, if organised communities remain in the north of the islands, France must account for another direction. Castile needs time at the Pyrenees more than almost anything else."

Edward stood beside her. "That is why Isabella offered it."

"Yes. She also knows who is perhaps the only man who could receive that order without laughing in her face."

Victoria glanced at him. "Do not take that as praise too quickly."

She returned to the desk. "What do you need from Marrakesh?"

"For now, the cattle transfer. After that, if your archives contain copies of reports from English refugees who reached North Africa from the islands, I want the newest reliable ones."

"I'll have six years of records filtered, priority to sources that identify their departure point clearly. And your family's route?"

"They travel with the convoy to Gibraltar. From there Juliet and Remi continue under protection to Iberia. I separate from them when the mission requires it."

Victoria looked at the glass in his hand instead of his face. "You say that so calmly someone might assume it costs you nothing."

Edward rotated the wine once more. "Shouting does not make the road shorter."

"True."

Victoria returned to her chair. "You genuinely have not lost the habit of reading people poorly while pretending no one can read you."

"That is why you govern this city."

"And why you should listen when I tell you something."

She drew out a blank sheet. "When you leave, who takes over the civilian work the Spencer household does for the English district?"

Edward stopped moving the glass.

"Juliet manages most of it. Food distribution, sick households, medicine exchanges, records of who lacks fuel. I handle the stable, repairs, and the labour that needs strength."

"Then do not transfer only the cattle."

Victoria began writing. "Give me a list. Not so the government can steal her work. So that if winter arrives and one link disappears, I know what breaks. And when you tell Juliet, make it a discussion, not a military order. I have met your wife often enough to know how that ends."

"I'll speak with her tonight."

Edward smiled. "If the two of you ever spend more than an hour in the same room, I may need to request political asylum."

"You are very confident. We may simply spend the hour discussing how to manage you."

"Exactly what I fear."

A knock sounded before Victoria could answer.

She had not yet said come in when the door opened. Marco entered first. Romeo followed with fresh snow still caught in both men's hair.

Victoria looked at them. "Still entering other people's rooms before being invited, just like the Academy."

Marco stopped. "I knocked."

"After your hand was already on the handle."

Romeo walked directly towards the hearth. "We have just completed three assignments of forced labour under Mrs Spencer. I believe the laws of war permit us to seek warmth without procedural delay."

Edward looked at them. "Juliet released you?"

"After I repaired a feeding trough, moved fodder, carried two buckets of water, and answered seventeen questions from Remi about the Royal Guard." Marco removed his gloves. "I believe my sentence is served."

Romeo saw the wine and brightened. "At last. A government that understands how to treat its Royal Guards."

Victoria moved the bottle beyond his reach. "You serve this government. You do not raid its wine stores."

"I merely wished to inspect the quality."

"No."

Marco laughed. Edward poured a little more into his own glass solely to annoy Romeo. The four of them had not stood together in a room like this for a very long time.

Once, the same arrangement usually included an angry instructor outside the door or an examination none of them had prepared for. Now one was Governor of Marrakesh under the Castilian Crown, two were Royal Guards in Isabella's service, and Edward had just accepted Castilian commission for a mission into the ruins of his own country. Time had changed almost everything. Romeo staring too long at someone else's wine had survived.

Victoria pointed towards the chairs. "Sit. Edward and I are finished with his affairs. Now yours."

Marco pulled his chair towards the map table. "If Ed is going north, we should make the rest clear as well. Once his convoy leaves Marrakesh, I go to Fes and join the forward staff. Her Majesty wants Taza and Fes reviewed before Western Rome applies more pressure."

Victoria moved to the map. "Isabella has already drawn forces back to positions we can feed. We no longer have enough men to defend every piece of earth simply because a paper says it belongs to Castile."

Marco placed a finger on the eastern corridor. "As long as Taza stands, Fes can breathe. If Taza breaks, Fes becomes the last major stop before the pressure comes deeper into Morocco. I have no intention of playing hero. First I want real troop numbers, real provisions, and a real route of retreat."

Edward nodded. "Do not trust reports that look too clean."

"I went to school with you. I know."

Romeo leaned back. "I get to spend my time among Tangier, Ceuta, Casablanca, and Marrakesh. Transport, food, recruitment, and preventing warehouses from burning because some fool decided to warm his hands beside ammunition."

Victoria looked at him. "And while in Marrakesh, you report directly to my office."

Romeo grimaced. "You see? I told you I am being detained."

"You may ask the Queen for a replacement."

"No, thank you."

Edward laughed. "At least you're both serving the same state."

Marco looked at him. "You are about to accept a Castilian commission, even if only for one mission. It counts."

Romeo raised his empty glass in a mock toast. "Then congratulations. The four of us have finally ended up working for one Queen again. Just not the Queen we once imagined."

Victoria did not smile immediately. She returned to the desk, opened a wooden box, and withdrew a letter carrying the royal seal. "Speaking of Queens, Isabella sent this before leaving Marrakesh."

Edward looked at the wax.

Victoria unfolded the paper.

"Marrakesh is not to fall. Legion Eleven and more than ten thousand troops are coming as reinforcement."

Marco gave a low whistle.

Romeo stopped joking. "More than ten thousand while the Pyrenees need men?"

"Not all in one day," Victoria said. "But the message is clear. Marrakesh is no longer merely a production centre and a refuge hub. It is a strategic rear base for Castile in North Africa."

Edward looked at the city on the map. Four years ago, Marrakesh had been only the endpoint of an escape. Now it had become a link in an entire war system. "Can you hold it?" he asked.

Victoria looked directly at him. "I will."

Edward nodded.

Marco folded his arms. "So we scatter again."

War had sent the four graduates in different directions often enough. They had only just gathered long enough to recognise that this reunion, too, was temporary. Even beneath the same Castilian system, each of them was being pulled towards another front.

Romeo rested his elbows on the table. "At least this time Castile has a functioning postal system. No one is permitted to disappear for three years and then send a letter announcing that he is still alive."

Edward looked at him. "I remember you being the worst at answering letters."

"Incorrect. I write many letters. They do not all reach the intended recipient."

Marco laughed. "You sent one to me through three different regiments because you wrote the wrong unit."

"But you received it."

"Seven months later."

"Result achieved."

Victoria leaned against the desk. "You are all exactly the same."

Edward looked at her. "So are you."

"No." Her smile was small. "I have merely become better at pretending."

Edward looked at Victoria and remembered something. "Vic."

She turned.

He did not call her by the shortened name often any longer.

"Four years ago I left something here."

She did not ask what. Her smile disappeared. "You finally remembered."

Romeo and Marco exchanged a glance.

Victoria crossed to the door leading towards the private rooms behind her office. "Wait."

She left them there.

Edward stood beside the fire with both hands in his pockets. Neither man asked what they were waiting for. By the time Victoria returned several minutes later, both had guessed.

She carried a sabre in a black leather scabbard.

Edward did not move.

Four years earlier, that sword had remained at his side through the road from a dying England to North Africa. When he reached Marrakesh, thin enough that his uniform hung loose from his shoulders, he had unbuckled it and placed it on Victoria's desk. A cattle farmer does not need a sword. That had been his reasoning.

Victoria stopped before him and held the sabre in both hands. "Four years ago you gave me this and said that if you ever had to draw it again, you would have failed to build another life."

Edward looked at the familiar scabbard. "Did I really say it quite that dramatically?"

"You had an unfortunate fondness for sentences that sounded like inscriptions on graves."

Romeo laughed under his breath.

Victoria kept the weapon extended. "But you did not fail, Edward. Those four years happened. Juliet. Remi. The house. The cattle. Your neighbours." Her voice softened. "Taking the sword again does not erase any of them."

Edward reached out. The sabre weighed exactly as he remembered. He did not draw it immediately. The leather had been kept clean. The silver fittings showed no rust. Victoria had plainly done more than throw it in a storage chest and forget it.

He pulled the blade a few inches free. Firelight moved along the steel. "You kept it better than I expected."

"I knew you would ask for it one day."

Edward raised his eyes. "You knew?"

"Do not start again."

Marco approached and placed a hand on his shoulder. "Remember the graduation ritual?"

Edward looked at him, then Romeo. Romeo no longer smiled. One hand rested on the hilt of the sabre at his own hip. Victoria crossed to the weapon rack beside the desk and removed hers.

Four sabres, nearly identical in form. They were not ordinary ceremonial swords. Years ago, the Royal Academy had presented only four to the highest-ranked cadets of their class. The smiths had built their cores around fragments identified as remnants of Excalibur. There had never been enough to resurrect the legendary blade, but enough remained for the four weapons to share a common resonance.

Four Miracle-grade Vestigia. Four swords once given to four young people who believed their empire would outlive them all.

Edward drew his sabre completely. Steel sang through the stone room. Marco and Romeo followed. Victoria drew last.

The four formed a loose circle as they had once done in the Academy yard, when their uniforms were new and none yet knew the true smell of a burning city.

Edward raised his blade. The others did the same. Four sabre points met above them. Gold light burst from the contact point and ran through the channels in the steel until it outshone the fire. Marco drew breath. Romeo and Victoria looked at Edward. Together, in the solemn cadence they had once practised until it became instinct, the four spoke.

"The Queen lights our way. Glory to the Empire on Which the Sun Never Sets."

They kept the blades raised. For a second, no one moved. Then Romeo made a small sound.

"Pfft."

Marco looked at him. Romeo bit his lip with violent determination. Victoria's shoulders began to shake. Edward looked around the circle.

"Do not."

Romeo failed first. He burst out laughing. Marco folded nearly in half, still holding his sword. Victoria turned her face away and completely failed to conceal her own laughter. Edward lasted several seconds longer before joining them.

The four blades separated. The gold radiance weakened, though it did not vanish.

Romeo had to brace himself against a chair. "I'm sorry. I genuinely tried."

Marco wiped tears from his eyes. "It sounded more impressive when we were younger."

"The sun was warm enough then for people to believe it," Romeo said.

Victoria laughed again. "And the empire still existed."

Edward looked at his sword. "Even the Queen named in the oath is not the Queen we serve."

Marco raised his sabre. "Three of us now answer directly to Castile. You are accepting a Castilian commission. Shouting glory to a dead empire inside Isabella's Governor's office does sound mildly disrespectful."

Romeo immediately added, "I believe Her Majesty would forgive us as long as no one tells her the part about the sun."

Victoria lowered her blade, careful not to let the steel touch the stone floor. "No. That line belongs to its time."

When the laughter faded, the four looked at one another. None was a cadet any longer. The empire to which they had once sworn themselves was gone.

Edward spoke first. "Then we need another line."

Romeo raised a hand immediately. "Provided it is short."

Marco shook his head. "This is not a drinking call."

"I am offering professional advice."

Victoria turned her sabre in her hand, the last gold light moving down its groove. "Do not swear to a throne again."

Edward looked at her. "Why?"

"Because thrones change occupants. Countries change names. Flags are torn down. The four of us have spent six years learning that."

Marco thought for a moment. "Then swear for those still alive."

Romeo frowned. "That sounds like something engraved on a tomb."

"Do you have something better?"

"Yes. 'Do not die stupidly.' Short, memorable, useful on every battlefield."

Victoria angled the point of her sword towards him, only slightly. Romeo raised his free hand in surrender. "Withdrawn."

Edward looked at the four blades as their light continued to fade. For those still alive. They had lost enough in six years. The work left to do remained. "When the light dies, we open the way."

Silence. Romeo repeated it first, without laughing this time. "When the light dies, we open the way."

Marco nodded. "That works."

Victoria looked at Edward. "Very much like you."

He shook his head. "No. I don't want it to belong to me."

Edward raised the sabre. "If we use it, it belongs to all four."

Victoria smiled. "Then once more."

They stood straight, but none bothered to imitate the rigid Academy posture of their youth. Four blades rose. The points met. Gold light returned, flooding through all four sabres and across uniforms that no longer resembled those they had worn at graduation. This time they named no dead Queen and no vanished empire.

Four voices spoke together. "When the light dies, we open the way."

No one laughed. The light held several seconds before withdrawing into the steel. Edward lowered his arm. The new oath belonged to no army, no country, and no throne. It belonged only to the four people standing in the room.

Marco sheathed first. "I approve."

Romeo followed. "I still prefer 'do not die stupidly', but this will do."

Victoria returned her sword to the rack. "You may use yours privately."

Edward looked once more at his own sabre, then slid it into the scabbard. The silver catch clicked shut. Four years earlier, he had left this room without it. Today the sword remained at his side.

Victoria stepped forward and adjusted the strap as naturally as she once had during Academy uniform inspections. "It's crooked."

Edward looked down. "I can fix it myself."

"I know."

She tightened the buckle another notch anyway and stepped back. "Go home to your wife."

Edward smiled. "Are you throwing me out?"

"You have cattle, paperwork, and an entire house to settle. I do not want Juliet coming here to ask why I kept her husband too long."

Romeo immediately leaned forward. "I would like to see that."

Marco pulled him back. "If you want to survive long enough to reach Fes, you would not."

Edward fastened his coat over the sword belt and looked at the three of them. "Do not disappear before I leave Marrakesh."

Marco nodded. "I am not leaving immediately."

Romeo said, "And I still intend to collect the lunch Juliet promised by never promising it."

Victoria folded her arms. "I still require your cattle-transfer signature tomorrow."

Edward opened the door. Before stepping out, he looked back. "Vic."

She met his eyes.

"Thank you for keeping the sword."

For once, she did not dismiss the thanks. "Thank you for finally coming back to take it."

Edward nodded and went into the corridor.

Outside, the sky over Marrakesh remained grey. Snow covered the square, and wind moved through streets that had once been built for desert heat. The sabre pulled one side of his coat lower with every step. Edward had to adjust the belt again before reaching the bottom stair.

Ahead waited nearly two days in which to pack a house, transfer a herd, say goodbye to the people who had kept his family alive, and explain to a seven-year-old boy that his father was going somewhere very far away.

Edward raised his collar and turned towards home.

Behind him, three old friends remained in the Castilian government's stone office. Their rare reunion ended much as earlier ones had: none knew exactly when all four would stand together again.

For the first time in four years, Edward Spencer carried his sword home.

Forty-eight hours had sounded generous when Isabella first said it. By the following afternoon, after Edward returned from the Governor's residence with his sabre at his hip and Victoria's promise to settle the cattle transfer, he understood that four years of life could not be packed into a few chests merely by working faster.

The Spencer house became a maze of clothes, books, rope, blankets, and half-made decisions. Edward stood in the middle of the room holding a copper pot and looked at the two piles before him. "Taking this or leaving it? I am asking before acting, because I believe my independent authority in this room has been suspended."

Juliet did not look up from the blanket she was inspecting. "Leave it for the Thompsons. Theirs cracked last winter. Right-hand pile, not left."

Edward looked at the piles, then at the pot. "Left was taking things five minutes ago."

"Correct, before you mixed the piles yourself and announced that you were only moving one object." Juliet indicated his woollen shirt lying beside the medicines and two of Remi's books that had somehow migrated into the tool bag. "You've said that four times since you came home. A fifth will not reorganise the room."

Edward obediently moved the pot to the right. "At least I remember what I did. I consider that progress."

Juliet pulled a woollen coat from the chest, checked the stitching at both cuffs, then placed it with the travelling clothes. "This one comes. The grey one goes to Thompson. It is still good, which is exactly why someone else can use it."

Edward picked up the grey coat as though he had just discovered an unfavourable law of nature. "I am beginning to understand the system. The better the condition, the greater the risk that you give it away."

"You're learning faster than I expected."

Juliet moved to his heaviest goatskin coat, brushed dried mud from the hem, and tested every fastening. Into the inner pockets she placed dried garlic, a clean strip of cloth, and a small packet of needles and thread.

Edward watched the garlic disappear into his coat. "Is that mandatory equipment now?"

"You once sailed for three days with a button missing and insisted it wasn't a problem. I am not gambling my husband's life on his ability to look after himself. The garlic, cloth, and sewing kit stay."

"I remember the button differently."

"Naturally. I was the one who sewed it back on when your ship reached port."

Remi laughed.

Edward turned. The boy immediately lowered his face towards the toys around him and became suspiciously industrious.

Juliet drew Remi's bag closer. Pairs of goatskin socks were rolled together. Beneath them went cough medicine, a spare scarf, and the woollen cap patched beside the left ear. She checked everything twice before placing it inside the small chest.

When Edward saw her reach for the old leather map, he stopped her hand. "That comes."

"I know."

She wrapped the map in oiled cloth with several of Remi's schoolbooks. Six years ago it had belonged on an officer's desk. In Marrakesh, Edward used it to teach his son where the Atlantic lay and what shape England had.

He set the pot down. "I'll split more wood."

"No." Juliet pointed at the chest of books beside the bed. "Sit down and choose. We cannot take all of them."

Edward lifted an old naval gunnery manual. "What if we leave clothing instead?"

"We can buy books in Iberia. You cannot wear a book when it snows."

Remi looked up from his own stack. "Does Aunt Isabella have a library, Father? If she already has lots of books, could we send yours there?"

Edward was still considering how to explain that the Royal Library was not a storage warehouse when Juliet laughed.

"I know you're trying to help," he told his son. "The problem is that every time you help enthusiastically, Father's chest somehow remains exactly as heavy."

Remi hugged one book to his chest. "Then I'll think of something else."

"That is what worries me."

The boy was also meant to choose three toys. Half an hour later, all six remained around his feet.

Edward rested an elbow on his knee. "Have you chosen?"

"Yes."

Remi gathered all six into his arms. "Three things."

"I chose three times two."

Juliet turned towards the clothing chest to hide her laughter.

Edward pointed in order. "The ship. The cloth ball. The wooden horse with one leg. Three."

Remi pulled the ship closer. "What about these two people?"

Two little wooden figures lay beside his foot. One wore a sailor's cap. The other had something resembling the cloak of an explorer, though Juliet had always insisted it looked like a sack.

"That makes four."

"But two people are smaller than one normal thing."

Edward looked at Juliet. She continued folding clothes and offered no rescue.

Remi set the figures shoulder to shoulder. "They travel together, so they're one team."

"You are inventing the rules."

"You said I had to choose three things. You didn't say how big a thing had to be."

Edward studied him and surrendered. "Fine. Two people count as one. You tie your own bag."

Remi nodded immediately.

"What about the drum?" Juliet asked.

"I'll give it to Hassan. He likes making noise."

"I'll make certain Hassan's mother knows that was entirely your decision."

Remi appeared to regret the generosity but placed the drum in the leaving pile anyway. The broken wooden horse took longer. He turned it in both hands. "Tom Thompson likes this one. Can I give it to him myself?"

Edward nodded. "Write Tom's name on the tag. Give it to him tomorrow. Then he'll know you chose the gift instead of thinking your parents forced you to abandon it."

Remi set the horse aside, then hugged the cloth ball.

"This one stays. No negotiation."

Edward left it with the travelling things. The discussion was clearly over.

Remi began sorting the remaining toys by recipient while Edward returned to his books. In the end he kept the old sea chart, a copy of Shakespeare missing its cover, the notebook he used for Remi's lessons, and two histories. The rest were marked for the little refugee school and for families whose children could read.

Juliet looked at the gunnery manual in the leaving pile. "I thought you'd cling to that one."

Edward opened it, turned several pages, then closed it again. "I remember most of it. And if I ever need to open a textbook in the middle of a battle to remember how to fire a gun, I have a much larger problem than a missing book."

Juliet studied him. "I cannot decide whether that should reassure me."

"Keep both feelings. That seems fair."

By mid-afternoon, two of the three chests were closed.

Remi had been given responsibility for tying labels to each bag. He wrote slowly, misspelled Hassan once and corrected it himself. Edward occasionally had to remove a tag because his son had knotted it with the enthusiasm of a naval rigger securing a storm line.

Juliet put a medicine bag in front of Edward. "This comes. Enough for several emergency days. The escort has military surgeons."

Edward opened it and checked every packet. "I haven't seen their medical stores. Remi will be travelling in winter. I don't like leaving this much behind."

"I know. But the Thompsons have a child with a fever, and Hassan has two little ones. We have more medicine than most households. We keep enough for the road. The rest stays."

Edward disliked the arithmetic. He also could not justify locking medicine in a chest while children a few streets away needed it now. He wrote the quantities on both sides of the ledger and closed the bag.

Juliet watched him finish without argument and raised an eyebrow. "Very obedient today."

"I am maturing."

"No. You are calculating how much you can secretly put back tonight."

Edward set down the pen and turned towards her. "You live with your husband under an alarming degree of suspicion."

"I've lived with you long enough to know that when you go quiet, you are planning something."

Remi looked up from the labels. "Mama, is Father going to sneak things back tonight?"

Edward pointed at the name in front of him. "Continue writing. Certain domestic matters do not require expanded investigation."

By the time the light outside had darkened from pale grey to something heavier, the room looked noticeably emptier. Bare shelves and unused wall hooks made the house feel altered though no one had yet left.

Juliet shut one chest and dusted her hands. "While you were with Victoria, Remi and I made the rounds. Omar, the Thompsons, Hassan, and the families closest to us all know. I asked them to pass word further. By tonight most of the quarter will have heard."

Edward looked up from the tool box. "You visited everyone this afternoon? I thought you only went to the market."

"The market was last."

Juliet pulled a chair towards the table. "If we're leaving Marrakesh, I want to tell the people who lived beside us for four years myself. Anyone who can come tomorrow is welcome. I counted more than thirty already."

Edward looked at the small house and then at the snowy yard. "Where are we putting more than thirty people?"

"We aren't. Open the yard. Stretch canvas beside the stable and light both outdoor stoves. If the snow becomes heavy, the children and older people come inside. I've worked out the seating."

She pointed at him. "All you need to do is not invite half of Marrakesh on your own."

"I haven't invited anyone and my diplomatic authority is already restricted?"

"Correct. Now the cattle."

Remi abandoned his labels and crawled closer the moment he heard the word.

Edward sat opposite Juliet. "Victoria's sending someone tomorrow to inspect them here. The municipal breeding share must be marked before any transfer. Our share is ours to decide."

"I remember."

Juliet opened the ledger to the last page and turned it towards him. "Forty-three total. Thirty-one still belong to the municipal breeding fund. Twelve are our household share after four seasons. I want those twelve settled tonight so tomorrow no one is counting and arguing at the same time."

Edward looked at the number. "Four for the feast."

Juliet raised her eyes. "You were going to say three."

"I had not finished the sentence and the household treasury has already lost another cow."

"Three is enough only if you plan to issue ration tokens at the gate. One for stew, two roasted, and the fourth for bones and soup. Anything left becomes salted meat for people to carry home. Hides get divided afterwards."

She was already writing. "A meal warms them for a day. Food to take home lasts longer. If we're saying goodbye, we do it properly."

Edward leaned back and bowed his head in mock surrender.

"Yes, Mrs Spencer. I withdraw all efforts to defend the treasury."

Remi followed the figures. "What happens to the other eight?"

Edward pulled the ledger nearer to him. "Four go to Uncle Omar and the Thompsons. The other four transfer to households short of breeding stock, using the Governor's list. We take none."

Remi thought, then asked the question both parents had expected. "What about Number Seventeen?"

Juliet knew immediately which animal he meant: the bull with the white patch on its forehead, the one Remi secretly fed turnip peelings.

"He's one of our twelve."

The boy's face brightened.

Edward continued before hope could grow too large. "I want him to go to Uncle Omar. Omar needs a healthy bull, and Seventeen already knows him."

Remi looked disappointed but did not argue.

"Can I tell Uncle Omar that he likes turnip peel more than dry hay?" "Of course. That is the most important transfer information, and I would never take the honour from you."

Juliet underlined the final line. "Thirty-one municipal. Twelve ours. Four for the feast, eight transferred. Forty-three. This time none vanish between one calculation and the next."

Edward placed a hand over his chest. "I am insulted that you think a former Admiral incapable of counting cattle."

Juliet looked at the copper pot still sitting in the wrong place. "Earlier you could not remember which side of the room meant taking things. Forgive me if I do not rank naval honour above arithmetic."

"That was civilian logistics."

"So are cattle, Admiral."

Remi rested his chin on the table. "Will Aunt Isabella come to the feast?"

Edward and Juliet looked at one another.

"I don't know," Edward said. "She has a court to run and is probably already far beyond Marrakesh."

"Can I ask Uncle Marco to carry an invitation? He knows her."

Juliet raised an eyebrow. "You met a Royal Guard yesterday and already understand how to use him as a courier?"

Edward drew Remi's chair nearer. "You can ask. But invite her because you want her to eat with our family, not because she is a Queen."

Remi considered this carefully. "If she comes, do we have to give her the best chair?"

"No," Juliet answered first. "The best chair in this house is the only one that doesn't wobble, and Uncle Omar is older. If Isabella comes, she follows Spencer-house law."

Edward laughed.

Remi accepted this distribution of authority and requested only that Isabella be seated near the fire.

Juliet agreed and closed the ledger. "One more thing. Who is bringing the wine?"

Edward already knew he was about to be blamed for something. "Romeo said he would."

Juliet looked at the numbers on the page and drew another line. "Then prepare twice the food tomorrow. I do not trust two jars of wine travelling with Romeo not to create additional consequences."

Edward decided the battle was not worth fighting.

Romeo arrived after dark carrying two large wine jars behind his back as though Juliet might fail to see them if he approached at the right angle. Marco followed with a bag of dried bread and announced before crossing the threshold, "For the record, I told him one jar was enough."

Romeo placed both jars on the table with the solemnity of a man completing an important mission. "Tomorrow is the real feast. Tonight is only quality inspection. It would be irresponsible to discover a defect in front of guests."

Juliet looked at the jars, then at him. "Does quality inspection require reaching the bottom of both?"

"If duty demands it."

"Duty does not."

Romeo looked towards Edward.

Edward was tying the last cord around the book chest and did not bother raising his head. "I learned this morning that arguing with my wife about logistics only increases the time spent losing. Fight your own battle."

Marco placed the bread beside the wine. "At last you have matured. Very late, but worth acknowledging."

Remi ran from the back room when he heard Marco's voice. He approached with obvious purpose, then slowed in front of him. Both hands caught the hem of his own shirt.

"Uncle Marco."

Marco brushed snow from his shoulder and waited.

"Could you give Aunt Isabella an invitation for me?"

Marco stopped. He crouched until they were level, though he had to press his lips together once before answering. "Of course. I'll send someone after the Queen's party tonight. I cannot promise she'll be able to return in time, but she will receive your invitation."

Remi straightened at once.

"Really? Then tell her the place near the stove is still free."

Marco studied him with grave consideration. "Ah. I see. You have fallen for Isabella, haven't you?"

"I have not!"

Remi's face went scarlet to the tips of his ears.

"I just want her to come eat. And she was kind to me. That's completely different."

"Entirely different," Marco agreed with exquisite seriousness. "I said nothing. You explained everything yourself." Remi opened his mouth, realised every additional word would worsen his position, and turned sharply towards his father for rescue. Edward immediately bent over the chest cord as though the survival of Europe depended on the knot. Juliet turned away because she was trying not to laugh.

"What about me?" Romeo demanded. "I brought wine and receive no gratitude?"

Remi looked at the two jars. "Mama says because of you we need twice the food tomorrow." Marco turned away. Edward bit his lip. Juliet did not rescue Romeo either.

Supper should have been soup, bread, and what meat remained from the day before. Instead four old friends sat at one table after too many years apart, Remi asked endless questions about the Academy, and Romeo insisted on demonstrating that the second jar of wine "possessed a clearly different character" from the first.

By the time Juliet put Remi to bed, the conversation in the front room had moved from skipped lessons to the occasion Marco had set his sleeve on fire during practical Vestigium training. Juliet returned once to tell them to lower their voices. A second time to remove the wine jar from Romeo's hands. The third time, she did not return.

Near midnight, conversation faded into broken sentences. Then only the fire remained, along with a long snore Juliet did not need to see the room to identify as Romeo's.

She slept for some time, then woke cold. The place beside her was empty.

Juliet put on her fur-lined robe, tied the collar, and opened the bedroom door. The front room looked as though it had survived a very small and profoundly pointless battle. Marco was curled so close to the hearth that one turn could have taken him into the guard rail. Romeo lay face-down across the table with one hand still wrapped around an empty clay cup beside a plate of beef bones.

Juliet dragged Marco further from the fire, covered him, cleared the crockery around Romeo, and added a second blanket. By daylight both men were Royal Guards who could make sentries stand straighter simply by approaching. After midnight, one had nearly gone to sleep inside a fireplace and the other was embracing an empty cup as though guarding it from thieves.

She adjusted Marco's blanket and looked for her husband. Edward lay beneath the table on an old fur rug.

Juliet bent to cover him. The hand resting near his chest caught her wrist. "I thought you'd leave all three of us to freeze out here." His voice was rough with wine but clearer than she expected. He pulled her carefully beneath the table, making sure her head did not strike the boards above. "Or did you come because you missed your husband?"

Juliet put one hand against his chest and smelled the wine on his breath. "I came to stop those two from killing themselves in their sleep. You remain under consideration. How much did you drink?"

"Less than Romeo."

"That is not a unit of measurement."

Edward laughed and wrapped an arm around her waist. Juliet allowed him to kiss her temple, but when he tried to draw her closer she held his shoulder. "Marco is a few steps away. Romeo is directly above us. Remi is asleep in the next room. Do you truly want the household to wake tomorrow knowing what their parents were doing under the table?"

Edward looked up at the tabletop as though only now remembering its existence and released her. "When you phrase it that way, the plan becomes difficult to defend."

Juliet turned aside for a moment to keep from laughing.

"Good. Then lie still while I find a blanket."

She had barely started to crawl out when Edward caught her hand again. This time he held only enough to make her look back. He waited until Juliet leaned towards him of her own accord before kissing her. The kiss had lasted scarcely any time when the table shuddered above them as Romeo rolled in his sleep. They separated instantly. A thunderous snore descended through the boards, followed by several words no one could understand. Edward covered his mouth to stop himself laughing aloud.

Juliet pushed his shoulder. "Out. Before he rolls off the table."

Edward crawled free first and helped her up. Then he bent and lifted her.

Juliet put both arms around his neck for balance and spoke beside his ear.

"If you drop me in front of those two, I will tell Remi about it until he is grown."

"I am completely sober now."

"That makes me trust you less."

Edward stepped around Marco and Romeo, carried her back to the bedroom, and shut the door. When he placed Juliet on the bed and leaned closer, she set both hands against his chest.

"Wait. Those two are still outside. Remi is through the wall."

Edward stopped immediately. The wine remained on his breath, but his voice was sober.

"You're right. I'm sorry. I wasn't thinking."

Juliet watched him long enough to be certain that he truly meant to stop.

He began to step back.

She caught his collar.

"Lock the door."

Edward looked at her.

"Are you sure?"

"Lock it, Edward. Do not make me say it a third time."

He asked nothing more.

The latch clicked. His footsteps returned, then disappeared into the darkness beside the bed.

Outside the little house, snow hammered against stone and roof. In the front room, Marco and Romeo continued sleeping through everything.

What remained of the Spencer night needed no further words.

* * *

Much later, the room was quiet again. Their breathing had steadied with the wind beyond the walls.

Juliet lay on her side with the blanket drawn over one shoulder. Edward was close behind her, one arm resting across her waist. Firelight from the other room entered through a narrow gap beside the door and reached the sabre leaning near the foot of the bed.

Juliet watched it longer than anything else. For four years, that place usually held mud-stained boots, a splitting axe, or the knife used for slaughtering livestock. The black leather scabbard looked like an object from another house accidentally set down in this one. "Victoria gave it back this afternoon?"

Edward was awake. "Yes. I left it with her when we first reached Marrakesh. At the time I thought I would never need a reason to take it again."

Juliet turned to face him. Edward's hand lay between them. Four years of farm work had laid new calluses over some of the old scars. "I'm not asking whether you should have taken it. I want to know what you felt when you held it again."

Edward looked towards the sword and flexed his right hand. "Familiar. Uncomfortably familiar. Vic put it in my hand and my fingers already knew where to settle, where the thumb rested, what angle the wrist wanted when I drew." He lowered his head to the pillow. "I remembered nothing first. My body remembered before I did."

Juliet listened.

"Then Marco and Romeo stood beside me, and all four of us raised our swords like the Academy. It lasted only minutes, but I remembered the command room too. Looking down at a map and knowing thousands of people were waiting for a sentence from me."

His hand closed and opened. "In the middle of gunfire, my mind used to become frighteningly clear."

Juliet did not interrupt.

Edward stared at his palm. "What frightens me is not that I remember. It is that some part of me still likes the feeling of being good at it."

Juliet rested her hand on his chest. "I'm not asking you to choose again. We talked about England last night. I know why you're going. I'm beginning to worry about Remi."

Edward looked immediately towards the adjoining room.

"Tomorrow he'll sit among people who knew you before Marrakesh. Marco and Romeo will tell Academy stories. If Victoria comes, all it takes is one of them mentioning some old victory or using your old rank, and Remi will discover they are describing an Edward he has never known."

Edward propped himself on one elbow. "I hadn't thought of that. He knows I served in the Navy. I've never told him much beyond that."

"I know. There was never a reason to hurry." Juliet took his hand. "I'm not afraid of Remi learning that his father was a soldier. I'm afraid he will hear only the part that makes a child want to become one."

She glanced towards the sabre. "They'll tell him about warships, victories, the times people called you a hero. Very few people tell children about the nights you woke because you could hear guns that weren't there, or the men who never returned from orders you gave."

Edward looked down at his hands. "At the Academy we only saw the beautiful part too. Uniforms, medals, victory. By the time we understood the rest, every one of us was already carrying too much." He looked towards Remi's room. "If he wants to be a carpenter, a farmer, a teacher, or spend his life selling vegetables in a market, good. In this age he'll still need to know how to use a gun and a blade. But I do not want him growing up believing the only way to matter is to wear a uniform."

Juliet drew his hand closer. "Then tell him both sides. The victories are real. So is the price. Do not leave the second half for other people to tell."

Edward pulled the blanket over half his face. "The way you describe me, I sound both impressive and rather pathetic."

"You have always contained both."

Edward pinched her side.

Juliet swatted his hand away and retaliated by stealing most of the blanket.

After a while she looked again at the sabre. "I don't think the worst thing is that you took it back. I am afraid that one day Remi will ask what kind of man his father was, and the first things you remember to tell him will all be battles."

Remi turned in the next room and settled again.

Edward waited until the sound disappeared.

Juliet spoke before he could turn the thought into a promise too large to keep. "You are good at war, Edward. Perhaps some part of you even likes the feeling of being good at it. I do not need you to pretend that part never existed."

Her hand tightened around his. "Just do not let our son believe it is the most valuable thing about you."

Edward looked at her, then at the sword. "I understand."

"That is enough for tonight."

He left the bed and picked up the sabre. The simple movement straightened his back before he noticed it. His hand settled on the hilt automatically. Edward looked at his own fingers. Then he took an old piece of wool and wrapped it around the scabbard. He laid the sabre horizontally on the low chair against the wall, beneath the same goatskin coat he wore to the cattle shed. "When I leave, I'll carry it."

Edward returned to bed and drew the blanket over Juliet's shoulder. "But tonight it can stay there. I do not need to turn our bedroom into a watch station."

Juliet wrapped an arm around his waist.

In the front room, Romeo suddenly snored with the violence of a wood saw. Marco rolled over and muttered something no one understood.

Edward closed his eyes.

The last thing he saw was the edge of the black scabbard beneath his old goatskin coat. Tomorrow Victoria's inspectors would come for the cattle. Canvas had to be raised in the yard, more fires lit, and food prepared before the guests arrived. The Spencer house would be full from the moment they woke. Tonight, at least, everything was still where it belonged.

Later that same day, while Edward was at the Governor's residence, Juliet left the house with Remi shortly before noon. Wind came down from the Atlas in short bursts, driving powdery snow against earthen walls whose red had faded beneath the winter. The sun hung low behind a thin veil of cloud, bright enough to turn the ice channels white but too weak to offer much warmth.

Four years ago Juliet would have walked too quickly in weather like this, breathing hard and exhausting herself before she had gone far. Now she leaned into the wind without thinking, kept an even pace, and chose the taller walls so Remi could walk in their shelter.

The boy had been wrapped until only his eyes remained visible. Every few minutes Juliet squeezed his fingertips through the gloves to make sure they were still warm, then checked the tops of his boots for snow. Remi endured the inspections without complaint. He had known the procedure almost as long as he had been old enough to walk through winter on his own.

Beyond them, Marrakesh emerged through the haze. Moorish domes seemed to float like dark stone across a white sea. Chimney smoke lay flat beneath the wind. Road crews still cleared the fresh snow that had spilled into yesterday's channels, while the central market was already thickening with people.

Juliet looked at the city longer than usual. Roofs, stoves, and roads she crossed every week had suddenly become things to remember before leaving. Edward had wanted to come when she told him she intended to visit each household, but Juliet had pushed the transfer papers back into his hands and told him to deal with his side first. In the end he went to see Victoria while Juliet led Remi along the route she had planned.

The boy walked beside her with a scarf covering his nose and a stack of invitations safely tucked into his coat.

"Do you remember the first house?" Juliet asked.

Remi nodded and recited the route like a lesson. "Uncle Omar. Then the Thompsons. Aunt Hassan. Then the Mariabells."

He repeated the names to be certain. Juliet listened and realised that Remi knew the people of Marrakesh more clearly than any relatives they might still have had in England. These were the people who had actually existed inside his life.

They followed the trench in the snow opened by the road crews and continued towards Omar's home.

Remi tightened his hand around hers. "Mama, will we come back?"

Juliet remembered other promises. They would return to London when the fighting eased. They would return to England when the sea became safe again. Neither promise had survived reality. This time she would not give her son certainty merely because certainty made the road less painful.

"I don't know. Your father doesn't know either." She squeezed his hand. "That is why we say goodbye properly today. Do not leave things unsaid because you assume tomorrow will keep them for you."

Remi considered that and nodded.

Omar opened the door after the second knock. Steam still clung to his heavy beard, and he had thrown on his djellaba so quickly that one side sat higher than the other. "Juliet? Remi? Where are you two going in this cold?"

Juliet lowered her scarf. "We're having a farewell meal tomorrow. We wanted to invite you and your family."

Omar went still. A younger child peered from behind him and was immediately pulled back by his mother when cold wind entered through the doorway.

"Farewell?"

Omar looked at the papers in Juliet's hand, then at Remi. "Where are you going?"

"Iberia first. Edward accepted a mission from the Queen."

Omar stopped leaning against the frame. In an age like this, rulers rarely summoned men to send them somewhere safer. "He's becoming a soldier again?"

He looked at Juliet. "And you and the boy? North in the middle of winter?"

"Edward did leave the military," Juliet said. "But the Queen needs what he used to know how to do, and this time he agreed. Remi and I are travelling with an escort."

She did not romanticise the road. She did not ask Omar to approve it.

He rested one hand against the doorway. "Four years ago you couldn't even tie a scarf properly. One Sahara wind and your face cracked for a week."

"You charged me twice the market price for a new one."

"Life-saving price."

"You called it a friendship price."

Omar laughed, ruffled Remi's hair, then asked the departure date again to make sure he had heard correctly. "We'll come tomorrow. And if Edward plans to slaughter cattle for the feast, tell him to save the hides for me. I won't take them free. I'll trade firewood." "Bring your family. We can argue about hides afterwards."

Omar stepped fully outside and embraced Juliet in the Moorish manner reserved for kin. She needed half a step to keep her balance, then hugged him back. "Go safely, English girl."

The old name made Juliet blink before she could answer. "I'll try."

They left Omar's house with more of noon already gone.

On the way towards the English quarter, Remi asked, "Mama, Uncle Omar isn't English. Is he still family?" Juliet asked what he thought family meant.

"People from the same country."

"Marco comes from the same country as your father. Uncle Omar helped watch you when you had a fever. Aunt Hassan split her flour with us when ours ran out. The Thompsons crossed from Gibraltar with us." Juliet looked down at him. "Some people are born in the same place and never meet. Some are born a thousand miles apart and stand beside each other when everything becomes difficult."

Remi looked at their footprints. "So is a homeland people?"

Juliet thought about it. "I don't know." She would not give him a beautiful answer merely because she did not yet possess an honest one. The English quarter lay in western Marrakesh, where later waves of refugees had built homes from whatever the city could spare. Some structures had already become proper brick houses with tiled roofs. Others remained patchworks of ship timber, canvas, old sheet metal, and doors salvaged from buildings that no longer existed.

A Tudor rose had been carved into one door. On another house hung a London street sign someone had carried across the sea. Here, people tried to preserve England with things small enough to survive luggage.

Juliet stopped outside the Thompson house.

Martha opened the door with a scarf wrapped over hair gone prematurely grey. She was thinner than in autumn, but widened the door at once when she saw them. "Inside. Quickly. Don't let the wind in."

The room held only a small stove and three children pressed together beneath one blanket. The youngest coughed in dry spasms, folding inward with every breath.

Juliet did not offer the invitation immediately. She knelt, touched the back of her hand to the child's forehead, and frowned. "Still feverish?"

Martha nodded.

"Better than yesterday. I'm saving the medicine for tonight."

Juliet opened her bag and removed a packet of herbs. "Brew this in hot water. It won't replace the medicine, but it'll ease the breathing."

"You're giving us things again." Martha held the packet without putting it away, as though already calculating what she could offer in return.

"Tomorrow you repay me by coming over and eating all the soup I make."

Martha laughed once, then turned to adjust the child's blanket.

Only then did Juliet sit beside her. "We leave Marrakesh the day after tomorrow."

The smile vanished.

"Because of Edward?" "He accepted a mission from the Queen."

Martha did not need more explanation. In the English quarter, people remembered who Edward had been even though he never introduced himself by his old rank.

"So they finally found him."

Martha folded both hands. "Do you want to go?"

"I want Remi to attend school. I want him to sleep in a room where the water doesn't freeze every morning."

"That's what you want for the boy." Martha did not let Juliet hide inside the easier answer. "What do you want?"

Juliet looked around the small room where another family fought the same winter. "I don't know yet."

Martha took her hand. "Then remember to find out."

Juliet looked at their two rough hands, weathered by the same kind of cold, then changed the subject before the room became too heavy. "Come tomorrow. We're slaughtering four cattle."

"Four?"

Martha stared at her. Juliet admitted that this was currently the number in her own calculations and Edward had not yet necessarily agreed.

Martha shook her head.

"God above. You haven't left Marrakesh and you've already spent the man's cattle for him."

"Maybe. But at least the children will eat hot food tomorrow."

Juliet retucked the blanket around the little one.

Martha laughed and promised to bring barley bread if the children were well enough to walk. Remi had sat with them without Juliet noticing. He was showing the other children his wooden ship. He described schools in Iberia as though he had already seen them, including a map so large that it required two people to hang. Juliet had no idea where that particular detail came from. She did not correct him. At least one child in that room was talking about the future.

title_vi: Chapter 11 - The Names We Leave Behind
title_en: Chapter 11 - The Names We Leave Behind
text_en:
From the Thompsons, they crossed south to Hassan's row. The house was lower than the Spencer home. Its windows had been sealed beneath an extra layer of oiled cloth, and an old carpet hung inside the doorway to block the wind.

Hassan opened it with both arms dusted in flour to the elbows. One look at Juliet and Remi was enough for her to understand why they had come. "Don't tell me you're paying back the flour. I told you we'd settle that in spring."

"We're not." Juliet lowered her scarf. "We leave Marrakesh the day after tomorrow."

Hassan stopped. Her flour-covered hands fell to her sides. In the kitchen behind her, her mother, an old woman who could barely hear, continued rolling dough and did not notice the room had gone silent.

"Where?"

"Iberia first. Edward accepted a mission."

Hassan asked nothing about the mission itself. Four years among refugees had taught all of them that some questions did nothing except make answers harder to speak.

She wiped her hands on her apron and pulled Juliet into a quick, hard, awkward embrace. "Then tomorrow I bring couscous."

Juliet held up the invitation papers. "I haven't even invited you."

"You've been walking house to house with the boy and a stack of papers in your pocket. Half the quarter knows before you arrive."

Remi looked at his mother as though this represented an embarrassing failure of operational secrecy. Hassan crouched and asked whether he was truly going to school. When Remi nodded, the old woman at the kitchen table finally caught the word school. She turned and beckoned him closer. She placed a piece of still-warm bread into his hand and spoke in Castilian threaded with Arabic, enough that Remi understood only half.

Juliet translated the rest. Study your letters well. Do not forget how to light a fire. And wherever someone gives you warm bread when the weather is cold, remember to say thank you. Remi nodded and repeated all three instructions to make certain he had them.

The old woman smiled and pushed the bread towards him.

Before Juliet left, Hassan drew her aside. "I heard you're giving Martha the ledger."

Juliet checked the invitations, now almost gone. "News travels quickly."

"Useful news travels faster than bad news."

Hassan promised to watch the southern row and visit homes with older residents after every heavy storm.

"Go. Do not climb into the carriage and immediately imagine the entire quarter will die because you're missing."

Juliet opened her mouth to protest, then stopped. "I'll try."

"No. You'll do it."

Juliet laughed. They clasped hands and separated.

The houses after that went faster, though none felt lighter. A Castilian family of tanners gave Juliet two new lengths of strap for the luggage. An old man who had once helped Edward save a sick cow refused the last money owed to him and called it travel provision. An English widow pressed two hard sweets saved from the previous festival into Remi's palm and made him eat one immediately to prove they had not turned to stone. No one remained empty-handed after learning the Spencers were leaving Marrakesh. Juliet had begun with invitation cards in her coat. By the sixth house, they were nearly pointless. News of the departure, Edward's return to service, Remi's school, and tomorrow's feast had already travelled faster than mother and son. Worst of all, the number four cattle, spoken only once inside the Thompson house, seemed to have crossed half the quarter before Juliet.

She knocked again.

"Anne? It's Juliet."

Wind moved through the lane, pushing loose snow against the threshold. A man from the neighbouring house stepped outside. He removed his cap before speaking.

"Don't knock again, Mrs Spencer."

Juliet turned. The man lowered his eyes and told her the stove had gone out two nights before. By morning, when neighbours finally broke open the door, it was too late. Juliet did not ask whom the Mariabells had lost. There were five people in that family, and the way the man removed his cap had already answered. Remi looked at his mother. His hand tightened around hers. Juliet remained before the door for several seconds. The final invitation was still untouched in her pocket. She took it out. Having no idea what else to do, she folded it once and put it back.

"Come on." They walked to the end of the lane without speaking. Juliet did not continue towards the market as planned. At the junction, she stopped and pulled out the small ledger she used to track flour, firewood, and medicine exchanged between households.

"Do you remember the way back to Martha's?" Remi nodded. They turned around.

Martha was surprised to see them again. Juliet did not step far into the room where the child was still ill. She remained near the doorway and opened the ledger in her palm. "I need you to do something after we leave. During cold spells, don't let any house go more than two days without someone knocking, especially homes with children or older people."

Martha looked at her face.

"Mariabell?"

Juliet nodded.

She pointed to names already written in the book. Thompson. Hassan. An English widow near the tannery. Two newly arrived families who had not yet learned how to maintain a stove through the night. "I check these households when I go to market or distribute food. When I'm gone, someone else needs to keep watching." Martha took the ledger and frowned at the small marks beside each name. Juliet explained which symbol meant firewood, which meant illness, and which indicated food still owed but better left uncollected until winter passed. By the third page, Martha could read the rest without help.

"You can't visit all of them alone," Juliet said. "Hassan will take the southern row. Omar knows people in the Moorish quarter and has a cart. He'll know who can move firewood when needed. If medicine runs short, ask my house before the day after tomorrow. After that, use my name with the herbalist near Bab Doukkala. He knows what I usually take."

Martha closed the ledger.

"How long have you been preparing this?"

"I haven't."

Juliet looked back towards the lane they had just left.

"I simply don't want today to be the last time someone discovers a cold house after it is already too late."

Remi stood beside her and listened in silence. When they left the Thompson house for the second time, he asked whether she had just handed over her work.

Juliet adjusted his scarf. "Yes. The ledger is useless if the day after tomorrow it's locked inside a chest halfway to Iberia."

"Will you do the same thing wherever we go?"

Juliet watched the road before answering. "I don't know what people there need. I'll look first. Then I'll decide where I can help."

Remi accepted that and took her hand again. This time they did not leave the English quarter in complete silence. Remi asked about several names in the ledger, and Juliet answered until the noise of the market ahead began to overtake their footsteps.

* * *

By early afternoon, Marrakesh was much busier. Every market lane was open. Amber Vestigium lamps beneath the timber beams gave off enough heat that snow along the roofline dripped steadily. Moorish traders, Castilians, and English refugees moved through one another buying turnips, salted meat, lamp oil, and fuel. Juliet had once thought the scene impossibly strange. Now she was so accustomed to it that only the certainty of leaving allowed her to see it as an outsider might. Low-grade Vestigium lamps gave steadier heat than coal and cost far more than most households could afford. Even during shortages, the city still spent part of its treasury maintaining the whole market line. One official had once explained to Juliet that food, employment, and news all passed through this roof. If the market went dark, the city would lose its heartbeat before its walls lost soldiers.

The merchants had a simpler version. Keep customers from freezing before they pay.

A spice seller called Juliet by name.

A Moorish woman waved to Remi and asked when he was coming back for bread. A Castilian patrol crossed the lane with boots striking the snow in disciplined rhythm. Behind them, two English refugees carried bundled timber while speaking in a Yorkshire accent so heavy Juliet had once needed every sentence repeated three times. This city was not England. For four years, it had also never required her family to pretend they were still in England.

They stopped to buy pepper and cinnamon for the feast. Juliet inspected every cinnamon stick and bargained exactly as she always did.

Remi grew impatient beside her. "Mama, we're leaving. Do you still have to bargain?"

"Leaving Marrakesh does not mean I have to throw money away." She pushed the lower sum towards the merchant and waited until he complained, sighed, and accepted. "What's left can buy medicine or firewood. Those are the things worth carrying into tomorrow."

Remi nodded as though receiving a principle of civilisation.

Clouds opened slightly overhead. Weak sunlight reached the red domes and turned the snow almost silver. Juliet stopped in the market lane.

London had once had days like this, before fire and Portuguese guns covered most of her memory of the city. Westminster under snow, windows still lit. Flower sellers wrapped in scarves at street corners. Carriages crossing the bridge and spraying mud over pedestrians. Edward returning late with salt in his hair and powder smoke in his coat, still somehow finding time to buy something for her even though most of the things he chose were useless.

Once he had brought home a silver comb far too expensive for their means. Juliet had scolded him for half an hour. She kept it until London fell. When she fled the house, the comb remained on the table. The memory was absurdly small beside tens of thousands of dead people. It still made her eyes burn.

A wooden crate fell from a stall behind her. The lid struck the market floor with a short explosion of sound. It was nothing like a cannon. Juliet's body reacted before her mind could make the distinction.

For a moment the market roof disappeared. Vestigium lamps became fires reflected on the Thames. Bargaining voices lengthened into screaming at the docks. A cartwheel grinding across ice became the tearing of a hull under bombardment. Juliet stopped in the middle of the crowd. Her breath lodged too high in her chest.

London returned as it had truly been on the last day. Snow dirtied by mud and blood. People crushing towards the piers until children were lifted clear of the ground. Sailors shouting the number of remaining places. Edward running against the crowd, disappearing from her sight and returning again, each time with another person or another order. Remi so small that Juliet had pressed his face to her chest to keep smoke from his lungs.

A small hand squeezed her glove.

"Mama."

Juliet blinked twice.

Cinnamon. Warmth from the lamps. Low wooden beams. Snow melting on coats around her. Everything returned to Marrakesh one piece at a time.

Remi stood close, the bow of his wooden ship sticking from his coat pocket. His eyes showed worry even though he did not understand.

Juliet crouched. She did not tell him she was fine. At that moment, she was not. "I remembered London too strongly."

Remi glanced around as though London might be hiding at another stall.

"Because the box fell?"

"Yes." Juliet breathed more slowly. "I knew this was Marrakesh. But for a moment I heard that noise and thought I was in London again."

The boy considered this, then closed both hands around one of hers. "Then we stand here for a little while." Juliet almost said there was no need. Instead she remained. They stood beside a wooden post until her breathing settled and the market became only a market again.

Juliet looked at her son. He possessed almost no memory of London, yet somehow stood beside her inside that memory. "Thank you."
