Remi shrugged in exactly the way Edward did whenever he had no idea how to receive gratitude. "Are we still buying cinnamon?"

Juliet took back her purse.

"Yes. But we're still bargaining."

Several steps later he asked, "What did you remember in London?"

"The silver comb your father bought me." She wiped the last dampness from her cheek. "Only a comb. Sometimes we remember home through very small things."

Remi thought.

"Does Father still buy useless things?"

Juliet folded the cinnamon wrapping.

"Yes. Some disasters survived the end of the world."

A little later he asked whether London had been more beautiful than Marrakesh.

Juliet refused to make him choose.

"Not more beautiful. Different. One day, if you remember London, Marrakesh, or wherever we're going next, remember all of them. No one gets to tell you that you must choose one place and forget the rest."

By the time they left the market, the grey light had begun to sink towards evening. Remi carried the spices in both hands and still regarded his mother's victory over the pepper merchant as a significant achievement.

Juliet kept the unused Mariabell invitation in her coat. When they reached home, Edward had not yet returned from the Governor's residence.

On the table beside the window lay notes he had abandoned before leaving, an open ink bottle, and a chair pulled slightly out of place. Juliet set down the pepper and cinnamon, removed Remi's scarf, and stood for a moment in a house that already looked emptier.

"Father isn't home yet?"

"Not yet. Victoria probably kept him longer than expected."

Juliet took off her gloves and looked towards the road leading into the city. "We'll put things away while we can. Tonight we still have to settle the cattle with him, and tomorrow no one in this house is allowed to sleep late."

Remi placed the spice bag on the table and took the wooden ship from his coat. "Mama, tomorrow do we still leave a place for the Mariabells?"

Juliet stopped. Her fingers touched the final invitation still in her pocket. "Yes."

She pulled the chair nearest the stove into place. "We still leave a place for them."

Remi nodded and asked nothing more.

He sat on the floor to untie a knot on the wooden ship. Juliet began arranging the purchases and sorting the papers that still had to be handed over.

Outside, Marrakesh continued through the sounds of cart wheels, hammers, and Vestigium lamps growing brighter as afternoon faded. Four years earlier, the Spencers had arrived almost empty-handed. Two days before leaving, nearly every chest was packed. Juliet still had a ledger, a list of names, and an empty chair that could not be put into luggage.

The door remained closed. Edward was still at the Governor's residence. The afternoon had not yet finished with any of them.

title_vi: Chapter 12 - A Feast for Those Who Stay
title_en: Chapter 12 - A Feast for Those Who Stay
text_en:
Dawn came slowly to Marrakesh. The sun hung low behind cloud, bright enough to turn the snow in the yard from grey to white but far too weak to soften the ice over the water barrel.

Edward woke before anyone else in the house. He entered the front room already washed and dressed despite having drunk with Marco and Romeo until nearly midnight. Wine, ashes, and cold meat still scented the room.

Romeo lay across the table. Marco had curled so close to the hearth that the blanket Juliet placed over him during the night had slipped to the floor.

Edward picked it up, rolled it, and nudged Marco's boot. "Wake up. Today the Royal Guard has a mission far more important than guarding a city."

Marco opened one eye. "If that mission happens before I drink water, I'm resigning."

Edward turned to Romeo and slapped his shoulder twice. "You too. Up. Four cattle are waiting outside to discover whether the reputation of the Royal Guard is anything more than rumour."

Romeo pulled the blanket over his head. "Ed, I've saved your life more times than I care to count. Surely that buys me five more minutes."

"Not remotely."

Edward set a bucket beside the table. "Juliet has calculated this feast to exactly four cattle. If she wakes and finds the two of you still decomposing in here, I will not be able to protect anyone."

Marco pushed himself upright with both hands. "Water first. Otherwise the next thing on the butcher's table will be me."

The three men went outside while the snow was still fresh across the bricks. A thin sheet of ice covered the barrel. Romeo broke it with the bucket handle and plunged both hands into the water before splashing his face. Marco muttered something unprintable. Edward laughed and opened the stable.

Four animals had been separated the night before.

Edward checked the tags around each neck before removing his gloves. The decision was already in the ledger, but he stood several seconds beside the last animal. For four years, the herd had been more than meat or property. It had been the first thing the family could trade for flour and medicine. It had given Edward a reason to rise every morning when reasons had once been difficult to find.

Romeo glanced at him. "Want to change your mind? Still time."

Edward shook his head.

"No. Continue."

The work moved faster than any of them wished to admit. Romeo handled the most difficult part with enough precision for Marco to remind him that this was a cattle yard, not a battlefield. Edward divided the cuts. Marco managed ropes and hides.

They worked quickly enough to preserve the meat and slowly enough not to waste anything. They had barely finished the first animal when Juliet appeared at the stable door. Her hair had been tied back, a heavy cloth hung over one arm, and the household ledger was tucked beneath the other. "Three gentlemen, I need a favour."

Juliet opened the book directly to a marked page. Edward looked up. "Say it."

"Hides, bones, and fat into three separate groups. I explained this last night, but seeing all three of you together has convinced me repetition is wise."

Romeo placed one greasy hand over his chest. "Madam, you insult three of the finest graduates in Royal Academy history."

"Excellent." Juliet turned the page. "Then three elite graduates should have no difficulty cleaning the blood from my yard before the guests arrive."

Romeo leaned closer to Edward. "Keep your voice down."

Remi appeared behind his mother, scarf covering half his face as he tried to peer around the buckets, knives, and rope.

Edward pointed towards the storehouse at once. "Too dangerous. Stay back."

"I'm only looking."

"If you want to look, do it from somewhere useful. Bring the stack of wooden bowls from the storehouse. Ask your mother whether she needs more firewood while you're there."

Remi lowered his scarf just enough to reveal a deeply offended mouth, then ran to obey. Soon he returned carrying bowls almost as high as his chin. The moment he completed that task, Juliet sent him for cloth, then string, then paper tags for the meat.

By the fourth trip across the yard, Edward caught him and wrapped another turn of scarf around his neck. "I'm not cold." "Your ears are red. You're running everywhere. Slow down." "But Father, you're the one who told me to hurry for the bowls."

Edward looked towards his wife. "He's beginning to use logic against us." Juliet continued adding meat portions in the ledger. "Who taught him that?"

They were preparing the third animal when cart wheels creaked outside the gate. Victoria arrived with four Moorish women. Their wagon was piled with herbs, onions, turnips, fresh bread, and two enormous copper pots. She stepped down, looked across the yard at the three men covered in cattle blood, and stopped. "So these are three of the four greatest graduates of the class of 1700. Apparently the fourth demonstrated superior intelligence by avoiding this spectacle."

Edward kept hold of the rope. "Did you come to help, or simply to inspect how far we've fallen?"

"I came to assist the person who actually understands organisation." Victoria looked at Juliet. "The three of you may continue your careers as butchers."

Juliet put a stone over the ledger so the wind could not turn the pages. "Thank you. They behave as though killing a cow is the most difficult labour in creation."

Victoria removed her gloves and tucked them into her coat. "Let them enjoy the illusion."

Edward leaned towards Marco. "I appear to be losing authority inside my own house."

"You never possessed it."

Marco wiped his knife on the cloth beside the block.

From that point onward, the Spencer house knew no quiet. Victoria and Juliet organised two outdoor stoves, tables, and canvas against the stable. The Moorish women prepared vegetables, herbs, and bread. Marco and Romeo remained with the meat.

Edward moved constantly between them, carrying bones, tightening ropes, raising table legs, lifting pots, and responding whenever one of the women shouted his name.

Near noon, neighbours began arriving early to help. No one came empty-handed. Omar brought a cart of firewood and three large butchering knives. Hassan's family arrived with couscous, dill, and a pot of spice mixture. A Castilian family from the tannery brought new leather straps. The Thompsons carried barley bread and extra chairs. News of the feast had spread well beyond Juliet's invitation list. Invited households brought relatives. Families who had merely heard that the Spencers were leaving Marrakesh came with whatever they could offer.

By early afternoon, three joined canopies covered the yard. Vestigium lamps hung from rope lines. Long tables had been built from storehouse doors, cart boards, and anything else flat enough to hold plates. Almost nothing from the four cattle went to waste. Brisket went into a wine-and-herb stew. Split bones simmered into soup. Tender cuts were seasoned for charcoal. Fat, offal, and anything that could be preserved went into separate trays. Excess meat was smoked and wrapped so each household could carry several meals home after the feast. The hides were rolled aside for Omar, Thompson, and the tannery. Juliet checked every portion in the ledger before anyone moved it, as though another cow might vanish from the arithmetic if she looked away.

Edward looked at Romeo. "I commanded fleets and never saw logistics this terrifying."

"Your fleets did not have Juliet."

"Fair point."

By the time the food was nearly ready, the Spencer yard resembled a small market. English, Castilian, and Arabic overlapped beneath the canvas. Children ran between tables until adults caught them and sent them back. Two English veterans argued with a Castilian smith over the proper way to roast beef. Omar guarded the stew pot and loudly accused everyone else of using the wrong amount of dill until Juliet physically moved him aside and corrected the seasoning herself.

Edward stood in the middle of it carrying a tray of bread and, for several seconds, forgot where he was supposed to go. For four years he had thought of his family as temporary residents in one corner of Marrakesh. Looking at almost a hundred and thirty people beneath the joined canopies, he finally saw how many connections had formed around the three Spencers without any of them ever sitting down to count. Juliet passed close enough to knock her elbow into his.

"Do not stand there staring like a guest." "I'm observing." "If you want to observe something, observe the soup. It's about to cook dry."

Edward hurried to the pot and picked up the ladle.

There was no formal opening to the feast. Juliet refused to make older people and children sit hungry while food cooled merely so Edward could deliver a beautiful speech. The first soup bowls went to the Thompson table.

Juliet broke bread for the child who was still coughing, checked the fever with the back of her hand, and reminded Martha to save the herbs for the evening. At the far end of the tables, one chair remained empty. The Mariabell invitation rested on the seat.

Edward noticed it from across the yard and did not ask who had placed it there. Only after the first bowls were nearly empty did Omar raise the handle of his knife and tap it against a cup. "Spencer." He waited until Edward looked at him. "Are you planning to let the whole city eat your cattle and then sneak away without saying anything?"

Laughter travelled down the tables.

Edward put down his drink and stepped onto the wooden porch. Juliet paused beside Martha. Remi stopped with half a piece of bread in one hand and stared eagerly towards his father.

Edward looked across the tables. He began with the simplest truth. "Four years ago, when my family arrived in Marrakesh, we had almost nothing."

He nodded towards Victoria. "Victoria gave us a roof and the cattle that allowed us to begin again. Omar taught me how to keep animals alive through this winter. The Thompsons gave up medicine when Remi was ill. Hassan's family helped repair our stable roof."

He looked further along the tables. "Many more of you gave things so small that if I listed every kindness, we would still be standing here tomorrow night."

Laughter rose from several tables.

Edward waited. "For a long time I believed Marrakesh was only where my family had stopped while searching for a way home."

He looked towards Remi. "But this is the city where my son knows the bread sellers by name. My wife cannot enter the market without half a street greeting her. I know which neighbour's cow is about to calve before its owner does."

A smile moved through the crowd. "A place like that is difficult to call temporary."

The yard quieted. "Tomorrow morning, we leave. Juliet and Remi travel towards Iberia. I have accepted a separate mission from the Queen. I do not yet know how far that road will take me."

Edward raised his cup. "These four cattle are not a gift from an admiral or a soldier. They are simply the Spencer family's thanks to the people who carried us through four winters."

Omar raised his cup first. "To those still living."

Juliet repeated it.

"To those still living."

The answer came from across the yard. Wooden cups and clay mugs struck together beneath the canvas. Conversations interrupted for Edward's speech resumed at every table.

Omar waited for him to sit, then pulled his chair closer. "You mentioned another mission. Where?"

Edward looked at Remi before answering. "England."

Omar stopped with his cup halfway to his mouth. "Back there? I thought the north was nothing now but ice, French troops, and stories nobody wants to remember."

"There may still be people alive. Units that were never fully destroyed." Edward drank once. "I need to see it before I agree to call England a dead country."

The news travelled faster through the yard than Edward expected. The feast did not become silent, but English faces began turning towards him.

For four years they had learned how to bury questions about home. Tonight he had dug them up again.

An old veteran stood first. "Are you Edward Spencer? The man who commanded HMS True Hero?"

Edward set down his cup.

"I was Admiral Spencer once. And yes, True Hero was my flagship."

"Was." The old man pressed one hand to his chest. "My son James Hartwell served aboard True Hero at La Coruña."

Edward repeated the name in his mind once and found the memory. A mid-deck gunner who had argued with a physician until they let him return to his gun despite a shoulder wound. "James Hartwell. He was wounded in the shoulder on the second day."

The old man's eyes filled. "You remember him?"

"He was extremely stubborn."

The man laughed through tears. "He got that from his mother."

Two nearby tables went quiet when a middle-aged woman stood at the end of the row. She clutched a folded paper whose edges had softened from years of handling. When Edward faced her, she asked with a trembling voice, "Timothy Beaumont. Do you remember him?"

Edward answered before he needed to search.

"Timothy Beaumont. Young gunner. English and French blood. He enlisted younger than he should have, only a few years older than Remi is now. Impossible to keep off the gun deck even when ordered away."

The woman tightened her fingers around the paper. "We have waited all these years. In his last letter he wrote that his unit had volunteered to cover the evacuation. Nothing after that."

She looked at Edward.

"Do you know whether he's alive?"

Edward read the name and unit on the paper before answering. "The last reliable report I saw confirmed he was alive at that time. I cannot tell you where Timothy is now. When London fell, the command network collapsed too quickly. Units vanished from the records before the men themselves had even reached the docks."

The woman's eyes lowered. "My family only wants to know whether there is still any reason to wait."

"I hope there is."

Edward did not offer comfort he could not support. "But I will promise only this. If my team finds ship registers, survivor lists, evacuation records, anything at all from the north, Timothy Beaumont will be among the first names I look for."

She gave him the paper. Timothy's name, old unit, and the last place from which his family had received a letter had been written carefully across it. Edward folded the page and placed it in the inside pocket of his coat. That simple act opened a door.

Another man asked about a younger brother in Portsmouth. A former marine wanted to know whether his old unit had escaped Dover. A Moorish woman whose husband had loaded English ships asked whether civilian dock workers were ever registered at all, or whether they had simply disappeared with a city's paperwork.

Edward said "I don't know" more often than he said "yes". Marco found an empty notebook and began writing names, units, and last-known locations. Victoria sent for a clerk from the Governor's office, but made him state clearly that no one was to promise what the government could not guarantee.

Half an hour later, several pages were full. No one cheered. Those who returned to their tables carried the same uncertainty they had brought, except the names now existed on paper rather than only inside individual homes. Remi stood beside his father and looked at the notebook.

"You remember Uncle Hartwell and Uncle Beaumont, but you still don't know where they are?" Edward nodded. "I remember faces. Names. Where they stood on a deck. After London broke, there were days when thousands disappeared from the record before I could learn where they had gone."

Remi looked towards the people returning to their seats. "Are they angry with you?"

"Some will be. They have the right."

Edward followed his son's gaze. "For a family, one name is an entire world. At headquarters, sometimes it becomes one line in a list. Those two things are not the same."

Remi watched Marco holding the notebook and asked nothing more. The feast continued, but many of the English guests had stopped drinking so heavily. The word England drew death lists, missing-person questions, and records no one had ever found.

Soon there were people waiting beside Marco's new ledger. Romeo looked around at the faces gathering towards Edward and set his cup down hard. "Will all of you stop looking at Ed as though he has already dug his own grave?"

Several people startled.

Romeo planted both hands on the table and raised his voice over the wind beating against the canvas. "You know him as a cattle farmer in Marrakesh. Has anyone here heard what happened in Flanders twelve years ago?"

A veteran at the far table answered. "The Second Agincourt?" "Exactly that madness."

Romeo pointed at Edward. "Six thousand Englishmen stepped off their ships. The French had several times the numbers, guns across the front, and cavalry enough to grind us into mud. Everyone expected him to retreat."

Romeo smiled. "He waited for rain."

Whispers spread.

"The rain dampened French powder. The ground became mud. Their horses could no longer charge the way they wanted. Ed formed the infantry into squares, broke the first cavalry attack, then drove straight into guns that had gone half-blind."

Victoria tilted her head. "Henry V at Agincourt."

"Call it whatever you like."

Romeo raised his cup towards Edward. "By afternoon, the French artillery was firing badly, their cavalry was dismounting, and six thousand men who expected to be buried in Flanders had opened their own road home."

Several veterans turned their chairs fully towards him. Marco, who had been eating in silence, put down the meat in his hand. "And La Coruña?"

Romeo grinned. "Your turn."

Marco stood. He used none of Romeo's gestures, but his voice carried clearly to the far tables. "Eleven years ago, four French Atlantic fleets entered La Coruña during a storm. The waves were high enough that gun crews tied themselves to railings to keep from being thrown overboard."

He looked at Edward. "His fleet fought for nearly sixteen hours through the night. At times the smoke and fog were so dense that the ships recognised each other only by muzzle flashes."

Marco lifted his cup. "By dawn, the French formation had broken. The ships still afloat withdrew."

He paused. "After that battle, sailors began calling him by the name you've heard tonight." An old English voice said it first. "The Pathmaker."

Another repeated it. Then several. Soon the name travelled through the yard from veterans who knew it to Moorish neighbours hearing it for the first time. "The Pathmaker!"

Edward stood among raised cups with his clay mug in one hand. He had heard that name thousands of times. Not for years.

Romeo continued telling some story. Veterans surrounded Marco with questions about La Coruña. The sounds remained. They simply began to recede, as though Edward were listening through a closed door.

Fire shifted beneath the canvas. A man stood on the other side of it. He wore the dark blue full dress uniform of a Royal Navy Admiral. Medals shone across the younger Edward's chest. A bicorne sat neatly over hair not yet touched by age. The boots were so clean they looked absurd in a yard full of snow and mud.

Edward knew the face. The younger man looked at the goatskin coat and smiled. "They tell it well."

Edward said nothing. "Flanders." The apparition inclined his head towards Romeo. "Rain arrived exactly when it needed to. La Coruña. The current changed after midnight, just as the French formation began to slip." His smile thinned. "You remember."

Edward's fingers tightened around the cup. "If the rain had come an hour later, or the water turned later, the stories would have different endings."

The younger man stepped along the edge of the fire. "You understand that better than any of the people raising cups out there."

"I left that behind." Edward heard his own voice very low.

"Did you?" The figure looked him up and down. "You traded dress uniform for goatskin. Battle maps for cattle sheds. Yet when Romeo described Flanders, you still remembered exactly where the French guns stood. When Marco said La Coruña, you knew which ship lost a mast before dawn."

Edward looked past him. The crowd beyond the flames still laughed. No one seemed to see the man standing between Edward and the fire.

"You hate being called a genius," the younger Edward said. "Because you remember every time disaster stood one decision, one storm, or one current away." He stepped closer. "But you also remember what it felt like when everything moved exactly as you ordered."

Edward did not deny it.

The younger man stopped smiling. "And what about the time it didn't?"

The cup became cold in Edward's hand though the fire burned hot against his face. The apparition moved closer. "Inverness."

Edward closed his eyes and opened them at once.

"Or shall I use the name you keep avoiding?"

Edward looked at him.

"Criston Wallace."

A faint crack came from the cup. Flanders vanished. La Coruña vanished. Edward saw dirty snow in Inverness. Lines stretched too thin. A gap he had mistaken for opportunity. Gunfire after that. Orders breaking apart. The moment he understood too late that the road ahead had been left open by Wallace precisely because Edward would take it.

His breath caught. Edward tried to open his fingers. The hand would not obey.

The younger man stood directly before him. "The Pathmaker." This time the title held no pride at all. "Wallace showed you a road you failed to see, then left you alive long enough to remember it."

A shard of clay pressed into Edward's palm. "You ran from that name for eleven years." The figure stepped backwards towards the flame. "Now you're walking towards it again."

The fire swayed. The voices of the feast returned all at once, close and loud enough to make Edward flinch. "THE PATHMAKER! THE PATHMAKER!"

He had not moved. The cup was cracked inside his fist. A thin line of blood had begun to run between his fingers, and Edward had not yet noticed. Surrounded by people raising drinks to his name, he stared only at the empty space across the fire where no one stood any longer.

Juliet saw the blood before Edward realised his hand was injured. She caught his elbow and drew him away from the crowd still calling "The Pathmaker" beneath the canvas. Marco glanced at Edward's hand, understood at once, and clapped Romeo hard on the shoulder. The two men immediately steered the gathering towards another old campaign, keeping the attention in the yard while Juliet led Edward into the kitchen.

Edward looked down at the broken clay cup. A crack ran from rim to base. One sharp shard had buried itself in his palm, and fresh blood was threading between fingers still clenched around it. "I broke the cup." He had to swallow before the words came out.

"We'll buy another one." Juliet gently removed it from his hand. "Right now you come inside and let me clean this."

Edward opened his mouth.

She looked directly into his eyes. "And do not tell me you're fine. I know exactly what you're about to say."

Edward closed his mouth and followed her.

The thick stone wall behind the kitchen muted most of the feast. Juliet rinsed the cut with warm water and wrapped his hand in clean gauze. Edward sat on a low stool, still looking towards the door into the yard.

"I heard his name."

Juliet held the bandage in place. "Criston Wallace?"

Edward turned sharply. "How do you know that name?"

She tied the dressing before answering. "You've said it in your sleep. More than once when Remi was little. Again during last winter's cold spell."

"I never told you about him."

"No."

Juliet pulled another chair closer. "You didn't want to. I wasn't going to force it out of you."

Edward looked at the white bandage around his palm. "I don't want Remi looking at me the way the people out there just did."

"The boy also watched his father crush a cup in his hand because of one name." Juliet leaned back against the wall. "That may be enough for him to understand that legends can still be afraid."

"I don't like him seeing that."

"I do."

Edward looked at her.

"If he sees that his father can be afraid and still do what needs doing, what is wrong with that? I only don't want him growing up afraid of something and hiding it until he does something stupid, exactly like you."

Edward rested his head against the wall. "You are exceptionally skilled at irritating me."

"Occupational requirement of being your wife."

Juliet put away the spare bandages.

Edward had just started to smile when the voices outside thinned all at once.

The change began at the gate. One table after another fell quiet until the crackle of the stove and the canvas snapping in the wind became the loudest sounds in the yard. Victoria stepped into the lane between the tables. "My Sultan."

Edward stood. Juliet turned towards the doorway.

A Moorish man entered the yard with only two guards. He was past fifty. Black hair had gone silver at the temples. His face was lean and sun-darkened, the lines around his eyes and mouth cut deep by age. A charcoal-grey robe edged in gold lay beneath a dark fur cloak. Had nearly everyone in the yard not risen at once, Edward might not have guessed his rank. The Sultan first looked towards the empty chair at the end of the Thompson table, where the Mariabell invitation still rested.

Victoria moved forward. This time her voice belonged to a Governor rather than an old Academy friend. "Please welcome Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad."

Every Moorish guest stood. The Castilians and English followed half a beat later.

Omar did not bow deeply, but one weathered hand came to his chest with a degree of respect Edward had never seen him offer any local official.

Abd al-Rahman raised his hand. "Sit. I came to eat, not inspect taxes."

Several people laughed, though most remained standing.

The Sultan looked at Victoria. "I heard the Spencer family was holding a farewell meal and half of Marrakesh had found its way here. If I stayed away, tomorrow people would decide their Sultan was too miserly to spare even one blessing for the road."

"I can have another table prepared."

"No need."

Abd al-Rahman looked at the rough tables built from cart planks, storehouse doors, and whatever other wood could carry a plate. "If this is a neighbours' feast, I will sit with neighbours."

Omar patted the empty chair beside him. "Then sit here. Though you are late, Your Majesty. Romeo has already conducted a campaign against the best cuts."

"For the record, I object to this characterisation," Romeo called from the next table.

Laughter spread through the yard.

Ignoring the ceremony available to him, Abd al-Rahman pulled out the chair and sat beside Omar.

Edward remained in the kitchen doorway. He had heard the Sultan's name throughout four years in Marrakesh and had seen him from a distance only a handful of times. Two guards did not impress him. Victoria's sudden formality did not either. What caught his attention was the way people relaxed almost as soon as Abd al-Rahman sat among them.

Juliet noticed him watching. "You've lived here four years and never asked why people respect him like that?"

"I assumed most of it was because he was Sultan." Edward looked towards the table where Omar had pulled out a chair for a monarch as casually as he might have for a neighbour. "I may have simplified the matter."

"In Marrakesh, a title is not enough to make Omar put his hand over his heart." Juliet tilted her head. "You earn that kind of respect by doing something people still remember."

Victoria passed the kitchen entrance and heard the last sentence. "During the first winter, when snow buried the foot of the Atlas, three great families tried to move their grain stores north and leave Marrakesh to survive as it could."

Edward waited. "The Sultan sealed the warehouses in front of them."

Victoria lowered her voice. "He opened the Ziyad stores first. Then he forced the other families to sell grain under a fixed ceiling. Two public squares became kitchens where nobles, Moorish families, Castilians, and refugees like you all stood in the same line."

Omar called from the yard in English loud enough for everyone to hear. "Don't forget the three merchants he hanged for hoarding."

Abd al-Rahman turned towards him.

"Two."

"Three."

"The third man fell down a staircase."

"Immediately after your soldiers entered his warehouse."

"I cannot be held responsible for another man's staircase."

The tables erupted. Even Edward laughed. When the noise fell away, Victoria said quietly, "That is why Marrakesh respects him. The reason Iberian courts never treat him as some provincial king is much longer."

Edward knew parts of that story. Near the end of Charles II's reign, Habsburg power in Spain had begun rotting from within. Abd al-Rahman was still a Moroccan prince Madrid often dismissed, but the Ziyads had money, ports, and merchants crossing Gibraltar. He used them. Habsburg representatives in Morocco found money and food suddenly unavailable. Rival factions gained access to ports. Couriers disappeared into safe houses. Lords who might alter a supply route discovered profitable reasons to remain neutral.

Madrid realised North Africa had ceased being obedient only after several networks were already broken. When Charles II died without an heir, Abd al-Rahman chose early. Isabella had been too young then to be the reason. He chose a new Castilian order because he believed Morocco would breathe more freely beneath it than beneath a restored Habsburg Spain. Morocco paid for that decision with coin, men, and ships that never came home. By the time Isabella took the throne, Abd al-Rahman was among the few men outside Castile who had helped make her accession possible.

"The Queen can become furious with him," Victoria said. "They have argued badly enough that the entire Council once walked outside to wait. She still listens."

Edward rested one shoulder against the doorframe. "Because she owes him, or because she trusts his judgement?"

"Both may be true. The important one is that he has been right at moments when everyone else merely repeated what the throne wanted to hear." Victoria almost smiled. "Isabella hates being contradicted. She hates discovering the contradiction was correct even more."

Outside, Abd al-Rahman asked Martha about the coughing child, switching into fluent enough English that the woman looked startled. Then he took a piece of almond sweet from his pocket and gave it to Remi, but made him break it in half with one of Hassan's children standing nearby.

Edward waited until the second half disappeared into the Sultan's pocket before stepping into the yard. Abd al-Rahman saw him and made no effort to summon him immediately. He finished eating. He discussed snow on the Atlas with Omar, lamp-oil shortages with the tanner, and listened to an elderly woman complain that patrolmen near the market were too fond of taking food without paying. Only when several families with small children began leaving did he put down his bowl.

"The celebrated Edward Spencer."

Edward approached. "My Sultan."

Abd al-Rahman indicated a chair near the fire. "Sit. Speak with me for a while."

The nearby tables lowered their voices.

Refusing would only make more people watch, so Edward sat. Juliet remained at the closest table. Marco, Romeo, and Victoria were near enough to hear without joining.

The Sultan nodded towards the white bandage. "A trophy won from a broken cup?"

Edward flexed two fingers. "Apparently."

"Excellent. It proves a legend can still bleed from pottery."

Edward settled back. "Did you come in person merely to insult me?"

Abd al-Rahman removed his hood and passed it to one of his guards. Then he rose and stepped closer to the fire, where every nearby table could see him clearly. "I remember the records of the class of 1700. Four names England once displayed as proof that the country would never run out of prodigies."

He raised a hand and pointed first at Edward. "Edward Spencer. The Pathmaker. Admiral of the Royal Navy of England."

His finger moved to Marco. "Marco Stones. The Balancer. Colonel of the English Army. Now a Castilian Royal Guard and commander of Tercio de la Balanza, Legion Two."

Romeo accepted his turn before the Sultan needed to point. "Romeo Harkon. The Headsman. Colonel of the English Expeditionary Force. Castilian Royal Guard, commander of Tercio del Filo, the infamous Legion Three."

Last came Victoria. "Victoria Valdes. The Final Wager. Major General of English Logistics. Now Governor of Marrakesh." Victoria said nothing. She merely straightened.

"Four people," Abd al-Rahman said. "Four Silver Crosses awarded before leaving the Academy. Four officers England once claimed could not be produced twice in a generation."

He turned back to Edward. "So explain something to me. How did a country possessing the four of you collapse so completely?"

Romeo's chair crashed backwards. A short flintlock left its holster before the chair hit the ground. The muzzle stopped at Abd al-Rahman's forehead. "Watch your mouth." Wine still roughened Romeo's voice. "You're standing at Ed's feast."

Victoria rose at once. "Romeo. Lower the weapon."

Marco was already on his feet.

Abd al-Rahman raised one finger and stopped both of them. His two guards did not draw. The Sultan did not so much as move his head away from the barrel. "If you intend to fire, fire. Otherwise lower it. I am speaking to Admiral Spencer."

Marco closed a hand around Romeo's wrist and forced the muzzle into the snow. "Enough. Put it away."

Romeo's jaw tightened. He held the Sultan's gaze several seconds longer, then shoved the flintlock back into its holster. The click of metal carried across the yard. Abd al-Rahman never looked after it.

"Why did you lose?"

Edward had answers ready. The cold. Harvest failure. Riots. France. Portugal. A court still trapped in the fantasy that one more victory would restore everything. The Sultan had publicly named all four of them before people who had just toasted Edward as a legend. It stripped away the possibility of hiding behind broad explanations. "Because of me."

Marco turned. Victoria's hands tightened in front of her. Romeo stopped moving.

Abd al-Rahman showed no mercy. "That is a sentence against yourself. It is not an answer."

Edward raised his head. "I am not asking how severely you wish to condemn Edward Spencer. I am asking what happened."

The Sultan stepped nearer. "Tell the truth."

Edward placed both hands on his knees to keep them still. "England was already collapsing from several directions. I was ordered to suppress Scotland. I believed I could strike quickly, finish the campaign, and return south before the rest of the country worsened."

He looked into the fire. "I was wrong from the beginning."

"And because of Criston Wallace." The Sultan spoke the name Edward had avoided all evening.

Edward did not answer. Juliet alone showed no surprise. Marco set down his cup. Romeo turned his chair fully towards the fire. Victoria watched Abd al-Rahman as though waiting to discover exactly how much he knew.

Edward needed one attempt before his voice returned. "You know about him?"

"I know he captured you alive at Inverness. I also know he chose to release you."

Pain flared beneath the bandage as Edward's hand closed around the fragment still buried in the cut. "What do you mean, you know?"

"Before the sea froze, Moroccan merchants traded between Edinburgh, Dublin, London, and Lisbon. I paid for information years before you could have placed Marrakesh on a map."

Abd al-Rahman inclined his head. "A Royal Admiral being captured and then released by the enemy is not the sort of event a few sealed court documents can conceal."

Edward remained silent.

"I know you took Edinburgh and lost it again. That part is old information. What I want you to explain is why, when the campaign had already moved beyond your control, you still drove north instead of stopping."

Marco shifted. Victoria touched his arm and shook her head. Edward saw them both and did not look away from the fire.

He turned the empty cup once in his hand. "I thought one more victory would leave Wallace nowhere to retreat. At Inverness he showed me exactly what I wanted to see: troops falling back, a headquarters exposed, a chance to end the campaign."

Edward set the cup down. "I knew I was angry. I called it decisiveness."

He met the Sultan's eyes. "I followed him into the trap."

Nearby conversations had stopped. Edward continued without waiting to be prompted. "The core force was destroyed. I was taken alive."

His mouth tightened. "Wallace did not kill me." Edward remembered the exact words eleven years later, and the precise way Criston had placed his name at the end. "Why should I take your life, Edward Spencer? So England can build itself another martyr?"

Edward drank some water. "He sent me home. Not from pity. He wanted England to watch me return defeated."

Remi stood near Juliet with the wooden ship held to his chest. He did not understand Inverness, but he understood enough not to interrupt his father.

Abd al-Rahman walked slowly around the edge of the fire. "While Marco was pinned around Rennes and Caen. Romeo was with the Danes. Victoria was trapped in North Africa. I do not need you to recite what the records already say." He stopped before Edward. "I want the rest. Who destroyed England?"

Edward watched a log collapse into coals. "I helped destroy it."

"Helped?"

Romeo moved as though to protest. Marco's hand landed on his shoulder first.

Abd al-Rahman leaned closer. "Answer honestly. Not in the language you've used to punish yourself for six years." His eyes narrowed. "Could you, alone, have destroyed England?"

The familiar verdict returned inside Edward. My fault. If I had not abandoned the south. If I had not followed Wallace.

If I had died at Inverness. If I had been stronger. For the first time, each sentence sounded worn from repetition rather than indisputably true.

"No." Edward spoke slowly. "I did not carry the collapse alone. I will also never blame crop failure, riots, weather, or other men's mistakes in order to wash my own hands clean."

Abd al-Rahman nodded. "Good. At least now you are taking responsibility without turning responsibility into a sentence against your own existence."

Edward sat straighter.

"You think saying that makes what I did less terrible?"

"I have no interest in making it less terrible." The Sultan's answer was almost casual. "You withdrew from the wrong position. Wallace manipulated you. You lost men, became trapped, and left the south exposed at a lethal moment. That is already bad enough. I have no need to decorate it."

He tapped the table once. "I merely refuse to let you collect crop failure, rebellion, winter, an incompetent court, and the failures of every other commander, pile them into one judgement, and write Edward Spencer beneath all of it."

Edward was silent.

Abd al-Rahman pointed towards the broken cup. "An hour ago these people were shouting The Pathmaker as if you had never failed. You despise that story, so you answered it with another fiction in which one Edward Spencer single-handedly brought down England." The Sultan leaned one hand on the table. "Either way, you are assigning yourself too much power."

Edward said nothing.

His bandaged fingers closed around the edge of the chair. For years, he had thought humility meant refusing every legend. It had never occurred to him that self-condemnation could be another way of placing himself at the centre of everything.

title_vi: Chapter 14 - The Weight of a Promise
title_en: Chapter 14 - The Weight of a Promise
text_en:
Abd al-Rahman straightened. "Now let us discuss promises."

He pointed towards the notebook of missing names beside Victoria. "You are going north to look for survivors, trace Vestigia, and attempt to bring Scotland, Ireland, and the Danes into a new front. Tonight you also accepted the names of sons, husbands, and brothers from the people sitting here."

Edward looked at the book. "I made it clear that I promise to bring no one home. If we find lists, records, or traces, I will search those names. Nothing more."

"At least you still understand the limit of a promise."

The Sultan stepped closer. "But I want something else answered. Are you going because of the mission, because of the living, or because you want to repair the name Edward Spencer?"

Romeo stood abruptly, though this time his hand stayed away from his weapon. "That is enough."

"Not yet." Abd al-Rahman barely looked at him before returning his attention to Edward.

Victoria spoke. "My Sultan, you are questioning a man who has just left his home to accept the Queen's commission."

"I know." The Sultan's answer remained calm. "But a seal cannot answer for the motives of the man carrying it."

He looked at Edward. "Castile? The people still alive? Or proof that you did not die at Inverness?"

Edward let the question remain between them for several seconds. "Perhaps all three."

Abd al-Rahman offered no praise. "At least this time you chose honesty."

Edward gestured towards the joined tables. "If you think I intend to restore an English throne, you are mistaken. If my homeland is now only a graveyard, I will not ask living people to bleed for a flag."

"The English throne does not concern me." The Sultan turned in a slow circle and encompassed the entire yard with one hand: the temporary tables, the stew pots scraped nearly empty, the patched canvas, and the vacant Mariabell chair. "Marrakesh does."

Edward waited.

"Four years ago you arrived here with an exhausted wife and a child who nearly died from the cold. Moorish families shared land and food with you. The Castilian government gave you legal papers. Your neighbours gave you animals, work, and enough time to remember who you were." Abd al-Rahman's eyes settled briefly on the empty chair. "Some people lived long enough to sit at this feast. Others did not."

Then he faced Edward again. "Now war is approaching, and you have decided to leave." His expression sharpened. "Before we discuss Scotland, answer me once. What is Marrakesh to you? A poor stopping place to discard the moment the Pathmaker discovers a grander purpose?"

Edward opened his mouth. The answer did not come quickly enough.

"No, sir." Remi's voice was small enough that several people behind him had to lean closer.

Edward turned. "Remi." The boy held the wooden ship against his chest and came towards his father. He did not place himself in front of Edward like some tiny defender. He merely rested one hand on Edward's knee, as though confirming that his father remained where he should be.

Abd al-Rahman looked down at him. His voice softened, but he did not use the false sweetness adults often reserved for children. "You say Marrakesh was never temporary. Why are you so certain?"

Remi swallowed and glanced at his father. Edward did not nod encouragement. He did not pull the boy back.

"Father says a homeland isn't snow or sand."

Remi tightened his arms around the ship. "I don't understand everything the adults were saying. But I know we never lived here like we were only waiting to leave."

He looked towards Omar. "Uncle Omar taught Father how to raise cattle. The Thompsons gave us flour when I was ill. Mama knows almost everyone at the market."

He hesitated. "The potato lady always gives me one extra even when Mama tells her not to."

Omar laughed. Juliet turned away to hide her own smile.

Remi continued. "Father says that without everyone here, our family wouldn't have survived the first winter. I don't remember England much. I remember this house. The market. The cattle shed."

Abd al-Rahman listened without interruption.

"Father says England is his homeland. But if I go to Iberia, I think I'll miss Marrakesh."

Remi looked up. "Can one person have more than one homeland?"

The Sultan watched him for a long moment, then lowered one knee to the stone so Remi would not need to crane his neck. "Yes. A person may belong to more than one place. Sometimes it takes most of a life to understand what he owes each of them."

Remi's uncertainty remained. He leaned closer to Edward and asked quietly, "Then if Father leaves tomorrow, is he abandoning Marrakesh?"

Instead of answering, Abd al-Rahman smiled and motioned towards Edward. Edward rose, stepped nearer, and knelt until he was level with his son. "No."

He put his bandaged hand on Remi's shoulder. "I'm leaving because I have work to do. Tomorrow we board the train, but Uncle Omar remains Uncle Omar. Your mother still knows every stall at the market. That cattle shed will still be the place where I cursed more than anywhere else in four years." A few nearby people laughed softly. "We lived here. Leaving cannot undo that."

Remi watched him with wide eyes. "Will you come back to Marrakesh?"

That question was harder than anything the Sultan had asked.

Edward did not look away. "I will do everything I can to come back."

He paused. "But I do not want to promise you something I cannot know I can keep."

Remi's mouth tightened. "'Try' again. Every time grown-ups don't want to promise, they say they'll try."

Edward managed a painful smile. "Yes. This time you're allowed to hate the word."

Remi remained unhappy with it, but nodded. Only then did Juliet step forward and draw him close.

Abd al-Rahman stood and brushed snow from the hem of his robe. "The boy argues better than you."

Edward gave him a dry smile. "I am beginning to notice."

"Do not relax." The Sultan's expression hardened again. "We are still not finished."

Edward stopped smiling.

Abd al-Rahman came close enough that only an arm's length remained. "You intend to contact Scotland. If you travel far enough north, there is a serious chance you will meet Criston Wallace again."

The Sultan watched Edward's hand close against his knee. "Do not answer as an admiral reading an operational plan. Tell me what you do when the man across the table is him."

Edward kept his voice even. "I talk. If Wallace refuses, I speak to local lords, surviving cities, the Church, whoever controls food, ports, or soldiers. Wallace is part of Scotland, not Scotland itself."

"That is the answer of an admiral who still possesses alternatives."

Abd al-Rahman stepped closer. "What if there are none? What if Wallace is the only man powerful enough to force all of them into one room? Can you keep that calm then?"

Edward said nothing.

His fingers closed more tightly.

The Sultan pressed further. "I will ask you plainly. When you face Criston Wallace again, do you approach him as an admiral negotiating with a symbol of Scotland, or as a frightened child standing beneath the shadow of the father you built inside your own mind?"

Edward pressed his tongue against his teeth and remained silent.

"If he demands that you kneel?"

Romeo lurched up from his chair. "My Sultan, that is enough."

Edward raised one hand to stop him. Then he answered. "I kneel."

Marco turned. Victoria's hands tightened around the edge of her chair. Juliet kept her eyes on her husband. Remi looked between the adults, unable to understand why the answer had stopped the table.

Abd al-Rahman gave no immediate reaction.

Edward continued before he could ask why. "If kneeling buys a civilian corridor, food, a Scottish agreement, or more time for Castile, then I kneel. Wallace defeated me. Whatever pride remains to me is not worth more than those things."

The Sultan waited.

"If he needs to see the defeated man bow before he agrees to sit at a table, I can give him that."

Edward's voice lowered. "I will not let Castile collapse to preserve my dignity."

"Enough." Abd al-Rahman cut him off.

Edward stopped.

"Edward Spencer, you disappoint me."

No one at the nearby tables dared move.

The Sultan walked behind Edward. "I do not despise your willingness to kneel. A man holding power sometimes swallows things far more bitter than pride." He came around the other side. "What disappoints me is how quickly you assumed you were the cheapest thing on the table."

Edward straightened. "You are turning a practical decision into a sermon."

"No. I am listening to your arithmetic." Abd al-Rahman pointed directly at his chest. "If sacrificing you truly saves a hundred people, I will personally push you through the door. I am not foolish enough to pretend every life carries identical strategic value in the middle of war."

He jerked his chin towards Marco. "But what if you die and your entire column loses command? What if your death kills another hundred behind you?"

Edward was silent. So was Marco, who now watched Edward rather than the Sultan.

"Years ago," Abd al-Rahman said, "I abandoned a fortress in the east to keep three cities. For two years people called me a coward who had surrendered ancestral ground."

"Because the cities were worth more."

"Exactly."

The Sultan's voice sharpened. "And I did not burn myself alive inside the fortress merely to prove that I regretted abandoning it." He stopped before Edward again. "You are coming dangerously close to becoming a man who fastens a chain around his own neck because he has decided he no longer possesses value."

Abd al-Rahman's eyes did not soften. "That man cannot save Marrakesh. He only teaches the enemy the exact price required to purchase him."

Edward's jaw tightened.

"You were not at Inverness."

"Correct." The Sultan acknowledged it without hesitation. "I did not stand on an English deck and watch the south burn. I possess no right to order you to forget the past. Wallace is under no obligation to forgive you. The dead cannot return to tell you how to make amends."

He stepped back half a pace. "But when you face him again, if circumstances require you to bow, then bow." His hand lowered. "Just make certain the man on his knees is an admiral conducting a negotiation, not a prisoner passing sentence upon himself."

Edward looked at his bandaged hand and then at the Sultan. "I'll remember."

"I don't need you to remember it for the rest of your life. I need you to remember long enough not to die pointlessly before completing the mission your Queen gave you."

Romeo let out one short laugh and immediately fell silent when the Sultan looked over.

Abd al-Rahman turned towards Remi. The boy still stood beside Juliet, following the Sultan's every movement. Abd al-Rahman laughed. "Very well. I have one more thing to do before a child begins passing judgement on my morals."

At his signal, one of the guards came forward carrying a cedar box longer than a man's forearm. Silver inlay across its lid formed waves braided with lightning. Age had darkened the metal, but the wood showed no cracks. The box was placed in front of Edward. "I intended to send this to your house tomorrow morning. Since I am already here, I see no reason to make one of my people travel twice."

Edward opened the lid. A flintlock pistol lay on dark fabric. The stock was black wood. The barrel had been forged from reddish copper alloy, ancient engravings running from chamber to muzzle. Deep inside the metal, a red light pulsed like a coal trapped within iron.

"I assume this is not merely a handsome firearm."

"Miracle-grade Vestigium."

Abd al-Rahman nodded towards it. "Stormroar. An old treasure of one branch of the Moroccan royal family, from before Castile and Morocco learned how to exist beneath the same political roof without trying to cut each other's throats every season."

Edward looked up. "A royal Miracle-grade treasure is not something people casually bring to a neighbour's feast. Are you giving it to me?"

"No. I am not that generous."

The Sultan put one hand on the edge of the box. "I am lending it to you until you return to Marrakesh." His eyes flicked towards Remi. "A loan requires a return date."

The Sultan smiled slightly. "I will not have that child grow up telling people the Sultan of Marrakesh sent his father into Scotland with one sword and several philosophical observations."

Edward lifted Stormroar from the box. The pistol was heavier than it appeared. Heat from the barrel passed through the bandage around his palm. He raised it to eye level without placing a finger near the trigger. "If you've gone to the trouble of bringing this, I need to know what it does before Remi decides Father has been given a new toy."

"Ordinary lead shot. The Vestigium within the barrel amplifies momentum and pressure at discharge. At close range, impact can approach a heavy cannon firing directly."

The Sultan saw Edward glance towards the house. "And before some idiotic experiment occurs to you, do not test it in your yard."

Edward lowered the weapon. "I appreciate your accurate assessment of my curiosity."

"I am assessing my experience with officers."

Abd al-Rahman tapped the box. "Stormroar reloads slowly, recoils brutally, and if fired indoors can deafen everyone you intended to save. It does not make the wielder immortal." His expression barely changed. "In other words, it is dangerous in precisely the way every good weapon is dangerous."

Edward placed the pistol back.

The Sultan closed the box, keeping one hand on the lid. "Stormroar is borrowed property. Do not turn it into a medal or an excuse to die beautifully."

Edward nodded. "I understand."

"Then return it to Marrakesh intact." Abd al-Rahman removed his hand. "If convenient, return the man carrying it intact as well."

The Sultan put on his cloak and started towards the gate. When he reached Edward, he stopped again. "One last thing."

Edward looked at him.

"When you meet Wallace, if kneeling buys something worthy, kneel."

Edward raised an eyebrow. Abd al-Rahman smiled. "But if he refuses to listen, Stormroar may help make the negotiation less theoretical."

For the first time since Criston Wallace's name entered the feast, Edward laughed without forcing it. The Sultan and his two guards passed through the gate and disappeared into the falling snow. Those remaining in the yard watched until all three figures were lost behind the neighbouring roofs.

Edward looked down at the cedar box in his hands. Borrowed weapon. Borrowed authority. Borrowed time. Unlike a promise, each of those things came with an expectation of return.

After the Sultan left, no one tried to force the feast back into its earlier mood. The remaining meat was divided, food wrapped for the road, and families began saying their farewells one by one.

Omar embraced Edward hard enough to press the bandage on his hand into the old man's back. Martha gave Juliet a small bag of bread for the journey and began crying before she managed to finish the sentence she had been trying to say.

Other households left carrying smoked meat, soup bones, or simply a scrap of paper with the Spencer family's new address written on it, provided letters still knew how to cross the sea. Victoria sent two clerks back to the Governor's residence with the missing-person ledger so it could be copied before Marco took the original north-east.

Edward kept the Beaumont note in the inside pocket of his own coat. Night had grown late. Fresh snow was already filling the trampled footprints in the yard. Beneath the emptied feast tents, only a handful of neighbours remained to help clear tables. The Spencers were left with Victoria, Marco, and Romeo.

Victoria fastened her cloak as if preparing to leave. Juliet stopped her. "You're truly waking your entire escort in the middle of the night just to ride a few streets back to the Governor's residence?"

Victoria paused at the clasp. "There is a proper bed there. And an entire city expects me to govern it tomorrow. Your house is already crowded. I see no need to wedge a Governor into it as well."

"My house just fed more than a hundred people in the yard." Juliet waved towards the back room. "One more person sleeping here will not bring the walls down. Besides, I would hate to acquire a reputation for treating Ed's closest old friend poorly."

Victoria looked towards Edward for judgement. He raised both hands immediately. "Do not appeal to me. I lost all authority over sleeping arrangements in this house some time ago."

Romeo added, "I can testify that he never possessed any."

Juliet ignored him.

She pointed at Marco and Romeo. "You two stay as well. We're going to the station early."

Marco nodded.

Romeo looked at the table on which he had fallen asleep the night before and shuddered. "But not face-down on that table again."

"You may sleep on the floor."

"Juliet, your hospitality is legendary."

"If you dislike it, the cattle shed still has space."

Romeo leaned towards Marco. "The floor sounds excellent."

Remi had reached the stage of exhaustion where he could barely stand but still insisted on carrying cups. Edward lifted him before the boy could protest. "I can walk." The words came while Remi's head was already falling against his father's neck.

"I know." Edward adjusted his hold. "If I put you down, you'll be asleep in the yard within ten paces. We have an early train. Save your strength so you can complain about the cold onboard."

Remi rubbed one eye. "Is Uncle Marco really coming with us? What if he changes his mind at the station?"

Marco, rolling the last of the canvas, answered for himself. "I'm travelling with you as far as Tangier. Then I separate for Fes. That means you have an entire train journey in which to annoy me."

"Then remember to tell me old stories about Father before we split up."

Edward looked at Marco with open threat. "If you tell him the stories currently entering your mind, I will throw you off at the first station."

Marco tossed the canvas onto the cart. "Then I shall make certain to select the most exciting one. Remi deserves to know his father endured a deeply embarrassing youth."

Remi was nearly asleep, but he still tightened both arms around Edward's neck. Edward carried him to bed, removed the boots, and tucked the blanket to his chin.

"Don't oversleep, Father."

"I have never overslept and missed a train in my life." Edward pulled the sleeping cap away from his eyes.

"But Uncle Romeo says you once fell asleep inside an ammunition store."

Edward's hand stopped.

From the front room came Romeo's voice. "I never said which day."

Remi giggled and pulled the blanket higher. "Good night, Father."

"Good night." Edward closed the bedroom door.

In the front room, Juliet had already laid three thin mattresses near the hearth. Marco removed his sword and rested it against the wall.

Romeo looked at the mattresses, then at the bedroom door, then back at Edward. "Wait." He pointed first at Edward, then at the floor. "This is his house. His wife is sleeping in the bedroom. Why is he on the floor with us?"

Juliet walked past carrying blankets without slowing. "Because Victoria is sharing the room with me. She is a guest. All three of you have slept on ship decks in freezing weather, so one night on a floor should not defeat you."

Edward raised an eyebrow. "I am impressed by how thoroughly this arrangement was decided before anyone informed me."

"You're becoming accustomed to marriage."

Juliet set down the blankets and looked at Victoria. "Does the arrangement suit you?"

Victoria leaned against the doorway. "Best logistical solution proposed all evening."

Edward pulled his blanket from the pile. "I knew you would describe it that way."

Marco lay down on the first mattress. "Stop resisting."

Romeo dropped onto the next one. "I prefer sleeping on deck. At least then two women do not seize the bed and expect gratitude."

Juliet threw a blanket directly into his face.

"Sleep, platinum hair."

The bedroom door closed.

None of the three men slept immediately.

The hearth had enough wood to last almost until morning, but the far corners of the room were still cold. Stormroar's cedar box rested beneath the chair by the wall. Edward's wrapped sabre lay beside his luggage.

Romeo lay on his back with both hands behind his head. "Every time I think about that old man, I become annoyed again. Not because of his manner. Because some of what he said is impossible to argue with."

Marco turned towards him. "Which part?"

Romeo pulled the blanket higher. "The part about lives not carrying equal value in war. I heard it and realised I have spent half my life operating on exactly that principle." He stared at the ceiling. "Once, on the Danish front, my unit slipped behind a force pressing our defence. I saw two things at once. A group of our men pinned beneath an embankment, and the enemy command carriage withdrawing north." Romeo brought one hand from the blanket. His index finger curled into the exact position it would take on a trigger. "I only had enough men for one objective." He paused. "I chased the carriage. Twelve of ours died beneath the embankment before help reached them. I took the enemy commander's head."

Romeo looked towards Edward. "Ten minutes later, three battalions ahead lost coordination. Their line broke in sections, and our left wing opened a retreat corridor." His hand lowered. "I remember all twelve names. If you put me back there tomorrow, I make the same choice." That was the part that angered him. "Twelve of ours against one man on the other side. His head really did weigh more than all twelve combined."

Edward watched him. Romeo had described hunting commanders many times, usually like a gambler recounting a successful hand. Edward had never heard him speak about the men left outside the chase.

Marco looked at the ceiling a while before answering. "I heard the Sultan differently." He pulled one arm from his blanket and rested it over his stomach. "At Rennes, the French had nearly four times my strength. If I met them in open ground, I would not hold until noon." Marco's voice took on the quiet precision of a report. "I destroyed two roads, blocked junctions with supply wagons, forced their guns into streets too narrow to turn, and made cavalry fight on foot."

He paused. "Then I placed one company inside the western workshops where I knew the enemy could see them." Marco looked at his palm. "Seventy-eight men held that sector for almost two hours. More than half never came back." No one interrupted. "Five French battalions diverted from the main axis just to crush them." He turned his hand, studying the calluses. "At midday, the French still outnumbered us four to one on paper. They simply could not find enough space anywhere to bring four men against one."

Marco's voice remained level. "I never believed those seventy-eight deserved life less than everyone else. But for exactly two hours, they were the weight holding five battalions in the wrong place." He exhaled. "I know the decision was correct. That is why the Sultan's words are uncomfortable."

A log split in the fire. For several seconds, no one spoke.

Edward folded his coat beneath his head. "Then where is the difference? Romeo exchanged twelve men for one commander. You exchanged seventy-eight to hold five battalions. We calculate like that in war." He looked from one man to the other. "Why am I different?"

Marco turned towards him. "Because you do not calculate your own life the way you calculate ours."

Edward frowned. "I calculate effect."

"If it were me, you would try to keep me alive because I could command tomorrow. If it were Romeo, you would also search for another option before throwing him away." Marco propped himself on one elbow. "When it is you, the only question you ask is what your death can purchase."

"Because I'm the commander."

"Exactly because you're the commander."

Marco pointed towards Romeo. "He hunts leaders because losing one man can disorient hundreds behind him. You understand that principle when it applies to an enemy, to me, to him." His eyes settled on Edward. "Only not to yourself."

Romeo tapped one finger against the mattress. "And if the enemy learns you will always exchange yourself for the right hostage, they no longer need to hunt you. They just put the right person in the right place."

Edward stared at the ceiling. "Then how do I know when I am paying a necessary price and when I am simply throwing myself away?"

Marco answered after a moment. "Alone? You don't." He settled back. "If you're already volunteering to step onto the scale, at least let someone else inspect the arithmetic."

Romeo shook his head and pulled the blanket to his chest. "This is a ridiculous sight. Three men almost thirty years old curled on a floor in Marrakesh, about to take three different roads at dawn, discussing what one human life is worth." He sighed. "If our Academy instructors could see us, they'd revoke every medal."

Edward looked between them. "If someone had told me fifteen years ago that one day we would lie in a snowbound Marrakesh after England collapsed while a Moorish Sultan lectured me about not dying stupidly, I would have told him to drink less."

Marco almost smiled. "No. You would have drawn your sword and challenged him."

Romeo waved one hand. "Nonsense. Young Ed challenged men. Put a woman in front of him and he became another species entirely."

Edward turned his head. "Do not begin."

Romeo rolled onto one elbow, suddenly much more awake. "Oh? You already know which story I mean?"

From beyond the bedroom door, Juliet's clear voice entered the room. "Ed, what colour was Victoria's corset?"

Edward went rigid. Marco turned his face into the wall. Romeo clamped both hands over his mouth before the laugh escaped. Edward stared at the bedroom door like a battery had just opened fire from it.

"Juliet."

"I'm asking seriously." Her voice remained perfectly calm. "Victoria says dark blue. I said if you truly did not look, you could not possibly know. We require a witness."

Edward opened his mouth and closed it again.

Romeo whispered, "Do not answer. Preserve what remains of Royal Navy honour."

Marco still faced the wall. "Too late. Look at him. He remembers. Very clearly."

"Both of you shut up."

Edward dragged the blanket over his chest as though cloth might protect what remained of his dignity.

Victoria spoke from the bedroom. "I would like an answer as well. For fifteen years I have not decided whether you passed the changing room accidentally, or whether the book you were holding upside down contained something unusually fascinating."

Romeo made a strangled sound and buried his face in a pillow. Edward pulled the blanket over half his face and surrendered. "Dark blue. Lavender lace." Silence lasted exactly one second. Marco and Romeo exploded. Romeo laughed loudly enough for Remi to turn in the next room. Marco sat upright clutching his stomach.

Inside the bedroom, Juliet laughed until she could speak again. "Thank you. I win."

Edward stared at the ceiling. "I hate everyone in this house."

Victoria answered at once. "Begin by blaming your excellent memory. I was changing behind a screen. You only saw a few seconds before I threw a towel at your face."

"It was not deliberate."

"And yet someone stood outside the door nearly a minute afterwards, holding a book upside down."

Marco sat up. "Wait. Was that the famous incident in the senior women's corridor?"

Edward snapped towards him. "You knew about that?"

"I gave you the book. You said you needed a legitimate reason to walk through that corridor. I genuinely thought you intended to return it to an instructor."

Romeo lifted his head from the pillow. "The book is new information to me. I remember him spending almost an hour choosing a coat."

"Forty minutes," Edward corrected automatically.

Romeo pointed at him in triumph. "See? He even remembers the duration."

Juliet's voice came through the door. "Forty minutes?"

Victoria answered, "And there are more stories."

Edward half-sat. "No. There are no more stories. Everyone sleep."

Victoria continued anyway. "Once he waited almost two hours in the rain to ask me to go walking. When I finally came down, he claimed he had simply happened to be passing."

Marco laughed. "I remember that. He spent the next day sick."

"I was not sick."

"You drank two kettles of hot tea and slept fourteen hours."

Romeo joined immediately. "What about the time he bought every pear tart in the dining hall because Vic casually mentioned wanting one?"

Edward glared at him.

"I bought them for the table."

"There were four people at the table," Marco said, "and you brought twelve."

Juliet sounded delighted. "Twelve?"

Victoria called through the wall. "I ate one."

Romeo put a hand over his chest. "Thanks to the leftovers, I learned to appreciate Ed's love. It fed his friends quite well."

Edward sat in the centre of the mattresses with both hands over his head. "I survived storms, Inverness, and a Sultan publicly dismantling my pride in front of a hundred people. None of that was as terrible as tonight."

"Take your time," Victoria said. "Juliet hasn't heard about the winter festival."

Edward looked up in alarm. "Victoria, please."

Juliet answered immediately.

"What happened at the winter festival?"

Marco lay down again. "Ah. The glove story."

Romeo whistled. "A classic."

Edward pointed at both men. "Traitors."

Victoria told it in a perfectly even voice. "That winter I lost one glove. Edward gave me his, then spent nearly three hours walking the festival with one bare hand. Afterwards he insisted he was not cold."

Juliet pulled the blanket to her shoulders. "That sounds familiar. My husband still has the habit."

"There's more," Marco added. "His hand was swollen the next day and he insisted it came from sword practice."

Romeo raised his hand as though taking an oath. "For the next three months, whenever Victoria appeared in the dining hall, Ed would suddenly discover he was hungry."

Edward collapsed onto his mattress. "I withdraw my earlier criticism. The Sultan was correct. There should be special circumstances under which a man is permitted to die."

"Do not borrow the Sultan's words to escape," Juliet called. "You still have to live long enough to answer me."

Edward resisted several seconds more, then began laughing himself. Marco joined him. Romeo had to shove the pillow over his face before he woke Remi.

Eventually the laughter softened.

Marco spoke first. "Actually, this is good."

Edward turned his head. "What is?"

"Remembering that before all the titles, we worried about who liked whom, who won at fencing, and what we were eating for supper." Marco looked towards the ceiling. "Sometimes we remember war so precisely that we forget we had lives between the battles."

Romeo lowered the pillow. "I never forget those parts. My memories generally smell of alcohol."

Edward adjusted his blanket. "At dawn, you stay in Marrakesh. Marco heads for Fes. I go to Tangier and farther." His eyes moved towards the closed bedroom door. "Tonight, perhaps the most important matter in the world may remain the dark-blue corset."

Juliet called back at once.

"I heard that. Are you nostalgic?" Edward closed his eyes. "I said it loudly so you would hear."

Victoria answered. "Liar. You were terrible at lying in the Academy too."

Romeo burst out laughing again.

"Enough stuttering. Sleep, Romeo," Edward and Marco said together.

On the other side of the wall, Juliet put the final shirt into its chest before lying down. Victoria drew her blanket over her legs and could still hear the three men arguing in the front room.

Juliet looked towards the wall.

"Thank you. I've lived with him nine years and apparently there are still entire archives."

"Do not use them all at once," Victoria said. "Edward has excellent defences against artillery. The past is another matter."

"I have all day on the train tomorrow. I'll ration them."

Edward's voice came through the wall.

"You do remember these walls are thin?"

"Yes," Juliet replied.

Victoria added, "That is why we made no effort to whisper."

Marco laughed. Romeo slapped the floor like an audience member applauding a particularly satisfying play.

Eventually the voices faded. None of the three men solved the question the Sultan had left behind, but neither did they turn it into another sentence against themselves on their final night in Marrakesh. Edward lay between two old friends listening to logs settle in the hearth and the voices of Victoria and Juliet finally quiet beyond the wall. Stormroar rested beneath the chair. His sabre lay wrapped beside the luggage. Outside, snow covered the last footprints from the feast. At dawn they would leave Marrakesh behind with the cattle shed, the market, and every road that had become familiar.

For one final night, however, the house still held all of them.

Marrakesh station was far busier than Edward expected the next morning. Thin bands of snow lay across the glass roof and iron ribs of the concourse. Beneath them, heat from great coal braziers filled the platforms with the smell of smoke and coffee.

Freight trains occupied the outer lines, every wagon stamped with military supply marks or food allotment seals. On platform three, the engine that would carry the Spencers towards Tangier sent columns of white steam into the roof.

Edward stood beside a collection of luggage he had believed packed the night before. At the station it had somehow acquired two more food bags from neighbours, a crate of Remi's books, the cedar box containing Stormroar, and the wrapped sabre Edward refused to let any porter touch.

Marco saw him wrestling with the heaviest chest and pulled the strap out of his hand. "You have a sword, a pistol, and an expression suggesting you're marching into battle. That is sufficient burden for one morning."

Edward glanced at the chest. "Half my household's clothes are in there."

"Then I shall take particular care." Marco adjusted the strap and carried it towards the passenger coach. "If I damage them, I suspect Juliet will kill me before war or my own wife gets the opportunity."

Juliet stood a short distance away checking tickets and travel papers. "He reads a situation more accurately than you do."

Edward had not yet answered when Victoria spoke behind him. "You've only just discovered that?"

The Governor arrived with two members of her staff. A dusting of snow had settled across the shoulders of her heavy cloak, and her blond hair was tucked beneath a fur hat.

Romeo pointed towards Marco. "I offered objections last night."

"Your objections lost value when you aimed a pistol at the Sultan."

Romeo put a hand over his chest and stepped back as though accused of a terrible injustice. "One day history will remember that I was a decorated officer."

"We all remember," Marco called from the luggage cart. "That is precisely what makes it concerning."

Edward looked at the four friends gathered around him beneath the station roof. The previous night they had slept beneath one roof and argued through a wall about things too trivial to deserve history. Now the luggage was stacked, Juliet held the tickets, and the rails ahead were preparing to divide them again. Victoria checked the station clock and touched Edward's sleeve.

"Edward Spencer."

"What?"

"Stand still."

Before he could ask why, Victoria turned to Juliet. The teasing left her face. "Juliet, there is something I should have done fifteen years ago. Would you object if I kissed your husband?"

Edward looked from one woman to the other. "Wait. Are the two of you negotiating this while I'm standing here?"

Juliet folded the travel paper and slipped it into her pocket. "One."

"Juliet."

"On the cheek," she added. "And I want to watch."

Marco released the chest strap. Romeo turned fully around. Victoria stepped closer. "Fifteen years is probably long enough to reward a young man who waited two hours in the rain, bought twelve pear tarts, and walked an entire winter festival with one bare hand without ever managing to take the next step."

Edward recognised danger too late. "Vic, those memories were thoroughly excavated last night. Leave them buried."

"Certainly not."

She placed one hand on his shoulder and kissed his cheek. Romeo's shout was loud enough to make several nearby passengers turn. Even Marco whistled, an image Edward had never expected from the Balancer at this hour of the morning. Edward still held one luggage strap and could not produce a response fast enough.

Romeo doubled over. "The Pathmaker has finally found a road he cannot take."

Edward noticed Juliet still smiling, but her hands had paused over the papers.

He straightened immediately. "I did absolutely nothing."

"I know."

"She initiated it."

"Edward, I am standing directly in front of you."

Victoria stepped back, plainly satisfied. "At last. The reward has reached its intended recipient."

Romeo leaned towards Marco. "I wager he sleeps in a corridor tonight."

Marco shook his head. "I never gamble on a result that certain."
