Edward pointed at both men. "Do not forget I once commanded you."

"Juliet decides where you sleep," Romeo replied. "I know which authority concerns me more."

Juliet walked over, brushed snow from Edward's shoulder, and straightened his collar. "All right. You have received your reward from youth." She touched his other cheek. "From now on, keep this side for me."

"I possess two cheeks."

"I know."

Edward wisely asked nothing else.

Remi had watched the whole exchange with the deep confusion of a child unable to understand how a kiss on the cheek could become a military incident. When Victoria turned away, he tugged gently at her sleeve. "Aunt Vic."

She looked back. "Yes?"

He hesitated. "Are you sad?"

Victoria lowered herself onto one knee despite the cold platform beneath her cloak. At that height, her blue eyes were level with his. "Of course I am."

She adjusted his woollen hat. "Your house has been so loud for the last few days that I almost forgot everyone would soon go in different directions." Her expression softened. "But before I become sad, I need to tell you something."

Remi immediately straightened.

Several steps away, Edward listened.

"When this journey is over, your father may not be home very often. Duty can carry him very far away. I don't know when the world will be calm enough for that to stop."

Edward's smile disappeared.

Juliet stood beside him with the travel papers pressed to her chest.

"But you do not need to hurry into becoming an adult just because your father is absent," Victoria continued. "You are still a child. Live like one." She touched his coat. "Study properly. Help your mother with the work you are old enough to do. And when she calls you, do not wait until the third time to answer."

Remi lowered his face at the mention of being called three times.

Juliet folded her arms but did not interrupt.

Victoria placed both hands on his shoulders. "When you are grown, I hope you become a man people can rely upon." She nodded towards Edward, Marco, and Romeo. "You don't need to be an admiral, a Royal Guard, or a hero. Only stand firm when someone turns towards you looking for support."

Romeo began to arrange his face into a moving expression.

Marco glanced at him.

"Do not ruin this."

"I haven't said anything."

For once, Romeo obeyed.

Remi looked at the three men and lingered longest on his father. Then he turned back to Victoria. "I'll try."

Victoria frowned immediately.

"That word again."

Remi hurried to correct himself.

"I will."

"Better."

He pulled down the edge of his hat. "The last few days were really fun." Victoria waited. "Aunt Isabella came to the house. Uncle Marco. Uncle Romeo. You. Everyone stayed last night and talked and laughed." Remi glanced towards his father, as though uncertain whether he had just disclosed something forbidden. "The house hasn't been that full in a long time. Now everyone has to say goodbye again. I don't like it."

The group stopped joking.

Remi looked at his boots, still holding one edge of Victoria's cloak. She put both hands on his shoulders again. "Then remember the good days first. Let the adults worry about the farewells."

Remi nodded.

"I'll write to you. And Uncle Romeo and Uncle Marco. And Aunt Isabella."

"I'll send a courier to your house as soon as I can." Victoria narrowed her eyes in mock severity. "But if the letter to Isabella is longer than the letter to me, I will consider it treason."

Edward folded his arms.

"Vic."

"You be quiet."

Remi laughed.

Romeo immediately tried to add something. Victoria ignored him and changed subjects while still kneeling before the boy. "Speaking of Isabella, I have one extremely important question before you board."

Remi gave her all his concentration. "What?"

Victoria straightened his collar. "Between me and Isabella, who is more beautiful?"

Marco bent over the luggage lock as though suddenly fascinated by it. Romeo turned away, shoulders shaking. Juliet stared at Victoria. The Governor had just given the boy a heartfelt lesson about childhood and reliability and had now voluntarily walked into the most obvious trap imaginable.

Remi thought carefully.

"Isabella."

Romeo broke first. Marco braced both hands on the chest and lowered his head. Edward tried and failed to remain dignified. Juliet managed an extra second before turning away. Victoria froze in her kneeling position. "I just gave you all that wisdom."

Remi realised the danger. "But you're very beautiful too."

"Too late."

Victoria pulled his hat down over his eyes, took both cheeks in her hands through the scarf, and shook him gently. "Little traitor."

"Aunt Vic!" Remi laughed while trying to push the hat back up. "I didn't say you weren't beautiful."

"You still chose her."

When he recovered his sight, he tried to explain. "Isabella has gold eyes. You have gold hair but blue eyes. You're different."

Victoria looked up at Edward in defeat. "Did you never teach your child to lie politely?"

Edward was still laughing. "I taught him to tell the truth."

Juliet added, "I tried to teach manners. His father destroyed the effort."

Remi tugged Victoria's sleeve. "Are you angry?"

She held the expression several seconds before surrendering. Victoria straightened his hat and smoothed the hair crushed across his forehead. "No. I have merely been reminded that gubernatorial power has extremely clear limits."

She stood and raised one hand. "Enough. Everyone quiet."

The first train whistle sounded at that exact moment. The joke vanished beneath the fact of departure. A railway employee moved down the platform calling passengers aboard. Steam thickened around the engine. Porters shut the luggage compartment and checked the locks one final time.

When the departure minute approached, Romeo turned first towards Remi. He knelt and held out a fist. "All right, little man. Next time I see you, you had better be at least one handspan taller."

Remi tapped his small fist against Romeo's. "What if I'm not?"

Romeo rubbed his chin. "Then I blame your father. I will invent the exact reason later."

Remi suddenly threw both arms around his neck. Romeo had to catch himself with one hand against the platform. He muttered a curse, then hugged the boy tightly.

"Write to me," Remi whispered.

"Of course."

"And don't lie in the letters."

Romeo patted his back. "That part I cannot confidently promise."

Remi released him and immediately hugged Victoria. She pulled him into the heavy cloak, chin resting on his woollen hat. "Be good to your mother. Do not irritate your father more than necessary. If you reach Madrid and meet Isabella, under no circumstances mention the question from five minutes ago."

Remi stepped back.

"Why?"

"Because I would like to retain enough dignity to govern Marrakesh."

"I'll try."

Victoria pressed two fingers to her temple.

"Again."

The phrase had begun the previous night and already become a private Spencer-family joke.

Edward laughed.

Victoria embraced Juliet next. It lasted longer than any greeting between them before. They spoke several sentences beyond Edward's hearing. Juliet nodded and held her a little longer before letting go. Then Victoria placed a thick envelope into Juliet's hand. "A letter of introduction. Use it or ignore it as you wish. Inside are the addresses of two people in Madrid who can help with work and local arrangements." Her voice sharpened slightly. "They are not caretakers and they are not there to supervise you."

Juliet placed the envelope carefully inside her coat. "Thank you."

"You don't need to thank me." Victoria nodded towards Edward. "Only make certain he does not turn moving house into a military deployment in which you have no vote."

"You can be confident. I have experience."

Edward lifted the strap of his bag.

"I remain clearly visible."

"That is why we are speaking loudly."

Romeo clasped Edward's hand, pulled him into a hard embrace, and struck his shoulder twice. "Promise me you won't die in the north."

Edward tightened a hand on his friend's shoulder. "You stay alive here."

"Easy. Marrakesh adores me."

Victoria answered, "Marrakesh is enduring you."

"Only a difference of phrasing."

Marco returned after the luggage had been loaded. He shook Victoria's hand, then drew Romeo into a fierce embrace. Neither man mentioned when they might meet again. Marco punched his chest lightly. "When I'm gone, do not point a pistol at another monarch."

Romeo put a hand over his heart. "I shall attempt restraint until you return."

"That is not the answer I wanted."

Romeo slapped Marco's shoulder. "Then you know me too well."

The second whistle sounded. Railway staff began closing the forward doors. Edward helped Juliet onto the step. Remi climbed after her by himself and firmly rejected every offer to be carried. Marco handed the final chest to a porter and boarded after Edward. The moment they reached the compartment, Remi pressed himself against the window.

Victoria stood below waving. Romeo cupped both hands around his mouth. "REMI! DON'T FORGET THAT ISABELLA IS PRETTIER!" Victoria struck him in the shoulder. The nearby carriage burst into laughter.

Remi turned red and hid half behind Edward, though he kept one hand visible to wave. Juliet bit her lower lip so hard it almost lost colour. Marco turned completely towards the interior. Edward stared at Romeo through the glass. "I should have let the Sultan shoot you." Romeo could not hear him. Somehow, he still raised a thumb.

The locomotive jerked. Steel wheels began to roll. Marrakesh station moved slowly backwards. Victoria walked several steps beside the train before stopping. Romeo kept waving until a steel support column covered him.

Remi knelt on the seat with both palms on the window. He tried to find them again through every gap between lamps and posts, but with each increase in speed the familiar faces became smaller. At the end of the platform, Victoria was only a dark shape beneath golden hair. Romeo was an arm still raised. Then a snow-covered warehouse hid them both.

Remi pressed his face close to the glass and watched Marrakesh begin to recede. Red earthen roofs under snow, watchtowers, chimneys, and the line of Vestigium lamps in the centre passed one after another. Farther away, Edward suddenly recognised the road leading towards the Spencer farm. The house disappeared behind other roofs before he could find the cattle shed. Juliet watched too, one hand on the back of Remi's seat until the final rows of buildings vanished. Across from them, Marco rested his hands on his knees beside a folded military cloak and followed the rails north.

Marrakesh disappeared from the window. Through all the years of exile, the city had never asked whether the Spencers still possessed a nation to return to. It had simply given them a roof beneath six years of ice. The train continued north. It carried the adopted children of Marrakesh away from red earth covered in snow, leaving behind a place they no longer needed blood or birthplace to call by the simplest name they knew.

Home.

The journey from Marrakesh to Tangier-Ceuta was quieter than Edward expected. After the morning at the station, nearly everyone in the compartment was short of sleep. The steady rhythm of iron wheels soon did what goodbyes could not.

Juliet rested her head beside the window, one hand holding the blanket across Remi. The boy had fallen asleep almost as soon as the train cleared the outskirts of Marrakesh, clutching a cloth bag against his chest as though the whole house they had just left were somehow inside it.

Marco sat opposite with his military cloak folded beside him and a file on Fes across his knees. He read several pages before sleep finally took him as the train passed through snow-covered fields in northern Morocco.

Only Edward remained awake. Signal posts flashed past the glass. A parallel rail vanished into mist ahead. Every time the train leaned through a curve, steel shrieked briefly and settled again into its steady cadence.

The long-distance carriages Edward had known in youth suddenly belonged to another age. Marco woke some time later and rubbed the back of his neck. Edward was still staring outside.

"England never built a railway system on this scale."

"Neither has France."

Edward looked over. "I remember the Academy years. Scholars were still arguing whether laying stone roads for carriages over a few dozen miles could ever justify the cost." He tapped the glass lightly. "We left Marrakesh not long ago and have already crossed a distance that once took nearly a week."

Marco lowered the file. "If you want to thank someone, thank Isabella. She forced every new line to use common rail gauges, engines, and parts. Then she forced workshops hundreds of miles apart to operate as one system." He nodded towards the floor beneath them. "Without that, the fastest engine in the world dies at the first station missing one particular component."

Edward smiled. "That sounds like her."

"How long the advantage lasts is another question. Anything that works will eventually attract someone who wants to take it apart and understand why."

Edward turned towards the window so his laughter would not wake Juliet and Remi.

Marco reopened his file.

The iron train carried the four of them along one final shared road before each went a different way.

Edward looked over the dense pages again. "Sleep a little longer. Tangier is still some distance."

Marco kept reading. "You should sleep. Men about to collapse from exhaustion always say, 'I'm not tired yet.'"

Edward looked back through the glass. "You've started talking like Juliet."

"I needed no teacher. Twenty-five years of friendship with you provided the evidence."

* * *

The train entered thick mist. Only when the vast steel roofs of Tangier-Ceuta station appeared behind a window clouded with steam did the compartment begin to wake.

Remi woke last. He sat upright with one side of his hair standing almost vertically and looked around as though he had missed something essential. "Mama, how long was I asleep?"

Juliet folded the blanket. "Long enough for me to enjoy most of the journey in peace."

The whistle sounded beyond the window. The locomotive slowed. Steel wheels ground along the track as the train entered a space that made both Juliet and Remi look up. Tangier-Ceuta station was so broad that the glass roof almost disappeared among black iron trusses. Pipes ran along the arches and released warm air over the platforms, melting snow as soon as it touched the glass. People below wore only light wool coats. For a family arriving from Marrakesh, the sight bordered on luxury.

The compartment door opened. Marco stepped down first, received the largest chest from a porter, and placed it on the platform before taking Remi's book crate. Edward followed. Juliet came next with a child who still looked only partly awake.

Isabella was waiting a short distance ahead. The Queen sat on a stone bench beside a steel column with her legs crossed and a ceramic cup of tea held in both hands. Instead of the crimson velvet cloak Edward usually associated with her, she wore a precise grey-white military uniform with a high collar. Her dark brown hair had been gathered neatly behind her head. Fredo stood behind her right shoulder, blond hair swept back, both hands clasped behind him.

Isabella saw Marco first and set down the tea. He approached, stopped at the proper distance, and bowed. "Your Majesty." Then he turned to Fredo. "Been a while." Fredo nodded. Marco gave exactly one nod in return.

Isabella observed the rigid greeting for only a moment before Fredo drew a thin file from inside his coat. "New intelligence from the east."

Marco broke the seal. He skimmed the first page and slowed on the second. Even from several paces away Edward saw his tongue press against the inside of his cheek. "When?"

"Confirmed during the night," Fredo said. "Western Roman forces breached the Algerian line earlier than expected. Several of our forward units are withdrawing towards western concentration points."

Marco read the line again. He closed the file between both hands. "Excellent. I haven't reached Fes and the enemy has already volunteered to revise my operational plan."

Isabella took the report back, read one additional line, and closed it. "I had hoped you would have several more days." Before Marco could answer, she stepped forward and embraced him. The embrace lasted only seconds. When she released him, both hands remained on his shoulders. "Do your best. Fes will not give you many opportunities to correct mistakes, and I do not have another person I can simply put in your place." Her grip tightened. "Hold the line for me, Marco. Then come back."

"Understood, Your Majesty."

Marco blinked once and lowered his voice as if sharing military intelligence. "But Your Majesty, if Millenia learns that you embraced me in the middle of a crowded station, Fes may not be the place posing the greatest threat to my life."

Isabella stepped back.

"I will issue a royal certificate confirming it was the will of the Queen."

"That certificate is exactly what would get me confined to the house."

Edward reached them as Marco turned back towards the Spencer family. Marco looked at the luggage scattered across the platform, then checked the station clock. "So this is where our journey ends."

Juliet offered her hand first. "Thank you for travelling with us."

Marco took it in both of his. "Juliet, if you have any difficulty in Madrid, find Millenia. She is already there with Dante."

"Your son is seven now, isn't he?"

"Seven." Marco nodded. "Dante Stones. Much gentler than his father. Fortunately."

Isabella answered before Juliet could ask more. "Millenia and Dante were moved to Madrid early. The Spencer family is going there as well."

Juliet turned. "Wasn't our destination Barcelona, Your Majesty?"

"Not any longer." Isabella's tone made the change sound already carved into law. "I received three more reports from the Pyrenees after leaving Marrakesh. French pressure is rising faster than projected, and Barcelona is nearer the threat axis than I am willing to accept. Last night I ordered the essential administrative organs transferred to Madrid."

Marco looked at Edward. "You sleep through one railway journey and the location of the capital changes."

Edward turned to Isabella. "Now I understand why Marco says the railway can never match your speed."

Isabella raised her chin. "At least you're keeping up."

Marco bent to retrieve his bag. "All right. If I survive Fes and come back..."

Edward raised a finger immediately. "Stop. Sentences beginning that way have never improved anyone's luck."

Marco stared. "I wasn't finished. I meant if I return before you do, I intend to eat a full meal at your house in Madrid."

Edward considered that. "You've planted your own funeral banner, then tried to repair it with dinner."

Marco shrugged. "Then it should be harmless."

Edward stepped forward. They embraced. Marco struck his back twice. Edward kept a hand on his shoulder several seconds before releasing him.

Steam roared beneath the station roof. Edward raised a fist. Marco looked at it and brought his own forward. Their knuckles met. Neither withdrew. Marco's thumb tapped Edward's knuckles twice, the old rhythm they had used since the Academy. Edward answered with one beat.

To the east side of the station, Legion Two, Tercio de la Balanza, was already assembled. Artillery wagons and supply cars stretched almost beyond the roof. A whistle echoed through the beams. Marco looked towards the soldiers waiting for him, then back at Edward. Their fists still touched when he spoke the line the four of them once used whenever units had to separate. "See you on the other side of this war."

Edward held his eyes, gripped Marco's shoulder once, and let go. "Yes. We'll meet there."

Marco had barely turned when Remi came from Juliet's side and caught the edge of his cloak. "Uncle Marco, I'm sorry I slept almost the whole way." The words came quickly. "You said you would tell me stories from when Father was young. I thought I was only closing my eyes for a little while." Remi looked at his boots. "Father always says Uncle Romeo exaggerates and you tell the truth. I wanted to know which subjects Father was bad at, whether he ever got punished, whether he was as strict then as he is now."

Marco knelt until they were level. "You prepared an interrogation?"

Remi looked up and kept hold of the cloak. "I've been preparing since you said you'd travel with us. I also wanted to ask whether Father was ever afraid of anything." His voice dropped. "Now you're leaving and I don't know when I'll be able to ask."

Marco studied him several seconds and then ruffled the hair standing on one side. "Keep the list. Do not let your father see it, especially the last question."

Edward folded his arms behind them. "I heard everything."

Remi turned instantly.

"I didn't say anything bad."

"I know. That's the worrying part."

Marco smoothed several strands of hair from Remi's forehead. "In Madrid you'll meet Dante. My son. He's seven too, but the two of you are very different." Remi listened closely. "Dante is quiet. Gentle. It takes him a while to speak around strangers."

"Then I'll speak first. I can talk a lot."

"That I believe."

Marco almost smiled. "But do not use his silence as an excuse to drag him through every idea you invent. If he doesn't want to climb onto a roof, do not dare him. If he loses a game, do not keep laughing about it." His expression became slightly more serious. "And never decide that because he's gentle, he can be bullied."

Remi frowned as if accused. "I don't bully people. I just... talk too much sometimes." He brightened. "If Dante doesn't like roofs, I can show him maps. I have Father's map of England. I want to see your maps of Fes too."

At the mention of Fes, Marco tapped Remi lightly on the forehead. "Maps are fine. I have several at home. Millenia knows where they are. Ask her before you tear my study apart."

"I will." Remi adjusted the strap over his shoulder. "If you haven't come home before I meet Dante, I'll tell him you're still well." He thought a moment. "I'll play with him too, so he won't be lonely."

Marco rested a hand behind the boy's neck. "I don't need you to become an adult for Dante." His voice softened. "Both of you may simply be children. Play. Argue a reasonable amount. If he goes quiet, give him time. He's not weak. Only gentler than his father."

Remi tried to suppress a smile.

"I won't tell him that last part."

"Good judgement."

The boy stood there several seconds longer, then threw his arms around Marco's neck. This time Marco did not freeze. He embraced him immediately, one hand behind Remi's head, the other patting his back. "Come back," Remi whispered against his shoulder. "I still have questions. And if you don't come back, no one will tell me how foolish Father was when he was young."

Edward complained from behind them. Marco kept one hand at the back of Remi's neck. "I'll do everything I can to return and inspect whatever trouble you and Dante have caused in Madrid."

He released the boy enough to look at him. "If you meet Dante first, remember what I said. Do not bully my son."

Remi nodded firmly.

"I promise. But you have to come back too so you can watch him yourself."

"Fair bargain."

Marco ruffled his hair once more and rose. Isabella had been standing with folded arms. "Have the two of you just divided responsibility for managing children in the middle of my station?"

Marco fixed his collar. "Your Majesty may be reassured. I assigned the most dangerous part to Remi."

The boy immediately lifted his head.

"I can do it."

Juliet laughed.

Edward only shook his head.

Marco looked at each of them one last time, accepted his bag from Fredo, and pulled the strap over his shoulder. A short whistle came from the military lines. He did not delay again. Marco raised two fingers to his temple in farewell and entered the flow of soldiers, porters, and officers moving across the platform. Brown hair vanished behind felt hats. The dark cloak appeared several more times between gaps in the crowd, then was swallowed entirely.

Edward kept looking. Remi did the same, one hand holding the edge of Juliet's coat as though trying to memorise the exact point where Marco disappeared. Only when the Balancer could no longer be distinguished among his own legion did Isabella finish the last cold swallow of tea. "Come." Her eyes remained briefly on the eastern platform. "Marco has an entire front to reach, and we are not finished here either."

Isabella led them away from the military platforms through a broad corridor joining the civilian station. Tangier-Ceuta impressed Edward less through another great roof or another line of heating pipes than through what happened only a few dozen steps after the whistles of mobilisation faded.

Ordinary life immediately filled the space. A baker pulled trays of steaming brown loaves from an oven. Two elderly women sat beside a heating pillar sharing a newspaper. A group of children hurried past carrying slate boards, their woollen scarves tied loosely enough to suggest they had already forgotten the cold.

On the next track, a military train began to move. Field guns were chained to flat wagons. Soldiers crowded the windows. Two medical cars bearing Castilian insignia closed the line. People moved aside when the warning bell rang.

The moment the train passed, tea was poured again, children ran again, and a mother bent to correct her daughter's hat as though an army leaving the city were simply another event in the morning. Remi watched the military train vanish behind the steel columns, then looked back towards the civilian hall.

"Are we really at war here, Father? There are guns and soldiers, but people are buying things and going to school."

Edward rested a hand on his shoulder. "Yes. They have simply learned not to let war occupy the whole morning."

Isabella heard him and did not interrupt. She led them onward between vendors calling their prices and bowls being set down where the troop whistle had just left silence.

Fredo took two valises from Edward. Edward kept only the wrapped sabre and Stormroar's cedar case.

Isabella touched one finger to its lid. "The Sultan's pistol?"

"A loan. He said I have to return it myself."

"Then do not make him wait." She tapped the wood once and continued.

As they crossed the ticket hall, Isabella slowed beside Juliet. Her gaze settled on the hand around a luggage strap, where winter cracks and old calluses remained visible despite the ointment Juliet had used the previous night. "Is something wrong, Juliet?" Isabella extended her hand but did not touch until Juliet offered hers. "I had forgotten how hard the years in Marrakesh must have been on you." She turned Juliet's hand gently beneath the station light. "A woman's hands should be cared for. Instead you worked through cold and heavy labour to keep Edward and Remi alive. The skin is still split."

Her expression remained kind enough to make the words that followed more dangerous. "Do not worry. Once we reach Madrid, I will send for the best balms and herbal baths I can find. And I shall take you to proper dressmakers." Isabella's thumb moved lightly over one roughened knuckle. "A woman beside Edward should not have to look so worn by poverty."

Juliet held her gaze a moment longer. Then she drew her hand back and pulled the glove over her wrist. "They work. I'm not ashamed of them."

"I never said you should be." Isabella's court smile did not falter. "When we reach Madrid, I shall take you to the finest dressmakers at court myself. I shall have them choose the softest silks and brocades, to conceal the marks these years have left on you. A woman who sacrificed her youth to poverty for Edward deserves every luxury—even if it comes a little late."

Juliet did not lower her eyes. "Thank you for the offer. But Edward has seen me in torn clothes, covered in mud, covered in blood, and looking worse than this." Her tone remained perfectly civil. "He married me anyway. I think he can survive my hands."

Isabella went quiet for exactly one beat. Then the smile returned. "I know. Edward has always possessed certain remarkably consistent tastes."

Juliet raised an eyebrow. "At least we agree on one thing."

"Perhaps eventually there will be others." Isabella started walking again, then added as though returning to the practical matter. "I am still sending the balm. Cracked skin does not need to hurt simply to prove you can endure it."

Edward bent to correct Remi's scarf before anyone could ask him for an opinion. Fredo walked behind with the valises and became intensely interested in luggage.

* * *

The royal carriage waited outside the station. Warmth flowed from concealed metal vents beneath the seats, entirely free of coal smoke or sulphur. In its place drifted a light, sweet scent Edward did not recognise. He looked up. A silver pomander swayed near the window. "That smell is new. Don't tell me you've put another invention in the carriage."

Isabella turned the pomander between two fingers. "Cherry blossom. Oil from an island kingdom at the far edge of the East." She released it. "When the trees flower, people sit beneath them, drink, and spend whole afternoons watching petals fall."

Edward leaned back. "Now?"

"Especially now." Isabella watched the silver sphere swing. "Six years of winter and they still refuse to surrender something as useless as watching flowers. I find that admirable."

The carriage left the station square. Tangier-Ceuta did not resemble an enormous fortress, even though nearly everything in the city had been designed to become part of one if necessary. Main avenues were almost free of ice because heating pipes ran beneath the paving. Shops stood beneath glass-covered blocks. Bakeries displayed hot barley loaves. Tea houses set tables inside heated galleries. Coal workers leaving a shift crowded around a soup cart, their coats still grey with dust. A few buildings farther on, two elderly men played chess while a young woman led a child wrapped almost entirely in wool. Branch railway lines ran directly beside warehouses, taking coal, ammunition, and food towards the harbour.

Medical wagons crossed the avenues under military escort. Soldiers moved between civilians on their way to barracks. People yielded the road when necessary and continued with their lives.

Remi pressed his face against the glass. A passing cavalry unit held his attention only until he noticed children throwing snow in a schoolyard. Juliet had to pull his collar back twice because he kept leaning closer.

She watched a fish seller lift his basket out of the way of a supply wagon, then set it down and continue weighing the same fish. "In Marrakesh, one artillery convoy can stop a whole street. Here people step aside and continue."

"That is the difficult part," Isabella said. She rested against the seat. "I do not want Tangier-Ceuta to become a barracks large enough to contain civilians. I want a city capable of surviving war without turning itself into war."

Edward studied drainage channels and steam outlets along the street. "To achieve that, you have to make the whole place operate like a machine."

"Not a machine." Isabella pointed through the window. "Thousands of systems that must not obstruct one another. Military rail needs to move while civilian trains reach the market. Hospitals receive wounded men but must not sit beside ammunition stores. Industrial heat is reused before it returns to the boilers." She glanced towards Remi. "People only need the road clear of ice and the room warm enough to sleep. The rest is my problem."

Edward pointed towards snow piling beyond the heated district. "You speak as though ordering winter to move aside is an administrative matter."

Isabella looked at the white roofs. "Winter does not need to agree with me. Neither does anyone trying to kill my people."

The carriage continued towards the harbour. Across the plain joining Tangier and Ceuta, agricultural domes appeared between streets. Strips of living barley stretched beneath glass, a colour so green that it seemed almost obscene against the white world.

Juliet watched the domes recede and rubbed one thumb over the seam of her glove. "How long can the treasury carry all this?"

Isabella did not pretend the question was impolite. "Not long if every expense is examined in isolation. The Council reminds me each morning." She nodded towards grain stores and cranes near the water. "But however expensive Tangier-Ceuta becomes, it is cheaper than losing the strait."

Edward stopped looking at individual buildings. In the map inside his head, Iberia and North Africa suddenly connected through the city around them.

"Food, ammunition, coal, steel, wounded men, reinforcements all have to pass through here," Isabella said. "If Tangier-Ceuta is strangled, Fes begins starving before Western Rome runs out of shells." Her hand moved towards the opposite side of the carriage. "If Gibraltar opens, Portugal receives a door behind us."

Edward looked at her. "So you are spending here because the Pyrenees are already burning."

"Exactly." Isabella kept her eyes on the city. "I did not build Tangier-Ceuta so it would look impressive on a map. I built it so Castile still has a road left when another front breaks."

Outside, children leaving school passed workers changing shifts. On the other side of the avenue, a field gun rolled slowly towards the harbour. Edward watched the two streams cross. "How much have you slept this week?"

Isabella narrowed her eyes. "Less than I permit any general under my command." Then she pointed at him. "Before you lecture me about sleep, remember who spent six years hiding in Marrakesh."

Juliet folded her arms. "On that subject I can testify against both of you."

Isabella looked at her. Juliet looked back. Edward found no safe reason to enter the conversation.

* * *

A row of Castilian flags passed outside and reminded Remi of a question he had been saving since Marco mentioned Madrid. He turned from the window, tugged his mother's sleeve, and looked towards Isabella. "Aunt Isabella, in Marrakesh you said we'd live in Barcelona. Uncle Marco said Madrid. Where is our house actually going to be?"

"Madrid." Isabella answered without hesitation. "After leaving Marrakesh I received three more reports from the Pyrenees. French pressure is increasing faster than expected. Barcelona lies closer to the threat than I am willing to accept." She pulled straight the cuff of her glove. "Last night I signed orders transferring the necessary central offices to Madrid."

Juliet looked at her. "Can an entire court truly move because of one signature?"

"One signature does not pack chests or remove maps from walls." Isabella's tone sharpened. "But there must be a moment when debate ends. I chose it." She continued. "Moving the machinery of government will take days. My responsibility is to make them begin before France forces us to do it in panic."

Madrid, she explained, lay deeper inland and offered better control over the three major directions of war. It was safer for Remi. Millenia and Dante Stones were already there. Three possible houses had been prepared for the Spencer family: one near a school, one close to the medical quarter, and one near the palace.

Edward turned fully towards her. "You prepared three houses before you knew whether I'd accept?"

"Of course." Isabella made no attempt at innocence. "Did you imagine I travelled to Marrakesh carrying nothing but hope? I respected your right to choose. That did not require me to want a different answer."

Juliet asked, "And if I dislike all three?"

"Then tell me what you need, and I find a fourth." Isabella looked directly at her. "I want Edward's family in Madrid. I do not want you trapped inside a house you hate."

Juliet considered that and nodded.

Remi cared about only two questions. Would he attend school? Would he meet Dante? Isabella answered yes to the first and said the second depended on Millenia. For a seven-year-old, that was sufficient grounds to accept the new capital.

Isabella opened a silver box and took out a warm butter biscuit. Remi reached for it. Juliet reminded him he had already eaten on the train. The Queen's hand stopped instantly. She looked towards Juliet. "One, if you agree. He's still your son."

Juliet looked at the biscuit and then at Remi's spectacularly poor attempt to hide hope. "One."

"Thank your mother first." Only after Remi did so did Isabella give him the biscuit and smooth his hair.

Juliet looked at her. "So the Queen does know how to ask."

"I have always known how." Isabella settled against the seat again. "I simply do not always enjoy the answer. Remi is different."

Juliet leaned back. "Good. Then perhaps we can survive living in the same city."

"Enough progress for the first day."

Edward closed his eyes for one second. Fredo remained in front and continued performing the role of a man entirely uninvolved.

* * *

The farther they travelled into Ceuta, the more civilian life receded. Bakeries and schools gave way to steel warehouses, machine halls, drill yards, ammunition stores, and dry docks. Freight rails multiplied along the road. Civilian wagons became less common than soldiers, artillery teams, and sealed crates. Fredo opened a small panel from the front of the carriage. "Five minutes."

Isabella sat straighter and turned towards Edward. "The city is what I needed you to understand." A smile appeared. "What comes next is what I actually wanted to show you."

Edward laughed. "I'm beginning to pity your treasury."

"Wait. You haven't seen why it cries."

The carriage stopped at the military gate of Ceuta harbour. When the door opened, sea wind struck hard enough to make Remi curl inward. The controlled warmth of the city vanished within several paces, replaced by salt, machine oil, and cold metal. Fredo opened the rear chest and handed out four heavy wool coats. Isabella threw one over her shoulders. "In the city I can make winter wait outside the door. On the docks, the cold has yet to learn manners."

Edward helped Juliet with hers, then knelt to close Remi's sleeves tightly. Isabella watched without interrupting. Only after the boy was properly wrapped did she lead them through the military checkpoint.

Hammers struck steel throughout the docks. White steam rolled from great pipes and mixed with coal smoke and sea fog. Traditional sailing warships lay along the distant piers, their masts forming the familiar forest Edward had known all his life. Then he saw what lay ahead.

A black mass pressed against the dock like a fortress cut from land and dropped into the sea. It stood lower than the three-masted ships Edward once commanded, but its hull was broader and immensely heavier. Metal armour plates ran from bow to stern. A large funnel rose from the centre of the deck. Around it crowded valves, pipes, vents, and machinery that made a sailor's mind require several seconds before accepting that the object was a warship and not a floating factory. Edward had not yet spoken when steam behind the dry dock parted.

More black hulls appeared under scaffolding. One was plated only halfway. Another still exposed ribs and propeller shafts. A crane lowered an enormous slab of armour onto a third amid the rattle of chains.

Edward stopped walking. He removed one glove and placed his palm against the cold hull. Metal did not move with the sea in the way timber did. The entire mass returned only the steady vibration of machinery below deck. "Isabella." He looked up. "What the hell have you built?"

The Queen had climbed several steps onto the gangway. She turned. Wind pulled the tails of her grey-white uniform. Steam folded behind her. Beneath her feet, the black ship growled softly like an animal not yet awake. "You said my railway was faster than anything England possessed." She placed one hand on the rail. "Then the first thing you must do is stop using old England as the measure of the new world."

Edward looked up at her. "You were raised in an age when warships asked permission from wind before they could move. When the whole hull had to turn simply to bring guns into line. When one red-hot shot reaching a timber magazine could kill hundreds." Her fingers tightened on the rail. "Admirals called that tradition. I call it a list of limitations no one had yet become sufficiently annoyed to tear apart."

Edward lifted his head. "Boilers from the railways. Pumps from deep mines. Toledo steel. Valencia machine tools. Naval experience from Ceuta." Isabella tapped one finger against the rail. "Every place told me its part could not be joined to the others." A small smile. "I made them join."

She pointed towards the hulls growing beneath the scaffolds. "One ship does not change the world. The ability of workshops hundreds of miles apart to build the second, the third, the tenth does." Isabella climbed higher. Halfway along the gangway she stopped, with the completed ironclad below and other hulls behind her among cranes, boilers, and scaffolding. "Look carefully, Edward Spencer." She used his full name like a summons.

"Europe still builds ships as if its ancestors will live forever. Lisbon trusts sails. Ravenna trusts rams and Greek fire. France counts broadside guns and calls the larger number progress." Her arm opened towards the yards. "I do not intend to win the next war by becoming better at what the world already knows." Isabella's voice carried without needing to rise. "I intend to make what they know obsolete."

A steam hammer struck somewhere behind the dock. "The day these ships sail, wind will no longer decide where a fleet may go. Rain will not cripple them merely by soaking lines and canvas. Cannon shot will have to learn what iron means instead of timber." She looked across the harbour. "Every admiral from Lisbon to Ravenna will have to relearn his maps, his doctrine, and every victory he believed permanent."

Edward looked up. "So you don't only want to change war."

Isabella turned half towards Ceuta and the hulls taking shape. "They call Tangier-Ceuta the Lighthouse of Europe." Her gaze returned to him. "I like the name because a lighthouse does not ask permission from the darkness before it shines."

Edward's hand remained on the armour. "And you truly believe these ships change warfare?"

"No."

A valve opened somewhere beneath the deck. Steam screamed across the pause. "War is simply the first thing they change." Isabella tapped two fingers against the rail. "The age of wood and sail is expiring, Edward. Those who learn quickly enough will enter what comes next." Her eyes moved towards the old sailing ships beyond the yard. "Those who do not will sink with the world they understood."

A series of valves opened across the ironclad and the neighbouring dry docks. White steam flooded the pier, rolled around the gangway, and dissolved into the sea wind. Edward remained beside the armour with his bare hand against cold steel. The world had moved during six years in Marrakesh.

And to the north, war was not going to give him much time to admire what replaced it.

Edward was still staring at the ironclad when running boots struck the deck behind them. A young officer reached Isabella out of breath. "Your Majesty, urgent intelligence from the northern frontier. The main French force has begun moving through the Pyrenees."

Isabella's hand went immediately to the rail. "Which formations? Which passes?"

The officer unfolded the map he had brought. After two questions, she turned. "Fredo. Take Edward and his family to their quarters. Make certain they have everything they need." She was already walking towards the command section before he answered. Fredo collected the Spencer luggage and led them below.

Their cabin lay near the middle of the hull, broad enough for a family and kept surprisingly warm by a small heating line set into the steel wall. Once Fredo placed the luggage inside, he bowed and closed the door.

Machinery beneath the floor transmitted a constant low vibration through the metal. Remi removed his boots, climbed into the narrow bed, and fell asleep within minutes.

Juliet waited until his breathing settled before sitting at the small table. Her hands remained linked for a long time. "Isabella doesn't hate me."

Edward pulled the other chair closer. "But?"

Juliet glanced towards Remi and lowered her voice. "She knows you too well." She looked back at him. "Things I needed six years of marriage to learn, she sees after one look. I'm not afraid she'll steal you. I'm afraid you'll become Sir Edward again for so long that one day the man who comes home won't be the man I know."

Edward moved his chair aside, lowered to one knee before her, and took both roughened hands. "Bella knew me before London. You knew me after London." He tightened his hold. "Both men are me. I am not going to put on a uniform and pretend the last six years never happened."

"You cannot promise you won't change."

"No." Edward did not insult her with that promise. "But I can promise something else. If there comes a day when all I can see are maps, battles, and whatever must be done next, pull me back." His thumb moved over one cracked knuckle. "Do not stand outside waiting for me to remember on my own."

Juliet studied him, then nodded. "All right."

Edward bent and kissed the hands she had spent six years using to keep their family alive. "I need to visit the command deck for a while. I want to know how bad the north is before we reach Gibraltar."

Juliet caught his hand before he could stand. "Go. But come back before they have time to turn you into an admiral."

Edward kissed her. "I'll try." When the steel door closed behind him, Juliet lay beside Remi. She kept watching that door for a long time.

* * *

Edward tightened his collar and followed the steel passage towards the bridge. The command room was stifling with heat from machinery, steam pipes, and more than a dozen people packed around the chart table. At its centre rested a transparent glass sphere the size of a human head. The Miracle-grade communications Vestigium pulsed with blue light while static hissed through the metal framework supporting it. Edward stopped outside the doorway rather than entering the meeting. Inside, Isabella stood over the charts with one hand gripping the table as a voice from the north broke through the sphere.

"Your Majesty, Legion One, Tercio del Rayo, can no longer hold the western Pyrenean corridor." Cannon fire boomed behind the speaker. "French artillery pressure is overwhelming. The main force is withdrawing towards San Sebastián and neighbouring cities to combine with local garrisons."

Isabella interrupted. "Cut the connection with Legion One." She turned sharply to the communications officer. "Priority line to Northern Theatre Headquarters at Bilbao. I want the men responsible for the whole front, not fragments."

The officer adjusted copper joints beneath the sphere. Blue light flared and died. A second attempt produced only static. A third failed completely. On the fourth, a hard click came from the base and the sphere shuddered. The noise of a full argument burst into the room from the headquarters of the Northern Family Councils.

"Give me the overall situation immediately." Isabella spoke the moment the line stabilised. "Do not feed me separate reports. I want the whole front before we descend into individual units."

A staff general answered through artillery and shouted orders. "Your Majesty, the Pyrenean line is failing at multiple points. Without reinforcements we cannot hold the entire front." Papers moved at the far end. "Legion Four, Tercio del León, Legion Five, Tercio de la Sombra, and Legion Six, Tercio del Trueno are holding every strongpoint they can. Legion Four and the Navarre family knights are under severe siege at Pamplona." The voice hesitated. "In the east, Legion Seven, Tercio del Sol, still holds Perpignan, but ammunition is nearly gone."

Isabella looked along the rail lines feeding San Sebastián. "Move the nearest reserve legions into San Sebastián immediately." She struck the chart table with her palm. "The Pyrenees do not fall completely. Whatever it costs."

Bilbao erupted in voices. A senior general forced his way onto the channel. "Move what, Your Majesty? You are sitting aboard a warm steel ship. You have no idea what the ground looks like here." A chair crashed somewhere beyond the sphere. "The coastal cities around San Sebastián are being shelled by the French fleet. Harbours are burning. Supply roads are cut. We have done everything possible." His voice rose. "You cannot order us to throw soldiers into fire and call that reinforcement."

"Everything possible?" Isabella's shout filled the bridge. "You control five hardened legions equipped with the best this kingdom can provide, and in three days you have allowed the French to pass the Pyrenean approaches as though they were taking a morning walk." Her fist closed against the table. "Is that incompetence or betrayal?"

"Do not accuse us of treason." The answer came back with the slap of a hand against a desk. "The weather is killing us. Snowstorms are ruining weapons. The French are using new siege Vestigia." Then the accusation Isabella had been expecting. "And you personally tore a hole in the front when you withdrew ten thousand elite soldiers of Legion Eleven, Tercio del Acero, and sent them to that corner of North Africa." The general nearly shouted. "Take away ten thousand of our best rifles, then demand to know why we cannot hold."

Fredo drew his dagger. He moved towards the sphere before Isabella could stop him. "Mind your words." His voice dropped colder than the steel underfoot. "Those ten thousand were redeployed to defend the rear. You still possess five legions and a chain of fortresses." He leaned towards the blue light. "If you wish to challenge the Queen's decision, first explain how all of that strength allowed a line to break in three days."

"Enough, Fredo." Isabella raised one hand. Three days was too fast for her to accept a story consisting only of blizzards and missing troops. Yet Bilbao still commanded forces the front desperately required. She possessed suspicion, not proof. Arresting the theatre staff in the middle of a collapse could turn uncertainty into mutiny exactly where discipline mattered most. She set the question aside and looked at the map again. The problem she could solve now was keeping living units alive. Her finger moved over Perpignan, Barcelona, and the eastern rail lines. For several seconds she closed her eyes and reordered the commands in her head. Then she opened them. "Change frequency."

The communications officer moved. "Connect me to Barcelona Military District. Colonel Cassandra."

Copper rings turned. Blue light returned. After several bursts of static, a woman's voice came through low, disciplined, and immediately alert. "Colonel Cassandra speaking. What has happened, Your Majesty?"

Cassandra, Isabella's close companion since youth, carried the number Diez among the Castilian Royal Guard and currently commanded the Barcelona urban defence.

"Cassandra, listen carefully." Isabella stepped nearer the sphere. "The Pyrenean line has been breached. Mobilise two hundred Conquistadores immediately."

Several officers turned away from the chart table. One senior fleet staff officer stepped into Isabella's path. "Your Majesty, reconsider." He pointed towards the sphere. "Two hundred Conquistadores cannot be replaced in a winter. If we lose them at Perpignan, we possess no equivalent force to seal the next breach."

"Step back."

The officer refused. Voices rose around the table. "It is a suicide mission. Sending them into a French encirclement is throwing gold against stone." "And if three thousand garrison troops leave Barcelona, Catalonia is open. An internal revolt could cost the entire eastern region."

Isabella walked around the man and returned to the sphere. "Barcelona station runs at full military capacity. Move directly to Perpignan and break the siege of Legion Seven."

Cassandra waited until the argument at Isabella's end quietened. "After Perpignan?"

"Gather every surviving formation of Legion Seven." Isabella drew her finger west across the map. "Then turn the attack west along the southern Pyrenean flank. Hit the French spearheads from the side. Use the Conquistadores to destroy their reinforcement lines."

Cassandra repeated the order once. "Understood. I will assemble the Conquistadores and have the trains moving immediately."

The channel closed. Isabella turned back to the staff. She stamped one boot against the steel floor. "Enough. Silence and listen." No one interrupted. "Castile has not fallen. I do not require any of you to look brave. I require you to perform your function."

She faced the map. "If San Sebastián falls, the Pyrenees open. Then none of us will be debating which reserves to preserve. War will make that choice for us." Her hand moved south. "The armoured fleet at Ceuta was not built to die at anchor. If it can save the northern coast, I will use it."

A naval colonel stepped forward. "Your Majesty." His voice remained respectful but firm. "If the entire armoured fleet leaves Gibraltar, the rear opens. Western Rome is concentrating at Palma and Portugal may return at any time." Several officers nodded. "Saving the north by opening the south is not reinforcement. It is exchanging one crisis for another."

Isabella did not shout. She went back to the sea chart. Ceuta to San Sebastián. Palma. Lisbon. Gibraltar.

Keep the fleet at the strait and protect the rear. Send it north and perhaps save San Sebastián. Both needs were real. There was not enough strength to satisfy both.

Isabella measured the distance once more. "Correct. The rear will be exposed." She raised her head. "But if San Sebastián falls, the northern door opens as well. I accept the wager." The decision came. "Tonight, concentrate every naval formation around Gibraltar. This ship and every remaining armoured warship at Ceuta will sail north." Her finger struck the northern coast. "We relieve San Sebastián ourselves and destroy the French fleet offshore."

Orders began to move. The communications officer reached for the sphere. Edward spoke from the doorway. "Apologies, Your Majesty, but the armoured fleet cannot go to San Sebastián."

The entire bridge turned. Edward stepped out of the corridor, the heavy wool coat still carrying cold air from the deck. One officer moved to stop him. Fredo raised his hand. "Stand down. Let him finish."

Isabella frowned. "How much did you hear?"

"Enough to know you're about to ask your newest ships to perform a job they were never built to do." Edward approached the chart table. "Give me three minutes."

She folded her arms. "You have three."

Edward put one finger on Ceuta and drew it north along the Atlantic coast. "These ironclads possess armour and firepower timber ships cannot meet directly." His finger stopped. "But they're first-generation designs. Their weakness is not the guns. It is range." He tapped the Strait. "Here they are beside Vestigium fuel stores, repair yards, and supply on both shores. A boiler fails, they have somewhere to fix it. Consumption exceeds estimates, they have somewhere to refuel."

His hand moved north. "Take the whole fleet around the Atlantic coast towards San Sebastián and you force unproven boilers into continuous winter operation on a voyage they have never attempted." Edward looked at the naval officers. "One storm. One delayed tender. One machinery failure beyond what can be repaired at sea. Your strongest warship becomes a steel island incapable of moving under its own power."

The naval colonel bent closer. "But if we leave them here, San Sebastián..."

"Still needs help." Edward cut him off. "From ships able to reach it." He looked at Isabella. "The sailing fleet is slower, weaker, and older. It also knows how to live for weeks on open water."

Edward placed his hand over Gibraltar. "Right now your ironclads are a steel wall. Leave the wall here and it locks the rear door of Iberia and North Africa." He drew the alternative line. "Send it north and you expose that door while wagering all your new technology on a long voyage you've never tested."

The colonel followed the route again. Isabella measured Ceuta to San Sebastián. Then Lisbon. "What would you do?"

"Keep every ironclad at the Strait. Make Portugal and Western Rome think twice before entering." Edward moved his finger to Lisbon. "For San Sebastián, gather long-range sailing warships. Reprovision at Lisbon, then strike the French fleet from the sea."

Isabella looked at the line he had drawn. "You've just stopped me from turning the thing I spent all afternoon showing you into dead iron in the Atlantic."

Edward shrugged. "I've known the design for several minutes and already found quite a lot to dislike." Several officers bent over the map to hide their reactions.

Isabella looked towards Fredo. "Fredo. Draw your sabre." Fredo met her eyes once. Then he drew the blade and offered it across both hands. Isabella took the hilt. She walked around the chart table and stopped in front of Edward. "Kneel, Edward Spencer."

He did not move immediately. Edward looked at the sabre, then at Isabella, and understood. "Isabella." "Kneel." Her volume did not change. The bridge became silent anyway.

Edward lowered one knee onto the steel floor. Cold came through the fabric at once. He had not knelt in military ceremony for six years. Long enough that the old titles felt like they belonged to a man who had died somewhere behind London. Isabella placed the flat of the blade against his left shoulder. Then the right. "On behalf of the lost Kingdom of England, and under the authority of the Castilian Crown, I restore the knighthood war took from you but never made you unworthy to bear." The blade left his shoulder. "Rise, Sir Edward Spencer."

No one on the bridge repeated the title. Edward did not rise immediately. One hand closed over his knee. The calluses from reins, shovels, cargo crates, and cattle sheds rubbed against his palm. They were still there. The old Marrakesh coat did not vanish because steel had touched his shoulders. Then Edward stood.

Isabella lowered the sabre. "This title does not return England to you." He kept his eyes on hers. "But you never lost the right to carry it," Isabella added. She returned the weapon to Fredo and turned towards the chart table. "Sir Edward Spencer, as sovereign of the Castilian realm, I place you in command of the fleet assembling at Lisbon." She indicated the northward route. "The sailing warships you once commanded are there. One hundred Conquistadores will accompany you north."

Edward looked from Lisbon to San Sebastián. "And the ironclads?"

"Remain at Gibraltar, as you advised." Isabella placed a steel marker on the Strait. "You want a road back to England. I cannot give England to you." She looked at the sea. "But I can give you the ocean."

Edward remained over the chart. "You may refuse." Isabella's voice became quieter. "I need an admiral capable of contradicting me when I am about to do something foolish. If I wanted a head that only nods, this room has no shortage." Several officers found the map extraordinarily interesting.

Edward looked at Isabella. Under the blue light of the communications Vestigium, the shadows beneath her eyes were far clearer than they had been on the dock.

"Juliet and Remi?"

"Madrid." The answer came instantly. "Barcelona is no longer safe enough after tonight. Millenia and Dante are already in Madrid. Your family will live near them." Isabella placed both palms on the table. "I will take Juliet and Remi there myself. No one touches them."

Edward set both hands on the chart table. "If I accept command, I command my way."

Isabella handed Fredo the sabre. "That is why I just put a blade on your shoulders."

Edward looked at the northern route one final time. Then he nodded. "I accept."

Isabella did not allow the moment to become ceremony. "Fredo. Prepare full admiral's dress for Sir Edward. Check weapons, luggage, and the route to Lisbon. When this ship reaches Gibraltar, I want him able to depart immediately." Fredo struck his heel to the floor. "Yes, Your Majesty."

Edward remained beside the chart. For the first time in six years, someone behind him said "Sir Edward" and he did not feel the need to turn around to discover whom they meant.

* * *

Juliet had been asleep only a short time when a knock woke her. She sat up, closed the collar of her dress, and opened the steel door. Then she stood still. Edward waited in the passage with Fredo. Only a few hours earlier he had worn the old wool coat that had followed the family from Marrakesh. Now his hair had been cut clean, his face shaved, and a dark navy-blue admiral's uniform fitted his body. Gold thread edged the high collar. Brass buttons ran in a perfect line down the front. The uniform fit him so well that Juliet hated the moment she noticed.

Her eyes travelled from the buttons to his face. "I told you to come back before they turned you into an admiral."

Edward looked down at himself. "I thought I had more time too."

Fredo, discovering a powerful interest in tact, stepped inside, collected the prepared luggage, and carried it back into the corridor. When the door closed, Juliet put her hand on Edward's collar. One finger moved across the gold stitching as if verifying it was real. "It suits you." After a moment she added, "I hate that."

Edward did not joke. "I know."

"Where are you going?"

"Lisbon first. Then north to relieve San Sebastián." He took the hand against his chest. "As soon as we reach Gibraltar, I leave."

Juliet did not release the gold thread. "Could you refuse?"

"Yes."

"And you accepted." Edward nodded. She held his collar between two fingers. "I do not need you to become a legend again. I do not need anyone returning every old title to you if the price is standing in another harbour wondering which version of you comes back."

"Neither do I." Edward lifted her hand and pressed it to his lips. "I accepted because I can do this." His voice remained steady. "And this time I have a home to return to. I will not throw my life at the first useful exchange and call it responsibility." A faint smile. "The Sultan has already shouted enough at me."

Juliet wiped beneath one eye with the back of her hand. "Then remember him." Her fingers tightened on the uniform. "I'm not afraid of this coat. I'm afraid you'll wear it long enough to forget there are two people in Madrid waiting for you."

Edward rested his forehead against hers. "If I forget, call me Edward."

"I have always called you that."

Behind them, blankets moved. Remi was awake. One side of his hair stood upright. He rubbed his eyes, looked at his father from head to foot, and sat straight up. "Father, you look like the men in paintings."

Edward turned. "Is that a polite way of saying I look ridiculous?"

Remi shook his head violently, jumped from the bed, and ran over to touch the brass buttons. "No. You look incredible." He looked up. "Are you wearing this because you're going to fight?"

"Yes." Edward knelt. "I have to do something at sea."

Remi became quiet. Both small hands remained on the dark blue coat. "Will you come back to Mama and me?"

Edward corrected the disordered hair. "I will do everything I can." He met his son's eyes. "But while I'm gone, you do not take over my job." Remi blinked. "No games about protecting your mother. Listen to her. Go to school. Play with Dante if the two of you like each other."

Edward tried to smile. "And save as many stories as you can for when I come back."

Remi thought seriously. "I'll keep the list of questions about when you were young too."

"That is beginning to worry me."

"Uncle Marco said I wasn't allowed to show you."

Juliet laughed through tears. Edward gathered both wife and son into his arms. Remi held tight around his neck. Juliet pressed her face into his shoulder and closed both hands around the stiff new uniform. For a while, no one spoke. Only the ship's machinery continued beneath them, its rhythm passing through the three bodies locked together.

* * *

By the time they left the cabin, the lights of Gibraltar had appeared through snow and mist. Isabella and Fredo waited on deck. A long steam whistle sounded as the ironclad entered the harbour. Two carriages stood ready below. One carried the royal crest and would take Isabella, Juliet, and Remi towards Madrid. The other was a dark military grey and waited for Edward and Fredo on the road to Lisbon.

Remi clung around his father's neck once more in the harbour yard. Edward let him hold on. Only then did he put the boy down. Juliet stepped forward and straightened Edward's collar twice even though nothing was wrong with it. "Edward."

"I'm here."

The tears finally escaped her eyes, but her voice remained steady. "Come home."

Edward wiped one away with his thumb. "Yes."

Juliet held his lapel. "Sir Edward Spencer may go and fight his war." She looked at him. "But the man who comes home to me has to be Edward."

He covered her hand with his. "I remember."

Edward kissed her slowly, without urgency, then bent and kissed Remi's forehead. When he straightened, he kept hold of Juliet's hand until Fredo called from beside the second carriage.

Edward walked to Isabella. "I know you'll keep your word. But Bella, do not provoke Juliet merely because you cannot resist."

Isabella looked towards the woman holding Remi beside the royal carriage. "Do you honestly imagine I have that much free time?" She looked back. "I may dislike certain facts. I do not harm the woman who kept you alive for six years." Her chin lifted. "Take care of your ocean."

Edward nodded. "Thank you."

Fredo struck his heel. "Your Majesty, permission to take Sir Edward on the road."

"Go." Isabella looked at both men. "And both of you come back."

The two carriages left the harbour in opposite directions. Through the royal window, Remi pressed both hands against the glass. Juliet remained seated, eyes following the grey military carriage until it began shrinking into the snow. Inside the westbound carriage, Edward continued looking back longer than necessary. Fredo waited until Gibraltar had become only a narrow line of lights behind them. "I used to think Sir Edward Spencer was a man who had lost nearly everything."

Edward turned. "So did I."

Fredo looked towards the road behind. "It seems you calculated badly."

Edward rested his head against the carriage wall. "Fortunately."

Fredo extended a scarred hand. "From this moment I serve under your command." His expression remained formal, but not cold. "It will be an honour to stand beside you, Sir Edward."

Edward took the hand. The restored title still felt strange. This time, he did not move away from it. "Take care of me, Fredo."

The carriage wheels beat steadily across the road. Gibraltar disappeared behind them. Ahead, through the snowstorm, the road to Lisbon opened west.

title_vi: Chapter 20 - Things Not Yet Tried in Blood
title_en: Chapter 20 - Things Not Yet Tried in Blood
text_en:
Events from Ceuta to Gibraltar had moved faster than Edward had managed to arrange them in his mind. On the train leaving Jerez de la Frontera, he sat beside the window reading through the Lisbon orders Fredo had prepared. The moment their carriage reached the station, Fredo had secured two seats on the earliest westbound service. Trains running deep inside Iberia felt different from those Edward had seen in North Africa. The same steel, steam, and machine oil remained, but here the wheels were softened by suspension beneath the floor and heat travelled evenly through the walls and seats. Edward stared at an armchair fitted with more brass valves than he considered reasonable.

Fredo set the luggage down and pointed at the armrest. "Make yourself comfortable, Sir Edward. Heated piping runs beneath the cushion. Turn the brass valve and adjust it as you like." He poured warm water and pushed the glass across. "The first prototypes ran in North Africa. After several years of discovering everything that could break, these coaches were introduced on the interior lines." Fredo settled opposite him. "They ride a little better and hold heat far better. In Castile now, those two things are worth more than luxury."

Edward drank. "You know an impressive amount about everything Isabella is doing."

"That is my job." Fredo adjusted one cuff. "If Her Majesty signs an order, I need to know which machine, unit, and person it touches. Otherwise I'm only a man carrying papers through a palace."

Edward's attention shifted to the dark grey leather notebook Fredo always kept at his side. The surface had grown rough. Its corners had worn pale from use. "I assumed that was a book of secret orders."

Fredo held the spine with one hand. "No, Sir Edward. Royal schedules are kept elsewhere." He rotated the notebook once. "This is only an unfinished novel I write during long watches."

Edward looked at it again. "A novel?" He leaned back. "What about?"

Fredo watched his reflection in the misted glass. "A person very much like you. Someone spending what little strength remains, walking into a snowstorm in search of the road back to his homeland." He glanced at Edward and immediately added, "Coincidence. I began the idea before the Queen ever ordered us to Marrakesh."

Edward smiled. "An interesting coincidence. What made a man more accustomed to sword and pistol write about a lonely exile?"

Fredo ran a fingertip along the worn page edge. "I don't trust writing that needs to shout that someone is in pain." Outside, snowfields slid past. "On a battlefield, people rarely have time to announce that they're frightened. They do something small. Hide an unsent letter inside the coat before charging. Check one boot twice. Give someone else the last mouthful of water." He turned his pen slowly. "The man beside them already understands."

Fredo lowered his eyes. "Perhaps that is why I write slowly. I've killed too many people to believe pain should be decorated with beautiful words." His thumb pressed the page. "Sometimes I wonder whether every sentence I put down drags behind it the voices of people who died."

Edward looked at the notebook. "And the answer?"

"Not in the lines I manage to write." Fredo closed two fingers over the page. "They usually live in the lines I cannot." He left the notebook partly open. "Maybe that is why it remains unfinished. During palace watches I keep writing about somewhere to return to." His gaze went towards the winter beyond the window. "The colder it becomes outside, the more clearly people remember how warm their houses once were."

Edward watched him smooth a bent corner. "Speaking of houses. Where is your family now?"

Fredo closed the book before answering. "My father is dead, sir. I have only my mother." He looked through the glass. "She still lives in a small house by the sea in San Sebastián."

The name stayed in the compartment. Then the whistle screamed. Another train raced beside them in the opposite direction. Behind fogged windows Edward saw black cars full of wounded men heading towards the rear. High-pressure exhaust drowned conversation until the last carriage passed. Fredo still had one hand on the notebook. Edward watched the retreating medical train. Then he spoke before Fredo could change the subject.

"I was born outside Nottingham." Fredo turned. "As a boy I spent half my life in Sherwood. I heard Robin Hood stories often enough to believe a bow was all a man needed to become a hero." Edward looked at the empty glass in his hand. "My father was a garrison soldier. My mother worked in a brothel before I was born. Afterwards she left, learned weaving, and supported us with her hands." He smiled faintly. "We were poor. It was still home."

Fredo hesitated. "And your parents?"

Edward rubbed his thumb around the rim. "Both dead." He did not look away. "They were killed defending Nottingham during the Portuguese raids."

Fredo lowered his eyes. "I'm sorry, sir."

Edward set down the glass and stood long enough to place a hand on Fredo's shoulder. "Don't apologise." His hand remained there a moment. "Orders I gave helped carry England towards the day they died. I spent years waking and using that sentence to put myself on trial again." Edward released him. "Your mother is alive. Do not bury her in your mind before war manages the task."

Fredo looked directly at him. "You're telling me everything will be all right?"

"No." Edward sat again. "I'm telling you to prepare for the worst without treating it as certainty." He glanced outside at a freight train running beside them. "Before Inverness, I believed an admiral who doubted himself was not good enough. After Inverness, I became so afraid of hesitation that I wanted every decision closed immediately." His mouth tightened. "Both habits made me misread battlefields."

Fredo asked, "And now? Do you doubt yourself?"

"Yes." Edward tapped one finger against the glass. "Now I use doubt to check the arithmetic. I don't use it to decide whether I'm still worthy to command."

Fredo shook his head. "You're only in your thirties and speak like an old man who's lived three separate lives."

Edward laughed as he returned fully to the seat.

Fredo pulled a chain from beneath his collar. "I have no intention of writing San Sebastián's obituary either. My mother is more frightening than the Queen. Her talent for calculation has infected me since childhood."

A Castilian lion hung from the chain. Two red-orange Vestigium crystals burned in its eyes. Beneath the jaw, one word had been engraved deep into the metal. Tres. Fredo tapped the lion with his thumb. "To save us another introduction. Tres. Number Three."

He tucked it back. "Marco is Ocho. Romeo is Doce. If you're about to ask whether I'm better than either of them, the answer remains yes."

Edward looked from the lion to its owner. "Ah. Royal Guard Number Three has returned."

"I never left."

"Unfortunate."

They both laughed.

Fredo leaned back and put a hand over his stomach. "Are you hungry, Sir Edward? Because mine is beginning to complain."

Edward looked at the empty plate on the side table. He had not eaten a proper meal since Ceuta. "Very."

"Excellent." Fredo pulled the brass bell cord. "I'll have them bring something decent. Eat properly. The moment we reach Lisbon, we board and sail."

While they waited, Edward looked again at the lion hidden beneath Fredo's collar. "Tres. Ocho. Doce." He tapped the table. "What do those numbers actually mean? A ranking of strength?"

"No." Fredo shook his head. "Think of it this way. The less a task is permitted to fail, the more likely Isabella is to call a smaller number."

Edward raised an eyebrow.

"It measures how willing the Queen is to place someone close to the centre of power, or throw that person into a problem that must be solved without supervision."

"So Number Three does not mean you automatically defeat Marco at Number Eight."

"In a serious fight, I still win."

Edward shook his head.

"I'm beginning to understand why you're irritating."

Fredo reopened the notebook. The nib touched paper. He drew one small circle and wrote Isabella in the centre. "If you want to understand the Castilian war machine, begin here." Around the name he left empty space. "One hundred Royal Guards answer directly to the Queen. We are bodyguards, but that is only the most visible meaning." Lines grew from the circle. "Those suited for it become commanding generals, inspectors, political officers, staff officers. We are inserted into important formations so that royal orders do not deform after passing through too many intermediate hands."

Edward studied the lone circle. "One hundred people to keep the whole army loyal?"

"No. One hundred people so the Queen always has eyes, ears, and hands where she needs them." Fredo tapped the paper. "An army may contain hundreds of thousands. It still operates through specific people." He stopped writing. "And privately, there is something else."

Edward waited.

"I think Isabella possesses another pair of eyes even the Guard does not fully understand."

"A Vestigium?"

"There are moments when Her Majesty knows something too early." Fredo's expression changed. "A report has not arrived. A name no one has dared mention. Yet she already prepared an answer." He lowered his voice. "I have seen signs of a Legendary-grade Vestigium around incidents like that. I have never met the entity itself." Fredo's finger rested on Isabella's name. "Whatever it is, it stands very close to her. Perhaps closer than the Royal Guard."

Edward remembered too many times when Isabella had prepared for news before official reports reached her. "So from now on, whenever the girl answers too quickly, I have another thing to suspect." He did not ask more.

The compartment door opened before Fredo could extend another branch from the circle. "Your meal, gentlemen." A woman pushed in a small cart. Two plates of lamb stewed with vegetables, toasted bread, and buttered potatoes soon covered the table. Fredo snatched the notebook away before sauce could reach it.

"A saviour arriving precisely on time." He tore bread and dragged it through the stew. "At least railway cooks remember soldiers are human."

Edward cut into the soft lamb while watching black freight wagons outside. Through the steamed glass he could see sacks of wheat, salted meat, and sealed military stores marked with the royal stamp moving north. "You said one hundred Guards are Isabella's eyes and hands. Who actually carries the war?" "It cannot be one hundred people."

Fredo swallowed and pointed his fork towards the freight line. "Look outside."

Edward followed.

"The war lives in those grain crates, ammunition boxes, and rails before it lives on any general's shoulders." Fredo set down the fork. "Then come the Tercios. They hold lines, seize ground, defend fortresses, and pay most of the bill in human bodies." He indicated south on the folded map. "Terrain means different fronts require different people. In the south, Moorish, Berber, and Algerian formations fight conditions continental soldiers often cannot endure." His fork moved north. "And the English exiles are being consolidated into the Exiled English Legions."

Edward's fork stopped several inches from his mouth. "Exiled." Fredo did not continue. He returned to his food and allowed Edward to watch the lit freight windows slide behind them. Edward's eyes remained outside. "One day those words won't need to stand before the name English." Then he lifted the fork and deliberately changed the subject. "Worst field rations you've ever eaten?"

Fredo planted his fork on the edge of the plate. "Perpignan." He considered. "During the siege our supply line broke repeatedly. Dried meat hard enough to use as building material. Biscuits so tasteless chewing them felt like eating bark." A faint smile. "Eventually my section stormed an abandoned bakery and found several croissants still inside. I swear the butter tasted better than anything in the palace."

Edward laughed aloud. "English troops in northern France did no better. Weeks of rain. Twice-baked bread arrived and turned green within two days." He used the knife to imitate cutting.
