"We shaved mould off it like turnip skin and swallowed the rest with our eyes closed. By the end of the campaign half the unit was fighting for the privies."

Their conversation moved from rations to stomach illness and the inventive dishonesty of wartime cooks until both plates were almost empty. Fredo used the last bread to wipe sauce from the plate.

"Conquistadores and Reliquiarios only appear when the battlefield moves beyond ordinary infantry."

Edward put down his fork.

"Go on."

"Conquistador is the hammer." Fredo drew a straight line through a bead of water on the table. "They carry military Vestigia heavy enough to break formations, artillery sites, or sections of a front that ordinary infantry might pay hundreds of lives to breach. Under special conditions, their equipment can even carry Miracle-grade transmission for a short period." His finger moved in another direction. "Reliquiarios hunt things rifles cannot solve. Original Vestigia. Mutated creatures. Formless entities an entire regiment could stand before and still not know where to shoot."

Edward nodded. "One breaks military lines. The other handles things that should not exist on a battlefield."

"Exactly."

The train began to slow. Through the window, station lights appeared among falling snow. Seville.

"And the lowest layer?" Edward stood and put on his coat.

"Garrison troops." Fredo closed the notebook. "The least celebrated and always necessary. Port towns, commercial cities, great fortresses. They maintain order, protect stores, and survive the first blow until a regular Tercio arrives." A small smile. "You'll see immediately."

They stepped onto the platform for a thirty-minute stop. Near a brass lamp, a disturbance had formed at the ticket barrier. A drunken man wearing a coat marked with old red-and-gold heraldry shouted at several station employees. He waved a tarnished metal badge and demanded priority boarding because he still carried the title Don from the previous dynasty. Most of the staff facing him were women.

Fredo handed his valise to Edward. "Everyone step back. I'll handle it." The employees recognised the Royal Guard uniform and gave him room. Fredo put one hand on the man's shoulder. "Good evening, sir. You've plainly had too much to drink. Give me your ticket and I'll arrange somewhere suitable for you to rest."

The man knocked the hand aside. "Who the hell are you to lecture me? Some brat hardly old enough to shave?" He stabbed one wine-stinking finger towards Fredo and the women behind the barrier. "These stupid women don't know who I am, and you..." He drew breath for the next insult.

Fredo punched him once. The blow landed under the jaw. The man went slack and struck the stone like a dropped sack. Fredo took out a handkerchief, wiped his knuckles, and turned towards the garrison soldiers who had just arrived. "Cell for a week. Then transport him to Toledo for Council judgement."

"Yes, sir."

No soldier asked Fredo's family, title, or exact office. They dragged the unconscious Don away while the crowd opened on its own. Edward watched them go. "I understand the garrison layer." He gave the valise back. "But now I have another question."

Fredo folded the handkerchief. "I assume it involves the word Don."

"And why a man carrying one can still be knocked unconscious and jailed by you in front of a station full of witnesses."

The whistle sounded. They returned to the train before the doors closed. When Seville vanished behind insulated glass, Edward poured more tea. "So where exactly does the title Sir or Don fit? How does Isabella's Council of Knights work?"

Fredo did not immediately open the notebook. He turned his teacup slowly and watched the surface roll with the rhythm of the rails. "The Council is where the old lands are forced to sit at one table." His voice became more formal. "Castile. Aragon. Navarre. León. Valencia. Andalusia. The great families besides." Fredo looked at Edward. "They hold land, retainers, local soldiers, and something the Crown cannot manufacture in a workshop: inherited loyalty."

"But the garrison outside obeyed you before a Don."

"Because being respected by a population and holding authority over royal forces are different things." Fredo leaned back. "A great Don may make a square bow. That does not give him the right to send Royal Guards or Tercios wherever he pleases."

"Local forces remain?"

"For territorial defence. The Crown watches them closely." Fredo placed three grains of sugar on the table. "The Council holds one hundred and twenty seats. Forty are occupied by members of the Royal Guard." He moved another cluster. "Twenty-five belong to nobles who have sworn absolute loyalty to Isabella. Your Victoria Valdes sits among that group."

Edward used the tip of the spoon to push the two clusters together. "So before debate begins, Isabella already has a hand on more than half the room."

"Her Majesty calls it ensuring the state cannot bite through its own throat." Fredo gathered the sugar. "She does not lock competent nobles outside. If a man can command, he can still receive troops. I may dislike certain houses, but battlefields have no interest in my preferences."

Edward settled into the seat. "So restoring my title placed me inside that structure? It gives me legitimate standing before the Council?"

"Possibly part of it." Fredo thought, then shook his head. "If you ask for the Queen's entire intention, I won't invent one. I do not know everything."

Edward did not press. Steam trembled on the tea. After a while Fredo tapped the window. "Look outside."

Snow-covered fields stretched to the horizon. Farther away, a frozen river had become an improvised road for sledges and carts. "You ruled the Atlantic before this winter began." Fredo watched the landscape. "How different is naval war now?"

Edward studied the temporary road across the ice, then removed a notebook from the valise. "Different from the land beneath it to the sea itself." He drew a curve. "The north is locked by the Ice Drift Boundary. The North Sea, Baltic, and Channel are mazes of broken ice and icebergs." His pen moved west. "It has not yet reached every stretch of water west of France and England, but leave a safe corridor by the wrong margin and an entire fleet may vanish without ever seeing an enemy flag." He drew into the continent. "The Seine, Rhine, Danube, and other great rivers freeze hard enough to become roads for armies and gun sledges."

A second line. "Meanwhile water locked on land lowers sea level. Shoals and reefs rise where old charts show clear water." The pen went south. "The Mediterranean and southern Atlantic remain among the few large reservoirs of heat and moisture. Northern cold meets warmer equatorial air." Edward looked up. "So the water still navigable becomes the place storms are born again and again." He closed one hand over the page. "A navy no longer fights only an enemy. It fights a map changing every year."

Fredo studied the drawing. "Your body left the service. Your head never left the sea."

"Running away did not make the ocean cease to exist." Edward pushed the notebook towards the middle. "I prepared for anything that might eventually come to my door." He gestured for the pen. "What does Castile believe?"

Fredo took it. "Under traditional naval doctrine, two things still dominate. Line of Battle and the Weather Gage." He drew parallel ship lines. "A good admiral preserves formation, takes the windward position, chooses range, then grinds the enemy with broadside fire." His pen crossed the lines. "Formation discipline, reload speed, direction of wind. Those decided most old battles."

Then he drew broken shapes. "But Ice Age winds shift violently with cold high-pressure systems. A long battle line among drifting ice can become a row of targets tied to one another." He wrote a title. "Castile therefore developed the doctrine of Open Corridor and Extreme Close Boarding."

Edward gave no opinion. He motioned for Fredo to continue.

"First pillar: restructure the fleet." Fredo drew smaller hulls. "Three-deck ships of the line carry enormous firepower but draw too much water and turn too slowly. Falling sea level exposes reefs while drifting ice closes narrow water." His pen touched each hull. "So the core shifts to frigates, corvettes, and galleys drawing less than four metres. Bows are reinforced with Vestigium alloy to break thin ice and survive collision."

Edward immediately pointed at the masts. "Smaller hull. More sensitive centre of gravity." He looked at Fredo. "A snowstorm freezes standing rigging and canvas beneath inches of ice. That puts tonnes of weight at the highest point of a frigate already rolling in heavy water." His finger tapped the drawing. "How does she survive?"

"Crew continuously breaks ice and reduces sail as the storm arrives."

"If they have time. What if the storm catches them during combat?"

Fredo looked at the design. "Staff doctrine has no complete answer."

Edward simply nodded. "Continue."

Fredo moved to the next line. "Second pillar: range." He wrote while speaking. "Low temperature makes metal brittle, fuses damp, long-range artillery less reliable. Gunners therefore hold fire until close approach." His pen became a ship. "At very close range, grapeshot can clear a deck. The priority is not always sinking the enemy. Break rigging, masts, anchor lines." He drew a vessel drifting sideways. "Take steering away among current, ice, and shoals. The sea finishes the work."

"If the enemy agrees to come close." Edward touched the diagram.

Fredo looked up. "You mean?"

"Fire ships. Mortar vessels. Gunships carrying incendiary Vestigia." Edward leaned over the page. "Or simply a man with better guns who remains outside your preferred range and forces you to approach." He tapped the written doctrine. "A system built around a few dozen yards only matters if you can compel the enemy to accept those yards."

Fredo did not argue. He wrote one note in the margin. "Force the range."

"Last pillar?"

"Terrain." Fredo opened a clean page and sketched San Sebastián Bay. "We avoid great open-sea engagements where possible. Emphasis shifts to coastal channels and bay mouths. Small ships act as bait, drawing the enemy across shoals or moving ice." A few marks represented fog. "Boats use bells or false signal guns to misdirect movement."

Edward traced the route from the bay towards Biscay. "Who owns the better chart?"

"Depends on the region."

"I'm asking San Sebastián and Biscay." Fredo did not have a name ready. Edward placed a fingertip at the mouth of the bay. "A terrain trap works only when the hunter understands the ground better than the prey." His finger moved along the narrow lane. "If the opposing captain knows the shoals, currents, and false signals, this same channel locks your retreat. The bait becomes the ship cut off."

Fredo set down the pen. He reread three pages and marked each question Edward had raised. "Light ships suffer from icing. Close boarding needs a way to compel range. Coastal traps depend on superior charts." He looked up. "Anything else, Admiral?"

Edward rested both elbows on the table. "One question matters more than all of them."

"Ask."

"Since the Ice Age began, has Castile won a true naval battle because of this doctrine?"

Fredo had no answer. He read the question again. Then he looked at the pages of theory and found no battle he could place beneath them.

Edward drew the notebook back and closed it. "Theory is not useless, Fredo." He stood and stretched. "It becomes dangerous when men start treating something never tried in blood as truth." Night had deepened beyond the glass. "Get some sleep."

Fredo nodded but left the notebook open across his knees. "Yes, Admiral."

Edward leaned back. For several seconds, the compartment held only the rails. Then his eyes opened again. The theory had given him problems.

Problems could become orders.

title_vi: Chapter 21 - The Price of a Plan
title_en: Chapter 21 - The Price of a Plan
text_en:
"Wait." Edward sat upright again. "Before you sleep, use the Vestigium communications sphere to contact Naval Command in Lisbon."

Fredo straightened immediately. "You want to change the doctrine?"

"Not yet. I want to remove something that can kill us before the enemy does." Edward pointed at the frost gathering around the carriage window. "Tell them to mix heat-producing Vestigium powder with whale fat and coat every sail and line on every combat-ready ship."

Fredo reached for his notebook. Edward continued, "The fat holds heat and resists water. The Vestigium keeps the surface warm enough to slow ice formation." He leaned back. "At minimum, I don't want a snowstorm capsizing us because every man on deck is busy shooting someone."

Fredo pulled the small communications sphere from the luggage. Edward raised one finger before he could activate it. "And tell them I want at least three heavy ships of the line prepared."

Fredo stopped.

"Four gun decks. Full maintenance. Ready to sail the moment we reach Lisbon."

He blinked. "You just spent half an hour explaining how cumbersome ships of the line have become."

"I said removing them entirely from doctrine is a wager. I did not say they are useless." Edward took the pen from him and wrote beside the three requests. "Light ships give us manoeuvrability. Heavy ships give us something drifting ice cannot replace: a firing platform able to absorb punishment when the enemy refuses to play by our preferred rules."

Fredo read the list. "I understand."

The communications sphere flared blue in his hands. Light spilled across the notebook, illuminating three new lines written among pages once reserved for an unfinished novel. Fredo transmitted each requirement to Lisbon and made the officer on the other end repeat every item back. Only after confirmation did the sphere go dark. Edward leaned into the heated chair. Fredo continued writing beside the notes for his fictional exile. Outside the window, the first distant lights of Lisbon appeared along the horizon.

A plan had begun as criticism in a railway carriage. By the time they reached the coast, men he had never met were already coating sails, moving powder, and preparing guns because of it. That was the price of command Edward had missed least. A thought stopped being his the moment another person was ordered to act upon it.

* * *

The day before, another part of Edward's decision had already become someone else's life. The long-distance train from Gibraltar had entered Madrid shortly after noon, steam rolling across the outer walls of the capital. Juliet, Remi, and Isabella now sat inside a royal carriage lined with black velvet as it moved along broad stone avenues. Juliet had lost track of how long she had been sitting near the window. Her rough hands lay carefully in her lap, fingers unconsciously gripping the coarse goatskin fabric of the dress she had brought from Marrakesh. Beside her, Remi had pressed his face so close to the glass that his breath kept fogging it.

"Mama. Look!"

"I see it, Remi. Don't press your face to the glass. It's cold."

"But look. The snow on the roofs is melting."

Juliet raised her eyes. Madrid stretched beneath the grey Ice Age sky like a different world. Red and grey sandstone buildings crowded the streets. Great glass canopies arched over iron frames throughout the centre, shielding the avenues so snow rarely touched the roads beneath. Along both sides, thick copper pipes disappeared beneath the paving stones and released steady threads of steam. Snow landing near the heated routes melted almost at once and ran into drainage channels.

There were no sagging earthen houses preserving the last scraps of heat from cheap red lime. No thin cattle dragging carts through wind-blown snow. Instead, carriages moved easily over dry streets. Soldiers marched in winter uniforms. Shop windows burned with Vestigium light bright enough to make Juliet squint.

Then she saw the fountain. Water rose in shining arcs across a broad square and fell again without freezing. Juliet stared. Every winter morning in Marrakesh, she had broken ice from the water bucket before she could wash, cook, or give anything to Edward and Remi. Here people sent clear water into the air simply because it was beautiful.

The feeling in her chest was difficult to name. Not admiration. Not quite joy. It felt more like having lived in darkness too long, then being forced to narrow the eyes when a door opened suddenly onto light.

"Beautiful, isn't it, Juliet?" Isabella sat opposite in her grey-white uniform, one leg crossed over the other. The journey from the south appeared not to have tired her at all. Her dark hair remained pinned neatly behind her head. Even the cream gloves showed no coal soot from the train.

Juliet turned from the window. "Your Majesty... it's magnificent."

"Only magnificent?" A smile touched Isabella's mouth.

Juliet looked down at her worn shoes, searching for something appropriate to say. "In Marrakesh, if a street remained this free of ice, I think half the neighbourhood would carry their beds outside simply to enjoy it."

Isabella stared at her. Then she laughed. Even the driver glanced away to hide a smile. "You may test the idea if you wish." Isabella's eyes brightened with amusement. "If you truly want to put a bed in Calle Mayor, I'll order the army to close the entire street."

"No, no. That isn't what I meant." Juliet waved both hands, horrified by the image of soldiers obeying such an order.

Isabella laughed harder. Remi joined in without understanding why. Juliet finally lowered her face, ears burning.

The embarrassment only sharpened the feeling that had followed her throughout the journey. People here seemed to know how to behave. When to laugh. How to sit. Which spoon belonged to which course. Where to place a hand. How far to bow without appearing foolish or excessive. Juliet knew none of those things instinctively.

She knew how many frosts a turnip had survived by looking at the skin. She knew how much wood a pot required to simmer overnight without burning dry. She could read cloud shapes and guess when a storm would reach the house. She could listen to a cow's breathing and know when labour had begun. Madrid did not make those skills useless. It was simply the first place in years where her family's survival did not depend on performing them correctly every day. The carriage stopped before a three-storey villa in a quiet private district.

Isabella stepped down first and helped Remi to the pavement. Then she moved aside for Juliet. Six years of displacement had left mother and son with very little. Juliet carried one worn leather valise. Remi clutched a faded cloth bag containing carved scraps of wood and the small sailing ship he refused to leave behind. Their possessions looked painfully poor against the polished buildings around them.

Isabella unlocked a thick oak door. "This is yours from now on." She stepped aside. "The ground floor contains the main living spaces and the master bedroom. Remi's room and the guest room are on the first floor. Upstairs you'll find a study, a sewing room, and a balcony overlooking the canal."

Juliet crossed the threshold cautiously. Waxed pine boards shone without dust. A built-in hearth burned low and clean, spreading the scent of dry wood instead of the sharp smell of red lime and cattle she had associated with every winter night in Marrakesh.

Isabella remained near the doorway. "The house is paid for. My people cover both ends of the street." Her voice was practical rather than ceremonial. "Millenia Stones will visit tomorrow morning. After that, someone from Interior Affairs will ask what else you need. If anything is missing, say so directly."

Juliet set down the old valise. Her hands closed around the worn grey dress. "Thank you, Your Majesty." She bowed her head. "You've done too much for Remi and me."

Isabella looked once at Juliet's tired face and weather-cracked hands, then turned towards the door. She pulled up the hood of her cloak. "Rest. You and Remi have travelled far enough." Then she left.

The royal carriage rolled away from the gate without Isabella looking back. Its wheels faded along the stone road until silence settled over the house. Remi released a breath he seemed to have held the entire time. He loosened his grip on the cloth bag and stared at the high ceiling.

"Mama." His eyes widened. "This house is enormous." He ran to the sheepskin sofa and dropped one hand onto the cushion. "And the fire doesn't make my eyes sting like the old one."

Juliet watched him move through the warm room. The plan Edward had accepted in Marrakesh had already divided their family across countries, oceans, and orders. Yet here was one part of its price that could not be written on a military map.

A mother and son standing inside a house too large to feel like theirs.

"Mama, there's fire under the floor, isn't there? It's so warm!"

"It won't be fire, sweetheart. They'll have hot-water pipes beneath the boards."

Juliet set the old leather valise beside the staircase and knelt next to Remi. Warmth rose steadily through the polished wood beneath her palms. In Marrakesh, winter meant cracked heels against damp floors, ash from the red-lime stove, and waking every few hours to make certain the house had not lost its fire. Here warmth came from somewhere she could not see and asked nothing from her hands. That simple fact made her throat tighten.

Remi had already discovered the kitchen. A brass tap curved like a swan's neck over a white stone sink. He rose onto his toes, twisted the handle, and immediately jumped backwards. Clear water burst into the basin with enough force to splash his shirt.

"Mama!"

Juliet hurried over, grabbed the unfamiliar lever, and received a thin stream of water directly across her nose before she found the right angle and shut it off. Remi stared at her dripping face. Then he folded over laughing. "You look like a drowned mouse!"

"Very proud of yourself, are you?" Juliet wiped her nose and flicked several drops straight back at him. Remi yelped with delight and fled the kitchen before she could retaliate again.

He found the master bedroom at the end of the ground floor and launched himself onto the broad fur mattress. His entire body sank into it. "Mama! Your bed is twice as big as the one in Marrakesh!"

Juliet followed more slowly. Tall windows looked into a small garden and the warm-water canal behind the house. Beside the bedroom lay a tiled bathing room with a deep stone tub and a system of brass valves that already made her uneasy. She put one hand to a wall and felt warmth beneath the marble, then smiled despite herself at how carefully Isabella had prepared the house for them.

"All right, sailor. Off the bed." She clapped once. "Let's see whether your room is as impressive."

Remi sprang up and ran upstairs. His room faced the street. Daylight poured through a large window across an oak desk and a neat wall of shelves. The boy entered cautiously now. He placed his small wooden ship on the polished desk and ran his fingertips across the grain. "Will I sit here and write Latin like Father said?"

Juliet came behind him and put both arms around his head. "Yes. And you'll learn properly."

They inspected the guest room and a smaller study next. Remi found the wardrobe more interesting than either and hid inside it until Juliet pretended to search the room with exaggerated despair before dragging him out by one ankle.

"There is still another floor."

The highest level was quieter. Edward's study occupied most of one side. A large chart table stood at its centre. Shelves reached almost to the ceiling. A brass telescope waited beside the window as though whoever furnished the house expected its owner to arrive at any moment.

Remi pressed one eye to the eyepiece. "Mama! I can see the carriages on the avenue!"

Juliet crossed to the room opposite. This one had been prepared for her. An ebony sewing table stood beneath the window beside a proper embroidery frame, with drawers waiting for thread and cloth. She rested her fingertips on the polished edge of the table, quietly taking in the thought that had gone into making the room hers.

At the end of the corridor, double doors opened onto a balcony overlooking the heated canal. Winter wind lifted several strands of her hair. Remi ran out and wrapped both arms around her waist. Together they leaned against the sandstone rail. Red maples bowed over water still moving beneath the cold. For several minutes, neither needed to say anything.

* * *

By late afternoon the little luggage they had brought from Marrakesh had spread through the house. Remi sat on the rug beside his bed with both hands over his stomach. "Mama. My belly is growling. What are we eating?"

Juliet stopped folding a shirt. Through all the anxiety about travel, safety, the house, and Remi's future, she had forgotten supper. "Wait here. I'll look downstairs."

The pantry door opened to shelves so full that Juliet actually stepped back. Fine flour. Oats. Butter wrapped in waxed paper. Smoked sausage. Hard cheeses. Fresh eggs. Preserved fruit. Everything had been sorted by type.

A note had been pinned neatly to the inside of the cupboard door. Food in this pantry has been sanitised and stored under royal standard. If anything approaches spoilage, wrap it in waxed paper and place it on the wooden shelf beside the gate rather than discarding it with household refuse.

The logistics team collects the shelf each morning. Suitable food will be transferred to farms outside the city for animal feed.

Isabella Testarossa

Juliet read it twice. The Queen's attention to detail inspired gratitude and unease in equal measure. Even food approaching spoilage had a route, a rule, and someone assigned to collect it. Juliet rolled up her sleeves. Butter, flour, eggs, and sausage soon produced the first smell in the villa that belonged to the Spencers rather than the people who had prepared it. Remi devoured dinner and repeatedly announced that the food in Madrid was excellent, apparently crediting the entire capital for his mother's cooking.

Afterwards Juliet led him into the bathing room. They spent several embarrassing minutes discovering which valve controlled hot water and which merely changed pressure. Eventually steam blurred the mirror. Juliet washed the road dust from Remi's hair with jasmine soap.

"This is the only time I'm helping you with the whole bath," she told him while rinsing away the foam. "Tomorrow you are old enough to wash yourself properly before bed."

"Yes, Mama."

His eyes were squeezed shut, but his smile remained broad. Once dry and dressed in soft linen sleep clothes, Remi took a small lamp upstairs by himself. Juliet stayed behind. For the first time in days, no one needed her immediately. She removed the old grey travelling dress and sank into the hot bath.

Her body softened almost by surprise. Six years of labour, train seats, cold floors, and tight shoulders seemed to loosen all at once in the water. The comfort should have been complete. Instead the silence became louder.

When Juliet finally rose, wrapped herself in a thick towel, and reached automatically towards the clothes hook, her hand found nothing. She stared. The hook was empty. Every clean dress she had unpacked lay two floors above in the sewing room. "Oh, for God's sake." Juliet covered her face. She had organised food, medicine, documents, Remi's belongings, cattle, ledgers, train tickets, and an entire departure from Marrakesh. She had forgotten to bring clean clothes into the bathroom.

To reach the second floor in only a towel meant crossing the ground-floor hall, taking the main stairs past Remi's room, then climbing another flight. With seven years of experience raising her son, Juliet considered the probability that he would remain quietly in bed during that expedition disastrously low. If he heard one footstep, the untidy little head would appear around the door. And if the towel chose that exact moment to fail... "No." Juliet tightened it around her chest. "Absolutely not."

The other option was the grey travelling dress lying across a chair, carrying coal dust and locomotive smoke after the whole journey from Gibraltar. She looked at it. The dress seemed to look back. Juliet wrinkled her nose. "I would rather die." She pinned the towel firmly beneath one arm, opened the bathroom door a fraction, and inspected the corridor like a thief studying a sentry route.

No Remi. She hurried into the master bedroom and shut the door behind her. A massive walnut wardrobe waited in one corner. Juliet opened both doors. The left side contained Edward. Crisp white shirts, heavy coats, a black-blue formal officer's uniform, gloves, belts, and clothing cut to his measurements. The care was too precise to be accidental; the royal household had prepared an entire life for him in this house before he had ever seen it.

The right side contained a problem. Women's clothing filled it from top to bottom. Satin evening gowns. Fine silk nightwear. Dresses in colours Juliet had never owned. Garments whose necklines appeared to assume a confidence she did not possess. She lifted one nearly weightless silk piece by its narrow straps and turned it over twice. "Is this worn underneath or outside?" Holding it against herself answered the question at once; the neckline plunged far enough to make her put it back as though it had burned her fingers. Then she opened the lower drawer. Juliet froze. Small pieces of silk lay arranged by colour, some attached to ribbons so narrow she could not understand what portion of a respectable woman they were supposed to cover. She lifted one between two fingertips.

"Is this... a handkerchief?" She tried it against her forearm. No. Juliet looked down at herself. The conclusion arrived. Her face went hot. She dropped the thing back into the drawer and stepped away as if it contained unstable Vestigium.

"Women in Madrid actually wear these?" A second, more charitable explanation occurred to her. "Is fabric so expensive that they have to save this much?" She slammed the drawer shut. "Never."

All she wanted now was something clean, modest, and recognisably constructed as clothing. A smaller wardrobe nearby offered several evening gowns. The first was dark red embroidered with gold and looked suitable for a coronation. The second was cream with a neckline Juliet considered nearly as threatening as the silk drawer. At last she found a deep blue-grey dress with a modest collar, sleeves past the elbow, and a skirt falling almost to the ankles. She embraced it like a drowning woman discovering a plank. "At least you resemble clothes."

Minutes later she left the bedroom wearing enough formal fabric for a royal dinner merely because it was the first thing she understood. The skirt caught against her legs twice while she climbed to the sewing room to collect her ordinary dresses.

On the way down she stopped beside Remi's room. He was already asleep, curled beneath the white wool blanket with the small wooden ship still against his chest. Juliet raised the cover over his shoulder and kissed his forehead. Jasmine replaced the coal smoke and dust that had clung to his hair in Marrakesh. Only after she closed the door did the villa's silence fully reach her.

Back downstairs, Juliet removed the ridiculous evening dress and put on her familiar cotton nightgown. She pushed the luxury clothing towards one end of the wardrobe. Beside Edward's immaculate new uniforms, she hung her old grey dresses, faded sleeves and all. The contrast was almost comic. Still, when one frayed hem brushed the dark cloth of Edward's officer's coat, something inside her quieted.

Juliet extinguished the candle and lay down. The bed was too soft. The house was too warm. In Marrakesh she had been trained by necessity to wake when the stove grew quiet, when wind moved a window cloth, when the water bucket needed moving nearer the fire. Her body tightened from habit. She began to sit up. Then she stopped.

Double glass sealed the window. No draught entered. Pipes beneath the floor maintained their quiet heat. The built-in hearth had been designed to last the night without someone rising to feed it. There was nothing to save.

Juliet sat motionless. In Marrakesh, fear had always given her a task. Block the window. Add wood. Move the water. Lift Remi's blanket. Here her hands lay useless on the bed.

She slowly lowered herself again. Street lamps cast pale gold through the windows. Snow still fell in the garden, but none of it could reach her. A bar of light crossed the other half of the mattress. Juliet looked at it. The room had been prepared for husband and wife. Edward's clothes hung behind her. Upstairs waited a study built for him, chart table and telescope already in place. The entire house contained spaces made for Edward. Edward had never entered any of them. His half of the bed remained perfectly flat.

Juliet drew her knees closer. For the first time, she missed the cramped Marrakesh bed where turning in sleep almost always meant accidentally touching the person beside her. Here she had to reach. Her hand moved over the smooth sheet until it reached the middle of the empty half. There was no warm chest beneath her palm. She did not pull back.

"Is the sea very cold tonight, Edward?" The words were barely more than breath. Exhaustion finally claimed her. Hot water continued travelling through the pipes beneath the floor. Juliet slept with one hand still stretched across her husband's untouched side of the bed.

Knock. Knock. Knock. Juliet woke beneath a grey dawn. For several seconds she stared at an unfamiliar ceiling and had no idea where she was. One hand still lay extended across the cold, flat half of the mattress. Memory returned. Madrid. The house. Edward at sea. Knock. Knock. Knock. "Oh, Lord."

Juliet scrambled up, smoothed her hair with both palms, pulled the front of her nightdress straight, and hurried barefoot through the corridor. Cold morning air entered the moment she cracked open the oak door. With it came an unexpectedly bright voice. "Good morning!" Juliet stopped.

A woman about her own age stood on the threshold in a simple cream wool coat. Short blond hair ended near the collarbone, several strands still carrying tiny crystals of snow. Her face held almost no make-up, only a little powder and cheeks pink from the cold. What Juliet noticed first were the eyes. They were clear and gentle, curving immediately with the woman's smile. Not the exact smile of a noblewoman measuring etiquette. Not the kind that made Juliet wonder how deeply to bow, what phrase she should return, or whether she had already violated a rule. Simply the smile of someone genuinely pleased to see her. "You're Juliet Spencer, aren't you?"

Juliet straightened automatically. "Y-yes. I am."

"Good." The woman sighed in exaggerated relief. "I'm Millenia Stones. Marco Stones is my husband."

Juliet blinked. "Marco?"

"Yes. The enormous loud one who drinks wine and becomes convinced his singing improves." A small laugh escaped Juliet before she could stop it. It was the first since waking.

Millenia brushed snow from her shoulder and lifted the large bag in one hand. "He wrote several days ago and repeated at least three times that you and Remi were coming to Madrid. I had to arrive early this morning or you would never know when opening day at the Royal Academy begins."

Juliet went pale. "Opening day is today?"

"Yes."

"Oh, God." Juliet spun towards the house. "I haven't prepared anything. Remi has no uniform, his hair will be impossible, I don't know how to get to the Academy, and..."

"Juliet." Millenia's warm voice stopped the spiral. She lifted the bag higher. "I brought his uniform."

Juliet fell silent.

Millenia raised one finger. "One, I know the road to the Academy." A second. "Two, I know the schedule." A third. "Three, the carriage is already waiting outside." She tilted her head. "So the only thing you need to do right now is invite me in before Madrid freezes me solid."

Juliet stared several seconds before realising she was still blocking the doorway. "Oh! I'm sorry." She jumped aside. "Please come in."

Millenia laughed and crossed the threshold. "Call me Millenia. We are both wives of men with an extraordinary talent for creating problems other people have to worry about."

Juliet laughed again, more clearly this time. Millenia removed her gloves and placed them neatly on the shelf. Instead of touring the villa like a guest inspecting someone else's house, she simply stamped snow from her boots with the ease of someone already welcome.

Small footsteps sounded on the stairs. Remi appeared behind the railing, wooden ship against his chest and hair violently disordered from sleep. Millenia recognised him immediately. "Ah!"

The boy startled and nearly vanished again. She crouched. "Let me guess. That hair, that ship, and the face of a sailor caught sleeping on watch..." Her expression became comically serious. "You must be Remi."

The boy blinked, hugged the ship tighter, then failed to resist smiling. "How did you know?"

"Adult secrets." Millenia put one finger to her lips. "But I know something else."

"What?"

"In the carriage outside, a boy your age has asked me four separate times when Remi Spencer is finally going to come out so the two of you can go to school."

Remi ran down two more steps. "What's his name?"

"You'll have to ask him yourself."

Less than a minute after Millenia entered, the reserve had vanished from Remi's face. Juliet leaned against the hall and watched. The day before, every conversation in Madrid had required her to measure words. Millenia did not give her enough time to feel like an outsider.

"Now." The blond woman stood. "Your turn."

"Mine?"

"That outfit." Millenia pointed at Juliet's plain sleep dress. "Unless you're planning to attend the Royal Academy wearing it. I personally have no objection. You would certainly become the most memorable parent on the first morning."

Juliet looked down. Her cheeks went red. "Oh, Lord."

Millenia laughed. Strangely, Juliet did not feel mocked. "Come on. Let's see what Her Majesty put in the wardrobe."

Juliet hesitated, then led her into the master bedroom. The wardrobe still stood partly open from the night before. Silks, evening gowns, and luxurious nightwear crowded one side beside Juliet's old grey dresses. Embarrassment returned immediately. Juliet pointed towards the shelves. "Honestly... I don't know what order women in Madrid are supposed to wear any of this."

Millenia leaned in. "Hmm."

"And these..." Juliet opened the lower drawer as cautiously as if reporting hazardous Vestigium. "I spent half the night wondering what parts these little pieces are even supposed to cover."

Millenia peered inside. Silence. One second. Two. She turned away and clapped a hand over her mouth. Her shoulders shook.

Juliet's face burned. "Was that a ridiculous question?"

"I'm sorry." Millenia inhaled slowly and turned back, attempting dignity. "There is nothing ridiculous about you." She pulled the drawer wider. "If anyone is to blame, Her Majesty's household prepared far too much."

Juliet blinked. "Really?"

"Completely." Millenia lifted one tiny piece of silk between two fingers. "And, incidentally, most of these designs are mine."

Juliet stared. "You made them?"

"Yes." Millenia waved the silk. "I licensed the patterns to several Madrid dressmakers about two years ago. Interior Affairs apparently decided that if they were furnishing your wardrobe, they should buy almost the entire collection."

Juliet looked from Millenia to the drawer and back. "You design undergarments?"

"Please don't look at me as though I've confessed to storing forbidden Vestigium." Millenia laughed. This time Juliet joined her.

"Come here." Millenia dragged a stool beside the dressing table and arranged garments across it with the care of a craftsman laying out tools. "If Her Majesty spent this much money, the least I can do is make sure you know what to do with it."

She held up a light cotton underlayer. "This touches the skin first. It absorbs sweat and keeps wool, silk, and stiff seams from rubbing directly against you."

Next came the item that had terrified Juliet most. "This is a newer style of drawers. Much shorter and lighter than the old long ones."

Juliet narrowed her eyes. "That little cloth is the entire thing?"

"Yes."

"Won't I freeze?"

"Juliet, Madrid women do not put this on and then run naked through the streets buying bread." Millenia laughed again. "It's for wearing beneath a dress, especially fitted clothing where heavy layers show through. Wider section behind, narrow section in front. The side ribbons sit at the hips. Do not pull them too tight."

Juliet picked up a sturdier cotton version and tested the seams between thumb and forefinger. Years of mending clothes for the family in Marrakesh had taught her to recognise good stitching at once. "This one is useful. Strong stitching."

"That's the everyday version. Warm, easy to wash, difficult to tear."

"Good. If I have to chase Remi across a schoolyard, I prefer not to spend the entire pursuit praying the seam doesn't open."

Juliet covered her mouth, still smiling. "You make that sound as though you've actually split a seam in public." Millenia went silent. Juliet stared. The designer looked away. "Let's examine something else."

Juliet burst out laughing.

Millenia reached for a short supportive garment. "This is a bust support."

Juliet stopped laughing.

"A what?"

"Nothing frightening."

Millenia turned it around to show the front hooks and adjustable shoulder straps. "Old underclothes depend heavily on corsets shaping the whole torso. This only supports the chest. Much easier under dresses that do not require a narrow waist."

"You invented that too?"

"Yes."

"Because corsets are unbearable?"

Millenia placed one hand on Juliet's shoulder. "Have you worn one?"

"Once."

"How did it feel?"

"As though it intended to break my ribs."

Millenia nodded. "You understand me." They both laughed.

Millenia next produced a cream-coloured corset, softer and far less rigid than the old-fashioned kind Juliet remembered. "I call this a soft stay. It uses only a few flexible supports, enough to smooth the shape beneath a formal gown without trying to squeeze your waist into something unnatural." She held it against Juliet for a moment. "For an evening dress, perhaps. For taking Remi to school this morning, absolutely not."

"Thank God," Juliet said, with such relief that Millenia laughed.

Then came a pair of cream stockings and two simple garters. Juliet brightened. "Those I know."

"Then I only have one improvement to offer." Millenia looped a garter loosely above her own knee to demonstrate. "Just tight enough to keep the stocking from slipping. Never tight enough to make you regret having legs."

Juliet took one, examined it, and nodded with genuine approval. "Useful."

"At last," Millenia said. "One design you liked before interrogating it."

"How many more things have you invented?" Juliet asked.

"More than you need to learn in one morning." Millenia began returning the fussier pieces to the wardrobe, then summarised the rules on four fingers. "Softest layer against the skin. Then support or shaping if you need it. Then warmth. Dress and coat last." She pointed at Juliet. "If anything prevents you from sitting, breathing, eating, or chasing your son, do not wear it."

Juliet nodded firmly. "That final rule makes the most sense."

"It is the most important."

Millenia turned to the dresses. She dismissed one elaborate gown at once. "Three hours sitting in that and your back will hate you." A second had a neckline she considered excessive for a school morning. Then a spectacular wine-red gown earned a longer frown. "Wear this to the Academy and half the parents will assume Edward conquered another country and you're attending the triumph."

Juliet laughed. "Put it away."

At last she drew out a moss-green wool dress with a modest collar, long sleeves, and a waist shaped without stiffness. "This." She held it against Juliet and stepped back. "Perfect. The colour suits your hair. Respectable without making you disappear among Madrid society."

On the bed she arranged the full set in order: cotton underlayer, practical cotton drawers, cream wool stockings, soft chest support, a light wool underskirt, the green dress, then a long coat.

"No corset?"

"Absolutely not. You need to stand, sit, walk, crouch beside Remi, and perhaps run if the boys discover a bad idea."

Juliet smiled. The night before, the clothes had felt like evidence that she had entered a world designed for someone else. Now they had become fabric again. Layers for warmth, comfort, movement, and choice.

She looked at Millenia. "Most of these really are your designs?"

"Most." Millenia shrugged. "Women have suffered inconvenient clothing long enough. If men can spend decades making guns fire faster, women deserve some time making dresses easier to breathe in."

Juliet stared several seconds. Then she laughed, fully and without restraint. The sound surprised even her.

Millenia pressed the clothes into her arms. "Go change." She started towards the door. "If you forget the order, call me."

"Millenia."

Millenia turned. "Yes?"

"The... drawers."

"Yes?"

Juliet's face reddened. "The wider part goes behind, correct?"

Millenia froze. Her shoulders began to shake.

"You promised not to laugh at me."

"I'm not laughing."

"You are clearly laughing."

"I'm sorry."

Their laughter filled the room again.

Outside the window, Madrid's morning light was beginning to break through the thin fog. Millenia returned to the sitting room and opened the large bag she had brought. Inside lay a navy-blue Academy uniform pressed to perfection, with thick wool stockings and a child's scarf. Remi ran over. "Oh!"

"Stand still." Millenia held the coat against him and narrowed her eyes. "Good. Very good."

Then she looked towards Juliet, who now stood at the bedroom doorway in the moss-green dress. "See?" Her playful smile returned. "Nothing to worry about."

Juliet paused. The sentence was simple. The weight it removed was not. Since leaving Marrakesh, Madrid, the villa, the etiquette, the clothes, and every unfamiliar system had made Juliet feel she would have to solve everything alone. Now Remi was firing questions about school while Millenia fought cheerfully with the uniform buttons and occasionally called Juliet over to help as though they had known one another for years. Morning light spread across the wooden floor.

Juliet stood in the room holding the edge of her green dress. For the first time since reaching Madrid, she no longer felt entirely alone.

The train began to slow, steel wheels screaming along the rails until the iron-and-glass arches of Lisbon station appeared through the cold morning mist. Edward had risen early; his uniform coat was properly fastened, and the night aboard had left little visible trace on him. Fredo looked very different. The Royal Guard was fighting his last button with sleep-deprived hands. Dark circles under his eyes made him look as though he had spent several days under siege rather than one night in a heated railway carriage.

Edward folded his scarf. "One night on a train has reduced you to this. I'm beginning to suspect the carriage did not carry us from Seville. It made you pull it."

Fredo stopped at the final button. "For the record, I did lie down and attempt to sleep like a normal person." He straightened one cuff. "Every time I closed my eyes, your questions returned. By dawn I realised I wasn't arguing with you any longer. I was arguing with things I had spent years treating as obvious."

Edward's smile faded. "Then one sleepless night is still a small price." He clapped Fredo on the shoulder. He had paid far more dearly for things he had refused to question in time.

"What troubles you on paper often saves lives at sea. But enough of doctrine. Find some cold water to clear your head. Lisbon won't let us sit around philosophising until noon."

Fredo gathered the valise and leather notebook. They followed the crowd onto the platform beneath a roof white with breath and thin morning light. Edward washed at a stone basin beside the waiting hall and found a wooden bench near the ticket gates. For several minutes he allowed his body to remain still. Nearby, a father bent to wrap his son's scarf more tightly while the mother held the boy's other hand. The three walked away arguing over whether they could still catch a carriage to the eastern district. Edward watched until they vanished through the gate. His fingers touched the place on his collar Juliet had straightened before they separated at Gibraltar.

Fredo returned with wet hair combed neatly back. Only the dark circles remained. "If you continue staring at other people's families like that, I may have to explain to the constables that Sir Edward Spencer has no intention of abducting children. He merely misses his wife and son with unusual clarity."

Edward laughed and lowered his hand. "I miss Juliet and Remi." He looked once more towards the gate. "Let's settle Lisbon quickly and come home. I don't want the first news Juliet receives about her husband to be a casualty report."

Fredo straightened his sleeve. "I support that objective completely. I have no desire to stand before Juliet and explain why I allowed her husband to die in a naval base before he even saw the enemy."

Only then did Edward notice that Fredo's admiral's shoulder boards had been arranged perfectly beneath his coat and the lion pendant marked Tres now rested outside the collar. He stood and lifted the valise. "In a few minutes you've transformed from a man dying on a bench into an Admiral of the Royal Guard." Edward looked from the shoulder boards to the polished buttons. "Was there cold water in that washroom, or a ceremony for replacing souls?"

"Cold water, a comb, and fear of appearing before the Council Navy with a crooked collar." Fredo checked it again. "Those three things preserve honour better than you imagine. Especially when standing beside a former English Admiral with a habit of staring at other people's insignia and asking questions that prevent sleep."

Edward looked again at the two shoulder boards. "Wait." He pointed. "A relief operation at San Sebastián already requires both you and me to carry admiral's authority. Do not tell me Lisbon contains more."

Fredo secured the lion against his chest and walked towards the main gate. "More." He did not turn. "You're still counting too few, Sir Edward. You'll understand at the naval base."

* * *

The carriage waiting outside had heating Vestigia mounted beneath the floor. Weak warmth rose through the boards as wheels cut through snow-covered Lisbon streets towards the Tagus. The military harbour appeared through fog before Edward could see individual ships. He heard it first. Hammers striking rivets. Wooden blocks knocking against hauling lines. Capstans groaning under load. Officers calling the changing watch.

Tar, salt, and gun oil entered the carriage with every gust from the river. Edward stepped onto the quay and immediately found himself checking mast angles, rigging tension, powder crates moving towards the decks, and the spacing between ships in the channel. Six years away from a flagship had not erased the habits. Marrakesh had simply never needed them.

Then an English voice shouted from the low deck of the nearest frigate. "Keep the pull even on the left! Don't let the brake line twist!" Edward turned. Two other sailors in grey-white Castilian uniform counted the hauling rhythm in English before their voices disappeared back into the surrounding Castilian orders. Fredo heard them too but said nothing. Edward slowed. An older gunner carried a faded anchor tattoo on his wrist. Another sailor tied his scarf in a style common in English squadrons before London fell.

No one ran to call him the Pathmaker. No one shouted his name. Several men merely looked at him a little too long before returning to work. That was enough. The English had not vanished entirely from the sea. They had changed uniforms, changed the flag above their heads, and learned to draw wages from another kingdom so they could continue doing what they had once done for a homeland that no longer existed.

Two Admirals waited through the fog at the main quay. The first was a broad, scarred middle-aged man with a red beard curled down at either side of his mouth. Gold insignia of the Castilian Council of Knights covered his chest. The second was a tall woman built as straight and spare as a blade. Black hair had been pinned high behind her head. The Castilian lion at her throat carried the mark Veinticinco. Martinez struck her heel in salute before they reached her. "All preparations under the sealed orders are complete." She handed Fredo a file. "One hundred Conquistadores transferred in full. Cold-weather equipment and weapon stores inspected twice. Ship officers await only final order before closing the rolls."

Fredo flipped through the pages. Martinez looked at the shadows beneath his eyes. "You look terrible, Fredo." She waited until he glanced up. "One night on a train and you appear to have spent three days inside a siege. If Sir Edward caused this, remember that a council of war is not required to continue until dawn."

Fredo did not deny it. "Don't put all of it on Sir Edward." He tapped the notebook. "He asked one question. I did the rest to myself. In exchange, I have more notes than when we left Seville. Not an absolute loss."

Martinez tapped the book once and stepped back.

At the same time, the red-bearded man looked over and froze. "Damn me." Don Trafalgar barged past two sailors carrying a crate. He stared Edward from boots to face. "Edward Spencer?" Edward barely had time to smile before Trafalgar seized his arm. "It really is you." The older Admiral laughed and dragged him into an embrace strong enough to knock Edward's valise against both their legs. "All these years without one damned scrap of news. I thought you had at least possessed the decency to die somewhere in the Channel."

"I considered it." Edward struck his back twice and shoved him away far enough to inspect the wild red beard. "Then I heard that ugly face of yours was still alive and decided death could wait."

Trafalgar glared. Edward pointed at the beard. "Someone still has to remind you that La Coruña was not Don Trafalgar's personal victory."

"Damn your whole bloodline." Trafalgar laughed so hard he had to bend forward. He kept one hand on Edward's shoulder as though letting go might allow the man to disappear for another six years.

Then he turned towards Fredo and Martinez. "Do not let him rewrite history. The last time this bastard and I fought together at La Coruña, if my squadron had not torn open the French flank, his English gunships would have been fish stew before dawn."

Edward folded his arms. "If my gunships had not held the covering line, your proud squadron would have been on the bottom of the bay before it had the privilege of tearing anything." He smiled. "Keep the beard. Keep the honour. Do not steal everyone else's share as well."

Several dockworkers turned at the laughter. Edward noticed something else. When Trafalgar crossed the quay, older sailors saluted with the ease of men who had served under him long enough not to stiffen unnecessarily. When Martinez turned, two nearby ranks of Conquistadores corrected their spacing without a shouted order. Fredo merely opened his notebook and a naval clerk brought the personnel ledger at once. Edward had no formation in Lisbon carrying his name. Even so, several English gunners on distant decks paused when he passed.

Trafalgar followed his gaze. "Looking for True Hero?"

Edward looked at the harbour.

Trafalgar shook his head. "Don't waste the search. Since England fell, she has never appeared on the Lisbon register. I have heard no report worth believing."

"I know." Edward continued scanning the dark hulls. "I don't expect her to be here. My eyes simply still look for that bow, that spacing of masts, every time I enter a naval base."

He finally stopped. Trafalgar led them towards the outer edge of the quay. "Old ghosts later. Look at what Lisbon has managed to keep alive. If we intend to reach San Sebastián, these ships are what will carry us out of the Tagus."

The fog thinned. Edward counted bows, masts, rigging lines, then counted again. "Fourteen that can leave harbour." He pointed. "The outer three need rigging inspected. That one replaced her mizzen recently. The next has two gun ports temporarily sealed." He looked at Trafalgar. "The number on paper is prettier than the fleet."

Trafalgar did not object. "Correct. Eleven frigates and corvettes. Three four-deck ships of the line." He indicated the heavy hulls. "Ice-breaking bows reinforced. Rigging and sails on the three largest coated with whale fat and Vestigium powder according to the method sent overnight."

They walked. One frigate carried a hull patch of fresh pale timber against older oak. Another had a new upper mast and hauling lines assembled from three different kinds of rope as though stores had been stripped to the last serviceable coils. Below deck, Edward found a watch list where several names had been crossed out and replaced in different ink. An eight-man gun crew had six men in position. Two young sail handlers ran below to fill the missing places when an officer inspected the drill. Trafalgar stopped beside the patched frigate. "Do not trust paint." He slapped the new timber. "Lisbon has repaired these ships too many times. Some look worse than they are. Some look better." His voice lowered. "But they float. The guns fire. The sailors still board when ordered."

Edward watched a man rewrap a bandage around his wrist and return to the hauling line. "Then I need two numbers." He nodded towards the depleted gun crew. "How many ships can leave harbour, and how many can survive another battle without making three men do the work of five?"

Trafalgar looked over the crews before answering. "Five thousand eight hundred, including Martinez's hundred Conquistadores." He tightened one glove. "Not pretty. Still enough to operate fourteen ships if we do not lose people before contact."

Fredo opened the sealed orders and checked the ledger twice. Then he stopped. "Wait." He reread the personnel column. "The Queen's order lists six Admirals and nearly three thousand more troops. I see only the four of us and five thousand eight hundred." He closed the book. "Where are the other three thousand? Where are the other two Admirals?"

Trafalgar did not answer quickly enough. Fredo continued. "If they remain on the Lisbon establishment, then they must be in the barracks around the harbour." He folded the document. "I need that answer before we discuss departure time."

A voice came from behind the fog before Trafalgar could reply. "Do not force Trafalgar to answer alone." The voice moved closer. "The people you're looking for are still in Lisbon. We kept them ashore." Two figures emerged. The man in front had silver entering his hair and a carefully trimmed grey beard. Dark shadows beneath his eyes showed the cost of command more clearly than any decoration. Beside him walked a slender woman in a black velvet cloak edged with silver. Her step remained steady as she inspected the ships and sailors around her as though those mattered more than the ceremony awaiting at the quay.

Edward recognised Don José and Dame Elizabeth before they arrived. Both names had occupied Castilian naval reports for years. Yet their reputations mattered less to Edward than the harbour's response. A supply officer automatically brought José the manpower ledger before he raised a hand. Elizabeth merely looked towards the nearest frigate and its officer stopped shouting, came down the gangway, and waited. Six Admirals now stood within the same piece of quay. Edward did not see a unified command. The Royal Guards carried direct authority from Isabella. The Council of Knights held ships, crews, and local influence. Trafalgar possessed loyalty built through campaigns. Edward carried a restored title but not one squadron of his own.

He looked from one face to the next. "Before we continue, I need one thing answered." No one interrupted. "If all six of us go to sea and formation breaks after the first broadside, who has the authority to issue one order for all fourteen ships?" Edward did not wait for an easier version of the question. "I'm not asking who can stamp documents on shore. I'm asking out there, in the first ten minutes, who speaks and the whole fleet obeys?"

Fredo closed his ledger. Martinez looked towards Trafalgar. José rested one hand on the manpower book. No one claimed the authority. At last José answered. "On paper, the Queen's sealed order defines the objective and gives the Royal Guard power to enforce its execution. But the squadrons still belong to the admirals who hold them. Anything beyond the authority of a single squadron requires agreement among us."

Edward looked at the masts moving in the wind. "Then that is the first hole." He pointed towards the water. "A storm does not wait for six people to agree. Neither does the enemy. If our formation breaks and we still have to negotiate among ourselves, the first enemy broadside makes the decision for us."

Martinez did not object. Elizabeth watched him. José closed the ledger. "Correct question. But today we have not yet reached the point of choosing who commands at sea." He tilted his head towards the barracks beyond the stores. "The remaining three thousand are there. I signed the order keeping them ashore."

Martinez's shoulders squared. José continued. "I know what the Queen's orders say. I also know the Royal Guard will dislike my decision." He looked towards the patched ships. "But a seal does not transform a bad plan into a good one." His eyes returned to the harbour. "Castile has not won a naval victory large enough to force Portugal to change the way it fights." He counted on his fingers. "They have better charts. They know storms better. And they possess seven Legendary-grade Vestigia we still do not understand."

Elizabeth nodded towards the pale timber patch on the frigate. "Look at that." She waited until Edward did. "Our experience in the last several years was purchased by ships returning home in that condition." Her voice remained cool. "Courage does not solve a weapon you do not understand. If you want to call caution cowardice, do so. First look at who pays for the remainder of the calculation."

Fredo reopened the sealed order. "Then let me make certain I understand you." He folded the page. "You do not require another legal reason to deploy." Fredo looked at José. "You require a plan clear enough that you believe the three thousand men ashore will not go to sea merely to repeat the last defeat."

José met his eyes. "Yes." He removed one glove and folded it inside the other hand. "If one of you can show me how, I open the gates myself and sail with them." He looked towards the barracks. "But I will not throw three thousand more men into the water because the report sent to Madrid would look cleaner. Families in Lisbon do not bury paperwork. They bury people."

Trafalgar tightened his glove but said nothing. Elizabeth looked towards the nearest frigate. A gunner tied the same wrist bandage again. A young sailor beside the gun port stared at the water. The officer behind them continued counting his crew as though rhythm alone could keep the whole structure from breaking. "They will still board if ordered," she said.

José looked at the young sailor. "That is exactly what worries me." He pulled the glove back on. "Discipline can carry a man onto a deck even when he believes he will die." José faced the six Admirals. "I do not need more men obedient enough to sink with the ship. I need them to believe they still have a chance to win."

Elizabeth turned fully towards Edward. "Sir Edward, if you want those remaining men, do not speak to them again about courage, honour, or the past." She pointed at the decks waiting in the mist. "Give them a specific reason to believe they will not die the same way this time." Her eyes shifted towards the Admirals around him. "After that, we may discuss command."

Wind swept in from the Tagus, pulling the flags taut and then letting them fall again above the fogged water. Edward looked from José to the repaired hulls, the English gunners in Castilian grey-white, and the crowded decks waiting for an order no one had yet agreed would come from whom. From that moment, he stopped counting ships.

He began counting the questions a plan had to answer before it had any right to take them to sea.

The sun had risen above the mist over Lisbon Bay, but its light only made the ice along the railings shine more sharply. It did nothing to soften the cold. Don José straightened the front of his coat, exchanged a few words with Elizabeth, and turned towards the barracks as though the argument on the quay had ended. "Wait, Don José." Edward followed him two paces. José stopped, looked him over, and tilted his head.

"At last, Sir Edward? Let me guess. You will mention La Coruña, remind us of the naval battles you never lost, then tell five thousand men out there that all they need do is trust the Pathmaker and the ocean itself will move aside."

Edward had been about to begin almost exactly that way. He knew it the instant José said it, and the irritation on his face lingered long enough for Elizabeth to notice. "You are half right." Edward looked beyond the masts in the bay. Fourteen warships still lay there, patched and battered, but afloat, armed, and crewed. "I used to treat old victories as proof that my next decision had to be right. I have paid enough for that habit." He turned back to José. "But San Sebastián is still being strangled. If it falls, the northern sea route opens. That does not stop being true because we hate the plan in front of us."

José did not answer immediately. He set the strength ledger on a crate and held the page open with one finger. "Correct. San Sebastián must be relieved." He tapped the casualty figure at the bottom. "But a worthy objective does not make every road leading to it worthy. I can love Castile enough to die for it and still have enough sense not to throw three thousand men into an unfinished calculation."

Elizabeth stepped back into the conversation. Her anger did not flare, but Edward could tell it had been there since José first mentioned the dead. "If you want to speak about the price of losing San Sebastián, then speak about the price of the way you like to win, Edward." She pointed towards Trafalgar and then towards the ships in the bay. "La Coruña. You remember it. You turned into the French gun line, dragged the squadron behind you, and won. All England called you invincible." Her jaw tightened. "My closest friend did not come home from that victory."

Edward did not interrupt. "I do not deny that you saved the battle. I deny the idea that a beautiful result makes every life spent to buy it reasonable." Elizabeth gestured towards the sailors. "These men have heard 'one more battle' more times than you think."

She pointed down towards the nearest frigate. The gun crew Edward had noticed on arriving was still replacing its breeching ropes with too few hands. "That crew should have eight men. Today it has six. The two empty places are not there because someone overslept in the barracks. I know the names of the men who did not return. José knows where their families live. Trafalgar has written so many death letters that he no longer lets a secretary do it for him."

Trafalgar did not object. He pulled his glove tight at the wrist, his eyes still on the decks beyond the quay. "My men do not need anyone to teach them how to die for Castile," he said. "What they are asking is whether this death will buy anything besides a handsome report sent back to Madrid."

Martinez stepped forward, one hand resting on the hilt of her longsword without drawing it. "Dame Elizabeth, criticising Sir Edward does not alter the fact that the mobilisation order bears the Queen's seal. The Council may oppose the plan, but withholding ships and manpower already assigned exceeds your authority. If every squadron obeys only the orders it agrees with, there is no unified navy left."

José closed the ledger and turned fully towards her. "Then before you speak further of authority, answer one question. If Madrid believes San Sebastián is worth risking a fleet, why is the first fleet placed on the table the Council fleet at Lisbon?" He indicated the fourteen hulls in the bay. "Lisbon feeds these ships. Those sailors live on Council pay and Council stores. These yards have patched them back together after every defeat. The Queen's order arrived. What did not arrive was an explanation of why the Crown's own warships were not placed into the calculation before ours."

Fredo closed the notebook in his hand. "I do not control the complete disposition of every Royal squadron. The sealed order assigns Lisbon the relief because this is the force able to assemble in time. If another fleet were close enough to replace it, that would have been written into the order."

José nodded without looking satisfied. "So you do not know where the Crown fleet is. You only know mine is nearest. Can you see why my sailors hear that and conclude they are the cheapest part of the calculation?"

Elizabeth looked towards Martinez. "Do not call our people cowards because they ask why Madrid will not place its own ships into the equation first. If the Crown lacks ships, say the Crown lacks ships. If Lisbon is the only force capable of reaching San Sebastián in time, prove it. Do not use discipline as a substitute for an answer."

Martinez removed her hand from the sword, though her voice remained hard. "Military duty does not permit high command to display the entire war before every deployment. If every unit demands that Madrid spread the strategic map across the quay before deciding whether to obey, the Empire would have collapsed in the first winter."

"True," José said. "A soldier does not need the whole map. An Admiral needs enough of it to know where he is taking his men. I am not asking for a guarantee of victory. I am asking for a plan that explains why this time we are not repeating the same method that killed them last time." He pointed towards the mouth of the Tagus. "If a Portuguese warship appeared out there today, I would be the first man aboard. Give me an answer to their seven Legendary Vestigia and I will lead this squadron to sea myself. I do not need pretty survival odds, and I do not need anyone to promise we return intact." José looked directly at Fredo. "But do not mistake my refusal to waste my men for fear of battle."

Several Council officers nearby adjusted their grips on their weapons, not lowering them, merely holding them more firmly. The sailors aboard remained at their stations. A corporal continued checking strength while the nearest frigate's gun crew kept changing ropes even though the argument might turn into a firefight at any moment. Edward looked along the harbour. He had seen mutineers before, and he had seen sailors panic when rumours of a sinking ship spread through a deck. This looked like neither.

Fredo stepped forward. "The Queen's order remains in force. I have heard your arguments, but continued detention of the ships is still disobedience in wartime. The Royal Guard has the authority to strip your commissions and send you to Madrid for trial."

Elizabeth gave a short laugh and spread her hands. "Then arrest me. But before you do, ask yourself why several thousand people are still standing behind us when they know Madrid may call this refusal of orders. They are here because when a ship sinks, the first officers they see in the rescue boats are Council officers, not the seal on a dispatch."

Martinez looked across the ranks. No one cheered. No one stirred them up. No one left position either.

José walked to the edge of the quay. "Listen!" The call travelled along the ships. Gun crews stopped working, officers of the watch turned towards the quay, and men hauling lines stood still without dropping their tools. "I will order no one to desert, and I will order no one to rise against the Queen. But I will not force my people into a campaign when command has not shown how it intends to bring them back, or at least shown that their deaths can purchase a real military result." He looked from deck to deck. "Anyone who stands with the Council's decision will finish the task in hand, safe the guns, seal the powder magazines, and disembark by unit. No disorder. No damage to the ships. We are refusing an order. We are not destroying our own navy."

The first man down the gangway was a gunner whose hair had gone more than half grey. Before leaving the deck, he checked the recoil tackle one last time, shut the powder chest, and only then slung his musket over his shoulder. A six-man gun crew followed. Their corporal called the pace, and they crossed the gangway in two files. The last man even turned back to chock the wheels of the gun nearest the port. Then another deck went quiet. Across fourteen warships, sailors closed compartments, secured lines, lowered ammunition into safe storage, and left by organised units. Within minutes, thousands had formed orderly blocks along the harbour, muskets upright at their shoulders and officers standing before their ranks.

Fredo watched them. The anger had not left his face, but it now had to share space with a more difficult fact. These were not men running from battle. "You understand what you are doing?"

José looked over his formation before answering. "We do. If Madrid wishes to call this wartime disobedience, call it by its proper name. If an arrest order arrives tomorrow, I will stand here and let them take me." He pointed to the packed ranks. "But do not call them cowards."

Fredo pushed the notebook inside his coat. His pistol came free of the holster in one clean motion. "Article Fourteen of the Royal Code authorises the Guard to act immediately against any noble or officer whose conduct threatens the security of the Empire. Don José, if you continue driving this naval base into confrontation with the Crown, you leave me no other choice."

Two hammers clicked back almost together. Elizabeth had drawn both pistols. One muzzle rested close to Fredo's temple. The other covered Martinez as she began to draw her sword. "Then do not choose."

Dozens of Council soldiers in the front line raised their weapons at once, but no one charged. They spread according to their officers' commands, closed angles, and kept their distance from the Royal Guards as though this were a drill practised a hundred times. Fredo did not lower his pistol from José. "You are pointing weapons at the Royal Guard."

"And you are pointing one at their Admiral." Elizabeth never took her eyes off him. "Do not make them decide which oath deserves to survive."

José refused to let the standoff stretch any further. He turned towards Trafalgar. Fredo followed his gaze. "Admiral Trafalgar, order your men to lower their weapons."

Trafalgar stood still for several seconds. Then he drew his sidearm, but the muzzle did not point at José. "Sorry, Fredo." The pistol settled towards the Royal Guards. "I will not shoot my own people to prove that I am loyal to the same country they are trying to defend."

Edward looked from one side to the other. Fredo had the Queen's seal. José and Elizabeth had the people who had survived defeat beside them. Edward himself had only an old title and memories of a navy that no longer existed. One shot here would answer none of their questions. "Fuck." He said it quietly enough for himself alone.

Among the clicks of gunlocks and the wind through the masts, a figure appeared against the rail of the nearest frigate. Edward recognised the dark blue uniform, gold epaulettes, and white gloves before the face became clear. His younger self leaned on the rail as though he still stood aboard an English warship. "You are looking in the wrong place."

Edward kept his eyes on the weapons before him. "I am looking at three Admirals preparing to shoot two Royal Guards. Difficult to miss."

The younger Edward laughed and nodded towards José, Elizabeth, and Trafalgar. "That is the problem. You are still trying to beat them."

Edward turned. "If I do not beat them, how do I get the ships to sea?" "You asked that in Scotland."

The younger man stopped smiling. Edward knew the name before it was spoken.

"Wallace."

"Wallace."

A rope snapped hard in the wind. The apparition stepped down from the rail and walked between armed men as though no one but Edward could see him.

"Remember what was most irritating about him? Not the swordsmanship. Not the speeches. Before he appeared, the Scottish houses hated one another almost as much as they hated us. They fought over who marched first, who controlled the grain, even which side of a field each camp occupied." Edward remembered. The early reports had convinced the English staff that the rebellion would tear itself apart before a major battle became necessary. It had not. "Wallace did not make them love one another. He did not settle every old feud. He did one thing better than we did."

Edward looked at him. "He made each clan understand that if the line beside it broke, it died too."

The apparition nodded. "Finally."

Edward frowned. "You want me to turn the Council and the Crown into one fighting formation here on the quay?"

"No. I want you to stop imagining your task is to end their disagreement." His younger self pointed towards Fredo and José. "Those two can hate each other's use of power for the rest of their lives. It does not matter." He turned, his finger moving across the sailors. "Look at their hands."

Edward did. A gunner in the second rank wore the fingerless gloves of the old Royal Navy. Another man had tied his rifle sling with a familiar double knot. Farther down the formation, a corporal shifting his section used the same three-beat cadence English gun crews once used to change position on cramped decks. Edward had noticed fragments of it since arriving in Lisbon. Forced now to look instead of count, he saw them everywhere.

"You see Council, Crown, Castilian, Moroccan, English exile," the apparition said. "They see gun crew, watch, command, the man who hauled them out of the water, the man who stood beside them when a gunport blew in."

"The officers divide them into factions."

"The deck divides them by work." His younger self tilted his head towards the ranks. "You lost to Wallace because you tried to break the clans one at a time. He bound them into a system before you realised you were fighting a system."

Edward clenched his jaw. "Thank you for reminding me."

"You paid the tuition in blood. It would be wasteful not to learn." Edward almost laughed. Then another hammer drew back and his attention returned to the guns.

"Suppose you are right. What do I do? Call every former English sailor out of formation? That only creates a third faction."

"Correct, if you call them out to restore a country." The apparition stepped close. "But if you call them out because they know a fighting system you know how to command, that is different.
