You do not need all Lisbon to love you. You do not need six Admirals to agree on politics. You need one crew that trusts that when you call a turn, the man beside them understands what happens next." Wind struck the quay and pulled the Castilian flags taut. "Start with the man who is most afraid."

Edward followed his gaze. "The most afraid?"

"People assume the most frightened man is the weakest. Wrong. In a formation that has lost too much, he is often the one who remembers most clearly why it broke." In the second rank to the left stood a gaunt young man with a small crescent scar beside one eye. His musket still covered the Royal Guards, but the hand around the stock would not stay steady. A name returned to Edward. The apparition stepped backwards into the thin harbour mist. "Do not ask the Admirals who is right, Edward." He faded behind rigging and masts. "Ask the sailors what they still believe."

Edward searched the faces again. Castilians, Moroccans, a few French exiles, and there in the second rank the gaunt face with the crescent scar. "Timothy Beaumont!" The young man flinched. His weapon still pointed towards the Guards, but his finger came away from the trigger when Edward called his name. "You still remember me, sir?"

Edward stepped out despite Fredo's attempt to stop him. "You were the youngest powder assistant aboard my ship. You nearly burned your hair off at Skagerrak because you ran a powder bag against the wind."

A strangled laugh escaped Timothy before he lowered his head. The musket came down. "I thought you had forgotten."

"No." Edward stopped before him. "But I want to know why a man who once stood a deck with me is now pointing a weapon at someone under the same flag."

Timothy tightened his grip. "Because I am tired, sir." He looked up. His voice began to fracture. "For years, every time we sail, someone tells us the next battle will be different. Then another ship sinks, more people disappear, and when we come home there is another officer explaining why the last defeat was necessary." Timothy pointed towards Trafalgar. "Vila do Porto." The name tightened his shoulders as though someone had pulled a wire along his spine. He no longer looked at Trafalgar. He looked through him, down towards the black water between quay and frigate. "My ship was torn in half offshore. More than a hundred men died before sunrise."

Trafalgar did not evade the accusation. He lowered his pistol beside his thigh. "That battle was my responsibility. If you need a head to put it on, put it on mine first."

Timothy laughed once without humour. "You think I am only angry because the order was wrong?" He turned to Edward. His breaths shortened, not enough to lose control, but enough that every sentence had to pass through a swallow. "I clung to a plank for two days. On the first day I could still hear people calling to one another. By the second night there were hardly any voices left. A man who slept in the hammock above mine for almost a year froze with both hands locked around the edge of the plank. I had to break his fingers one by one to get his body off because the wood could not carry another man." No one laughed. No one told him to calm down. "When they pulled me out, I kept vomiting seawater even though there was nothing left in my stomach. Three days later I woke in the infirmary and asked whether gun number six had survived. I did not ask who was alive. I did not ask when the ship sank. I asked about the gun."

A metal hook struck a hull behind them. Timothy snapped his head towards the sound before anyone else reacted. Edward saw it. Timothy saw that he had seen it. "It has been like that for years. Every time there is an order to sail, I check the ladder down to the gun deck before I check the guns. I count the nearest ports. I sleep in my boots because if the ship lists, I do not want to waste time looking for them. Some nights a line only has to creak harder than usual and I wake thinking the hull is splitting again." He looked towards the warships. There was less anger in his voice now than shame. "And the worst part is that before I even see the enemy, I am already thinking about sinking." A few Council sailors shifted their feet. "Once I stepped onto a deck thinking which enemy I would hit first. Now I step aboard wondering which port will flood first. Do you understand, Admiral? I am not afraid of a bullet killing me. I am afraid that I have already lost before the anchor line is loose."

Edward said nothing. Neither did Trafalgar.

Elizabeth moved first. She lowered one pistol, though the other still kept Fredo covered. "Timothy."

He shook his head. "I am not finished, Elizabeth."

"I know." Her voice did not soften. "But you are about to turn what happened to you into a sentence against an entire navy."

Timothy swung towards her. "Because they are Castilian, sir." He spoke to Edward, though his eyes remained on Elizabeth. "Everyone knows it and no one wants to say it. Without the Royal Navy beside it, the Castilian Navy has too often been nothing more than wooden targets waiting for another fleet to tear apart."

A curse came from the ranks. The sailor with the burn scar stepped half a pace out. "Say that again."

Several Council muskets shifted. Men near Timothy turned towards him while their officers raised hands to stop the formation surging forward. Timothy faced the sailor. "I said you have been losing too long."

"No. You said we were wooden targets." The sailor pulled his collar aside, revealing a white scar from collarbone to ear. "I got this jumping into the water to pull two Englishmen out of a burning gun deck. One lived. One died in my arms before the boat reached the ship." Timothy opened his mouth and found no immediate answer.

Only then did Elizabeth approach. She did not embrace him or touch his shoulder. She struck two fingers against the centre of his chest. "I sat outside the infirmary for three nights after Vila do Porto. I know you woke asking for gun number six. I also know that on the fourth night you crawled out of bed because someone called a watch change in the corridor and you thought you were back aboard."

Timothy ground his teeth. "Then you should understand."

"I understand. That is why I am telling you not to talk like an idiot." She pointed towards the burned sailor. "You want to curse Trafalgar, curse me, curse José, then do it. We sign orders. We wear rank. We have the power to be wrong, and we answer when we are wrong. But do not take the night you nearly died and throw it at the men who jumped into the sea to pull you and your people out."

Timothy drew a long breath. "I did not call them cowards."

"Then say what you mean."

He looked back towards the ships. When he spoke again, he no longer shouted. "I mean this navy has lost for too long. So long that people no longer discuss how to win. They discuss how many ships are acceptable to lose. So long that when an order to sail arrives, my first thought is not to check the powder. It is whether I should write to my mother before or after supper." The burned sailor did not interrupt. "The Portuguese and the French taught us to fear the sea. You may hate me for saying it. I hate myself because every time I hear the signal to prepare for departure, my knees want to turn back towards the barracks." He crushed the sling in his hand. "But I still board the ship. Every time."

Trafalgar held his gaze until Timothy looked back. "And we still send you."

"Yes."

One word, and no one heard it now as a simple accusation. Trafalgar nodded. "Then the shame is not that you are afraid. The shame is that we let you carry that fear onto deck voyage after voyage without yet showing you why the next one will be different."

José said nothing. Neither did Fredo. Elizabeth folded her arms. "And the stupid part is turning command's failures into proof that every Castilian is incompetent. Do that and you are no better than the nobles in Madrid who think the men down here are numbers." Timothy's mouth twitched, ready to argue. "Go on," Elizabeth said. "I know you want to."

"I still mean what I said." Timothy looked back to Edward. "When the Royal Navy fought beside us, I never stepped onto a deck feeling defeated before I saw the enemy. Arrogant or not, offensive or not, I do not know how to lie about that."

The burned sailor answered from the line. "Then do not lie. Just remember all of it. When a ship sinks, English blood and Castilian blood are the same colour on the water." Timothy looked down at his musket. For the first time since he began speaking, his hands stopped shifting.

Trafalgar lowered his pistol completely. "Enough. Beaumont has the right to remember defeat in his own way. You have the right to hate the way he says it. But none of you gets to make the man beside you a coward just to make yourselves feel better."

Edward let the silence hold until the clink of chains beneath the quay filled it. "Are you afraid to die?"

"No, sir." Timothy answered immediately. "I am afraid of dying without knowing what my life bought. I am afraid of boarding because someone calls it duty, then learning when the water comes through the gunport that no one ashore truly knew what we had been sent to do."

Edward remained silent. He had heard another version of that thought in Marrakesh, from a Sultan who had taught him that sacrifice meant something only when the commander understood the value of what he spent. "If I show you a plan clearly enough that you know what we are doing, will you board?"

Timothy studied him. "A real plan? Not a speech. Not 'trust me because I used to win.' A real plan."

"I can promise you one thing. I will not ask anyone to board because I won somewhere ten years ago." Edward pointed towards the fleet. "Before we weigh anchor, you will know which ship we intend to use, how we intend to fight, and what this battle is meant to achieve. If you still believe I am trading lives for reputation, you may walk off."

Timothy looked towards Elizabeth. She neither nodded nor shook her head. "If you can prove it, I will go."

Edward turned to the ranks crowding the quay. He did not shout immediately. He did not invoke England or restoration as bait. "Those of you who once served under the flag of the Royal Navy, step forward so I can see you." Men looked at one another, but no one moved at once. Edward gave them time. "I am not asking you to betray Castile. This country gave many of us a bed, food, and a deck when England had nothing left to give. Some of the people here have fought beside you longer than many Englishmen still alive." He looked from Fredo to José. "But if I am to take a ship out of Lisbon, I need to know who still remembers how we once fought together. Not to resurrect a dead empire. I need people who know the command system, gun handling, and deck coordination I know how to lead."

The first to step out was an old sailor missing two fingers. He removed his cap, looked first at his Council officer, and only then went to stand near Timothy. "Eight years under the Royal flag." No one cheered. Another man stepped out from the gun crews and gave only the city of his birth. "Portsmouth." Then four more. A group of gunners left the Council line, slung their muskets, and joined Timothy. Before going, their corporal turned to say something to the Castilian officer holding the unit. The officer simply nodded. Gaps began to open along the harbour.

Elizabeth looked at Timothy. "Are you sure?"

He faced her. The anger had faded. The fear had not. "No. But I am going anyway."

Elizabeth cursed under her breath, straightened his collar, and shoved him back towards Edward. "Then do not die stupid."

"I will try to die according to plan."

"Fuck off." A few men nearby laughed, including the Castilian sailor who had challenged him. The laughter lasted only seconds, but it was enough to make the raised guns feel less likely to fire.

English voices began to rise from the Council ranks. Portsmouth. Bristol. Kent. Yorkshire. Accents Edward had thought he would hear only in memory. A former gunner with a scar across his forehead stepped forward. "Sir Edward. If you take the helm and show us the plan before asking us to die for it, we will board. Many of us owe Castile a home, so do not ask us to pretend we never belonged here." He tightened his rifle sling. "But we have not forgotten what we were either. If the red cross has a chance to fly from a mast once more, I doubt many of us would object."

Agreement spread, not as one roar but as a movement through the ranks. A sailmaker stepped out. Two gunners followed. Three men in garrison uniforms left the far end of the quay. A Castilian caught his friend's arm before he went, said something in Spanish, then struck him once on the shoulder. Edward stopped trying to count them. More than eight hundred English veterans eventually stood together beside him. They were not a restoration army, and they were not yet the crew of any ship. They were simply eight hundred people who had decided that if they were to go to sea once more, they wanted to know who held the helm and why they were sailing.

Timothy looked at Edward and then at the men who had stepped out with him. "We have not forgotten, Admiral."

Edward answered with no speech. He looked across their faces, then towards José, Elizabeth, and Trafalgar. Wind from the river mouth moved through the gaps now opened in the Council formations and pulled the Castilian flags taut above the quay. No one lowered a weapon, but from that moment the dispute in Lisbon was no longer merely about whether a fleet would leave harbour.

Clap. Clap. Clap. Three measured claps sounded across the quay just as the noise began to settle. Elizabeth stepped out from the Council ranks without drawing a weapon and without looking at the eight hundred and three English veterans as though they had suddenly become enemies. She looked first at Edward, then at the gaps they had left in the Castilian formation. "Beautiful, Sir Edward. You failed to persuade the Council, so you found the men who still remember how to obey your commands and built yourself a crew in the middle of our harbour."

Timothy stiffened. Several veterans behind him adjusted their rifle slings, but Elizabeth raised one finger. "Do not misunderstand me. I heard why each of you stepped out, and I will not call it treason simply because that would make the story easier to handle." She turned back to Edward. "But eight hundred Castilian servicemen have just left a Council formation to stand beneath a newly restored Admiral. If you think I can watch that happen and smile while wishing you a pleasant voyage, six years in Marrakesh have made you far too optimistic."

Fredo closed the strength ledger and put it inside his coat. His pistol remained in his hand, though he had lowered it from José after Timothy began speaking about Vila do Porto. "No one here has declared a force outside Castile, Dame Elizabeth. Sir Edward made it clear that these men are neither restoring England nor abandoning their duty to the Empire. They have volunteered to place themselves under a command system they believe can take them to San Sebastián."

"And that is exactly the part that concerns me." Elizabeth pointed towards the Castilian flag above the harbour fortress. "An army cannot survive if every soldier who loses faith in a superior is allowed to choose another commander and call it reorganisation."

Martinez moved beside Fredo, one hand resting on her sword as a reminder that the Royal Guard still carried a sealed order. "Nor can a navy survive if fourteen warships and thousands of sailors refuse a mobilisation order without offering an alternative. The Council has given its reasons. We have heard them. San Sebastián remains under blockade."

José raised a hand before Elizabeth could answer. He looked from the English veterans to the Council sailors still standing in formation behind them. "Then we have reached the useful part. No one here lacks arguments. What we lack is a solution that can leave this quay without turning Lisbon into the first battle of a civil war."

A gunlock clicked somewhere behind them. One sound was enough to make the Conquistadores nearest Martinez shift their stance. Fredo turned. One hundred elite Castilian soldiers who had been dispersed around the harbour compressed themselves into two lines. They did not aim at the Council sailors, but they sealed every route leading directly to Edward and Martinez. Their officers needed no second order. The Council answered almost at once. José rotated one wrist, and reserve units emerged from the barracks behind the warehouses in formation, neither running nor shouting. More than three thousand men occupied the approaches to the harbour, bringing field guns and sealed ammunition chests with them.

Martinez watched the artillery wheels turn into position. "You prepared three thousand reserves in advance?"

"Lisbon is the largest naval base in the west. Did you imagine we placed every soldier on the quay merely to make the argument look crowded?"

Fredo exhaled through his nose. "If anyone fires, neither side wins."

"At last," José said. "Something we agree on."

Edward looked through the layers of armed men around him. The Royal Guard had the authority of the throne. The Council had eight thousand troops and officers who had fought beside them for years. The Englishmen behind Edward had only his promise that he would show them a real plan. He did not need all of Lisbon. The thought was so simple he nearly laughed. His younger self had already explained it in the most irritating way possible. A fighting system did not require every person inside it to believe the same thing. It required them to understand one another well enough to act when the order came.

Edward stepped past Fredo and looked along the fourteen ships anchored in the bay. "José."

The old Admiral raised his head.

"I do not need fourteen." The men nearest them fell silent. Edward pointed towards the four-gun-deck warship lying apart from the main formation. Its dark hull carried Castilian repairs over lines of construction he had recognised the moment he arrived. "That one."

Trafalgar frowned. "Red Baron?"

"Yes."

Fredo followed his hand. "One ship?"

"One." Edward turned back. "If the Council believes sending the entire fleet is a wager without an answer, I will not force them to stake the entire fleet. I need a hull large enough for nine hundred and three people, enough guns to deliver meaningful firepower, and a design familiar enough that these sailors can operate it without learning from the beginning."

José studied Red Baron longer than the others. "She is one of the oldest ships here."

"That is why I chose her."

Trafalgar laughed for the first time since the confrontation began. "Bloody hell. You really recognised her?"

"The stern has been rebuilt. The upper gun deck is not original either. But I walked the plans of that class before some people here knew how to hold a sword." Edward looked at him. "Red Baron was transferred from the Royal Navy to Castile fifteen years ago."

Trafalgar nodded. "Three gun decks when she arrived. Castile added the fourth."

Edward left the matter there. Whatever needed to be done about that fourth deck could wait until the ship was under his command. First he had to get her out of Lisbon.

Fredo understood before anyone else. He turned to José, no longer sounding like a Royal Guard reciting law but like an officer trying to disarm a shell lying between two armed formations. "Don José, the Council keeps thirteen warships, every Castilian sailor who does not volunteer to accompany Sir Edward, the harbour magazines, and the garrison. We take Red Baron, eight hundred and three English veterans, and one hundred Conquistadores."

José did not answer. "I will record this as a command dispute during an emergency, not a mass desertion. I cannot erase every legal responsibility of the Council, but I can refuse to turn Lisbon into a battlefield today, and I can refuse to submit a charge of treason before the San Sebastián campaign is concluded."

Elizabeth studied him.

"You are proposing to postpone the confrontation, not forgive it."

"Correct. If we live long enough to continue arguing, Madrid can argue later."

Trafalgar shook his head. "You are beginning to sound like Edward."

Fredo started to answer, but José raised a hand. He walked to the edge of the quay, looked at Red Baron, then at the eight hundred and three Englishmen behind Edward. "You want one ship. I can give you one ship." He turned. "But if you leave Lisbon aboard Red Baron, today's crisis leaves with you. Fredo does not call Royal reinforcements the moment your sails disappear. And you do not stop at Council ports on the way north to pull more sailors from our formations."

Martinez narrowed her eyes. "You want conditions."

"Three."

Fredo rubbed his forehead. "Of course."

José raised one finger. "First. The Vestigium communication spheres carried by Royal Guards Tres and Veinticinco will be sealed in Lisbon until the San Sebastián campaign has a result. Not destroyed. Not permanently confiscated. Sealed."

Martinez objected at once. "Cutting us off from Madrid while we execute a sealed order is a substantial demand."

"And allowing two Royal Guards to summon Crown forces into a naval base that has just refused an order is a substantial risk." José met her gaze. "If you expect me to hand over a ship in front of eight thousand people who believe the Council just protected them from a meaningless deployment, give them reason to believe Royal troops will not arrive tomorrow morning to close the harbour."

Fredo looked at Martinez. She disliked it, but she could not dismiss the logic.

José raised a second finger. "Red Baron carries enough heating crystals for a four-deck warship with an oversized crew. You take half the current reserve."

Timothy spoke from behind them. "Half?"

Elizabeth turned towards him. "Lisbon is also in the middle of winter." He looked at the barracks, warehouses, and thousands of people behind her and swallowed whatever argument had been coming.

"You take the ship, provisions for the voyage, fresh water, and enough crystals to keep the occupied compartments from freezing," José continued. "The rest remains here. I will not strip Lisbon's heat reserves to fund a campaign I have just refused."

Edward calculated quickly. Half would be uncomfortable, but with rotating watches, restricted heated zones, and no attempt to warm all four decks at once, they could live. "Acceptable."

Martinez turned sharply.

"Sir Edward."

"We need enough to fight. We do not need enough to turn the Atlantic into a sitting room."

José did not smile. He raised the third finger. "Finally, from the moment Red Baron clears the Tagus until Lekeitio or San Sebastián, she enters no Council port. No recruiting. No additional ships. No armed landing parties forcing local units to choose a side."

Fredo watched him. "If the ship is damaged?"

"Anchor offshore and signal as civilians. We will provide rescue if we can. But the Royal Guard does not walk into a Council harbour with eight hundred English soldiers behind it while this remains unresolved."

This time Trafalgar spoke. "That is not unreasonable."

Martinez looked at him. "You support this condition as well?"

"I support preventing one dispute in Lisbon from becoming three more disputes along the coast." Trafalgar tightened his glove. "I still want San Sebastián saved. I would also prefer not to spend tomorrow deciding whether to shoot the French or the Queen's own troops."

Elizabeth looked at Edward. Her anger remained, but the cold contempt from earlier was gone. "You promised Timothy that before anchor was raised, everyone sailing with you would know the ship, the objective, and why they were placing their lives into it." She inclined her head towards Red Baron. "You have the ship. Do not spend the rest of the morning performing."

"I do not intend to."

Timothy stood a few paces behind her. Elizabeth looked at him as if she wanted to add something, then stopped. He did not approach either. Enough had already been said between them on this quay.

Fredo removed the Vestigium communication sphere from his belt and set it carefully on a crate. "Seal it in front of us. Record the recipient, the time, and the conditions of return."

José called a clerk immediately. Martinez surrendered hers after Fredo, wearing the expression of someone memorising the name of every person who touched it for later investigation. When the Council seal was pressed into wax over both boxes, the weapons around the harbour began to lower. José ordered the reserve artillery back to storage. Front-line officers dismissed units by formation, and the Conquistadores returned their weapons to carry position. No one had won the confrontation. Perhaps that was why Lisbon had not bled.

Edward did not allow the quiet to linger. He turned to the eight hundred and three English veterans and pointed towards Red Baron. "You wanted a real plan. First we learn what we actually have."

He called Timothy forward. "Choose two hundred gunners. Board first. Inspect every gun deck, the powder, breeching ropes, flints, and every round that can be fired immediately. I do not want a beautiful report. If a gun is dead, mark it dead. If it needs two hours, tell me two hours."

Timothy brought his heels together. "Yes, Admiral."

"Then inspect the hand pumps and every gunport near the waterline. I do not intend to win our first battle and sink because of a rotten seal." For the first time since his confrontation with Elizabeth, Timothy smiled. "Yes, sir."

Edward divided the remaining sailors. One group would inspect sails, standing rigging, winches, and anchors. Another would go below to examine the hull, water stores, and old repairs. The last would count provisions and the heating crystals they were actually permitted to carry after the Council took its half. No major repairs were to begin before they reported back. For now there was one task: determine exactly how alive Red Baron still was.

The one hundred Conquistadores were called forward as well. Edward walked the line, taking in the thick fur cloaks, long rifles, rows of pistols, and sabres at their hips. "Are you preparing to fight on a ship or move house?"

Several men glanced at one another. Edward tapped the commander's rifle barrel. "Keep the leather armour. Keep the sabre. One pistol each. Long rifles and the rest of the spare weapons go into the magazine under seal. If you have to swing across to another ship, I do not want half of you falling into the sea because you brought the armoury with you."

The commander looked towards Martinez. She nodded once. "Do as Sir Edward says."

"Yes, ma'am."

Fredo stood beside a crate, watching the harbour transform from a standoff into departure preparations quickly enough that he needed several seconds to catch up. "What about me?"

Edward turned. "Do you know how to find tea?"

Fredo stared at him. "I know how to find an artillery battery, an assassination team, or a classified file. Tea was never part of Royal Guard training."

"Then today you broaden your expertise."

Martinez failed to suppress a laugh. Fredo looked at her as though betrayed. Edward pointed towards the supply warehouses. "Three crates of black tea. Good enough that eight hundred and three Englishmen do not mutiny a second time before luncheon."

"Sir Edward, I do not believe tea is a tactical priority."

"I have just watched eight hundred and three men prove that sailor morale is a tactical priority."

Fredo had no answer. Martinez struck him lightly on the shoulder. "Come on, Tres. At least this assignment is unlikely to kill you."

"You are coming with me."

"Why?"

"Because if I have to explain to a merchant that the future of San Sebastián depends upon tea, I require a witness."

The two Royal Guards left to the laughter of several veterans nearby. Edward turned back towards Red Baron.

The first report reached him an hour later. The ship was not ready for a major battle, but neither was she the floating corpse her exterior suggested. Most guns on the lower three decks remained usable. Several carriages needed new pins, two hand pumps required repair, the powder magazines were reasonably dry, and the hull showed no dangerous leak. The fourth gun deck made her top-heavy, while aristocratic cabins in the stern consumed enough useless volume to irritate Edward merely by reading the figures. He ordered nothing removed yet.

Timothy returned to the upper deck with soot on one cheek and an old roll of cloth under his arm. "Admiral. You should see this." He laid it on a crate and unrolled it. Inside was the red cross edged in gold of the Royal Navy of England. Time had darkened the fabric, but the embroidery remained intact. The Englishmen nearby fell quiet. Edward touched the edge of the cloth. He did not need to ask how long it had lain in storage or why Castile had never thrown it away.

José and Elizabeth had not yet left the quay. Both looked over when Timothy brought the flag. Edward turned towards them before giving the order. "Castilian flag above."

José watched him. "And this one?"

"Below it. Red Baron is a Castilian warship. The people operating her today simply wish to remember beneath which flag they first learned to go to sea."

José remained silent for several seconds, then nodded. "Keep them in that order."

Timothy carried the flag towards the halyards. When the red cross rose beneath the Castilian colours, the cheer did not become a frenzy for restoration. It began among a few men, spread through gunners, sailmakers, and old sailors, then stopped at a volume just loud enough for the harbour to hear. Elizabeth watched Timothy among them. This time she did not scold him.

Trafalgar approached Edward as the first anchor cable began to move. "You truly need only one?"

Edward watched Red Baron's sails begin to fill in the wind from the mouth of the Tagus. "I need a crew that knows what I mean when I call a turn. One is enough."

"You still have not told me what you intend to do at La Concha."

"Because I do not yet know everything this ship can do."

Trafalgar stared at him, then burst out laughing. "That is a more decent answer than the old 'I have never lost.'"

Edward held out his hand. "I am getting old."

"No. You are becoming less stupid." They clasped hands hard. Trafalgar did not pull him into another embrace, only held his old friend's wrist for one extra second before letting go. "Edward." He stopped. Trafalgar looked towards Red Baron. "Do not make your people write another death letter merely to protect the legend of the Pathmaker."

Edward did not smile. "I know." It was the only answer Trafalgar needed.

Fredo and Martinez returned with three crates of tea just as the final boat prepared to leave the quay. Fredo threw one crate down to two sailors and climbed the rope ladder while cursing that no sealed mission had ever humiliated the Royal Guard as thoroughly as the one he had just completed. Edward waited on Red Baron's deck until both were aboard before ordering the gangway withdrawn. José remained on the quay. The two communication spheres rested in sealed boxes. Half the heating crystals had gone back into Lisbon's stores, and the other thirteen warships remained under Council control. The dispute had not disappeared. Only the guns had come down. No one wore chains, and no one spoke the word coward again. Red Baron still had men, guns, provisions, two flags, and an open sea gate before her.

Edward put both hands on the wheel. "Weigh anchor." The order travelled down through every deck. Chain ran through the capstan, sails took the wind, and the four-gun-deck hull began moving out of the calmer water of the bay towards the Atlantic.

Fredo stood beside Edward with the smell of tea still clinging to his gloves.

"Sir Edward."

"Hm?"

"Can you tell us what we are doing now?"

Edward felt the heavy ship answer the wheel with a delay and glanced up at the fourth gun deck raising her centre of gravity higher than it had any right to be. An idea began to form. "First?" He slapped the wheel. "Put the kettle on. I need to decide what to do with this floating four-storey cupboard before we see the French."

Red Baron passed the mouth of the Tagus beneath straining sails, carrying nine hundred and three people and a war that no one aboard still expected to unfold according to plan.

Outside, the Atlantic struck the flanks of Red Baron in slow, heavy blows. Inside the captain's cabin, a brass kettle had only just begun to sing over the coal stove when Edward poured the water through black tea, set three cups on the chart table, and finally allowed himself to sit.

Fredo took the first cup but did not drink. He looked instead at the small sandglass beside the charts, then back at Edward. "You have just taken nine hundred and three people out of Lisbon aboard a ship you freely admit you do not entirely understand. If this is how Englishmen relax after an attempted mutiny, I begin to see why your empire gives the rest of Europe headaches."

"Tea first. Headaches later." Edward pushed the remaining cup towards Martinez.

She lifted it, tested the heat with one fingertip, and set it beside the inspection report Timothy had sent up from below. "You told us we had to know what ship we were fighting with, what target we were taking, and why any of us should put our lives into it before we reached La Concha. I assume three chests of tea are not one of those answers."

"No. They merely improve the people giving them."

Fredo tasted the tea, frowned at the bitterness, and opened the report. "Then talk. I have read this twice. Most of the guns on the lower three decks still work, two hand pumps need repair, the powder is dry, and the hull has no dangerous leak. The worst problem is the upper deck and the way it makes the ship answer the helm like a drunk mule."

Edward drew the chart of La Concha into the centre of the table. He placed a small model of Red Baron north of the bay entrance, then used two carved pieces to mark Santa Clara Island and the French flagship at its expected position. "That is the worst problem if we intend to fight conventionally," he said. "I do not."

Martinez leaned over the chart, one hand holding its edge as the ship rolled through a swell. "The western channel is deeper. The eastern channel is narrow and full of rock. The French will keep their lighter ships outside as pickets, with the heavy warships nearer the mouth of the bay where they can support the troops ashore. If we arrive in a four-deck ship of the line, they will see us long before we have a firing angle."

Edward touched the northern edge of the chart. "Unless they do not see us until it is too late."

Fredo's eyes went to the weather notes along the margin. "Fog."

"And wind." Edward moved a piece in a long arc from the north. He did not draw a direct attack through the outer screen; the course stayed wide of the bay before cutting in behind the pickets and towards the French flagship's stern.

"We use the fog to close from a quarter they will not expect. Then we cross the flagship's stern. One rake at close range should wreck the rudder, the command deck, and enough of her rigging to leave her half blind. The moment we strike, Martinez takes the Conquistadores across. You are not there to conquer every deck. Lock down the command section and cut the anchor cables."

Martinez did not nod yet. "And if the flagship carries Gendarmes?"

"Do not go looking for a gentleman's duel. Hold the approaches. Pull their soldiers away from the anchors and the command deck. Put pistol rounds into armour joints when you get the angle. If the numbers become ridiculous, abandon the idea of controlling the whole ship. I only need her unable to control herself."

"And how do my people come back?"

Edward pushed Red Baron close behind the French model, then separated the two by a narrow gap. "Grappling lines keep the ships together during boarding. Fredo holds our side, protects the lines and the hauling parties. If it turns bad, you withdraw by groups. No one stays behind merely to finish an objective that has stopped being worth the lives."

Fredo planted both hands on the table. "I like that sentence more than most speeches about honour. But there is a problem. Red Baron, as she stands, cannot make the run you have just drawn."

"Correct."

"So the tea was only here while you waited for us to say it?"

Edward lifted his cup. "I needed to make certain two Royal Guards still knew how to think after Lisbon."

Martinez studied him, then tapped one fingernail against the model of Red Baron. "You want her back in her old configuration."

Edward stopped with the cup halfway to his mouth.

Fredo looked at her, then at the inspection report. "Three gun decks."

Martinez pulled the papers closer. "The fourth deck makes her top-heavy. It gives crosswinds more of the ship's side to push against, and it puts extra guns, ammunition, water, stores, and people where the ship feels them most. If you want her to turn sharply at the mouth of the bay, you do not need more cannon. You need the ship to stop fighting the rudder."

Edward set the cup down. "That is why I wanted both of you here." He did not praise them like pupils who had found the right answer. Instead, he took a piece of charcoal, turned over a manifest sheet, and drew a cross-section of the hull in several firm strokes. The original three gun decks came first. Above them, the Castilian addition sat like another building laid on top of a house.

Fredo followed the lines. "I have read the refit records. The fourth deck was added after the fighting with Portugal, when Madrid wanted a ship that could sit outside a harbour and throw more metal in one direction for longer. The Queen never asked it to race frigates."

"Exactly." Edward tapped the upper tier with the charcoal. "Isabella did not design a bad ship. She designed one for another job. As a floating fortress, Red Baron makes sense. For slipping into La Concha, turning inside the bay, going alongside and getting out again before the fog burns off, she is a four-storey cupboard that happens to float."

Martinez leaned back. "Then the argument is not about who was right when she was built. It is about forcing a defensive design to do the work of a raider."

"And we have only a few days to persuade her."

Fredo rotated the paper towards himself. "How much do you intend to remove?"

"At minimum, every gun on the fourth deck, the ammunition assigned to them, the partitions, the noble cabins, and everything built above the original weather deck that the shipwrights confirm was added later."

"At minimum?"

"I decide the rest after the shipwrights mark what belongs to the old structure and what does not."

Martinez raised an eyebrow. "So you are not planning to hand nine hundred men axes and tell them to cut anything that looks expensive?"

"You wound me."

"You just called the ship a cupboard."

"The cupboard still has to live long enough to reach La Concha."

Fredo laughed under his breath and stole the charcoal. He drew a line down both sides of the upper deck. "Suppose we remove the guns in pairs, port then starboard. Lowering them into the hold improves the centre of gravity, but it does not reduce the total load. If you genuinely want the ship lighter, something has to go."

"Correct."

"The Council's cannon."

"Also correct."

Fredo looked up. "José will kill us if we come back."

"The condition was that we return Red Baron, not every gun she left with."

"You are relying on semantics."

"I am English. It is an old national tradition."

Martinez put her cup down before she laughed aloud. She pointed to the middle of the hull. "Do not throw them all away. Keep some of the heavy pieces low as reserve weight and emergency guns. The rest, if they cannot help in this battle, should not be allowed to kill us simply because they were expensive."

Edward nodded. "That was my thought."

Fredo folded his arms. "I want numbers before a single gun goes overboard. How much weight we remove, how much we move lower, how much water and food change position. And I want stopping limits."

Edward looked at him. "Stopping limits?"

"You are proposing surgery on a ship at sea. If a carpenter reports that a main beam has shifted, we stop. If the mast step begins taking load in a way it was not meant to, we stop. If she heels beyond the agreed limit after any stage of the work, we stop. I refuse to approve a plan in which failure is discovered only when the deck reaches ninety degrees."

Silence stretched briefly across the table. Edward took back the charcoal and wrote three large words along the edge of the sheet.

STOP FOR STRUCTURAL FAILURE.

"Agreed."

Martinez tapped the crew list. "And nine hundred and three people. If you remove sleeping space from the upper tier, where do they go? We already have half the heating we should have. A faster ship is useless if, three days from now, the gun crews are shaking too badly to light their fuses."

Edward wrote another line.

STOP FOR CREW EXHAUSTION.

"You take that."

"No. Fredo and I take it."

Fredo turned. "How have I been dragged into this?"

"You just demanded a weight table, work rotations, and stopping limits. Do not pretend now that all you know how to do is hold a sword."

Edward rested both hands on the table and looked between them. "Now you sound like two admirals."

Fredo lifted his cup. "If you had said that in Lisbon, I might have wanted to shoot fewer people."

"In Lisbon, you were busy pointing a pistol."

"A minor detail."

Edward spread another sheet of paper over the table. From that point, no one sat there merely listening to his plan. The three of them divided the problem. First came inspection. Two English shipwrights who had served aboard the original class, together with three Castilian carpenters, would walk the entire fourth deck and mark every beam, mast support, brace, and connection that must never be cut in red chalk. White chalk would mark later additions. No axe would touch timber until both groups signed the same list. Second came weight. Guns, shot, tool chests, furnishings, partitions, decorative fittings, and every heavy object would come off symmetrically. Whenever a load left the port side, a matching load would leave starboard before the next stage began. The guns they retained would be lowered and secured near the centreline; the rest would be discarded. Third, no one would rebuild Red Baron while she was carrying full sail through rough water. They would reduce sail as soon as they reached a stable stretch of sea, hold the bow against the swell, and work in measured stages. After each one, Edward would make the ship run, turn her both ways, and listen to what the hull told them before authorising another cut.

Fredo read the watch rotation twice. "Three shifts. No more than four hours of heavy labour each. Anyone who spends a watch on capstans, hauling lines, or sawing timber does not go straight to a gun crew. They get at least one watch off first."

Martinez added a note beneath his. "Conquistadores are not carpenters. Use them on hoists, cables, timber hauling, and safety lines. No one who does not understand the structure gets a saw near a beam."

"I will tell them you have just saved the honour of their branch."

"Try saying that within hearing distance."

Edward did not answer. He was staring at the final two lines of the inspection report. "The fourth deck carries twelve of the heaviest guns. Six go lower. Six go overboard."

Fredo whistled. "José is definitely going to kill us."

Martinez lifted her cup. "Then we should win before we go home."

By the time Timothy was called into the cabin, the table no longer held an Edward Spencer plan. Three sets of handwriting crossed over one another, entire sections had been struck out, three columns of duties filled one page, and the stopping conditions had grown long enough to satisfy even the most suspicious shipwright. Timothy read from top to bottom, lips tightening at the paragraph about throwing guns into the sea. "Admiral, may I ask one question?"

"Go on."

"Are we truly throwing six cannon overboard?"

Fredo pointed at Edward. "His idea."

Martinez pointed at Fredo. "He demanded the weight reduction."

Edward pointed at both of them. "Two Royal Guards approved it."

Timothy looked from one face to the next, then pulled the plan towards himself. "Understood. If José asks, I know nothing." This time all four laughed.

The laughter ended when Timothy put a finger on the target speed. "Ten knots."

"Target, not prophecy." Edward rose. "If the trials give us nine and a half but the helm answers better and she is stable enough for the stern cut, I still fight. If she gives us ten while trying to disassemble herself, we abandon the plan."

Timothy nodded. "I like the number much more now."

The work began before noon. Red Baron shortened sail in a relatively calm stretch of water, her bow held at an angle to the swell. Red and white chalk soon covered the fourth deck. Two English carpenters argued with a Castilian shipwright for nearly ten minutes over a row of transverse beams until Edward climbed up himself, knocked along each length with the back of an axe, and ordered the entire set left alone. No one mocked them for being careful.

The guns came first. Hoists creaked across the deck as one iron barrel after another rose from its carriage. Fredo stood to starboard with the load sheet in hand; he did not tell the crews how to rig the tackle, but he checked every paired weight, every man responsible, and every time entry. Whenever a party tried to hurry, he stopped them. "Do not compete with the rope to see which of you is stronger. If it snaps, the rope wins." One broad-shouldered Conquistador looked personally insulted. Ten minutes later, an auxiliary hook slipped out of its groove and smashed hard against the rail. The man did not argue again.

Martinez worked the opposite side. She divided the sleeping spaces by watch and moved men with fever, old injuries, or a history of cold collapse nearer the surviving heat points. Canvas stripped from dismantled cabins became windbreaks below decks, while hammocks were rehung in double tiers where the overhead clearance allowed it. When an officer suggested packing more men into the central compartment to preserve heat, Martinez crouched and measured the space between the lowest hammock and the escape route. She shook her head. "If we take water, they have to get out in the dark. Leave this clear."

"That costs us two more heat lamps."

"Then turn off the lamps in the officers' compartment."

The officer stared at her. "Your place is in there too."

"I know." Fredo heard the exchange from the ladder and said nothing. He simply crossed two lamps off the old allocation and wrote them into the new one.

By mid-afternoon, six of the fourth-deck guns had been lowered, secured low and close to the centreline. The remaining six were unlashed, marked, and taken to the rail. No one cheered when each block of iron fell from the deck and vanished beneath the grey water. Edward stood beside the rail for the last one. "Expensive."

Fredo handed him the revised load sheet. "You can jump after it if you are sentimental."

"You are learning the insolence of the Royal Navy."

"Three days with you is enough."

After every discarded gun, they checked the painted draught marks fore and aft. Carpenters walked the red-chalk points, pressed hands to the timber, and listened to the hull work in the swell. Nothing moved that should not have moved. Only then did the upper works begin to come apart. No one touched the main posts. No one cut a load-bearing beam belonging to the original three-deck hull. Cabin walls, raised rails, light roof frames, decorative platforms, storage partitions, and sections of light flooring added during the Castilian refit came away in order, lowered whole when possible and cut only when they had to be. Some timber became emergency bracing. Some repaired damaged gun carriages. The rest was bundled for the galley and heating stations, not because it could warm an entire warship, but because at sea one did not throw away anything that still possessed a use.

Timothy ran between gun decks with two assistants, marking which cannon remained serviceable, which needed new pins, and which were not worth carrying into battle. By the end of the first labour watch, soot had blackened him from forehead to collar. "Admiral!"

Edward was holding one end of a lever while the carpenters shifted a frame. "What?"

"Port pump is running again. Starboard still leaks at the lower valve, but the men say two hours. And gun fourteen should be retired before it kills us."

"Mark it dead."

"You do not want one more test?"

"No one dies to prove an old cannon still has pride." Timothy grinned and disappeared down the ladder.

Fredo came to take Edward's place on the lever. No one ordered him. He pulled off his outer gloves, wrapped the line across his palms, and put his weight into it beside two sailors. "When did you learn to use that?" "I did not. I know when two men are about to collapse." One of the sailors laughed. Edward surrendered the lever and moved on to inspect another station.

By late afternoon, Red Baron no longer looked like the ship that had left Lisbon. She was still a heavy three-decker, still carried nearly nine hundred people, and no single day of labour could turn her into a frigate. Yet her upper line had dropped and tightened. The heaviest loads had come away from the places where they hurt her most, and what remained had been brought lower and closer to the middle of the hull.

Edward refused to celebrate. "Trial first."

Sail was increased by stages. Timothy went aft with the log line while a sailor threw the small float astern; cord ran between counting fingers as the sandglass turned. "Seven point eight!" Edward did not react.

On the second run they carried more sail and adjusted the trim. "Eight point six!" Fredo stood near the helm, feeling the ship begin her turn before he looked at Edward. "Faster, yes. But the real difference is that she agrees to turn now." "Again."

Martinez watched a rough inclinometer fixed beside the mainmast, a plumb line moving across a marked board. When Edward ordered a hard turn to port, then to starboard, she called out each angle. "Stable. Still below the red mark."

The wind improved towards evening. Red Baron filled her treated sails and began to tremble beneath their feet. Timothy cast the log a third time. He watched the sandglass, watched the knots run between his hands, then snapped his head up. "Nine point seven!" A few men began to cheer. Edward raised one hand. "Again."

Fredo glanced sideways. "You are the sort of man who receives a gift and asks for the receipt."

"Again."

On the fourth run they altered the headsails and let Red Baron hold the favourable wind for a short stretch. Timothy counted, then kept the line in his hand for another heartbeat as though checking that the answer had not changed. "Ten point one!" The cheer broke across the deck. Edward kept his eyes on the mainmast, the standing rigging, and the response of the helm. No timber gave a wrong complaint. Martinez's plumb line settled inside the safe band. Only then did Edward take his hand off the wheel. "Ten is a beautiful number. Remember that it exists because the wind has chosen to cooperate. If La Concha changes the wind on us, do not expect a miracle."

Fredo raised the load sheet. "I am writing that down. Next time you boast about your genius, I want evidence for the prosecution."

"Go ahead. You are the novelist."

Martinez gave the back of Fredo's hand a light knock as she passed. "Write down the part where he demanded stopping limits too. You were more useful today than when you went looking for tea."

"You still drank the tea I found."

"That is irrelevant."

That evening, supper was served from low wooden crates on the middle deck. There was no victory feast, only bean soup, salt meat, hard biscuit, and tea hot enough to put feeling back into cold fingers. Edward raised his mug towards the men nearest him. "No one performed a miracle today. We merely stopped forcing Red Baron to do a job she was never built to do." Timothy swallowed his mouthful of biscuit. "So ten point one does not count?"

"It counts as the ship not killing us."

"Your standards are low."

"Lisbon made me practical." Laughter moved through the small group. No one required a speech longer than that.

Late that night, Edward stood at the bow with a cup of tea gone cold between his hands. Salt wind clung to his hair and collar; ahead lay only darkness and the long black road of water towards the Bay of Biscay. Martinez came up carrying a folded sheet. There was none of the exasperation she had worn earlier while reorganising blankets and bunks. "The new rest rotation is holding. Officers' quarters keep one heat lamp. The others go to the gun crews and the sleeping compartments near the waterline." Edward read the list. "You cut your own heat?"

"I was the one who said we should not freeze the gunners before battle. It becomes difficult to retain authority if I then sleep beside three lamps."

He returned the sheet. "Thank you."

Martinez rested her forearms on the rail. "You know, in Lisbon I thought you were dangerous because you trusted yourself too much. Today I watched you stop a man from cutting one piece of timber simply because you did not yet know what it was holding."

"Disappointed?"

"Less than before."

Fredo appeared behind them with two fresh cups, gave one to Martinez, and kept the other. "He is still dangerous. At least now we know where to stand when he has an axe."

Edward turned. "Should you not be asleep?"

"Someone wrote three pages of stopping conditions and made me sign them. I am enjoying my achievement."

Martinez took the cup. "You wrote half of them yourself."

"A detail."

For a while the three of them stood together without mentioning Lisbon. Edward watched the horizon. "I miss Juliet and Remi." The words came out more easily than he expected. Fredo did not hunt for consolation. He drank his tea and looked towards the same darkness.

Martinez asked, "Do you believe they are safe in Madrid?"

"Yes. I trust Isabella to keep her word."

"Then the rest is homesickness."

Edward laughed once, though the word felt far too small for the weight in his chest. He corrected himself with a tired nod. "Yes. Home."

Martinez pulled her collar higher against the wind. "Then live long enough to open your own front door. Do not make somebody else do it for you."

Edward looked at her. "You make that sound like an order."

"I am a Royal Guard. Occupational habit."

Fredo lifted his cup. "I support the order. At least it does not require me to find tea." "You are holding tea." Fredo stared at the cup in his hand, then swore quietly.

Night went on around them. Below decks, the watches slept in the spaces the three had rearranged; carpenters rechecked the marked timbers after every hour of rougher sea, while Timothy ran the repaired pumps one final time before locking the powder magazine. Red Baron had not become a new ship in a day. She had merely been pulled closer to what she once was, close enough for Edward to ask something dangerous of her without pretending her limits had disappeared. Before going below, he rested one hand on the helm again. The ship answered more quickly than she had that morning, yet the wheel still carried the stubborn weight of thousands of tons of timber, iron, men, and decisions. He preferred it that way.

A ship did not have to become a miracle. It only had to be good enough to carry them where they needed to go, and strong enough to bring the survivors home.

title_vi: Chapter 30 - The Night Before La Concha
title_en: Chapter 30 - The Night Before La Concha
text_en:
In the darkness north of the Bay of Biscay, Red Baron drove south with the wind behind her, holding close to ten knots. The surgery of the previous day had made her quicker to answer the helm, though every roll still carried the immense weight of three gun decks through the oak wheel.

Edward sat with his back against the helm housing on the quarterdeck, turning the pages of an old leather-bound notebook worn pale at the edges. A storm lantern swung from the rail above him, and in its wavering yellow light the charcoal marks on each page came alive: abbreviations, arrows, firing angles, and small corrections that drew his mind back through the hours of tactical briefings below deck.

He remembered Timothy's sharp nod when the young gunner received responsibility for coordinating the entire broadside. No one was to pull a firing lanyard until Red Baron had crossed close behind the enemy flagship, near enough for the rake to enter through the stern rather than merely batter its armour.

He remembered Martinez studying the boarding plan in silence. Her Conquistadores were to pin the French naval Gendarmes aboard the flagship and keep them away from the anchors and command spaces; Fredo, meanwhile, had been given the opposite problem, holding Red Baron's flank and preventing the enemy from cutting the grappling lines that would bind the two hulls together.

Edward's finger stopped at the final diagonal stroke on the page: reinforcements arrive while one hundred Conquistadores remain aboard the French flagship. He had placed that possibility in front of Martinez and Fredo over the chart table. "If they close your route back, do not try to retreat through the space between two broadsides," he had told them, pointing to the flagship. "Break their command, cut the anchors, and use the hull itself to screen the fire. We open a path for our people back to Red Baron."

Now Edward looked away from the writing and tilted his head towards the sky. The notebook remained open across his knees. For once, the endless winter had given them a clear night. The usual leaden cloud had broken apart, exposing a scattering of cold stars. Above the mainmast, the great Castilian standard and the red cross of the English Royal Navy snapped side by side in the sea wind. Only days ago, Edward had been standing in a cattle shed in Marrakesh waiting for a batch of lime to cool. San Sebastián now lay somewhere ahead in the darkness, while nine hundred people beneath his boots slept, pretended to sleep, or lay awake counting the same hours he was counting. His eyes returned to the slash at the bottom of the page. If they failed to seize the flagship quickly enough, how much time would he have to bring his people home?

Edward half closed the notebook, though his hand remained tight around the cover. In his mind, the front door of the house in Madrid appeared with impossible clarity, along with Remi's voice whenever footsteps sounded outside. He feared the day that door might open for someone else.

The lantern blurred before him. One moment he saw its trembling flame; the next, memory dragged him six years backwards to a freezing London night. There had been screaming in the streets, the hard chaos of evacuation, and cold sharp enough to turn every breath painful. Edward had forced a path towards the refugee ship with Juliet beside him and their one-year-old son bundled against her chest. Remi had been little more than a knot of cloth in those days. Each breath came so softly that Edward had sometimes bent down to make certain winter had not stolen the next one. Inside the damp refugee compartment, Juliet had sat close to a storm lantern with both hands wrapped around their son's feet. Whenever his breathing became too faint, she lowered her face to listen, then pulled her coat farther over him.

Edward stared at the lantern on Red Baron until his eyes watered. For years in Marrakesh, no matter how late he came home, he had always been able to lie beside Juliet and listen while she told him whatever trouble Remi had caused that day. "Juliet..." His voice broke before he could steady it. He covered his face with one hand. "God, I miss you." The next words slipped through his fingers. "And you, little man."

Wind found its way under his collar. Edward bowed his head and tried to swallow the sound in his throat when boots came up the ladder. Martinez stopped beside the helm housing and put a hand on his shoulder. She said nothing at first. Fredo stood a few paces away with Timothy. Both men turned towards the sea and gave Edward enough time to wipe his face.

"The wind is vicious up here, Sir Edward." Martinez dragged a wooden chest into the shelter of the helm housing. "Move over. Sit where it cannot cut through you." Edward meant to answer, but his throat still refused him. He shifted aside and let her pull the chest close.

"I had the firing lines and sequence checked again," Timothy said as he came nearer. "If we have to shoot while the ship is still turning, I will let each gun take the stern as it crosses the angle. We do not need to wait for the whole broadside to align."

Edward looked at him. "And you? Did you sleep at all?" "For a while." Timothy rubbed his hands together. "Then I went down to look at the guns again. I know we already checked them. I just lie there thinking I missed something."

Edward nodded and pulled another chest towards him. Timothy sat, but his hands remained locked together between his knees. Edward wiped the last wetness from his face with the back of his hand and looked at the three men around him. "This late at night, and you have all decided to freeze up here with me?"

"I had just finished handing over the watch," Fredo said. He leaned against the helm housing but kept the helmsman's path clear. "Saw you sitting here. Thought I would stop."

"Thank you." Edward placed the notebook on his knees. It took him a moment before he managed to let go of it. Martinez sat on the chest beside him. "Tomorrow we may not say anything to one another except whatever has to be shouted over cannon. We can spend a little time tonight speaking about something else."

"We still need sleep," Timothy said. "I would rather not discover tomorrow that all three of you answer orders by nodding off."

Fredo pulled his collar higher over his neck. "A little while. You keep the time. When it is enough, throw me below."

They gathered the chests around the storm lantern without blocking the approach to the wheel. Martinez had barely settled before she tilted her head towards Fredo. "Sir Edward, have you ever read anything by our novelist here? In Madrid he can spend half an afternoon repairing one sentence about a lady crossing a corridor."

"Because someone stands over my shoulder reading and criticising," Fredo said. He turned his chest until it stopped rocking. "You even corrected the way a man held a sword during a dance scene."

"He held it incorrectly." Martinez glanced at Edward. "And when this one goes on patrol, he studies the ladies-in-waiting so intently that I once had to remind him the Queen was standing in front of them."

"I was looking at the person behind the Queen." Fredo stopped as her smile widened. "Right. That sounded worse." Timothy laughed into his collar. Edward joined him, the sound still rough from the cold and what had come before.

"Speaking of observation," Fredo said, "how many arranged meetings has the Queen forced upon you now? Ten? I remember one gentleman who asked what you enjoyed, and you gave him a complete explanation of how to break his guard." "He asked about swords first," Martinez protested.

"And you answered until he asked permission to leave," Fredo said. Martinez nudged Fredo's chest with the toe of her boot. He caught the edge before it tipped, raised one hand in surrender, and lost the fight against his own grin.

Timothy looked across the lantern at Edward. "Neither of them knows about the Admiral's tea." Edward rested one hand on the notebook. "Timothy. Think very carefully about your next sentence." "If he misses his morning cup, the rest of us generally hope the French start trouble early so he has someone else to be angry with."

Fredo turned towards Edward. "That bad?" Timothy was already committed. "Once, in northern France, he led us into a farmhouse on a hill. The family was so terrified they had all pressed themselves against one wall. I was waiting for an order to search the place. The Admiral asked what kind of tea they were drying behind the house."

"I still needed directions," Edward said. He raised one finger towards Timothy. "And I paid for the tea." "Yes, sir. You also ordered me to carry it back and warned me not to get it wet. The powder bags received almost the same instruction."

Martinez laughed hard enough that she had to lean away from the lantern. Fredo wanted to know whether the tea had at least been worth it, and Edward had to wait for all three to stop before he could answer. They traded more stories after that. Several never reached the ending because the teller began laughing first, and for a little while Red Baron became less a warship approaching battle than a cold deck occupied by four people who had been given one quiet hour.

When the bell for the change of watch sounded, Timothy pointed at the time. Fredo kept his promise; he and Martinez went below to rest before assembly.

At four in the morning, boots returned to the ladder. Edward closed the lid of his silver watch as Timothy came up last, tugging his collar into place. "Has the galley fire been lit?" "Yes, Admiral."

"If there is time, ask them for four cups of tea. I owe you a proper dawn service." Timothy stared at him. "You spent the night telling me to remind everyone to sleep, and now you are sending me for tea." Edward looked towards Fredo. Timothy followed the look, sighed, and shook his head. "Fine. I will see what they have."

He returned soon after with a steaming tin tray. Four cream-coloured cups held dark brown tea, its bitter warmth strong enough to overcome the smell of salt, whale oil, damp rope, and the sea washing across the deck. The east was still black beneath a shelf of cloud. They stood near the rail with both hands around the cups, lifting their boots whenever cold water ran across the planks.

Edward raised his tea. "Still hot. Drink before somebody finds work for us again." "To victory," Fredo said. Martinez touched her cup to his. Timothy watched the steam curl in front of his face before lifting his own. "And to the road home."

Five thirty in the morning. Fog had closed over the bay. Moisture silvered the rails and rigging, and beyond the carefully hooded deck lamps Edward could make out little more than human shapes moving towards battle stations. The world ahead of Red Baron had become a wall of white-grey silence. Edward settled his bicorne and drew the grey-white admiral's dress coat tight across his shoulders. Then he walked the oak deck at an even pace, past the long ranks already forming for action. Eight hundred English veterans stood with flintlock rifles at the shoulder, their ammunition including Rare-grade Vestigium rounds intended for armour. Between them waited one hundred Conquistadores in polished leather armour, weapons ready and expressions gone still.

Edward stopped where the first ranks could see him. "Eyes on me." The murmur died. He walked slowly along the line, meeting face after face hardened by cold and waiting. "Out there is a French fleet full of men arrogant enough to believe polished cannon and a few miles of ice are enough to keep us in a cage. Remember this: I brought you here to tear that cage open. I did not bring you here to waste your lives."

His voice carried farther down the deck. "No one aboard this ship gets to die cheaply. If your powder is gone, use the bayonet. If the bayonet breaks, use the stock. Lose the rifle, take your knife. Lose the knife, use your teeth and fingernails if that is what remains. Whatever is still in your hand, put it somewhere the bastard in front of you will remember." A few grim smiles appeared among the veterans.

Edward stopped before a group of young gunners. The corner of his mouth lifted, and when he spoke again the edge in his voice had shifted from command to the coarser humour of a man who belonged on a deck more than in any palace. "The perfumed gentlemen of Paris are very brave when someone else is loading the cannon. I would wager the French admiral's mother is praying this very moment that her son does not piss through his expensive silk trousers when he sees the red cross come out of the fog." Laughter rolled through the ranks, elbows struck ribs, and one Conquistador made a noise that might have been a cough if anyone wished to be polite.

Edward let the grin remain for one heartbeat. "Let us send the lot of them to the bottom so they can complain to their mothers in person."

The laughter broke louder, then vanished when Edward raised one hand and pointed into the fog. "Our estimate gives us cover until roughly eight. Wind changes, and it may disappear sooner. That means two and a half hours, and I do not intend to spend all of them." He pointed towards the bow. "Take the flagship. Break the blockade. Keep a road open for the landing force and a road back for our own people."

Edward's eyes moved across the ranks. "Clear?" Nine hundred voices struck back at once. "CLEAR, ADMIRAL!" Rifle locks snapped. Steel struck steel. Beneath it all, the sea continued to hammer the hull as Red Baron vanished deeper into the fog.

title_vi: Chapter 31 - Battle of La Concha I
title_en: Chapter 31 - Battle of La Concha I
text_en:
Fog cut visibility to less than thirty fathoms. Red Baron slipped into the bay with the wind behind her, the silhouettes of her masts vanishing into banks of low grey mist. Whale grease mixed with Vestigium powder kept the rigging from freezing solid and softened the complaint of the blocks. Sailors held loose lengths of line away from the hull wherever they might strike the planking, and what little noise remained disappeared beneath the wash of the sea.

At the helm, Edward locked both hands around the oak wheel and watched the rhythm of the swell along the quarter. Fredo and Martinez stood close beside the rail, bodies lowered against the wind as they searched the fog for movement.

Fredo lowered his Vestigium scope and pointed towards eleven o'clock. "Two patrol frigates, roughly three hundred metres. Sails slack. Looks as though they're drifting."

Through the specially ground Vestigium lenses of his telescope, Edward could make out French sentries huddled on the enemy decks. They crouched in their cloaks around weak charcoal braziers, fighting the cold while frost packed itself over gun tackles and standing rigging. The French cannon sat inside that white crust like frozen iron, slow to wake and slower still to train.

"To hell with them." Edward put the helm to starboard. "I'm not wasting powder on minnows. Keep quiet."

Martinez passed the signal down to the gun decks. Below, the English veterans pulled back from the open ports and waited with their weapons held close. Red Baron seemed to swallow every sound as she slid through a gap scarcely a hundred metres wide between the two French patrol ships. The water sheared beneath her hull, but even that vanished into the slap and surge of the waves. Neither frigate gave the slightest sign that it had seen her.

Beyond the outer screen, the true target emerged from the fog. The French flagship towered above the water beneath the golden fleur-de-lis of the Holy Kingdom of France, a four-deck monster that looked less like a ship than a fortress cut loose from land. She lay anchored beside the deep-water approach into San Sebastián Bay, broadside turned towards the coast to support the bombardment ashore. Hundreds of gunports faced the land, leaving the lighter timber of her stern exposed towards the open sea.

"There she is." Edward handed the wheel to Timothy and waited until the younger man had a firm grip before drawing Stormroar.

The patterns running along the weapon's body flared red. Snow trapped in the metal grooves hissed into steam, and heat bit into fingers that had gone numb in the cold. Edward stepped to the rail and aimed at the rudder assembly beneath the French flagship's stern. He waited for the rise of the swell to expose the joint, then held Stormroar steady on the mark. Click. His finger closed around the trigger.

BOOM!

The weapon's report tore through the fog like a siege gun fired at arm's length. Red fire burst from the bronze muzzle, carving a burning tunnel through the mist. The explosive round struck the rudder joint squarely. Vestigium force stored inside the projectile detonated on impact, breaking iron pins as thick as a man's wrist as though they were dry sticks. The flagship's steering gear erupted into splintered oak and torn steel, thousands of fragments scything out across the black water. The shock wave drove blistering heat upwards and blew the armoured glass from the stern navigation room. Oak beams groaned, split, and folded. The chart table vanished beneath flying wreckage, the compass shattered, and the officer of the watch was hurled into a broken bulkhead.

"Hard to port! Cut across her stern!" Edward lowered the smoking weapon and caught the rail as Red Baron began to swing.

The oak wheel spun through Timothy's hands. Red Baron heeled into the turn, crossing behind the crippled flagship at a clean right angle and locking the French ship into the oldest cruelty of line warfare: a raking position. Three Castilian gun decks opened at once, black muzzles sliding through the ports until they pointed into the shattered stern windows from less than twenty metres away.

"Gunners! Double shot, chain shot... FIRE!"

Timothy's shout cracked across the deck.

BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

Dozens of cannon discharged together. Grey-white powder smoke rolled from the broadside in one solid wall and darkened the sea. Solid iron and spinning lengths of chain drove through the flagship from stern to bow, sweeping along the decks like the teeth of some immense machine. Oak burst apart. French gun carriages tore free and smashed into bulkheads. Men disappeared beneath splinters, broken equipment, and one another as screams merged with the thunder of collapsing timber.

By the time the broadside finished raking forward, the enemy's upper deck had become a field of wreckage streaked red with blood. Edward waited until their guns had cleared the line of the French stern, then threw up one hand. "Furl the mainsail and forecourse! Starboard anchor, let it bite!"

Canvas climbed under the shouts of the line crews. The anchor cable snapped taut, Red Baron's hull shuddered beneath them, and the ship lost speed. Timothy fought the wheel and held the broadside facing the enemy stern. English soldiers rose in ordered ranks and levelled their muskets over the rail. Fredo drew his sword, waited until the first line had a target, then dropped the blade.

"Fire by volley!"

Armour-piercing rounds swept the exits from the enemy decks and pinned down French marines trying to climb through the wreckage. Martinez raised her sword towards the flagship's stern. "Conquistadores! Across!"

A hundred grappling hooks flew, their copper-braided lines following them through the air before iron teeth bit into railings and broken frames. One hundred Conquistadores swung across the gap between the ships. Their fast-loading rifles began cracking almost as soon as boots struck French timber. Stocks slammed through the reload mechanism in disciplined rhythm, producing a wall of fire that swept forward from the stern. French sailors and marines rushed them with blades and were cut down at close range before they could turn the broken deck into a proper defence.

"Forward to the bow!" Martinez pointed towards the anchor windlass and led the first group across the torn midships.

They had barely passed the centre of the flagship when lower hatch covers burst open. French naval Gendarmes poured onto the deck in a mass of iron and blocked the only direct route forward. Unlike ordinary marines, these guards wore solid plate from head to foot. Vestigium worked into the forged metal took away much of the armour's natural burden, giving men in full iron an unnatural speed as they closed.

"Watch yourselves! Gendarmes!"

Martinez's longsword came up just in time to catch the first crushing blow.

"Split to both wings! No single combat! Change your angle and shoot for the gaps behind the knees and at the neck. Anchor team, flank them. I don't care what it costs, cut those chains!"

Conquistador rifles hammered in response. Lead struck the heavy armour in showers of sparks and skipped away. Sword edges fared little better, leaving pale scars across plates that had been built to survive far more than ordinary steel. The Gendarmes answered with solid war hammers and spiked maces. The Vestigium-treated leather of the Conquistadores could blunt cuts and resist shot with remarkable efficiency, but it offered little mercy against a weapon designed to crush through protection rather than pierce it. Every hammer blow carried the sound of bone breaking beneath intact armour. Shock travelled through ribcages and into organs; Castilian soldiers coughed blood and collapsed while the leather around them remained whole. The boarding wedge stalled amidships, then began to come apart under the weight of iron.

Bodies from both sides already covered the frozen planks when Martinez Testarossa roared above the gunfire. Her Miracle-grade Vestigium sword flared with brilliant emerald light. The blade lengthened in her hands, steel expanding until it became a towering claymore more than two metres long.

"Hold the flanks! These three are mine!"

Martinez stepped into the gap as three Gendarmes advanced. The first brought his war hammer down at her head. Martinez raised the claymore horizontally and took the blow on the blade.

CLANG!

The impact should have broken bone or torn the weapon from her hands. Instead, the Vestigium blade swallowed the crushing force so completely that Martinez did not give up a single step. The Gendarme hesitated at the absence of recoil. That heartbeat was enough. Martinez pivoted through ninety degrees, drove the turn through her hips, and sent the great blade screaming across his neck. Steel passed through armour, flesh, and bone in one clean line. The Gendarme's head spun away in a dark arc of blood before the armoured body crashed onto the deck. The remaining pair came in together. One swept a spiked mace at her waist while the other raised his weapon to smash down into her shoulder.

Martinez sank her weight, turned the claymore through a low arc to knock the first mace aside, then drove the point precisely through the gap at the second man's neck. Another helmeted head fell into the snow. She drew breath in the middle of the blood and wreckage, then bellowed towards her men.

"This deck has no room for cowards! Forward! Cut those anchors! For Castile! For Testarossa!"

She dropped the third Gendarme and drove the Conquistadores forward with her. Their line recovered around her, rifles firing as men pushed once more towards the bow. Human endurance, however, had limits even before a wall of iron. Five more Gendarmes flooded in and closed around her from every direction. Martinez checked her next stroke to avoid a falling Conquistador. The altered angle carried the claymore away from the neck joint and buried it in the commander's breastplate instead. She pulled once, but the blade remained lodged in the metal.
