A Gendarme struck her from the flank. The leather armour held. Two ribs beneath it did not. Martinez coughed blood and hit the deck, one hand slipping from the claymore still buried in the enemy plate. She kicked against the boards and forced herself up before the mace could come around again. Both hands found the hilt. She used it as a fixed point, hauled her body upwards, and locked her legs around the helmet of the man who had struck her. Then she twisted with all the strength left in her hips.

CRACK!

The Gendarme's neck broke inside the heavy gorget. His armoured body dropped like a load of scrap iron. Martinez landed, tore the claymore free from the fallen commander's chest, and swept the blade across the next attack hard enough to send the enemy weapon aside. She went straight back into the French formation.

"IS THAT ALL YOU'VE GOT?"

The words had barely left her mouth when she cut down another man. A shot cracked from somewhere beyond the smoke. Martinez jerked as the round punched through her shoulder and spun her half sideways. Before she found her balance, a Gendarme came from the blind quarter behind her and drove the haft of his iron mace into the centre of her back. The blow emptied the last strength from her legs. Darkness washed across her vision. The claymore slipped from numb fingers, and she collapsed into blood and frozen spray.

The Gendarme stepped over her and lifted his spiked mace for the killing blow.

BOOM!

Stormroar thundered in Edward's hands and blew the man apart. Edward was over the gap between the ships a heartbeat later. He landed hard on French timber and drew his sabre. The instant the weapon cleared its scabbard, the fragment of Excalibur worked into the ancient blade erupted in golden light. Heat rolled out across the deck, turning snow to steam beneath his boots. He drove forward like fire pushed by a gale. The first French plate he met opened under the glowing edge as though the Vestigium iron were rotten wood, blood spraying across the white deck.

Edward reached Martinez with one hand still cutting at anyone who came too close. With the other he seized the strap of her armour and hauled her upright. His eyes went once to the bullet wound in her shoulder, then to the great sword she had dropped.

"Still breathing, Lady Martinez?"

She coughed up a mouthful of dark blood. One corner of her split lip managed something close to a smile.

"Not dead yet... much as you worry."

Edward glanced at the claymore and crooked his mouth. "Good. That transformation was bloody spectacular." He turned his back towards her and lowered himself. "Hold on to me. Can you cover my right?"

Martinez clenched her teeth and hooked her left arm across his shoulder. "Yes. Just don't crush me against the rail."

Edward raised his sabre and shouted to the nearest men. "Conquistadores, hold both flanks! Get the anchor team through!"

Seeing their commander-in-chief carrying their wounded admiral into the fight did more for the surviving Conquistadores than any speech could have managed. They closed into a narrow wedge, rifles firing from the sides as they shielded Edward's advance. With Martinez on his back, Edward forced his way through the iron line like a battering ram. His burning sabre cut mace shafts, opened plate, and dropped Gendarmes one after another. Behind and beside him, the Conquistadores pressed forward through the gap his blade made. The whole formation fought its way to the bow. Axes and Edward's incandescent edge fell together on the anchor gear until the massive iron links broke apart and plunged into the dark water below. Without steering and with her anchor chains severed, the French four-decker began to yaw under the current. The flagship moved helplessly towards the reefs inside San Sebastián Bay.

"Anchors are gone! Everybody back to Red Baron!"

Edward turned to force a path towards the stern. The instant the formation moved, gunfire crashed into them.

BANG! BANG! BANG!

The remaining Conquistadores collapsed towards the sound, covering Edward and Martinez while firing back from behind shattered gun carriages. Heavy rounds hammered their leather armour. Men at the edge of the line went to their knees; the protection remained unbroken, yet blood ran from their mouths.

As the powder smoke thinned, another rank of Gendarmes emerged through it. This time they were accompanied by men in black wool uniforms embroidered with the French royal arms: the feared Mousquetaires Noirs. The black musketeers carried long-barrelled flintlocks built around a specialised firing mechanism. Their steel-cored ammunition had been designed to punch through the plate armour of the Holy Roman Empire, and at this distance the weapons needed little invitation.

Dark muzzles rose behind the advancing Gendarmes. Hammermen moved with them, narrowing the space around the Castilians and driving Edward's battered force towards the confined bow. Then a young aristocrat stepped out from behind the French line. He was handsome in the cold way of a portrait meant to intimidate visitors. Golden hair had been tied neatly at the nape with a black ribbon, and his dark blue naval dress coat carried silver embroidery fine enough for a royal audience. A pair of narrow curved sabres gleamed in his hands.

He moved like a ghost. The first Conquistador lunged and died before his sword had finished the motion. The Frenchman's twin blades slipped through the vulnerable seams beneath arm and jaw, cutting where the leather armour could not protect. Three elite Castilian soldiers fell within seconds.

"Target the man with the tied hair! Pin him down! FIRE!"

Timothy shouted from Red Baron's rail and threw his arm forward. The Gendarmes instantly locked their plate together and formed a living wall around their commander. Armour-piercing shot struck in a deafening series of metallic blows. Some rounds began to bite through, but the iron screen held long enough to preserve the man behind it. Before the English could cycle their rifles again, the Gendarmes lowered themselves in perfect coordination and opened firing lanes for the Mousquetaires Noirs.

BANG! BANG! BANG!

Long flintlocks spat blue-grey flame. Steel-cored rounds crossed the gap and struck Red Baron. Oak exploded into sprays of splinters. Bullets punched through sandbag breastworks and tore into the thick wool coats of English veterans. Men fell backwards across the deck, blood striking sailcloth while their cries disappeared beneath the cannonade rolling across the bay. The blond officer flicked blood from his sabres and lifted clear blue eyes towards Edward.

"Do you see it, Admiral? Every dark-red flower opening in the white snow..." His smile deepened. "Beautiful. Like the red spider lilies I once saw growing at the edge of death in a kingdom far to the East. War has always been the finest symphony."

He bowed with courtly elegance amid the dead.

"Pierrot de Kenway, captain of Le Triomphant. It is a pleasure to witness the legend of England reach its final movement."

Edward eased Martinez against a broken section of bulwark and bent to retrieve the sabre beside the limp hand of a dead Conquistador. In his right hand, the Excalibur fragment still burned inside his own weapon, flooding the snow with gold and steam. The ordinary grey blade rested cold in his left. He angled that borrowed steel towards Pierrot while keeping the glowing sabre close enough to defend Martinez.

"Pierrot de Kenway. Pierrot, as in the clown?" Edward bared his teeth. "Ten years ago, when we were shitting all over the forts of northern France, were you old enough to hold a sword, or were you still under your mother's skirts crying for milk?"

Pierrot looked at the plain sabre in Edward's left hand and smiled. He did not enter its reach.

"What a pity, Edward. The vulgarity of a relic cannot alter the field before him. I did not come here to quarrel with you over the past."

He turned one of his sabres and pointed its tip towards the changing sky.

"I came only to tell you this: your time has run out."

A hard wind swept in from the west and tore strips of fog from the sea. Edward glanced at his watch. Six forty-five. An hour and fifteen minutes early. French signal lamps appeared all across the mouth of the bay as the mist opened. Ships of the line and frigates had already closed the circle, their broadsides turned towards Red Baron and Le Triomphant. Then the western horizon revealed something worse. Four immense black spreads of canvas emerged from the last of the thinning fog over the Atlantic. At the mastheads, the flag of the Portuguese Empire cracked in the wind. Four heavy ships of the line, each carrying the unnatural power of Vestigium, drove towards the bay like executioners who had arrived ahead of schedule.

The worst version of Edward's forecast had become real. Two jaws. One ship trapped between them. Pierrot turned away as though the matter had already been settled.

"There. Farewell, Edward Spencer. Your age is over."

The Gendarmes and Mousquetaires Noirs surged forward at once. Maces struck armour at killing distance while steel-cored rounds flashed between bodies. One Conquistador after another went down, their blood running across the cramped bow. Edward tightened his grip on both swords. His mind raced through routes, angles, currents, distances, every possible way out of the trap. Each one ended in the same wall of fire. For the first time that morning, the hand holding his blade began to shake. Warm fingers, wet with blood, closed around them. Edward looked down.

Martinez was staring at him. Her breathing came broken and shallow, yet her voice cut cleanly through the battle.

"Look at me, Sir Edward." She tightened her grip until his eyes stayed on hers. "Isabella is still waiting. We are getting out of here."

She fought down a cough, reached to her throat, and tore away the gold chain bearing the Castilian royal lion. Martinez pressed the metal emblem against the bleeding wound in her shoulder. Golden light burst from the pendant and washed across her grey face. At the same moment, the towering claymore on the deck lost its glow and contracted into the plain grey longsword it had been before. With what strength she still possessed, Martinez pushed the warm, blood-slick chain into Edward's hand.

"Put it on. It will take one mortal blow in your place." She stopped to breathe, but kept the pendant pressed towards him. "And the sword... you can release its form."

Edward looked from the weapon at her feet to the lion in his palm. Then he turned his body between Martinez and the French line and slipped the chain over his head. The lion touched his chest. The number 25 vanished. Heat ran the length of Edward's spine. Martinez caught his wrist before her hand dropped away.

"Close your eyes. Think of the weapon you want." Each breath cost her now. "You choose once. Whatever shape you give it will remain yours."

The dead Conquistador's sabre slipped from Edward's left hand and struck the deck. His right closed around the hilt of the Miracle-grade Vestigium sword. French boots hammered closer. Iron weapons rose. Edward closed his eyes.

CRASH!

A column of golden light erupted around him. The nearest French soldiers were lifted from their feet and thrown backwards across the deck. In Edward's hand, the blade lengthened and changed, becoming a great two-edged longsword whose proportions seemed at once ancient and absolute. Along the fuller, old Celtic letters ignited one after another until the steel appeared inlaid with living gold. Only Edward could read what they said.

Excalibur.

title_vi: Chapter 32 - Battle of La Concha II
title_en: Chapter 32 - Battle of La Concha II
text_en:
The wind blowing ahead of the Portuguese squadron swept the last fog from La Concha Bay. As the full shape of the battle emerged offshore, the coastal batteries of San Sebastián sent word at once to the most powerful woman still commanding the city.

"Governor Frenesia! Fighting in the bay. One ship under Castilian colours is engaged with the French."

Frenesia set down her pen. The officer in the doorway was still breathing hard, and she motioned him towards the desk.

"One ship? Have we received her signals?"

"No, madam. Her upper deck is gone, so the watchtowers cannot identify the class. But we can see the lion banner, and beneath it..." He stopped. "The red cross of England."

A drop of ink spread at the corner of the page. Frenesia watched it for a moment before looking up.

"You checked?"

"Three times from the North Tower. Four black-sailed Portuguese ships are also closing from the west."

Frenesia rose. She was past sixty, yet her back remained straight beneath a dark service coat with a rigid standing collar. She took the leather gloves from her desk and pulled them on as she crossed the room.

"Come with me to Monte Urgull."

The heavy oak door of the governor's residence closed behind them. Bitter sea wind struck through the streets of San Sebastián carrying sulphur, salt, and the first clear smell of gun smoke from the bay. The road towards Monte Urgull was clogged with ammunition carts. Frenesia went on foot beside the officer, threading past militia passing sandbags beneath an awning. Their leader shoved an empty handcart aside as soon as he saw her and cleared a path. She stopped at a field ration station. An older woman in a thick wool shawl was trembling as she measured dried turnip with a wooden scoop. At the sight of the familiar dark coat she began to bow.

"Keep serving." Frenesia looked into the soup barrel. "How long can the kitchen hold the heat?"

"With the red lime, until early afternoon, madam. We still have two streets to feed."

"Cut the salt in the next batch by a fifth. Send the difference to the curing workshop." Frenesia turned to the officer beside her. "Tell the well guards to keep the children away from the mouth. I will not have another one falling in."

She moved on towards Santa Catalina Bridge, the defensive throat that kept the French on the eastern bank from pouring into the centre of the city. Two tiers of oak barricades had been built across the span. Dozens of rifled barrels pointed through embrasures towards the far end. A young lieutenant, face streaked with soot and frost crusting the edge of his cap, stamped to attention when Frenesia approached.

"Governor! Third Garrison Battalion still controls the bridgehead. French long guns fired three harassment salvos, but all of them fell into the river."

Frenesia looked down along the nearest pier and asked how far from the supports the rounds had struck. After hearing the distances, she ordered another inspection after the next French salvo and told him to hold his men exactly where they were. Through the narrow lanes of Parte Vieja, Frenesia kept finding small failures before they became large ones. She sent the surgical station deeper into the cellars where shell fragments could not reach it and ordered patrols to collect old blankets from the churches for the coastal watch posts.

Behind her, two orderlies carried a stretcher down a basement stair. The liaison officer had to run several paces to catch up when Frenesia turned onto the road climbing towards the fortress. The stone way rose gradually towards Monte Urgull. By then the sea wind had become a shriek between the walls, carrying the deep roll of cannon from offshore. Frenesia passed through the gate of La Mota and went straight to the western rampart, where La Concha Bay burned beneath a lead-grey dawn. She climbed to the highest stone step and took a brass telescope from the engineering commander.

The whole mouth of the bay lay open through the glass. With the fog gone, the sea revealed a battlefield of black water, powder smoke, wreckage, and torn canvas. The strange ship whose fourth deck had been planed away, exactly as the watchman had reported, was holding itself against the stern of the French flagship Le Triomphant. Frenesia swept the telescope along the vessel. Hundreds of grey-and-white uniformed marksmen were firing without pause. Then she stopped on one man moving along the rail and shooting French soldiers who tried to swing across.

Muzzle flame flashed against the lion pendant on his chest. Tres.

"Fredo..." Frenesia kept the glass there until he vanished behind the mainmast.

Beside her, the artillery commander cleared his throat.

"Madam... that ship is caught between the French fleet and four Portuguese heavies. Should we order the coastal batteries to suppress the enemy and support her?"

Frenesia's eye stayed to the telescope. She shifted it towards the bow of the French flagship just as a burst of golden light exploded across the deck and threw armoured men away from its centre. A man stood inside that radiance with a two-edged longsword blazing in his hands. Even through distance and smoke, the figure held the deck with the immovable pressure of a stone wall. Frenesia lowered the glass.

"Beyond effective shore range. We fire from here, we waste ammunition."

She returned the telescope and pointed down towards the harbour.

"Prepare every warship that can move. The moment we draw them inside range, the fortress supports us. Whoever is aboard that ship comes home."

* * *

Golden light rolled from Excalibur and ran along the old Celtic letters in its fuller until every mark shone as though plated in fire. Clean warmth spread across the deck, driving the killing cold from the planks and burning away the stink of blood and powder. Martinez leaned against the broken bulwark and watched light travel through the sword. She caught the hem of Edward's coat and coughed blood before she managed to speak.

"This power... it doesn't feel Miracle-grade anymore." She looked up at him. "It may have reached Legendary. Use it. Open the road."

Her hand slid from his coat. Edward saw her chest still rising and turned towards the maces coming through the smoke. He said nothing. Both scarred hands closed around Excalibur's hilt. The moment all ten fingers locked into place, an unnatural quiet descended over his mind. Cannon fire, the scream of wind through shattered oak, the cries of French musketeers, all of it receded as though the world had been pushed to some distant shore. Time slowed. Snow hung in the air long enough for him to count the flakes. He saw every shift of muscle beneath the Gendarmes' armour, every twitch before a mace changed angle. Pierrot's sabres moved with glacial slowness. Gaps appeared in plate, dead ground between lines, openings that had been invisible a heartbeat before.

"Well. Here we are again."

A familiar voice spoke beside him. Edward turned his eyes without moving his head. The man walking through the frozen battlefield wore an English admiral's uniform from years ago. His younger face carried all the insolence Edward remembered because it was his own. The apparition stopped beside him and looked at Excalibur. The usual mockery faded.

"Not bad." A gloved hand settled on Edward's shoulder. "But you've still got people to get home."

For one instant Edward heard timber breaking at Inverness, brief and sharp inside the silence. His eyes stayed on the road towards the stern. His younger self drew the Miracle-grade Vestigium sabre at his hip. Gold ran along its edge, mirroring the light on Excalibur. Then the old sea wolf smiled.

"Come on, brother. Let's fight."

Reality slammed back into place. Edward drew one deep breath, tightened both hands around the hilt, and swung.

WHOOM!

The cut carried all the precision of the sabre work he had learned years ago, but the force behind it belonged to something else entirely. Steel passed through steel. The first Gendarme came apart through breastplate and body without slowing the blade. Before the two halves could fall, compressed air burst behind the stroke.

BOOM!

The pressure wave hit like a wall. Two more Gendarmes were ripped from their feet and thrown several fathoms across the deck. Edward reversed the blade. A second horizontal cut released another blast, clearing one whole section of planking and hurling Mousquetaires Noirs over the rail into the black water below. The moment the road opened, every Conquistador still able to stand dragged a wounded man with him. One shouted for the push. Others fired into both flanks, buying Edward another few steps towards Red Baron each time the sword threw the French line apart.

Blood streamed down one marksman's chin. He had to rest his stock on another man's shoulder to keep the muzzle level. Still he fired. Then Edward saw through the thinning smoke and looked beyond the wrecked flagship. A French three-decker had taken position roughly two hundred metres beyond Le Triomphant's bow. Her yards were squared, her dark broadside presented perfectly across the French flagship's axis. A classic rake.

"EVERYONE OFF THE SHIP!"

Edward's warning had barely left his throat when the deck bucked beneath him.

BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

The explosions came from deep inside Le Triomphant's hull. Dozens of powder charges hidden through the lower holds detonated together. Oak frames burst apart. The upper deck split open as red columns of flame and black smoke punched through it, throwing French and Castilian soldiers into the air. The shock wave ripped across the flagship and swept men into the freezing sea. Broken timber became shrapnel. Fire rolled through the wreckage until the whole deck seemed to collapse into a single man-made hell. French and Castilian bodies went down together. The most terrible part was what the survivors did next.

Mousquetaires Noirs and Gendarmes staggered out of the smoke with uniforms burning, skin blackened, blood matting their armour. Their eyes remained dull and empty. They showed no fear of the flames eating into them and no instinct to flee. They simply charged. Boots trampled dead comrades. Maces rose. Bayonets drove forwards.

"Damn it... he rigged his own ship to die."

Edward bit hard enough to taste blood. He could no longer keep both hands on Excalibur. One arm had to catch Martinez around the waist and pull her half-conscious weight against him, her arm dragged over his shoulders as he turned towards the stern. The instant he shifted to a one-handed grip, the Celtic letters dimmed. Edward cut through one mace shaft, but no pressure wave followed the stroke. The French flooded into the gap.

"PROTECT THE ADMIRAL!"

A Conquistador's roar tore through the explosions. The survivors closed around Edward and Martinez. They fired while falling back, then used rifle stocks to stop maces before the blows could land. Whenever one man fell, the soldier beside him stepped into the opening. A Conquistador with broken ribs still locked his teeth into a Frenchman's throat when the mace brought him down. Another took a round through the shoulder and used his last stroke to sever the tendon behind an enemy knee before collapsing.

"ADMIRAL, MOVE!"

One man had both hands wrapped around enemy bayonets. Blood filled his mouth as he turned his head and screamed at Edward.

"WE DON'T NEED YOU DYING WITH US! GET LADY MARTINEZ BACK TO THE SHIP! BACK TO RED BARON, NOW!"

Edward reached the stern with Martinez. Of the hundred Conquistadores who had boarded Le Triomphant, perhaps three or four were still close enough to follow, their leather armour torn and soaked dark. Another chain of explosions ran through the lower decks. Seawater poured into the opened hull and dragged the bow down. The stern rose higher and higher while the planking folded beneath anyone who had failed to seize a handhold. The surge struck Red Baron and lifted her port side. Gun carriages rolled until their restraining lines snapped tight. Grappling cables between the vessels began dragging the Castilian ship towards the sinking French hull.

The angle beneath Edward's boots steepened. He looked across the widening gap. More than thirty metres now separated the ships, far beyond the range of any ordinary hook. The earlier blast had burned or torn away every usable line hanging from the after rigging. The road back was gone. Martinez sagged against his chest, unconscious now, breath barely visible in the snow gathering on her pale lips. On Red Baron, Timothy and the English sailors were hacking at the grapples with axes, but muscle alone could not overcome the pull of a four-decker taking the sea with it.

Edward looked at the men cutting from the other side, then lowered Martinez against the base of the steering platform. He drew Stormroar and aimed at the bundle of grapples still carrying the strain. If they held much longer, Red Baron would capsize with them.

BOOM!

The shot struck the connection point and exploded in red fire. Heat and metal tore through the last grappling heads. The bond between the ships vanished.

Red Baron rolled violently, recovered, and began sliding away from the deadly pull of the sinking flagship. Edward shoved the empty Stormroar into his belt and went back to Martinez. With the stern now lifted into the highest part of the wreck, he placed her in the angle between the helm housing and the rear cabin wall where gravity could not drag her towards the water. He stripped off his formal coat, covered her with it, and wedged a broken timber across the edge so the gale could not tear it away.

Then Edward planted his boots on the sloping deck and stood. Both hands closed around Excalibur. The moment the two-handed grip returned, golden power erupted through the blade. Light rose from the stern like a beacon at sea and drove smoke and snow away from the wreck. The old Celtic letters burned bright along the steel. Below him, surviving Gendarmes and Mousquetaires Noirs clawed their way up the incline through shattered planking. Men with burned faces used broken beams as handholds, climbing with maces and rifles raised towards him. Edward lowered his centre of gravity and held Excalibur across his body.

The French came on. Then a shout fell from above.

"EDWARD! GET YOUR HEAD DOWN!"

Edward looked up. A figure tore through smoke and salt spray and landed on the steep stern beside him. Boots struck cracked oak hard enough to scatter frozen snow. Fredo. His cloak had been ripped open. Segments of steel were folding back into the weapon in his hand. Edward followed the retreating line of a metal whip towards its last anchor point, then looked past Fredo. Red Baron had already drifted more than forty metres away.

"You... how the hell did you get over here?"

"Later!"

Fredo wiped soot from his cheek, breath coming hard, grey eyes fixed on the French climbing towards them.

"Pick Martinez up! Hold on to me, now!"

Edward collapsed Excalibur back into sabre form and sheathed it. He lifted Martinez into his arms, then locked his free arm around Fredo's waist as the deck tilted farther beneath them. Fredo drew the longsword at his hip. Click. A sharp mechanical release sounded. Purple light burst down the blade. The straight steel separated into hundreds of thin, flat segments linked by Vestigium cables fine as spider silk. In the gale, the pieces shook and turned like pages of a metal manuscript, each one answering the smallest movement of Fredo's wrist.

Mousquetaires Noirs raised their muskets below. Fredo swung.

WHIP!

The segmented blade tore through the air and extended more than twenty metres in an instant. Razor-edged plates slipped through openings in armour, looped around five musket barrels, and cinched across the throats of the two leading Gendarmes. Fredo snapped his wrist back.

CRACK!

Both armoured men dropped with broken necks. The five muskets flew from their owners and vanished over the side. Fredo rotated his wrist again and opened the segmented weapon into a killing spiral. Steel plates drove into knee joints and armour seams, clearing a swathe of the climbing French in a storm of screams. The moment their advance broke, Fredo changed direction. He aimed the weapon towards Red Baron's mainmast, now nearly fifty metres away.

"Fifty-five metres is the limit! Hold on, Sir Edward!"

The whip flew. Le Triomphant answered with her final death rattle. The aft structure burst apart. White water boiled around the wreck as the four-deck flagship gave up the last of its buoyancy and plunged into the bay. The sinking hull pulled the sea down after it. Water dropped into a vast funnel of foam and wreckage. The deck vanished beneath Edward, Martinez, and Fredo. All three fell. Fredo drove his arm forward. Every flat steel segment opened to its full length, the weapon stretching through the smoke like a silver thread.

But the violent current and the shock from the sinking flagship had pushed Red Baron farther than he had judged. The hooked tip passed beneath the main yard. It missed. The distance had opened to nearly fifty-seven metres. Fredo's weapon had fifty-five. The chain reached full extension and the hook hung in open air while all three bodies continued to fall. On Red Baron's deck, Timothy stared at the steel line stretched towards nothing. He saw the hook begin to drop and understood the distance at once.

"ALL PORT GUN CREWS! EVERY MAN TO STARBOARD, NOW!"

His voice broke with the force of the shout. Timothy seized the restraining line of the nearest thirty-two-pounder and threw his whole weight into it.

"SLACK THE BREECHING, HOLD THE TACKLE! RUN THE GUNS TO STARBOARD!" He pointed towards the three falling figures. "LOWER THE YARDS TOWARDS THEM!"

Gun crews put shoulders against carriages and drove them across with the ship's roll. Men on the tackles checked each gun before its wheels could run too far. Everyone else who could move crossed to the same side. Red Baron began to heel. Timber groaned through the hull. Starboard sank towards the water and the great masts leaned more than twenty degrees over the whirlpool, their yards reaching out like wooden arms. The tip of the main yard dropped and swung closer. Fifty-four metres. Fredo's hook struck wood.

The final segments wrapped and locked around the spar while the chain remained inside its fifty-five-metre limit.

"GOT IT!"

Timothy's scream carried across the deck. The segmented weapon snapped taut like a string about to break under the weight of three people. Fredo used the recoil. With both hands locked and his body swinging beneath the line, he converted the Vestigium cable's stored tension into one long arc. Edward and Martinez rose with him out of the spray, all three bodies flying through powder smoke towards Red Baron.

CRASH!

They struck the oak deck and slid through loose snow before stopping beside the mainmast. Edward rolled at once and put his body around Martinez. Fredo dropped to one knee, dragging cold air into his lungs while trembling hands began pulling the steel segments back into their sword form.

"LEVEL THE SHIP! BACK TO STATIONS! LOCK EVERY GUN CARRIAGE!"

The crews hauled the guns home and retightened the restraining lines as men moved back towards port. Red Baron rolled hard once more, then began to right herself. Timothy kept both hands on the tackle until the final carriage had been chocked. Only then did he let go.

"WE SAVED THEM!"

title_vi: Chapter 33 - Battle of La Concha III
title_en: Chapter 33 - Battle of La Concha III
text_en:
"THE ADMIRAL'S ALIVE!"

The cheer rolled through every deck of Red Baron, fists lifting into the smoke as relief broke across men who had been holding their breath for far too long. It lasted less than three seconds.

BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

Black columns of seawater erupted around the hull. French ships of the line had closed the ring from every direction and were firing at short range, broadside after broadside converging on Red Baron. Solid shot and explosive shells hammered the planking. The oak hull shook under every impact and answered with the deep groan of a wounded animal. Red Baron had been built from ancient Sherwood oaks, timber grown in soil altered by Vestigium and saturated through generations with its strange energy. The grain was denser, tougher, and more resilient than ordinary oak. That was the only reason the ship remained afloat after so many direct hits.

Even Sherwood timber had limits. Deep cracks opened along the starboard side. Whole sections of splintered planking peeled away and smoked around glowing impact scars. Another concentrated broadside or two would tear through into the gun decks and let the freezing sea into the belly of the ship. Timothy dragged Edward to his feet and pointed towards the damage.

"Starboard's coming apart! Two more salvos like that and we'll flood the gun deck."

Edward narrowed his eyes and fixed south by the ship's bow. The trap was complete. French line ships held the north, east, and west in a curved killing arc, firing continuously as they tightened around him. South was the only exit into the mouth of San Sebastián Bay. Four black-sailed Portuguese heavies were taking it away. Farther off, one French vessel had already broken from the ring. Edward caught a brief glimpse of Pierrot de Kenway on her deck, withdrawing while the wreck of Le Triomphant disappeared behind him.

"Set every scrap of fore and main canvas!" Edward watched the battle flags snap in the westerly. "Take the wind. Run south for the bay!"

Timothy stared at the black sails. "They're blocking the mouth. At this speed we can't clear the first one's bow."

"I need the wind they're bringing with them." Edward drew Stormroar and shoved the grip into Timothy's hand. "I'll steer. Break the French ships on our stern and keep them from forcing us to turn early."

Timothy checked the empty chamber, then took cartridges from Edward's pouch.

"I'll call when the stern is clear. Don't put the helm all the way over before that."

Edward sprinted for the shattered command deck and locked both hands around what remained of the oak wheel. Under the old sea wolf's hands, Red Baron answered. The whale-greased canvas filled with the western wind and drove the three-decker forwards like an arrow across black water. Both broadsides opened as she ran, firing continuously into French ships attempting to close. Below, Timothy rammed a fresh round into Stormroar and listened for Edward's voice through the decks.

"Ten o'clock! Second storage compartment below the French waterline... FIRE!"

BOOM!

Timothy pulled the trigger. The red Vestigium shell struck the protected magazine section of the French ship and detonated inside the timber. Fire burst through the hull and split the vessel almost in two. Edward held the helm and threaded Red Baron between shell splashes. The ship answered more quickly after the surgery in Lisbon, but her mass still needed time to follow every turn. He felt that delay through the wheel and never asked for more than the hull could give. Portuguese gunfire began to reach them. Their ammunition was nothing like the French iron that had been battering Red Baron all morning. The Portuguese rounds were cast from alloys charged with Vestigium energy. They did not arc across the water with the blunt roar of ordinary heavy shot.

They screamed. Purple traces tore through the air with frightening precision.

BOOM!

One Portuguese round punched through the upper deck and opened a smoking crater in the Sherwood oak. The angle spared the hull below the waterline, but the impact threw splinters across the deck and shook the whole ship from keel to masthead. Seeing Red Baron drive directly towards them, the Portuguese heavies spread every black sail they carried. Vestigium worked through the canvas and whipped the westerly harder, drawing the squadron forwards.

The wind they created reached Red Baron as well. Rigging shrieked under the extra load. Reinforcements shuddered in the hull as the ship found another burst of speed and the gap before the leading black-sailed vessel began to close. Timothy braced Stormroar against the edge of a gunport.

"Eight o'clock! Second ship of the line!"

"I see her!"

He waited for the hull to rise on the swell and fired. By the time Edward called a frigate at two o'clock, Timothy was already at the next port, forcing another round into the overheated weapon. Stormroar fired again and again. Four French pursuers exploded. Then five. Magazine fires turned the sea behind Red Baron into pillars of flame. The remaining French ships faltered at the sight of the destruction and the reckless vessel flying the English cross. Their line finally broke. Timothy shouted towards the helm.

"Stern is clear! You can turn!"

"HARD TO PORT! STARBOARD GUNS, READY TO GIVE HER EVERYTHING!"

Edward threw his weight against the wheel. Red Baron swept across the bow of the leading Portuguese monster. Dozens of starboard guns fired at point-blank range and raked the Portuguese forecastle from end to end. The Portuguese ship was carrying too much momentum. Red Baron cleared most of her length. Her stern did not.

CRASH!

A Vestigium-armoured ram drove into Red Baron's quarter like an immense spear. The steering platform and command deck disintegrated around Edward. Oak exploded into dust and splinters. The wheel vanished beneath him, and the impact threw him across the deck. Edward drove his sabre into the planking to stop the slide and forced himself upright amid the wreckage. Portuguese soldiers were gathering on the enemy bow.

"Infantry! Form a firing wall across the deck! Prepare to receive boarders!"

He turned towards the open gun deck.

"Timothy! Hold your gunners below! Free fire with every broadside gun and Stormroar. Their bow is inside our stern. Shoot through the bottom of the bastard until it opens!"

Then Edward looked beyond the collision. The other three black-sailed warships were curving in behind the leader, using the same western wind to form a closing T across Red Baron's path. Hundreds of gunports opened along their sides. Purple light began to build inside the muzzles. But the immediate threat came over the rail.

"KILL THE CASTILIANS!"

Hundreds of Portuguese Conquistadores poured from the bow of the ship locked into Red Baron. They looked nothing like Castile's mobile Conquistadores in their Vestigium-treated leather. The Portuguese soldiers wore crude full plate that belonged to another century, heavy iron wrapped around them from throat to boot. Grey Morion helmets hid much of their faces, and broad old-fashioned swords filled their hands.

"VOLLEY FIRE!"

Four hundred English veterans fired as one. Vestigium-cored rounds punched through rusted breastplates with ease. Black blood and fragments of metal burst through the Portuguese ranks. The men kept walking. Five rounds struck one in the chest and belly. He did not slow. Seven struck another. He kept coming. Whatever Vestigium power had been brought out of the New World had stripped pain from them and left only forward motion. It took nearly ten rounds tearing through a man's organs before one of them finally staggered and collapsed.

Then they reached the English line. The killing became immediate. The Portuguese did not need modern fencing or refined close-combat doctrine. They raised their broad swords and drove old steel forwards with both hands. Thick English wool stopped nothing. Every thrust into the chest meant another veteran falling. Blood spread across the oak until the deck shone red beneath frozen spray. Edward watched men he had brought from England die three at a time. Something in his face changed. He drew his sabre and called power through Martinez's pendant. The blade lengthened in golden light and became Excalibur once more.

Ancient Celtic letters burned along the fuller. Edward locked both hands on the hilt and charged into the iron mass.

WHUM!

Excalibur cut through the first two Portuguese necks in one stroke. Morion helmets spun into the air trailing dark blood before both bodies struck the deck. Those bodies stayed down. Edward pointed the blade towards the others still walking through gunfire.

"The neck! Take their heads off!"

Behind him, Fredo had hidden Martinez inside a sheltered recess near the foot of the mizzenmast. Then his own sword came free. Click. The blade opened into its segmented whip form. Hundreds of thin steel plates spun through the air and wrapped around Portuguese throats from a distance. Fredo pulled hard, breaking necks and opening windpipes before the armoured men could reach the firing line. It still was not enough. The Portuguese came like a tide that had forgotten exhaustion. English veterans fell by the dozens. Blood and snow froze together into slick red slabs across the deck.

Edward took the head from the tenth man and staggered back half a step for breath. Then he looked seaward. The remaining three Portuguese heavies had completed their turn. They lay across Red Baron's blind angle with hundreds of broadside guns exposed. Purple Vestigium light burned inside the muzzles. Less than a hundred metres separated them. No wooden ship survived that.

BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

The first thunder came from the south. Ships flying Castilian colours had burst out of San Sebastián under Frenesia's command. Triple-barrelled heavy guns mounted in their bows fired at long range, steel rounds crossing the bay and punching holes through the sides of the Portuguese line. The Portuguese squadron answered immediately. Every available broadside fired in both directions. Half the purple shot came for Red Baron. Masts exploded. English marksmen vanished in sprays of timber. Sections of deck lifted and broke apart beneath burning fragments.

The rest of the Portuguese broadside went south towards Frenesia's relief force. Then a much closer explosion tore through Red Baron's stern. Below deck, Timothy waited for the Portuguese bow to lift on the swell and expose the hull behind the collision point. He braced Stormroar into the opening. He fired. The Portuguese magazine detonated. The blast tore the two ships apart and shoved Red Baron out of the line of the next broadside. Seawater immediately began pouring through the section of hull that had been ripped open in the collision. Timothy was thrown away from the gunport.

By the time he crawled upright, water was already washing ammunition boxes around his boots. Above, Edward's order came down through the decks.

"ABANDON SHIP! EVERYONE INTO THE WATER, NOW!"

Edward kept both hands on Excalibur and cut down the last Portuguese boarders who stood between his men and the rail. Fredo ran for Martinez, carried her onto his back, and jumped. Timothy and the gun crews smashed open the gunports and forced themselves through into the sea. The surviving English veterans seized floating timber, broken boats, anything that would carry weight, and followed. The battle beyond them did not end. Frenesia's squadron fought for hours at the mouth of San Sebastián Bay. Once the Portuguese ships were forced into the effective range of Monte Urgull, the coastal batteries joined the triple-barrelled guns and sank the black-sailed heavies one after another.

All four Portuguese warships remained in La Concha. So did four of the six Castilian ships that had sailed out to meet them. Frenesia's flagship and one surviving escort turned among burning wrecks and lowered boats anywhere the gunfire had finally moved away. For the survivors of Red Baron, the worst part had already begun. The sea belonged to the Ice Age. Wind and battle carried wreckage far across the bay. Men who had survived shot, steel, and exploding ships drifted for hours while rescue crews fought through waves and wreckage to reach them.

By the time the first San Sebastián boats entered the densest field of debris, most of Edward's English veterans no longer answered when called. The water had taken the last heat from them. Hundreds floated rigid against broken timber, hands still locked around the pieces that had kept their faces above La Concha long after life itself had left them.

The sea wind still screamed across La Concha, but almost everything living on the surface had fallen silent. French, Portuguese, Castilian, and English dead drifted together across the bay until uniform and allegiance meant very little from a distance. Among them, four people clung to the largest surviving section of Red Baron's shattered hull. They pressed together around the timber, sharing what little heat remained between their bodies. Edward held the wreckage with one arm and kept Excalibur level with the water in the other. The Celtic letters had faded to a weak gold, but the sword still gave off enough warmth to hold a thin circle of life around them.

The lion pendant on Edward's chest was dimming. Fredo's was doing the same. Every wave stole back some of what the Vestigia gave them. Edward pulled Timothy closer and wedged the sword hilt against the timber so his numbed hand would not lose it.

"Stay with me... Timothy. Keep your eyes open."

His own teeth were striking together. Edward hooked one arm around the young gunner's neck and pulled his head against his chest, close to the last heat coming from Martinez's pendant. Timothy shook uncontrollably. His lips had turned blue-black, and cramped fingers clung to Edward's soaked wool coat. All he could manage were shallow breaths that came out as pale vapour. Across the timber, Fredo held Martinez against him and took the waves across his own back. Her face had gone grey.

Blood from the bullet wound through her shoulder and the crushing injury along her ribs froze almost as soon as it escaped, leaving dark crusted lines beneath the cold. Her chest barely moved. Salt frost gathered along her closed lashes.

"Martinez! Wake up, you stubborn girl!"

Fredo struck her cheek with trembling fingers, gentle despite the panic in his voice.

"Don't close your eyes. We're nearly ashore. My mother's coming for us, do you hear me?"

Martinez gave him nothing. Her head rested against his shoulder. The pulse at her wrist was so faint that Fredo had to keep checking whether he still felt it. Another wave broke over them. Fredo turned his body and kept Martinez's face above the water. Edward waited for the surge to pass before calling Timothy again. The boy answered, but the words had become too soft to understand. Cold moved through Edward layer by layer until pain gave way to absence. Fredo's shouting receded first. Then the sea.

Then everything. His eyes closed.

* * *

When Edward woke again, the cold and salt of La Concha were gone. Warm wind came off another sea, carrying grass, chalk, and the clean bitter smell of the English coast. He was sitting on a white limestone cliff somewhere along southern England. The Channel stretched below in deep blue folds. Above it lay a sky untouched by the grey prison of the Ice Age, filled instead with late sunlight and a few white gulls turning through open air. Someone sat beside him with both legs hanging over the edge. Edward knew the uniform before he looked at the face. The younger admiral from ten years ago rested a gold-trimmed bicorne across his knees.

Edward raised one hand. The scars were still there. So were the calluses and dried blood. The pain was gone.

"So..." he said. "Did we win? Or am I dead?"

His younger self kept looking out over the Channel and rolled the hat slowly between his hands.

"I don't know. When you closed your eyes, they were still beside you."

Edward looked down at his dry palms. He could still remember a sword hilt slipping inside his freezing grip.

"Timothy was answering me."

The younger man nodded. For a while, neither spoke. Then Edward watched the horizon and asked, "If you could choose, what would you want Remi to become?"

One eyebrow rose. The younger Edward picked up a pebble and tossed it from the cliff. He waited until it had disappeared towards the water.

"Anything he wants. Carpenter. Gardener. Schoolmaster in some village nobody's heard of." He glanced across. "Just keep him out of a military academy. And keep him away from thieves."

Edward looked at the admiral's coat.

"You saying that? Nobody could have stopped us."

"Exactly." The younger man looked down at the old blood on his sleeve. "That's why I don't want him becoming us."

Edward pulled up a blade of grass and rolled it between his fingers. After a moment, the younger man added, "If he likes books, let him read. Don't put him on a ship just because his father was an admiral."

Edward met his own eyes at twenty and nodded. They remained together on the cliff, watching gulls move through the free sky. Eventually the younger admiral dusted grass from his coat and stood. He no longer looked towards the sea. He turned inland. Edward watched him start along the path.

"Where are you going?"

The other man stopped for half a step but did not turn. He tipped the edge of his bicorne.

"Home."

Edward stood and followed. What came next felt like a journey across an entire country and the length of a single breath. They walked without speaking. South Downs came first, white chalk beneath green slopes and gorse bright against the grass. The air still carried the sea. Hampshire opened beyond, and old Winchester appeared beside the Itchen, slate roofs crouched beneath abbeys darkened by moss and age. Farther north, they crossed the Thames valley through Berkshire, water moving quietly beneath willow branches and fern. In Oxfordshire, sandstone church towers rose between trees while cobbled roads passed inns smelling of bread and fresh malt.

The red earth of the Midlands gave way to open pasture in Leicestershire and Warwickshire. Sheep moved behind clipped hawthorn hedges. Waterwheels turned beside thatched villages where thin evening smoke climbed into a sky that had forgotten war. Then the Trent curved through Nottinghamshire. Nottingham Castle caught the last light above the sandstone. Beyond old bridges, a familiar path entered Sherwood Forest. Ancient oaks spread their branches overhead. Edward slowed. He had known the shape of those shadows before he had known the shape of a ship.

His younger self stopped before a small timber house near the forest edge. The smile on his face was suddenly light.

"We're home, Edward."

Edward froze. Through the open window, a middle-aged man in an old garrison coat sat at a wooden table sharpening a small knife. Beside him, a woman moved a shuttle through rough linen and smiled at something he had said. His father. His mother. Whole. No artillery. No fire. The younger admiral pushed open the half-closed door and stepped inside.

The woman looked up and set down her shuttle.

"Edward? Is that you? What took you so long to come home?"

His father laid the whetstone on the table.

"Come sit down, son. Supper's nearly ready. Your mother baked barley bread today."

Edward remained on the porch. A chair scraped across the floor inside. He opened his mouth to answer his mother. Nothing came. Tears fell onto clothes that, in some impossible way, still felt wet with seawater. The door creaked again. The proud admiral did not step back outside. A boy of ten did. Blond hair stuck up in every direction above an oversized linen tunic. The child looked at the scarred man on the porch, reached up, and wrapped both small hands around one rough finger.

"Come in, big brother. Everyone's waiting."

Edward let the boy lead him. His father pulled a stool closer to the table and set a warm hand on his shoulder.

"Long road? How have you been? Has life at sea been too hard on you?"

His mother wiped her hands on her apron and touched the scars across Edward's brow.

"You've gone so thin. How long has it been since somebody put a warm meal in front of you?"

Edward sat. He looked at his mother's hand on his shoulder and closed his own around it. He had carried the apology for years. The words never made it out. Edward bent forwards into her apron. His mother worked her fingers into his tangled hair. He held her around the waist and cried until breathing itself became difficult. At the far side of the room, the figure by the window wore the admiral's uniform again. His bicorne rested against his chest.

He waited.

"I'm sorry," Edward finally managed. "I'm sorry, Mother. Father..."

His grip tightened on the apron.

"It was me. My arrogance, my stupidity. I left the southern coast open and the Portuguese came through it. I handed them our home. You died because I failed."

His mother lifted his face with work-worn hands. There was no accusation in her eyes. Only the unbearable kindness of someone who had once taught him how to stand.

"I heard you, son."

She wiped his face with the corner of her apron. Then wiped it again when the tears kept coming.

"Sit here for a while."

His father pulled his chair closer and set one hand at the back of Edward's neck. After some time, he pushed a bowl towards him.

"Eat whatever you can. Your mother just finished it."

They sat around the plain table together. Fresh barley bread and turnip soup filled the room with steam. The smell drove away the sea more effectively than Excalibur ever had. Edward tore off a piece of bread and chewed slowly. At the window, his younger self spoke without mockery.

"I still think they called our name that day. When the fire reached the forest."

Edward's fingers tightened around the spoon. He had never heard that call. Yet in Marrakesh, on certain nights, he had woken with it almost inside his ear. His mother pushed the soup closer.

"So. Tell me, Edward. What is your life like now?"

He looked up and tried to smile.

"I'm all right, Mother. Drifted through a few places. Met good people. Life hasn't been easy, but... it's been all right."

She studied him, then placed another piece of bread beside the bowl. Her hand remained on the table near his. She did not ask him to prove the answer. Supper passed in a quiet Edward had almost forgotten existed. When his father scraped up the final spoonful, he stood and took two wooden practice swords from the wall.

"Food's down. Move your arms a little, Admiral. Come outside and show your old father whether all those years at sea sharpened you or ruined you."

Late sunlight lay over the packed-earth yard beneath the Sherwood oaks. Edward took the wooden sword. His father lowered into an old garrison stance and raised the point to eye level.

"Come on, son."

He stepped and cut diagonally for Edward's shoulder. The technique was clean. To a man who had survived boarding actions, sieges, and fights where a late parry meant death, it was also painfully readable. Edward slipped outside the line, turned, caught the wooden blade, and let its momentum pass. His counter stopped at his father's throat before three breaths had gone by. The older man stared at the wooden point. Then he laughed.

"Good! Very good. The Atlantic really did make a swordsman of you. This old man can't keep up."

He dropped his practice sword, brushed dust from his trouser leg, and walked towards a bench cut from a fallen oak.

"Sit with me."

Edward put both wooden swords aside and joined him. His father plucked a dead leaf from Edward's sleeve.

"Juliet and the boy well?"

"They were when I left." Edward looked at the practice swords beside the tree. "I promised I'd come back."

"Then when you do, stay with them for a day. Don't sit down at the table already planning where you have to go next."

Edward lowered his head.

"There are things I can't abandon."

"I didn't ask you to." His father flicked the leaf away. "But when you're home, do you listen to your wife? Do you know what the boy likes?"

"Remi likes questions. Everything becomes a question."

Edward smiled. The smile faded.

"I have to bring my people home too. Out there... I don't know how many are left."

His father said nothing. Edward waited for an answer and received only a hand on his shoulder.

"I planned the retreat," Edward continued. "Then the fog cleared. Men died in front of me anyway."

"When you wake, listen to the ones who survived. Find out where you were wrong."

"And if I'm wrong again?"

The hand tightened.

"I can't promise that for you."

Edward looked into the forest. He allowed the next things he wanted to say to settle before he touched his father's hand. Oak leaves turned in the breeze and crossed the yard. After a long silence, Edward rolled another blade of grass between his fingers.

"Father... I've wondered about Isabella for years. My distant little cousin."

The memory came with it: a child waiting under the eaves for him to return from lessons.

"She was with our family for only a few years. Then people from Aragon appeared and took her back to Castile. Now I see her on a throne, and I can't stop wondering who she really was."

His father picked up a dry twig and drew meaningless lines through the soil. He thought for a long time.

"Edward... Isabella was never your cousin. There isn't a drop of our family's blood in her."

Edward stared at him. The twig stopped moving.

"About twenty years ago, your mother and I were travelling outside Nottingham. We found the girl after she'd been pushed into a filthy brothel near the edge of town. Six, perhaps seven years old."

His father's mouth tightened.

"She was skin and bone. Her face had gone empty. Your mother knew too much about what a place like that could do to a child. So we gathered every coin we could spare and bought the girl's freedom."

He shook his head.

"When she first came through our door, she disappeared into silence. No crying. No laughter. She hid in shadows as though she could erase the place she'd come from."

Then a small smile touched the old soldier's face.

"Until she met you."

Edward said nothing.

"With you, she began speaking. Then following you. Sherwood became her world. She learned to climb because you climbed. She ran after you until she remembered how to be a child."

His father threw the twig aside.

"Then royal English officials arrived with an emergency order. They took her into custody and handed her to an Aragonese delegation that had just landed from the continent."

He looked across the yard.

"When they returned her to her aunt, I asked where her parents were. I wanted to know how a child had been allowed to disappear that far."

Edward leaned forwards.

"What did her aunt say?"

The answer came slowly.

"One sentence. Cold as iron."

His father looked at him.

"'They fell for the unification of the Castilian nobility.'"

The breeze moved through the oaks.

"Then they put Isabella on a ship south. We never heard anything about her again."

Edward waited. His father looked towards the road.

"The day they came for her, she kept staring at you. I called for her to get into the carriage and she wouldn't move."

Edward remembered a small hand holding his sleeve. He tried to remember what Isabella had said that day. Only oak leaves answered.

"You should ask her yourself," his father said.

Edward sat a little longer, then stood without releasing the older man's hand. He filled his lungs with Sherwood air. His father rose beside him. Edward turned and gripped that rough hand with both of his.

"Thank you, Father. For everything."

Then he went back to the house. Sunlight filled the room. His mother had cleared the table and waited with the same gentle smile. Near the window, the Edward of ten years ago stood again in full Royal Navy dress, bicorne set properly on his head. The apparition looked at him.

"Well? Still want to stay?"

Edward looked at the chair his mother had drawn out. He wanted to sit there forever.

"Yes," he said. "But I have to go back."

He crossed the room and embraced his mother, burying his face against her shoulder.

"I miss you both."

She placed one warm hand against his cheek.

"Keep walking, my son. Your father, your mother, Sherwood... all of us belong to what has already been."

His father stood beside her and held out the bicorne.

"Juliet and Remi are waiting. Go home to them."

The younger admiral put a hand on Edward's shoulder for the last time, then stepped back towards the table with the two people who were waiting for him. Edward bowed his head. He embraced his parents and the man he had once been. Then he turned and crossed the wooden threshold.

* * *

His journey continued southeast. The low country of the Fens opened beneath a pale autumn mist, old canals lying flat as glass between reeds and fern. Cambridge rose beside the River Cam, stone bridges curving beneath old red-brick colleges. Through the quiet country of Essex, Edward kept walking towards London. The capital he remembered from evacuation and fear had become whole again inside the dream. He crossed the Thames over a stone bridge and made his way to Westminster. Beneath the old clock tower, bronze bells sounded over the city. Edward stopped at a moss-covered bench beneath an oak near the river. Another memory found him there.

Juliet, years younger, wrapped in a rough wool scarf while snow fell lightly around them. Her cheeks were pink from cold. She had sat tucked against him while they shared hot toasted bread and whispered about a future so ordinary that neither of them had understood how precious it was. Relief softened Edward's face. He nodded once to the memory and continued south. Kent opened in orchards and hop fields around old Canterbury. Red-brick villages passed beneath his feet. The smell of the sea grew stronger with every mile.

Then the white cliffs of Dover rose before him. They caught the evening light high above the Channel, brilliant against water turned gold by the setting sun. Edward stood at the edge and looked back across England. Childhood. Sherwood. His parents. The sea. Triumphs he no longer believed. Failures he still carried.

He stepped back half a pace, straightened, placed one hand over his heart, and bowed deeply. A final courtly salute to the country that had made him and buried him. Then Edward turned towards the cliff. The wind pulled at his coat. When he looked down, his hands were cold again.

"Juliet. Remi... I'm coming home."

Edward closed his eyes and stepped into the air. Wind tore past his ears. Then water took him. The sea folded around his body and carried him down into the deep. Golden sunlight receded above, smaller and smaller, until it vanished. Edward let go.

His mind sank into a long, dreamless dark.

The crack of firewood woke Edward. He opened his eyes to the scent of herbs rising from the bandages around his arm. The black depth of the sea was gone, along with the killing cold of La Concha. Above him stretched a sandstone ceiling crossed by dark oak beams. He lay in a proper bed beneath thick fur blankets, with heat rolling from a stone stove burning in the corner. Edward tried to move his arm. A small weight beside the mattress stopped him. He turned his head.

Isabella had fallen asleep sitting against the bed, her forehead resting near the edge of the mattress. The Castilian queen wore only a soft grey linen dress, without court ornaments or armour. Firelight showed the exhaustion in her face and the faint shadows beneath her eyes. One hand still rested over the corner of his blanket. Her fingers tightened slightly in sleep, as though even there she had been holding on to something. The familiar scent of cherry blossom lingered in her hair and softened the harsher smells of antiseptic herbs and dried salt.

Edward remembered a child's hand gripping his sleeve beneath the Sherwood oaks. He looked at Isabella and had no idea how he would ask her about what his father had told him in the dream. His expression softened. Edward reached from beneath the blanket and placed one rough hand on her hair, stroking it the way he once had when a little girl followed him everywhere beneath the ancient trees of home. The touch woke her at once. Isabella's eyes opened, unfocused at first. Then she saw him looking back.

"Edward... you're awake!"

She threw both arms around his neck. Edward barely had time to inhale before pain tore through his bruised chest and cracked muscles.

"Ah... Bella. Bella, that hurts."

Isabella released him at once.

"I'm sorry. I forgot." Her eyes dropped to his chest. "Where does it hurt?"

Edward had to wait for the spasm to ease before he could point. She helped him sit higher against the headboard, arranged another pillow behind his back, and reached for warm water. She held the ceramic cup while he drank in small mouthfuls. Then Isabella brought over the silver scissors and tray of clean dressings beside the bed and began removing the old bandages from his chest and arm.

"The cuts have been treated," she said, spreading salve around the bruised skin. Edward flinched, and her hand stopped immediately. "The physicians are still worried about the internal shock."

"From the pendant?"

Isabella nodded and opened a fresh roll of bandage.

"It was made for the bloodline of the Royal Guard. You used it to release a Legendary-grade Vestigium. Your body was never meant to carry that strain."

Edward looked towards the lion pendant resting beside the bed. Isabella wound the fresh bandage around his arm, but the end slipped from her fingers. She stared at it for a second, then unwound the poor turn and began again.

"And then you spent hours in that water." Her voice dropped. "When they pulled you aboard, I called your name and you didn't answer."

The bandage stopped in her hands.

"I was so afraid."

Her control broke. Isabella let the roll fall and bent over him, forehead pressed against his chest as her hands clenched the linen of his shirt.

"When I heard the French flagship had exploded, and then that the Portuguese had closed around you..." She struggled for air between the words. "I thought I had lost you. I thought I had sent you there myself and killed you with the order."

Edward put one hand behind her neck, careful not to draw her weight across the deepest bruise. He waited. Isabella kept hold of his shirt until she could breathe again.

"Thank you, Bella," Edward said quietly. "For worrying about me. For all of it."

She looked up at him through tears. His hand remained in her hair.

"I still remember the little girl who followed me through Sherwood." A tired smile touched his mouth. "I haven't forgotten you, Bella."

Isabella stopped wiping her face. After a moment, she bent down and retrieved the fallen bandage.

"I know."

She found the loose end and rolled it back into place.

"And I know where Juliet stands in your heart."

Edward opened his mouth. Isabella shook her head before he could begin. She wrapped the final turn around his arm and tied it with just enough pressure to hold without hurting him.

"At least you've stopped looking at me as though the moment I enter a room you ought to hide all the knives." Her smile was still wet with tears. "This is an improvement."

A knock came at the door.

"Your Majesty, I've brought more medicine."

Timothy.

"Come in."

He opened the door, saw Edward sitting upright, and nearly dropped the tray.

"Admiral!"

Timothy put the medicine down and crossed the room in two strides. Then he hugged him. Edward hissed through his teeth and struck the young man twice on the back.

"Let go. Are you trying to finish what the French started?"

Timothy released him so quickly he almost stepped on the blanket. Isabella caught Edward by the shoulder before he slipped against the headboard.

"He has only just woken. Be gentle."

"I'm sorry." Timothy stooped to retrieve the corner of the blanket he had dragged loose. "I thought you were still unconscious."

Isabella checked Edward's bandage one last time and rose.

"Stay with Sir Edward. If the pain grows worse, call the physician. And do not let him decide he can walk somewhere by himself."

She turned to Edward.

"I have a council meeting. Reinforcements are still moving, and the Pyrenean front has not settled." Her eyes held his for a moment. "Rest, Sir Edward. We will speak later."

Edward nodded. Timothy bowed until the sound of the Queen's steps had disappeared down the stone corridor. The room grew quiet again. Edward shifted himself higher and looked the young gunner over from head to toe.

"How are you, lad? Any pieces of you still frozen after that swim?"

"I'm all right. Fingers are still a little numb."

Timothy opened one hand to show him. Then, with visible hesitation, he placed Stormroar across the blanket. Edward's expression changed immediately.

"What happened? Who didn't make it?"

"No, sir. That's not why I've come." Timothy pushed the weapon closer. "It's Stormroar. I can't get her working again. Saltwater got into the loading mechanism. I've cleaned it, but the action still jams."

Edward stared at him for two seconds. Then he laughed. The movement hurt enough to make him wince, but he kept laughing anyway.

"Let the armourers in Toledo look at it. The poor thing has done enough." He pushed Stormroar back towards the medicine tray. "So have you. Don't dismantle it with bandaged fingers."

Timothy's shoulders loosened. Only then did Edward's voice become serious.

"Fredo and Martinez?"

"Both alive, sir." Timothy pulled the chair closer. "Fredo got all of us onto Lady Frenesia's ship."

Edward waited.

"He used the last of his strength to hook a steel chain onto the rescue vessel. Pulled us in himself." Timothy flexed his still-numb fingers. "He recovered frighteningly fast. As soon as he regained consciousness, he took command of First Legion, Tercio del Rayo. Her Majesty joined him with two hundred Conquistadores. Together they broke the French force on the eastern bank."

Edward let out a slow breath.

"And Martinez?"

"Recovering quickly too. I saw her at the training yard this morning trying to hold a sword." Timothy looked almost offended on behalf of her physicians. "Her attendant was standing close enough to tackle her."

"Good." Edward settled back against the pillow. "Good."

Relief lasted only a moment. The next question was already waiting.

"And our Englishmen, Timothy?"

The young man's expression changed.

"More than three hundred survived."

Edward said nothing. Timothy looked towards the door.

"The ones who can stand are waiting in the yard. Would you like to see them?"

Edward pushed the blankets aside. Timothy immediately stood.

"Sir, the Queen specifically said you were not to walk anywhere by yourself."

"Then you'll be useful."

Edward pointed towards the dark blue Castilian admiral's uniform hanging from the wooden stand.

"Help me with that."

Pain moved through his joints with every motion. The magical recoil inside his chest had not faded, and bruises pulled whenever he raised his arms. Even so, Edward fastened the polished brass buttons himself, one after another. Timothy settled the heavy cloak across his shoulders. Edward took his first step and nearly lost it. The young gunner caught him. With one hand braced on Timothy's shoulder, Edward made his way through the stone corridors and out beyond the gates of Monte Urgull. Cold sea wind caught the hem of his coat. They entered the broad packed-earth yard of the central barracks.

Edward stopped. Under the grey sky stood the men who had returned. English veterans filled the yard in thinning ranks, their uniforms worn, burned, and patched. Some leaned on crutches. Others held bandaged arms across their chests or stood with dressings visible beneath torn coats. More than three hundred. Eight hundred had sailed with him. The moment Edward appeared on the stone steps, hundreds of hands rose to their chests in the old salute of the Royal Navy.

Edward removed his hand from Timothy's shoulder. He straightened. Pain pulled across his ribs when he raised his arm, but he held the salute anyway. His eyes moved slowly along the broken ranks before him.

These were the survivors.

Wind from La Concha climbed the slope of Monte Urgull, passing through cracks in the stone with salt on it and the last faint traces of powder smoke. Timothy sat alone on a ledge above the hillside, legs hanging over open air. San Sebastián lay behind him. Hammers on roof timbers, cart wheels, and voices from the rebuilding city reached the height only as fragments before the wind broke them apart. Ahead, the mouth of the bay opened towards the Atlantic, where several broken masts still protruded from the water like blackened ribs.

Timothy raised both hands. Bandages covered several fingers. Salt and cold had split the skin around his knuckles, and powder still lived beneath his nails despite repeated scrubbing in warm water. He turned the right palm towards himself. That hand had loaded Stormroar until the metal burned him. It had held the weapon against a gunport and waited through splintering timber until the enemy hull rose on the swell. Then it had pulled the trigger. His left hand had done no better. It had seized the restraining line of a thirty-two-pounder, dragged with a dozen other men, and helped drive the whole carriage towards starboard until Red Baron heeled far enough for Fredo's chain to reach the yard.

Timothy studied both hands for another moment. Then he laughed. At first the sound was so small that the wind almost carried it away. His shoulders began to shake, and the laugh grew louder, awkward and broken. Tears reached his face before he noticed them.

"We won."

No one answered. Timothy lifted his face to the sea and let the cold wind strike the wetness on his cheeks.

"We actually bloody won."

He wiped his face on his sleeve. When he looked at his hands again, he remembered them without the calluses. Ten years old.

Black with coal and powder, both arms wrapped around a bag of gunpowder nearly half his size. Back then, those hands had never learned how long gun oil could cling to skin. They had never been frozen around wreckage in open water. Timothy had known only that he wanted to be aboard a warship, beside the guns, among the men he watched from the harbour with hunger in his eyes.

He remembered the heat of that first gun deck. The ship rolled beneath him. Boots struck overhead. Blocks and tackles creaked while Timothy crawled out from behind the old sailcloth where he had hidden since before dawn. The plan had seemed flawless. Wait until the ship had left harbour. Then reveal himself. Surely nobody would turn a warship around just to throw one boy back ashore. The plan of a ten-year-old genius survived less than half an hour. A gloved hand caught Timothy by the collar the moment he set the powder bag beside the first cannon.

He saw the black boots first. Then the hem of a Royal Navy dress coat. Only then did he look high enough to recognise the man holding him. Edward Spencer looked at Timothy. Then at the powder.

"What is this? How old are you?"

Timothy had prepared the answer.

"Fourteen, Admiral."

Edward looked at his thin arms. Then down at the oversized old boots slipping around his heels.

"I'll give you one final chance not to insult my intelligence."

Timothy swallowed.

"Ten."

A nearby gunner snorted. Edward turned his head. The man immediately bent over the gunlock with the intense concentration of someone who had heard nothing at all. Timothy argued anyway. He knew how to carry powder. He knew how to prime a piece. He knew how many men served a cannon. He had watched gun crews from the harbour hundreds of times.

Edward listened without interruption. Then he dragged Timothy the length of the gun deck by the same collar while the boy twisted hard enough to nearly lose one shoe.

"Admiral, I can do it! I'm not afraid!"

"I know."

"I can fight!"

"Perhaps."

Timothy twisted around in Edward's grip, furious and humiliated.

"Then why are you sending me ashore?"

Edward stopped. He released the collar and lowered himself onto one knee until their eyes were level. Leather, gunpowder, and black tea clung to the hot air of the gun deck.

"Because a boy who does not know fear is the most dangerous thing I can put beside a powder magazine."

Timothy hated that sentence for years. Edward took a blunt pencil and scrap of paper from his coat. He wrote several sums and a small table, then pushed it into Timothy's hands.

"If you truly want to come back, learn to read a powder table. Learn range. Learn gun commands. Learn the difference between a good shot and a stupid one." His eyes stayed on the boy. "When you're old enough to understand what can kill you and why, come find me."

"When will I be old enough?"

Edward stood and straightened his cuff.

"When you no longer need to ask me."

Two sailors took Timothy ashore in a small boat before the warship left the harbour. He stood on the pier and cursed Edward Spencer until the ship had become a pale shape on the horizon. Years later, Timothy went aboard again. This time nobody seized him by the collar. He started at the lowest station in a gun crew, passing powder, swabbing barrels, hauling line, and performing every dull task the boy he had once been considered beneath the grandeur of war. The men around him spoke of heroism far less often than children on the docks did.

They taught him how to keep his thumb from being crushed when a carriage recoiled and never to stand behind a gun wheel when the breeching rope had begun to fray. One old gunner once struck him on the head with a broom handle for putting powder too close to a lamp, then secretly gave him half a piece of bread that evening after learning Timothy had missed supper. The rope master made him tie the same knot until two fingertips bled.

The next morning he made Timothy tie it again. For years Timothy believed those men were the most unpleasant creatures in England. Only much later did he understand they had raised him on the deck. One taught him elevation tables. Another taught him to listen to the timber and hear where a hull was carrying strain. One insisted that before a good gunner pulled a lanyard, he should already know where the shot would go if the ship rolled another half degree. Edward appeared on the gun deck from time to time. Some days he merely passed through, ran one finger across a dirty carriage, and looked at the watch officer until the man understood his future had become unpleasant. One day he stopped in front of Timothy.

"How old are you now?"

Timothy kept cleaning the lock.

"Old enough not to ask you."

Edward stared for several seconds. Then he laughed and continued walking. It was the first time Timothy thought he had ever beaten the admiral in an exchange. The years after that passed faster than he expected. Night watches became campaigns. Campaigns became other campaigns. Ships returned to harbour with fewer men than they had carried away. Some died to shot. Some disappeared overboard in darkness and left only a cap caught in the rigging by morning. One man survived battle, lost a leg, and spent the rest of his life sitting on the quay to wave the others out to sea.

Timothy kept sailing. The English Navy of his memory had once seemed permanent. Flags could tear. Ships could burn. Admirals could be replaced. Yet the next morning someone would still ring the watch bell, and the gun crews would still swab their barrels. Then England ceased to exist. There were memories Timothy never learned where to put.

Crowds at the docks fighting for places in boats. Houses burning behind them. Soldiers who had argued the previous evening over half a bottle of rum standing shoulder to shoulder the next morning to hold a pier while civilians escaped. The red-cross flags vanished from the horizon more quickly than anyone had believed possible. Timothy could not remember the exact day he last called a vessel an English ship. He remembered only waking one morning and realising that the surviving men around him had begun serving beneath different colours.

He continued. Not because England had been forgotten. If Timothy had stopped, he did not know what he could have done except remember. Castilian service taught him another form of war.
