He learned new commands, learned to swear in another language, and learned to drink a local liquor sailors praised with religious conviction despite Timothy's belief that it tasted like barrel cleaner. The guns were still guns. Powder still burned the same way. A man struck by shot still fell. Then the defeats began to accumulate.

On some nights Timothy walked an entire gun deck before realising he was inspecting the escape route for the second time. He returned to his hammock and slept with his boots on until the next watch. Before inspecting the guns, he checked the exits. Before sailing, he counted the boats. Whenever rigging shrieked in darkness or timber cracked beneath him, his body reacted before his mind understood the sound. Vila do Porto was merely the place where all of that finally received a name. He remembered cold water. An ocean so wide he could not tell where land was. Two days clinging to wreckage beside men who had been fighting with him only hours earlier.

The man on Timothy's left died first. Timothy did not realise it at once. The dead sailor still held the timber, head resting on one arm as if asleep. Then a wave knocked their bodies together and Timothy saw eyes that were open but looking at nothing. The dead man's fingers had frozen around the wood. Timothy broke them away one by one. He heard the joints snap in the open sea. That sound remained with him longer than cannon fire. When the rescue party finally found him, Timothy remembered nothing of being pulled aboard. His next memory was the ceiling of a medical berth, the smell of disinfectant, and Elizabeth seated outside the door with her arms folded, wearing the irritated expression of someone who considered Timothy's near death a personal inconvenience.

She was not his sister by blood. She had never needed to be. Timothy woke feverish one night, heard a change-of-watch bell in the corridor, threw off his blanket, and tried to crawl out of bed because he believed the ship was under attack. Elizabeth caught him. Timothy cursed her. She cursed him back and pushed him into the mattress with one hand. The following days were much the same. Elizabeth brought food, changed dressings, and sat outside the door when he could not sleep. She never asked whether he was afraid.

Each time Timothy woke thinking he had heard a hull splitting open, Elizabeth was still there. Some nights she fell asleep in the chair with a cold bowl balanced on her knees. He would lie awake watching for a while, then pull his blanket higher. Timothy had never thanked her. The wind brought him back to San Sebastián. He wiped his face and watched a gull skim the bay before climbing on an updraft. Timothy followed it until it became a white point beyond the mouth of La Concha.

Then he looked at his right hand again. Lisbon came back. Thousands of men leaving ships in orderly ranks. José in front of his troops. Fredo and Martinez between lines of raised guns. Edward standing among people arguing over who possessed the right to decide who would die and for what. Timothy had said cruel things that day. Part of him still believed them. Another part knew Elizabeth had been right to tear into him.

What Timothy remembered most clearly was Edward's answer. He would ask no one to board a ship merely because he had won battles ten years earlier. If men sailed with him, he would show them enough of the plan to decide for themselves whether they wanted to place their lives inside it. Timothy boarded. Eight hundred English veterans and one hundred Conquistadores sailed aboard Red Baron. The night before La Concha they drank tea, insulted one another, laughed at death, and talked about stupid things that had nothing to do with war.

The next morning, fog covered the bay. Timothy stood near the helm and heard Edward give the order. For the first time in years, he did not look for the nearest escape route. He looked at the target. The first shot destroyed the French flagship's stern. Then everything escaped the plan. Martinez fell. The fog cleared early. The Portuguese appeared.

Le Triomphant exploded while Edward remained aboard, and Fredo crossed over to bring him and Martinez back. Timothy watched the end of Fredo's chain miss the yard. The distance grew. Fifty-five metres was not enough. Before fear could tell him that everything was about to end the way it always ended, Timothy looked down at the cannon around him. He ordered them moved to one side. Nobody asked why. Hundreds of men threw themselves onto restraining lines, levers, and iron carriages weighing thousands of pounds. Red Baron heeled.

Three metres. Only three. Three metres were enough. Timothy remembered the hook striking the yard and his own voice tearing itself raw as Fredo, Edward, and Martinez swung through open air and crashed onto the deck. Then came Stormroar. The weapon became so hot that the skin on Timothy's fingers blistered. Edward called firing angles through the speaking tube. Timothy loaded, aimed, fired, opened the action, and loaded again. One French ship exploded.

Then another. Fire rose behind Red Baron's stern. When the Portuguese ram struck the steering deck, Timothy hit the floor of the gun deck. He was moving before the last timber finished breaking. Stormroar in his arms, he dropped to a lower compartment and searched for an angle into the ship pinning Red Baron. He was still afraid. His legs shook. His throat was so dry that swallowing hurt. Vila do Porto spoke inside his head, telling him he would soon be back in the water, breaking frozen fingers from the last piece of wreckage while a friend died beside him.

Timothy fired anyway. The Portuguese magazine exploded. The blast separated the ships and pushed Red Baron out of the killing broadside. Then Red Baron sank too. Timothy went into the sea again. He had thought God's sense of humour was appalling. This time, when hands pulled him from the water, the first person he saw was breathing. So was the second. Edward lived.

Fredo lived. Martinez lived. Timothy lived. San Sebastián was still standing behind them. His head dropped. The laugh returned through his tears.

"We won."

This time he did not wipe his face. Under La Concha were men no boat had brought back. Some had been found still clinging to timber. Some had been damaged so badly there was no name left to attach to the body. Timothy had known some since he was shorter than a cannon barrel. Others he had met only in Lisbon. There were Castilian sailors he had hated enough to curse their entire navy a few days earlier. Now all of them occupied the same water. Timothy reached into his coat for a handkerchief. His fingers found folded paper instead.

He pulled it out and opened it across his knee, holding both corners against the wind. Edward's handwriting filled the scrap. No firing order. No angle. No tactical diagram. An address in Marrakesh. Beneath it, Edward had written two words. Beaumont family. Timothy stared at them.

He had received the paper before leaving Lisbon, pushed it into his pocket, and told himself he would study it after the battle. Now he read the address one line at a time. Somewhere in Marrakesh was a street he could walk down. A door where he could ask for the name Beaumont. He pressed the paper into his palm and folded over his knees. Laughter and a sob came out together.

"Damn you."

He laughed harder.

"You are an absolute bastard, Admiral."

The sea offered no opinion. Timothy sat there for a long time, holding the paper between both hands as though it were the most valuable thing he had ever owned. At last he drew another sheet and a short pencil from his inner pocket. He flattened the page against his knee. Dear Dame Elizabeth, The pencil stopped. Timothy frowned. He scratched the words out. Elizabeth,

That looked wrong too. He tried again. Sister Elizabeth, The pencil moved. I'm alive. Timothy read the sentence and nearly crossed it out for sounding stupid. He left it. We won. This is the first time in a very long while I can write that without feeling as though I am lying to myself. I don't know whether the news from San Sebastián has reached you yet, but I wanted to say it before someone turns everything into a ten-page report and sends it to Lisbon.

I boarded the ship. I was afraid, and this time I can admit that I was very afraid. Timothy paused until the pencil left a black dot on the paper. He remembered Elizabeth on the quay and continued. You once told me not to turn my fear into a sentence passed on everyone else. At the time I thought you were half wrong. I still do. Unfortunately, you were also half right.

If you are still reading, you are probably already swearing because I cannot write a thank-you letter without arguing. You may swear at me later. The Castilian Navy has lost too much. I still believe that. But at La Concha, I watched men I once called wooden targets sail out of San Sebastián under Portuguese fire to pull us from the sea. I saw Englishmen and Castilians move the same gun. I saw Conquistadores die to hold a road open for the Admiral. I saw men who had been pointing weapons at one another only days before jump into the same water to save one another.

You are going to enjoy knowing that I had to write those sentences myself. Timothy laughed and bent over the page again. The Admiral kept his word. The plan did not happen the way he expected. At one point everything became such a magnificent disaster that I decided if I lived, my first task would be forcing him to write the report explaining it. But we knew what we were doing. When the plan broke, he found the next thing that had to be done.

So did I. Timothy looked at his right hand. Then he wrote: I sank enemy ships, sister. Not the sort where a hundred guns fire and somebody later says ours may have struck something. I pulled the trigger. I saw the magazine. I saw the hull come apart.

I won a battle. The final word slanted down. Timothy pressed his wrist briefly against his eyes before continuing. I wish the old crew had been here to see it. A great many did not come back. I do not yet know how to write about them, so I will not pretend I can do it today. I only want you to know that I am alive. And I did not die stupidly. Timothy laughed aloud because he could almost hear Elizabeth's answer inside his skull.

He added another line. I also failed to die according to plan, so I suppose I kept half my promise. For a while he could not write because laughter and tears blurred the page. When it cleared, he lowered the pencil again. Thank you. For every night you sat outside the medical berth while I pretended to sleep. For never treating me like a broken soldier because I was afraid. And for shouting at me whenever I said something idiotic.

I cannot remember when I started calling you my sister. I am writing it here because you already understand, and I do not know how to say it more beautifully. Timothy put one hand on the Marrakesh address beside his knee. Then he wrote the last part. The Admiral found my family. They are in Marrakesh. I have their address in my hand. When the work here is finished, if nobody invents another stupid war to drag me elsewhere, I am going there. Perhaps I still have somewhere to go home to. The final words came more easily than the rest.

Do not worry anymore. I will come home. Timothy Beaumont. He read the letter from beginning to end. There were spelling mistakes, one line scratched out, and two places where water had blurred the graphite. Timothy corrected nothing. He folded the letter into quarters and returned it to the inside of his coat. The Marrakesh address received more care. He folded it separately, placed it in the small pocket nearest his chest, and fastened the button.

Timothy braced both palms against his knees and stood. His legs had gone numb. He staggered once, stamped his heels against the stone, brushed dust from his trousers, and pulled his creased uniform straight. The wind over the bay had strengthened. Timothy walked to the edge of the ledge where almost all of La Concha lay visible below him. The sea had swallowed most signs of battle. A few pieces of timber remained. Part of a mast. Oil shifting over the waves.

Timothy knew how much more lay beneath. Red Baron was down there somewhere with her guns, hammocks, tin mugs, blunt knives for cutting salted meat, and the men who had once stood beside him. Only days earlier, all those things had still been a ship. Timothy remembered the ten-year-old boy dragged away by his collar. The old gunner with the broom handle. The dead man at Vila do Porto whose frozen fingers broke around the timber. He remembered the faces in Lisbon that stepped out of formation when Edward called. The laughter aboard Red Baron on the night before battle. The men who entered the sea and did not wake when rescuers found them.

Timothy stood straight. He brought his heels together and lifted his chin towards the mouth of the bay. His right hand closed into a fist. He extended it towards La Concha. Wind pulled his coat behind him. His arm hurt badly enough that he had to lock his shoulder to keep the fist from dropping. He held it there until the wind changed and brought the smell of smoke from the city back across the sea. Then Timothy drew the fist to the centre of his chest. He bowed deeply towards the water.

"Thank you."

title_en: Chapter 37 - The Woman in the Mirror
text_en:
Only the crackle of oak in the stone hearth disturbed the sealed room inside Monte Urgull. Stacks of red-wax documents covered Isabella's dark wooden desk. Military maps lay beneath provincial reports, petitions, supply requests, and long lists of names. One month had passed since La Concha. In the streets of northern Castilian, people had already begun turning the victory into song. On Isabella's desk, victory had become paper. Fleet losses. Ships requiring refit. Treatment for the wounded.

Pensions for families of the dead. Pyrenean food stores drained by emergency transfers. Requests for heating coal from garrisons. Appeals from North Africa. Noble families composing elaborate arguments over which estates ought to bear the greater share of the new taxes. Near the centre of it all rested a thinner file marked with the red cross of the English exiles. Isabella stopped her pen above the page. The list was shorter than the strength of a single legion, yet every name made the quill feel heavier.

Men who had followed Edward into La Concha had spent years living quietly in refugee districts. More than half were now reduced to a line recording a name, a former home, and the pension due to whoever remained behind. Isabella signed the final sheet. She pressed the royal seal into the approval for compensation, closed the file, and looked at the red cross for several seconds before placing it among the completed work.

"It must nearly be time." She checked the lock on the door, changed her linen blouse for silk, and took the military coat from its stand. Even while fastening the first button, Isabella kept looking at the English file.

"Edward... how do you make hundreds of people choose to follow you that far?" Silver buttons engraved with lion and castle closed one after another. The stiff collar rose around her throat. She tightened the belt, smoothed every fold, and restored the precision the world expected from her. No maid or attendant was allowed into these private moments. The boots beside the stand still carried mud from a recent barracks inspection. Isabella wiped the leather clean herself and set them straight. In a short while, generals would be waiting for answers to the petitions on her desk. She crossed to the dressing table, drew an ivory comb through her hair, and used a little powder to hide the evidence of sleepless nights. Dark red wax passed over her lips. The Queen appeared in the mirror. Then Isabella remembered the Lisbon report. She was still angry that Edward had gone to sea with one ship. Yet the objections recorded in Lisbon had not been invented after the fact. The arguments over manpower, operational authority, and the danger of stripping other defensive lines were all there, signed by officers who would have been blamed if those lines had broken. Isabella turned the report face down. La Concha had been won. She still had to answer why those men had been forced into such a battle. Anger rose again.

The silver handle of the cosmetic brush broke in Isabella's hand. A sharp edge bit into her palm. Blood welled at once and ran across her wrist before falling onto the table. Isabella watched it. Then she lifted her eyes towards the polished bronze mirror. The room seemed to freeze. Her right eye remained clear amber. The left had turned red. Blood-red light gleamed from it inside the dim room.

The reflection moved. Isabella's real face remained still, but the woman in the mirror smiled. The reflection's left eye deepened to crimson. A voice entered Isabella's mind, clear and gentle, yet cold as deep water.

"Isabella. How careless of you." The reflection looked down at the bleeding hand with something almost like tenderness. "Why should vermin hiding in the corners of the peninsula be permitted to injure such precious skin through so ordinary an anger? Those hands should not be stained over matters beneath their worth."

Isabella kept the broken silver handle clenched in her fist. A veil of red mist slipped from the bronze and wound itself around her wrist. Coolness spread through the skin. The cut closed. Flesh joined cleanly until the palm showed no sign that blood had ever crossed it.

"I am the shadow born only to serve you." The woman inside the mirror raised a hand to the polished bronze. Red eyes held absolute devotion. "If harm were to reach Your Majesty, if that skin should suffer another wound, what purpose would this being possess in such a frozen world? Please do not injure yourself for anyone beneath heaven."

Isabella looked at her healed palm. Then at the English file on the desk. "Testarossa."

The name altered the reflection's smile.

"If you can mend flesh so easily, why could you not heal the men who died in the bay?"

The smile remained. "Because they are not you. And I am not omnipotent."

Isabella looked back at the pension file. Testarossa waited in the mirror, her hand resting where Isabella's had been.

"The lives of subjects, soldiers, or anyone else in this world can be weighed according to what they contribute. Your Majesty is different. Nothing alive has enough weight to share a scale with you."

Isabella withdrew her hand. Her voice grew quieter. "And if a city had to be exchanged for my life?"

"I would burn the city."

"A legion?"

"Bury the legion."

"Even the entire Castilian realm?"

For the first time, Testarossa stopped smiling. She studied Isabella before answering. "If the Castilian realm could survive only through your death, what purpose would its survival serve?" The red eyes softened around another sweet smile. "The kingdom exists for you. You do not exist for the kingdom."

Isabella stared into her own face. Her court smile had disappeared. "You are wrong."

Testarossa tilted her head. "Then please enlighten me, Your Majesty."

"I sit on the throne because Castilian needs someone to sit there. If one day my life must be traded to keep the country alive, I will be the first person to give that order."

Displeasure passed through Testarossa's crimson eyes. The mist around the mirror trembled. "I will not allow it."

"You possess no right to allow or forbid it."

Isabella did not raise her voice. She did not need to. Two women wearing the same face looked at one another through polished bronze. After a long moment, Testarossa lowered her head. When she looked up again, the smile had returned. "Then I will devote everything I possess to ensuring that day never arrives."

Isabella placed one fingertip against the mirror. "Do you know why I still keep you with me?"

"Because I understand you." Testarossa touched the same point from the other side. "Or because you still fear my strength?"

"Because you say things I have thought myself." Isabella removed her hand. "Things I am not permitted to do."

Testarossa's smile slowly widened. "Then do I not understand you better than anyone else alive?"

Isabella did not answer. She looked at the broken brush handle and covered the blood on the table with a cloth. "Then speak." She leaned against the dressing table. "Lisbon. The Council. Where would you begin?"

Testarossa looked past her towards the English file. Her smile widened further. "Why pluck thorns one at a time when a lighthouse has just ignited across the whole northern sea?"

Isabella frowned. "Edward?"

A light laugh came from the mirror. "My sovereign. Not only him." Testarossa moved closer and placed her spectral hand against the bronze as though she wished to touch Isabella's cheek. "The North is offering you a beautiful board. The Pathmaker has returned from death. English veterans hunger to rebuild a symbol of home. Loyal soldiers need a victory they can believe in. And there are those who kneel before your throne while waiting for it to become weak." She began pacing within the reflected room. "Do not arrest them yet. Let them believe they still have choices." Testarossa stopped at the edge of the mirror. "You will learn who follows willingly and who begins sabotaging the moment Edward's name grows too large."

Isabella turned fully towards her. "You want Edward used as bait?"

"I want you to use everything already on the board." There was no hesitation. "Edward. His reputation. The English exiles. The great houses. Even the hatred your enemies bear for you. Love, loyalty, fear, betrayal. All of them are strings. Pull at the proper moment and pieces move."

Isabella's expression chilled. "Edward accepted a military order as an admiral." She rested one hand against the desk. "Juliet and Remi are not soldiers in my service."

Testarossa's smile faltered. "You distinguish between two things that are both weaknesses in the same man?"

"Yes." Isabella did not allow her to continue. "I can order Edward into battle. I can use the victory to rally an army. But do not suggest that I use his wife or his child to force him again."

Testarossa watched her for a long time. "Because you love him?"

Isabella did not look away. "Because military authority has a boundary. Cross it, and I no longer have an admiral who chooses to stand beside me." Her fingers pressed against the wood. "I have a prisoner."

The woman in the mirror slowly bowed her head, even though disagreement remained plain in her face. "I will remember."

Isabella returned to the dressing table and placed the broken brush handle into a silver tray. "Continue."

Testarossa smiled again. "Blind loyalty and false obedience are both tools if placed correctly. Let war force each person to choose where they stand." Her fingertip touched the bronze. "Do not give them a purge that allows them to become victims. Give them enough freedom to cross the line they still pretend to honour." The red eye gleamed. "Once the thorns reveal themselves in the light, you will not need to dirty your hands searching for them."

Isabella drew the Lisbon report closer. "I will watch what they do. Opposition to an order is not treason. Anyone who crosses that boundary must leave evidence." She looked into the mirror. "Thank you, Testarossa."

The name she had given the entity carried her royal house within it. Testarossa trembled with delight. Her face brightened and she bowed deeply, like a worshipper receiving grace from the only god she recognised. "To bear your name is an eternal honour, Your Majesty." She rose slowly and pressed her palm to the bronze. The crimson eye burned with longing. "When Your Majesty finds the missing eye, I will tear away the limits of a Legendary-grade Vestigium. When both eyes are united, I will ascend to Mythic grade."

Isabella showed none of the excitement Testarossa expected. She watched her reflection. "If the eyes are united, what happens to you?"

"I become complete."

"I asked what happens to you."

Testarossa did not answer immediately. She lifted one hand and studied her own fingers. The smile softened into an unsettling peace. "If I can become a perfect part of you, does my separate existence still matter?"

Isabella's brow tightened. "I did not ask whether you were willing to disappear."

"But I am answering." Testarossa's voice became almost weightless. "I was born to protect you. If my existence can one day be exchanged for Your Majesty continuing to walk forward, I would consider that the most perfect conclusion possible."

Isabella said nothing. For a moment, firelight on the bronze laid both faces over one another until human and shadow became difficult to separate. Testarossa broke the silence. "When I am complete, even the vast power of the Crown of Ravenna will cease to be a meaningful threat. I will break every danger, master every backlash, and offer you lasting peace."

Isabella narrowed her eyes. "You have never seen the Crown of Ravenna. Why are you so certain?"

Testarossa laughed softly. "I am not."

The direct answer caught Isabella off guard. "But if that crown ever tries to make you its slave, I will find a way to kill it. If strength cannot kill it, I will find another method." The red light sharpened. "If I fail once, I will try again. As long as I exist, nothing is permitted to own Your Majesty's will except you." Her devotion was calm enough to make the fanaticism worse. "My only Queen."

Footsteps sounded beyond the locked door. A knock followed. Martinez's familiar voice came from the corridor, reporting that the generals had assembled in the great hall. Testarossa's smile faded. The red mist withdrew into the bronze. Light died in Isabella's left eye and amber returned. Isabella wiped the final drop of blood from the desk, put the broken brush handle into its case, and straightened the stiff collar of her uniform. She studied herself once more. Then she opened the door and stepped out to meet Martinez.

In the mirror left behind, firelight still caught one eye of the departing reflection and painted it red.

Martinez was waiting in the corridor with the conference file beneath one arm. When the Queen emerged, she stepped back to clear the way. The Royal Guard wore full dress uniform, collar fastened neatly, the place where her pendant should have hung still empty. She studied Isabella's face.

"Your Majesty. Are you well?"

"I'm fine." Isabella looked at Martinez's shoulder. "And your wound? Can you sit through a long council?"

"Healed, Your Majesty." Martinez rolled the shoulder to prove it, though she still carried the file on her uninjured side. "If I need to rest, I will say so."

Isabella nodded. Together they walked towards the great hall. Guards along the passage stepped aside as Queen and Royal Guard passed. Their boots struck the stone stairs in steady rhythm on the climb towards Monte Urgull's war room. The heavy oak doors opened. Noise from inside stopped both women at the threshold. Officers had gathered around Edward and were asking him about the battle in the bay. He sat beside Fredo with a cup of tea in one hand. Conversation died the moment Martinez announced the Queen.

Everyone stood. Isabella's eyes went at once to Edward's hand braced against the arm of his chair.

"Sir Edward, has a physician actually released you from your room?"

"I went to the yard with Timothy, then found Fredo." Edward set down his cup. "I want to hear the council. If I cannot manage it, I will ask to leave."

Isabella looked towards Fredo. He pulled the chair beside Edward closer so he could catch him if necessary. She turned towards the head of the table. "Then remain seated. Do not stand for ceremony."

Order returned to the hall as Isabella took the red-upholstered chair at the head of the long table. Fredo and Martinez occupied the two places nearest her. Governor Frenesia sat beyond them, composed and severe, with garrison commanders and artillery officers filling the remaining seats. At the far end, directly opposite Isabella across the enormous campaign map, sat Edward. Martinez broke the red wax on the leather file and stood beside the Queen.

"In the name of Queen Isabella Testarossa, I declare this extraordinary military council at Monte Urgull in session." She did not bury the room beneath a list of names. Each time she announced one, a staff officer placed a corresponding wooden marker around the map.

"Representatives of Navarre and the Pyrenean General Staff. Lord Franco Valdes, representing House Castile. Governor of San Sebastián, Lady Frenesia. Admiral of the Royal Castilian Navy, Sir Edward Spencer."

The principal political positions appeared first. Martinez turned towards the military officers along both sides of the table. "Commanders of Tercio I del Rayo, IV del León, V de la Sombra, VI del Trueno, VIII de la Roca, IX del Escudo, and X del Bastión." Seven grey markers formed a row beside the Pyrenees. Edward watched them take shape on the map instead of trying to memorise numbers in isolation. Martinez closed one page.

"Royal Guard Number Ten, Colonel Cassandra, attends directly from the Perpignan front through Vestigium transmission." The crystal sphere at the centre of the table flashed blue. Wind shrieked through it. Distant explosions followed. Then Cassandra's voice came through.

"Cassandra present. My respects to Her Majesty and the assembled commanders."

Isabella nodded. "Fredo. One front at a time. Try not to kill everyone with figures before the French get their turn." A few restrained laughs moved around the table. Fredo stepped to the map.

"First, the North." He used two fingers to push the French markers away from San Sebastián. "Following the defeat of the French and Portuguese fleets at La Concha, royal relief forces counterattacked from both the eastern and western Pyrenean sectors. French troops that had penetrated deep into our territory were driven back across the border. The western front is relieved for the moment."

The crystal sphere vibrated before Fredo could move on. "For the moment." Cassandra's voice cut in from Perpignan. "The East is nowhere near quiet. French artillery still hits the outer line every day. Aragon is holding my flank, but if they concentrate more men here, Perpignan becomes the first pressure point again."

Fredo nodded towards the sphere. "Exactly as reported. Perpignan remains the eastern throat. Cassandra and the Aragonese forces are holding, but the line must be reinforced before we discuss an offensive."

Edward looked again at the seven Tercio markers waiting at the edge of the map. Now he understood why nearly every one of their commanders had been brought to Monte Urgull at once. Fredo moved south. He picked up the marker labelled Taza. Then he removed it from the map entirely. Several officers stopped breathing. "North Africa. Taza has fallen after days of Western Roman bombardment. Their main army is now tightening around Fes. Intelligence estimates exceed five hundred thousand troops. Much of that force is sustained by forward depots and a continuous supply chain running from Mediterranean ports under Western Roman control."

"Five hundred thousand?" Whispers broke around the table. Martinez struck the tabletop once. The room went silent. "Let him finish."

Fredo laid a chain of smaller markers from Iberia and North Africa towards Fes. "Fes is not alive because of its walls. It is alive because of these convoys. Food from agricultural districts, ammunition, medicine, and fuel are being pushed through every route still functioning. At the same time, five Tercio legions, Sixteen through Twenty, have received orders to cross the sea as reinforcements."

A staff officer placed the pieces as Fredo named them. "Tercio XVI de la Hazaña. XVII del Pozo. XVIII de las Cadenas. XIX del Silencio. XX del Trono." Five new markers formed a defensive belt around Fes. Set against the red mass representing more than half a million Romans, the numbers became heavier than they had ever looked in a report. Fredo did not allow the room to remain there for long. He returned to Iberia and placed three markers over León, Galicia, and Valencia, but turned them sideways instead of aligning them with royal forces. "Behind our fronts, León and Galicia continue refusing to release grain stores or enforce Madrid's mobilisation orders. Valencia belonged to the same bloc but has reversed its decision. I will explain their deployment shortly."

A Council representative frowned. "Then why have charges of treason not been brought?"

Fredo tapped the three sideways pieces with the end of his pen. "Because none of them claims to oppose the Queen. Every refusal is wrapped in phrases such as 'the result of local consultation' and 'the will of the regional garrison.' If the Crown declares rebellion before there is armed action or clear evidence of conspiracy, we hand them the justification to turn disobedience into war."

Edward tightened his fingers around his tea. Three fronts. One city lost. One border only just pulled back from disaster. And a rear area beginning to bite itself. He watched Fredo turn the final page. "How long did all of this take?"

Fredo looked at him. "The last month, Admiral."

Edward stopped with the cup halfway to his mouth. "A month?"

He had thought himself unconscious for days. While he had been locked in darkness, the map had changed shape. Edward lowered the tea and fell quiet. Franco Valdes rose and drew four markers bearing the red cross into the centre of the table. "In that same month, we did more than lose ground. We created a new force." The old lord placed the four pieces in a line. "The general mobilisation of the English exile community is complete. Four Exile Legions have been formed: White Lion, Black Rose, Fallen Oak, and Fog. Supreme command has been assigned to four exceptional former officers of the old English Royal Academy."

He lifted the first marker and placed it on Madrid. "Sir Edward Spencer. You will not be sent directly to the French frontier. One legion follows you to the capital. Your task is Keeper of the Throne: protect the Queen, protect your own household, and prevent unrest behind the fronts from becoming a knife in Madrid's back."

Edward looked at the small red-cross marker on the capital and said nothing. Franco moved the second piece across Gibraltar and placed it at Fes. "Marco Stones takes one English legion and fights beside the Tercio forces holding Fes." The third went to Tangier-Ceuta. "Romeo Harkon commands the next. He will coordinate with Tercio III del Filo and Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad. That position serves as a reserve for Fes and as the vital gate if the forward line breaks."

The final marker settled over Marrakesh. "Victoria Valdes assumes command of the remaining legion with Tercio XI del Acero. She will protect the rear-area centre and the food and armament routes sustaining the North African theatre."

Franco stepped back. Three English markers now formed southern anchor points integrated with Tercio formations and Moorish forces. "If we total everything committed to North Africa, we have concentrated two hundred and thirty-five thousand soldiers there. Eight regular Tercio legions. Three English Exile Legions under Marco, Romeo, and Victoria. Sixty thousand elite Moorish troops under Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad." With his silver cane, Franco circled Fes, Tangier-Ceuta, and Marrakesh. "That is the present price of containing a Western Roman army exceeding half a million men while keeping North Africa connected to Iberia."

Nobody cheered for two hundred and thirty-five thousand. On the map, they were still the smaller mass. Franco returned his cane to the Pyrenees.

"Now we come to what the people inside this room must do." He pointed at the seven grey pieces Martinez had placed at the beginning. "Tercio I del Rayo, IV del León, V de la Sombra, VI del Trueno, VIII de la Roca, IX del Escudo, and X del Bastión will leave Monte Urgull immediately, march east, and enter Cassandra's direct command."

Her answer came from the crystal sphere. "I'll open an assembly area behind Perpignan. Send men, ammunition, and food before you send me any more speeches." A few officers laughed dryly. Franco's mouth almost moved into a smile. He added Tercio VII del Sol at Perpignan.

"Tercio VII del Sol remains in the strongpoint. The Navarre Knight Legion will reinforce the line, while Aragon commits local forces and funds to hold the route down to the Mediterranean. Once all seven legions have concentrated and Perpignan is reinforced, Cassandra will possess authority to launch a general counteroffensive across the Pyrenees into southern France."

This time the murmuring came from the Navarre delegation. Before objection could rise into open argument, Governor Frenesia stood. The woman in her sixties placed both palms on the table and looked directly at Isabella.

"The eastern wing belongs to Cassandra. San Sebastián will answer for the west.

"The old Pyrenean General Staff appointed by the Council has been dismissed after its recent failures. I give my personal honour on this: so long as the flag flies over La Mota, the Biscay bases will not permit the French to cross the western wing."

Franco nodded and closed the operational file. Every order now had a place on the map. Every number had somewhere it would be expected to live or die. Only the Navarre marker in the northeast remained unmoved. Then a hand struck the table. The Navarre representative stood and pulled the map towards him. "Your Majesty, we have held the mountain passes throughout this campaign. If the knights are sent into France, who guards the routes the French just used to enter our lands?" He pressed one finger onto the border. "An order to defend and an order to cross the frontier are not the same thing. I need to return to my Council with a limited mission, not a promise of a war with no end."

Fredo stepped beside the map. "The first task is reinforcement of Perpignan. No offensive begins until concentration is complete, the defensive line is strengthened, and Cassandra can sustain the supply route."

"Then write that into the order."

"I will."

Fredo pointed towards the remaining French positions. "But if we do nothing except block the mountain passes, they retain the staging ground for the next assault. We need Navarre to participate beyond that line, not wait permanently on this side."

The representative looked at the officers accompanying him. Then back to Isabella. She allowed him to continue. "Authority to send Navarre troops beyond our own territory still belongs to the Navarre Council. I cannot go home with my signature alone and tell every household to surrender its children to a new campaign." Two officers behind him nodded. Fredo opened the document file and laid the deployment order beside the map.

"Valencia accepted responsibility for Palma two weeks ago." He touched the seal. "They objected as well. They accepted once their mission and supply route were defined."

"Palma is not southern France."

"Correct. Which is why I am not handing you Valencia's order." Fredo pushed the Navarre document towards him. "Show me what is missing here."

The representative did not sit. His eyes moved across the seven Tercio markers, then back to Fredo. Fredo smiled. At first the expression looked harmless. "At present, seven of the Crown's most experienced legions happen to be assembled inside this fortress. If the noble houses of Navarre remain concerned that their local strength is insufficient to protect their homes, Her Majesty would be delighted to instruct the commanders here to visit and assist you in guarding Navarre for a time."

The representative removed his hand from the map. He looked at the Tercio commanders. Then he pulled the deployment order towards himself. "I understand the offer." No one laughed. "Write the border-defence conditions into it. I will take the order home."

Fredo signalled to the secretary. The Navarre officers sat and began conferring quietly over the amended document. Fredo folded his hands over the remaining papers and looked around the table. "The general allocation of forces and the operational strategy for every theatre have been stated. Does everyone understand the duties before them?"

Dozens of officers rose at once. Hands went to chests. "CLEAR, YOUR MAJESTY!" The answer rolled beneath the stone vault. Fredo nodded. "This operational council is adjourned. Return to your formations, prepare supply, and march according to the deadlines issued."

Generals, staff officers, and the Navarre delegation bowed and filed from the hall. When the room had emptied, only five remained around the long table. Isabella at the head. Fredo and Martinez beside her. Franco Valdes studying the map. Edward at the far end. Franco moved his chair closer only after the doors had shut behind the last Navarre representative. With the tip of his silver cane, he swept the ceremonial markers aside and revealed the western section of the map that had remained covered throughout the public council. "What we have just discussed is what can be said before the full Council, Your Majesty." He placed two black markers over León and Galicia. "This cannot." Martinez leaned one hand against the table. Franco continued. "If these houses openly revolt, their two core knight legions and the mercenaries they are quietly recruiting are already enough to push the rebel strength above fifty thousand. We also have indications that they are seeking contact with foreign powers. Nothing yet clean enough to place before the Council."

"Andalusia?" Martinez asked.

Franco took out another piece but did not set it down. He held it above the south, as uncertain as the house it represented. "Publicly compliant. Grain is still moving. Taxes are still being paid. Their garrison has done nothing abnormal. But House Castile intelligence has confirmed that Andalusian representatives secretly entered Lisbon's military harbour no fewer than three times this month to contact Don José's faction."

"Three meetings do not tell us what was promised," Fredo said. "I want the courier and the money trail before we decide what they mean."

Martinez drew a Conquistador marker towards Santiago. "If they begin concentrating troops, striking the command structure costs fewer lives than waiting for sixty thousand men to assemble. But we need a verified target. How many Conquistadores can we pull from the Pyrenees?"

Franco did not answer with a number. He opened the wooden box beside the map and placed fifteen small metal markers in three rows before Martinez. "This was our strength when the Pyrenean war began." He looked at the pieces. "More than fifteen hundred." Then he removed six markers. One by one, they struck the box with a dry metallic sound. "This is what remains." Nine pieces stayed on the table. "Nine hundred."

Martinez looked at the empty spaces. Franco pushed the open box towards her so she could see the six removed markers. "For the past month they have rotated against Gendarme heavy infantry across the Pyrenean slopes. Six hundred Conquistadores are dead, missing, or no longer capable of returning to combat. Every suit of military Vestigium equipment, every Miracle-grade transmission system, costs money the treasury is now scraping away from food trains and foundries running through the night. We are no longer rich enough to swing Conquistadores at every political problem like a sword."

Martinez's hand slowly loosened from her own weapon. "If we lose half of those who remain..."

"Castilian will have broken its last shield with its own hands," Franco finished.

Silence settled over the table. Martinez looked towards Isabella. "Then the Reliquiarios? Fewer of them, yes, but if the goal is decapitation rather than fighting an entire legion, aren't they better suited?"

"Suited to hunting a target. Not suited to becoming an army," Isabella said. She turned a small Reliquiario marker between her fingers. "There are already very few of them. They are trained to track original Vestigia, hunt altered creatures, infiltrate, seal, and deal with anomalies a conventional military formation cannot. If I spend them as elite infantry patching every breach in a civil conflict, a handful of battles will erase the entire force." She returned the piece to the box instead of the map. "I need them intact for jobs nobody else can replace. One day Edward will have to return to England. Or our army will advance deep into southern France, into regions saturated with magical ruins. When that day comes, a thousand good soldiers cannot replace one Reliquiario team that knows what it is hunting."

Isabella looked down the table. "Sir Edward. You will hold Madrid. With everything you have heard, what do you believe we should do first?"

Edward was still staring at the pieces. Several seconds passed before he realised all four of them were looking at him. "Truthfully... my head is stuck on something else." He put down the tea. "I woke up and discovered I'd missed an entire month. Before we decide who ought to be arrested or baited into rebellion, tell me how my wife and son are doing in Madrid."

The impatience in his face made Franco laugh quietly. The old lord put away the Andalusian piece still hanging between his fingers. "Lady Juliet and young Remi are safe, Spencer. Your family apartment lies inside the heavily protected central district. Heat and provisions are fully supplied. According to my household reports, Lady Juliet has adapted well to Madrid and has become particularly close to Lady Millenia, Colonel Marco's wife. They visit one another almost daily."

Fredo added, "Remi is enrolled at the Royal Academy. He studies in the same class as Marco's son. The two are attached badly enough that the professors now have to remember their names together."

Edward's shoulders lowered. He breathed out slowly and drew his chair closer. "Good." He looked at the map again. "Now tell me exactly what I have. No more reading statistics at me. Build Madrid on this table."

Franco pushed the marker box towards him. Edward placed the red-cross piece on the capital. "My English legion. Strength?"

"Eleven thousand rifles," Franco answered at once. "Assembly and equipment are complete in the outer barracks."

Edward kept one finger on the marker and looked towards Isabella. "Eleven thousand people who were scattered across the peninsula. How did the Queen gather them?"

Isabella left the head of the table and came beside the map. "News of La Concha reached the towns, mines, and refugee districts before the recruiters did." She touched the red cross. "I permitted them to assemble beneath the symbol of their homeland. They came." Her finger rested lightly on the piece. "They defend Castilian, the country that kept them alive through this winter. All four Exile Legions retain the right to carry the red cross on campaign."

Edward looked at the flag for a long time. "Equipment?"

"Equivalent to a regular Tercio," Isabella said. "Mutated-cattle leather armour. The best standard rifles the arsenals can supply. Only the uniform differs. Not royal grey and white." A faint smile touched her lips. "Dark red wool."

Edward looked up. "The same colour as the Redcoats Marco built at Fes. When the North African campaign ends, the Redcoats will be absorbed into the English Exile Legion under Marco."

Edward slowly set the marker firmly onto Madrid. Its red colour stood out among the grey blocks of the Castilian map. He selected another piece and placed it beside the English force, leaving room for local units. "What about Madrid itself? House Castile. How many men remain under your private banner?"

Franco leaned on his cane and laughed with unmistakable pride. "The Castile Knight Legion remains in the capital. Two thousand cavalry and heavy infantry."

Edward looked up. "Only two thousand? For House Castile?"

"Precisely because we are House Castile." Franco took the marker from him and placed it beside the English legion. "For centuries, most men of our lands who reached fighting age entered the royal Tercio legions instead of building some enormous private army for my family. Those two thousand exist to preserve tradition, the dignity of the house, and the capital itself. The real strength of Castile belongs in the national army, not behind the gates of my estate."

Edward nodded. Then he looked at Fredo and Martinez. "And those two? What authority do I have over them in Madrid?"

"They receive orders directly from you within the capital," Isabella answered. "They will coordinate Royal Guard operations."

Fredo touched one hand to his chest. Martinez gave a short nod. Edward pulled two smaller markers beside the red block. Then he frowned. "Something is missing."

Fredo followed his gaze.

"What?"

Edward ran one finger along the Tercio designations at the edge of the map. "In the council we had One, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, Nine, Ten. Others are in North Africa. Where are Twelve, Thirteen, Fourteen, and Fifteen?"

Fredo immediately drew four markers from the box. "Tercio XII de la Cima." He placed the first across a mountain passage. "Tercio XIII del Muro." The second blocked a major road. "Tercio XIV de la Venganza and XV del Colmillo." The final pair formed a rear arc. "All four hold the approaches between the Castilian heartland and territories showing signs of conspiracy. Their orders are to stop any unauthorised movement from León, Galicia, or Andalusia before it reaches the core."

Edward tested the arrangement by moving the León marker towards Madrid. It ran directly into the Tercio line. He studied the whole disposition. Eleven thousand English soldiers in the capital. Two thousand Castile knights. Fredo and Martinez at the centre. Four regular Tercio legions sealing the approaches. Conquistadores and Reliquiarios protected from becoming expendable pieces in a political meat grinder. Edward drew the map closer. Pain caught in his chest and forced him to adjust his position. Fredo quietly moved the tea tray away from the space where Edward was about to place more markers. "All right."

Edward pointed at the routes into Madrid. "Keep enough men visible here, at the food depots, and on every route that moves troops into the capital. The reserve does not need to advertise its full strength. Neither do the people watching the houses we suspect."

"You want them to underestimate us?" Isabella asked. "Even if they target me, Juliet, or Remi?"

"Then we protect those people before anything happens." Edward kept one hand on Madrid. "I am not suggesting we withdraw guards to create an opening. I am certainly not placing my family in danger and waiting to catch whoever brings the knife."

Martinez pulled a small marker beside the palace. "Royal Guard handles positions immediately around the Queen. Your troops hold roads and assigned strongpoints. Reliquiarios receive specific targets only. We do not scatter them through the city."

Franco looked at Edward. "And if the houses continue meeting but never move troops?"

"Keep watching. Record who travels where. Track money. Track weapons." Edward released the marker. "When there is an act that justifies intervention, we already need someone close enough to respond. If all they do is oppose the Crown, we do not yet have cause to arrest them."

Isabella studied the board. "Visible defence. Hidden reserve. Evidence collection. Civilians are never bait." She nodded once. "That is the plan."

Franco Valdes stood, put one hand to his chest, and bowed. "With Your Majesty's leave, I will withdraw and prepare for what comes next."

The silver tip of his cane receded along the stone floor. Four people remained. Fredo dropped into the nearest chair and loosened his collar before reorganising the amended orders. Martinez relaxed her sword belt. Isabella leaned back and rubbed the place where the edge of her hat had pressed against her forehead. She looked at Edward.

"When we return to Madrid, I need you healthy enough to do everything you just proposed."

"I would also like to make it home in time for supper." Edward put down his cup and braced himself to stand. He got halfway before stopping. Fredo was already beside him. Edward accepted the arm with a sigh.

"For now, get me back to my room."
